text:
Prologo.

Nocierto es, lamenos noble joia: dela recamara, dela predicacion evangelica, cimiento, delas cosas naturales: para poner exemplos, i comparaciones. Como v redemptiva, averlo vsado: iestos exemplos, i comparaciones: quanto mas familiares alos oientes ipor palabras, i lenguage mas vsadas, entellos, dichas: tanto sera mas zes: iprouechosas. Aeste proposito se hizo, ia tesoro: en harta costa, itrabaxo: este er que esta escriptas en lengua mexicana: las propiedades imaneras exteriores, i vezes que se pudiezon alcancar: delos animales, aves, ipezes: arboles, i ieruas, flores mas conocidos: i vsados, que ai en toda esta tierra: donde ai, gran copia de vocablos sho lenguage: muy propio, imui comun: imateria mui gustosa. Sera tambien esta oportuna, para dar los aentender, el valor delas criaturas: para que no las arrebatnjdad: porque aqualquiera cratura, que vian ser iminente: en bien o en mal, se llama teutil quisere dezir dios: demarceza que al sol, le llamauan teutil: yor su lndeza: al por su grandeza, i ferocidad: tambien a muchos delos animales los llamauan por esto por razon de su espantable disposicion, ibraveza. Donde se infiere, que este nombre se toma, en buena, i en mala parte. Imucho mas se conoce esto, quando esta en comp mo entere nombre, teuipiltontli, nino muy lindo: teuipiltontli, muchacho muy o malo. Otros muchos vocablos, se componen desta misma manera: dela significacion quales, se puede conjeturar: que este vocablo, teutil, quisiere dezir: cosa estremada o en mal. Ansi que, el presente Volumen, se podra tener, o estimar como vn tesoro, de la i vocablos desta lengua mexicana: i vna recamara, mui rica delas cosas que ai en esta

Al sincero lector.

Tienes, amigo lector, enel presente volumen: vn bosque con gran diuersidad de montes, riscos: donde hallaras, arboles siluestres, de todo genero: ibestias fieras, iserpientes, demandaras: tienes, vn jardin poblado, de todos arboles frutiferos: i de todas maneras: uas: donde ai fuertes, frios dedicarosas maneras. E sto lleno de aves, animales, ipeces de nero: tienes vna floresta, mui deleitosa, llena de todo genero de flores: ansi delas que se nacen arboles, arbustos, imatas: como delas que se hazen en tierras: enella ai aves, de dulces i ricas plumas: aitambien florestas, edificacias, alas mil marauillas: tienes diuersidad de ninos i edificios: tienes ansi mismo campos, illanuras, donde ai toda manera de matas ierbs: donde ai charcos, i lagunas: donde se crian canas, espadanas i juncos: i diuers ras de animalejos, aquatiles itterestres. Donde ai minas, de todas maneras de piedras preciosas: ide otras muchas cosas prouechosas, ala vida. Donde ai, nuestras maneras de tierras, i piedras, iaguas, i cerros. No procede, la orden arriba puesta: sino por la que se sigue. El primero capitulo, trata de los animales del agua: como son pezes, iotros animales, que biven p. 2. contiene siete parraphos. El segundo, trata delas aves: contiene diez parraphos. b. 20. cero capitulo trata delos animales del agua: como son pezes, iotros animales, que b. 61. enel agua: contiene cinco parraphos. El quarto, trata delos animales fieros: que b. 70. enel agua: contiene quatro parraphos. El quinto, trata de serpientes i otros b. 77.
translation:
Prologue.

It is certainly not the least noble jewel: of the treasury, of evangelical preaching, the foundation of natural things: for the purpose of providing examples and comparisons. As the redemptive use of such examples and comparisons: the more familiar they are to listeners, both in words and in the most commonly used language and expression, the more useful and beneficial they will be. For this purpose this work was made, a true treasure: at great cost and labor: written here in the Mexican language: the properties and outward characteristics, as far as could be attained: of animals, birds, and fish: trees, herbs, and flowers, the most well known and used, that exist throughout this land: where there is a great wealth of vocabulary in this language: very proper and very common: and very pleasing subject matter. It will also be useful for making understood the value of creatures: so that they are not belittled: because any creature that is seen as eminent, whether in good or in bad, is called teotl, which means god: thus the sun was called teotl: for its splendor: and others for their greatness and ferocity: and many animals were also called thus for their terrible disposition and bravery. From which it follows that this name is taken in both a good and a bad sense. And this is much better understood when the full word is used: teopiltontli, a very beautiful child: teopiltontli, a very wicked boy. Many other words are composed in this same manner: from whose meaning one can conjecture that this word teotl, means: something extreme, whether in good or in bad. Thus the present volume may be held or esteemed as a treasure, of the language and vocabulary of the Mexican tongue: and a very rich treasury of the things that exist in this land.

To the sincere reader.

You have, dear reader, in the present volume: a forest with a great diversity of mountains and crags: where you will find wild trees of every kind: fierce beasts and serpents. You have a garden populated with all manner of fruit-bearing trees, and of many kinds: where there are strong and cold streams of many sorts. It is full of birds, animals, and fish of every kind. You have a very delightful grove, full of all manner of flowers: both those that grow on trees, shrubs, and bushes: and those that grow in the fields: in it there are birds with sweet and rich plumage: and also gardens, built to a thousand wonders: you have a diversity of children and buildings: you have likewise fields and plains, where there are all manner of plants and herbs: where there are pools and lagoons: where reeds, cattails, and rushes grow: and a diversity of small aquatic and terrestrial animals. Where there are mines, of all manner of precious stones: and of many other things useful to life. Where there are our kinds of soils, stones, waters, and hills. The order set out above is not followed, but rather the following. The first chapter deals with the animals of the water: such as fish and other animals. p. 2. It contains seven paragraphs. The second deals with birds: it contains ten paragraphs. b. 20. The third chapter deals with the animals of the water: such as fish and other animals that live in the water: it contains five paragraphs. The fourth deals with fierce animals: b. 61. in the water: it contains four paragraphs. b. 70. The fifth deals with serpents and others. b. 77.

translation:
Book Eleventh

Book Eleventh on the properties of animals, birds, fish, trees, herbs, flowers, metals, and stones, and of colors.

Chapter One, on animals.

First paragraph on wild beasts.

The tiger walks and lives in the mountains, among the crags and cliffs, and also in the water. It is noble, and they say it is a prince and lord of the other animals. It is shrewd and cautious and pampers itself like a cat, and endures no labor whatsoever. It is disgusted to see filthy things and avoids them, and holds itself in high regard. It is low-bodied and stout, and has a long tail, and its forepaws are thick and wide, and it has a thick neck,

This eleventh book speaks of the various living creatures: of birds, of fish, of trees, of herbs, of things lying in the earth made of metal, of stone, of other things, and of various stones.

This first chapter speaks of living creatures and how they move about.

This first paragraph speaks of beasts of prey.

The ocelot: dweller of the forests, dweller of the rocky places, dweller of the water; a noble, a commoner. They say it surpasses all other animals in cunning. It is knowing, self-aware, ever attentive, never a scavenger, never an eater of filth, never a devourer of corruption. Noble, yet base. It is long, lean, cylindrical in body, broad and flat-headed, thick-bodied, thick-fleshed, thick with muscle, with a long tail, with a rounded tail, with large palms, with flat palms, with a thick neck, with a broad neck, with a round head, with a large round head...

¶The nature of the tiger [jaguar] is that it eats animals, such as deer and rabbits and other similar creatures. It is fastidious and not suited for labor; it takes great care to keep itself clean; and at night it can see the animals it is going to hunt — it has very keen sight, and even if it is very dark, or even if there is fog, it can see very small things.
When it sees the hunter with his bow and arrows, it does not flee, but rather sits looking at him, without hiding behind anything or pressing up against anything. Then it begins to hiss, and that breath it directs toward the hunter, in order to instill fear and dread in him and make his heart faint with the hissing. And the hunter then begins to shoot at it; and the first arrow, which is made of cane, the jaguar catches with its paw and breaks it to pieces with its teeth, and begins to snarl and growl, and as another arrow is shot at it...

[Nahuatl column:]
¶This is how it lives: the ocelot goes about seeking, pursuing, those it will eat — deer, rabbits, etc. And it is very fastidious: it is not crude; it is very refined, it grooms itself, it washes itself, it cleans its face, it licks itself; it is deceptive, boastful; it is very alert, it is very prepared. And with its sight it looks at, it observes, what it seeks to eat, what it hunts; it sees very well, its gaze is sharp and clear, seeing well at a distance: even in darkness, even in dimness, it sees. When it sees, when it encounters, when it faces its adversary — it does not lower its head, it does not look down; it stands facing it squarely. It settles itself well, it crouches for nothing — the jaguar. Then it begins to snort, to blow its breath, so as to terrify the hunter, to make his heart stop, the one shooting at it. And then the hunter begins to shoot at it; one arrow that he launches — of cane — the jaguar simply catches it and pulls it and snaps it apart, and slaps at it...

He does the same. The hunters kept the custom that they were not to shoot the jaguar more than four arrows: this was their tradition or devotion. And if they did not kill it with those four arrows, the hunter would consider himself defeated. And the jaguar then begins to stretch itself, and to shake itself, and to lick itself. Having done this, it gathers itself and leaps as if flying, and throws itself upon the hunter. Even if the hunter is ten or twenty fathoms away, it takes but one leap; it goes all bristled up, like a cat against a dog. Then it kills the hunter and eats him. Skilled hunters, upon shooting the first arrow — if the jaguar was not shattered by it — take a leaf from an oak tree, and from another similar tree, and fix it onto the arrow, and shoot the jaguar with it. The leaf placed thus makes a sound, just as when a grasshopper flies and falls to the ground halfway, or nearby.

[Nahuatl column:] Making noises with its throat, snarling, it becomes enraged, as it is said. It throws itself at him just as many times as it shoots arrows at him, doing so in the same manner. And if the count of arrows shot at it falls short, even by one, the arrow flies: then it looks at the hunter. At dawn it yawns, stretches, shakes, quivers, cleans itself, flutters its sides. Then it truly readies itself; it stretches out its claws and flies off — ten measures away, the arrow stands erect in the air; even to the far side, twenty measures: it goes seizing it, for once it leaps: it flies, curves, circles around, surrounds — there the arrow dies; there it is consumed. And when it recovers: the hunter shoots another arrow, takes a reed, pulls it toward himself the quauhxiuatlapalli [eagle-herb board], and places the reed-tip there, and the reed comes out singing. He shoots it again, and it rustles as it goes: the acazoatl reed. Just as a grasshopper goes: perhaps it strikes the ground, perhaps it lands beside it, flying, falling, into the quauhxiuatlapalli: it cures its eyes with it.

of the tiger: with this the tiger diverts itself from striking the leaf that falls, and the arrow reaches and passes through it or wounds it; and then the tiger leaps upward and coming back down to the ground, sits again as it was before. And there it dies seated, without closing its eyes; although it is dead, it appears alive. When the tiger hunts, it first breathes upon whatever it is going to catch with that breath, stunning it. The flesh of the tiger has a bad taste and burns.

¶ There was a people who were like assassins, who were called nonohzalequc; they were practiced and bold people, ready to kill. They carried with them the skin of the tiger — a piece of the forehead, another piece of the chest, and at the end of the tail the claws, and the heart, and the fangs, and the snouts. They said that with these things they were strong, and bold, and terrifying when bound together; and everyone feared them, and they feared no one, because of carrying these things of the tiger. These are also called pixeque teiolpachwanj.

¶ The wildcat [lynx], they call it by this name, which is to say tlaco ocelutl, tlacomjztli, because

[Nahuatl column:]
It shoots them, it strikes them from afar; it is very swift; and then the ocelot crouches down. And then it settles itself flat on the ground, stretches itself out, presses itself low; it thus positions itself as it was before, its eyes rolling; it dies thus; only with its eyes open. Though it appears yet alive. When the ocelot feeds: first it makes the prey afraid of it, it causes it to be stunned, it causes it to be confused. Its flesh is very hot and bitter.

¶ The nonohzalequc: it is said they go about with the skin of the ocelot's face, and the skin of its chest, and the tip of its tail, and its blood, and its heart, and its rattle — that is, its spine — and its muzzle; they say that thus they go about invulnerable, that thus they go about making others afraid of them, that thus they are feared: that no one dares face them, for they go about under their protection; they go by the name nonohzalequc, pixeque, teiolpathoanj.

which is small, the size of a cat: it is brown, has some dark spots like a tiger or painted animal.

There is an animal in this land called tlacaxolotl: it is large, bigger than a great ox, it has a large head, a long snout, very wide ears, it has large teeth and molars: but in the form of a person, it has a very thick and sturdy neck, it has thick feet and hands, hooves like an ox but larger: it has large and wide haunches, its tail is thick and long: it is the color of a red ox, it has very thick hide: its meat is edible: they say its meat and flavor contains that of all animals, roots, and even of men. This animal is rare, it lives in the provinces of Atzaccan, and of Tepuztontlan, and Tlanguylapan, which are toward Honduras, it lives in the mountains and in certain places among the cliffs: it eats wild peanuts.

Tlacaxolotl, it greatly surpasses the cow: its head is very large and long-necked: its flesh is very thick and meaty: its teeth are very large: it appears roughly person-like, its neck is very thick and very fleshy: its shin, its leg, its body is very hairy and rough, very large, its mane is rough and shaggy, not smooth: its snout very large, its tail very thick, very long, not easily cut: its hair all over is not very long, like a deer's hair: its hide is dark-colored. This tlacaxolotl eats many things: and the flavor of its flesh is not in one part only — it has the taste of all kinds of meat: of human meat, of wild beast meat, of deer, of turkey, of dog. This tlacaxolotl, it lives only midway between — it dwells in Atzaccan, Tepuztontlan, Tlangutylapan, there in the great forest where no one can reach the interior. When it feeds it [illegible] when...

translation:
Book Eleven

These are the cacahuates called quappatlachtli. It also eats green corn and corn cobs. When it comes upon a cornfield, it eats everything, leaving nothing behind. When food is scarce, it eats the leaves of shrubs and trees. When it defecates, it expels the cacao beans whole, nearly a jarful of them each time. The inhabitants of that land go searching for its dung in order to collect the cacao it has passed. This animal does not fear people, nor does it die from an arrow. They catch it by digging a large pit and covering it with branches and grass so that it falls in; there they kill it, and from there they pull it out with ropes and eat its flesh, which is very good to eat.

And it cries out among the trees in the forest. When it finds nothing to eat, this animal called Jeucacaoatl, also quappatlahtli, goes to the cornfields and takes corn one ear at a time. It scatters the cacao, and it is good at carrying loads on its back. The commoners go looking for it in the forest so that they can collect the cacao from it. It is not timid, nor does it die from arrows, even if it is wounded. It does not dig burrows; it goes all about searching among the stones and rocks, and it goes far into the woods. When they have found it, they lay logs and stones over it and cover it.

There is an animal called tzonistac. It is found toward the South Sea, in the province of Toztlan and Casepan. It is called tzonistac because it has a very white head only. Tzonistac: it is a beast of prey. It lives over there in Tozllantzapan, somewhat near the great sea. This animal, by its description, appears to be a bear; and if it is not a bear, I do not know what animal among those we know it can be compared to. It is a hairy animal, with long wool: it has a tail, very woolly, like that of a fox; but of a dark brownish color, it has shaggy wool; when it is old: it has small, narrow ears; it has a round face, wide, almost like that of a person; it has a thick snout; it has a little gland for being venomous, to poison whatever it encounters; the vapor or air that it emits is of many colors, like a rainbow; it is very cunning, and lies in ambush to kill.

The lion: it is the size of a tiger, it is not spotted; it also has sleek fur; and in body it is like a tiger, except that it has larger claws, and also small ones very long; it is rarely dark; there are red lions and others whitish: these are called white lions.

Cujtlachtli [the bear/wolverine]: or also called cueclachtli; it is thick, rounded, very large, with a broad tail base, [its tail hairs spread out]; its [fur] is very rounded and smooth; it cannot [easily] be compared to our [animals]; it is somewhat like a chichimec person in appearance, very large and broad; it is very round-faced, very clear-eyed, it sees those who approach it; it is just like a rainbow coming from its mouth; it is very knowing, it can imitate people and make itself known; it rolls upon people, it makes itself known, it causes flatulence.

Miztli [the mountain lion/puma]: it is just like the ocelot in size and appearance: there is nothing that can be placed alongside it; it is entirely slender, narrow, exactly alike, very long and lean, very lean and straight; it leaps very well, it is dark-smoked in color; the reddish puma is tawny-colored; the [other kind of] puma — in some [accounts] it is called the white puma.

translation:
Book Eleven

¶This animal, which is called the quaumiztli [tree-lion/ocelot], by its properties appears to be an onza [lynx/wildcat]. And if it is not one, no other animal seems so similar: they say it resembles a lion, except that it always lives in the trees, leaping from branch to branch, and there it seeks its food. It rarely comes down to the ground.

¶There is an animal in these parts called the maçamiztli [deer-lion]. The name means a certain kind of lion. It is not known whether it exists anywhere else. It is the size of a deer, and has the color of a deer, and has claws like a deer's, and the males have horns like a deer; but it has feet like a lion, very sharp, and teeth and fangs like a lion. It does not eat plants. It lives among the other deer. And when it wants to eat, it embraces a deer and grips it by the neck; it opens it through the belly, eating from the legs up to the throat, and in this way draws out all the intestines and eats them. In nothing do the other deer associate with it, except through a foul stench that it carries.

¶The quaumiztli [tree-lion]: it lives only as the mountain lion lives, always dwelling in the treetops and in the high crags. If it eats anything, it rarely comes down to the ground.

¶The maçamiztli [deer-lion]: it is called by this name because it resembles a deer in certain ways, yet is truly like a mountain lion. The females resemble doe-deer in appearance; it has a long tail. It approaches and comes near; it is truly like a mountain lion in its nature, and none can escape it, none can flee from it once it has seized a deer. Thereupon the deer-lion tears it: it tears it open and devours it. It is extremely large and very fat. It seizes prey in its claws like iron hooks. Whatever it takes, whatever it catches, it strips off the skin, peels it entirely. It is greatly to be feared; it wanders seeking to devour, it never rests in peace.

There is another animal in this land called the cujtlamjztli, which means "bastard lion." According to what is said of it, it is a wolf: it eats dogs and chickens and sheep. In wintertime it secludes itself until it can no more, and then it goes about hunting for three days without stopping. For this reason they call it "bastard lion," because it is a glutton; it has no den like the lions; and at night it eats the chickens and the sheep; and even so, this beast kills all the chickens and sheep it can.

The cujtlamjztli lives in the forest, it wanders through the ravines, like the mountain lion. It goes about at night, the cujtlamjztli. It seizes animals; it hunts and captures them; it takes four, or it seizes them in its jaws. Two days, three days it goes without eating, then all at once it gorges itself; it comes down from above, and thus it is called cujtlamjztli, because it is voracious and also because it does not shelter itself. At night it then comes to eat the turkey; it is like the large wild beast. It also looks like a wildcat and also like a dog.

There is another animal called iteujn quanjs, which means "camel of dogs," which is of the same kind as the one described above. They are called by this name iteujn quanjs, or camels of dogs, because at night—

It approaches the settlements and from nearby begins to howl; and all the dogs that hear it respond by howling, and go running to where it is. Once the dogs are together with it, they kill what is needed to eat, and it eats them; the rest go off — its food is the dogs — and it finds them very tasty. Second paragraph on animals such as foxes, wolves, and other similar animals.

There is in this land an animal called coyote, which some Spaniards call a fox and others call a wolf; but according to its characteristics, it is neither wolf nor fox, but an animal proper to this land. It is very shaggy with long fur, has a thick and very woolly tail; it has small, pointed ears; its snout is long and not very thick, and dark; its legs are sinewy; its claws are curved and black. It is very alert and cautious. To hunt, it crouches down and lies in wait, looking in all directions to catch its prey. It is very cunning in ambushing its game. When it wants to rush at the prey, it first hurls itself—

[Nahuatl column:]
Coyote: it has a long, blunt snout; it is wide-faced; it has long legs, long-legged, slender-legged; it is pinched at the temples, sleek-headed, dark-throated, white-eared, white-toed; its paws are dark, it shows well, it knows things. How it hunts: it stalks crouching, it presses itself low; it rolls in the grass, it stretches itself on the ground; it sets itself thus, it crouches. It watches keenly in all directions; it knows a person from afar. It launches itself forward. It seeks sheep(?); it seizes game...

its venom, against it, to infect it and discourage its spirit. This animal is diabolical: if someone takes away its prey, it takes note of them and seeks to take revenge, killing their chickens or other animals of their household. And if it notices any such thing, it waits for that person when they travel along the road, and places itself in front of them, gesturing as if it wants to eat them, to frighten them. And sometimes it also accompanies itself with three or four companions to frighten them further. They do this either by night or by day. This animal has exquisite qualities — it is grateful. Now in these times there occurred a noteworthy thing, concerning one of these little animals. A traveler, going along his road, saw one of these animals making a signal to him with its hand, that he should approach. The traveler was frightened by this, but went to where it was. And when he drew near, he saw a snake that was coiled around the neck of that animal, and had its head tucked under the armpit of that little creature, holding it very tightly. This snake was one of those called cincoatl. And the traveler

[Right column — Nahuatl:]
was watching it. And just then, like a person: when it had already called out, when it had already cried for help, it grabbed the fur from its back, so that it would come to its aid. And the heart said: it is addressing me, calling me. And if someone harms it, it will rebuke me, it will mock me, it will shame me, it will threaten me, it will terrify me: and also two, three, those it will set against you in the open field, or maybe people. And also when its spirit is restored, it is grateful, it gives thanks: as many as are gathered, it will approach them. A certain man came out onto a road in the ravine, following after his companion. And then the coyote came out onto the path ahead of them; it was very agitated and very alarmed about the companion — something was happening there. And having approached: he saw the snake, which had thrown itself upon him; it was coming out from between his legs, the snake: it was coming out from beside his ear, having wrapped itself around him: its name, cincoatl. And the traveler said: "I will help him." And then he took up his companion's walking staff.

When he saw what was happening, he thought to himself, saying: "Help those people there." And he decided to help that animal; and he took up a stick and began to strike the snake. Then the snake uncoiled and fell to the ground, and began to go away and hide itself among the grass. The little animal also fled, and after a while it came back and found the traveler again, among some cornfields. It was carrying two roosters in its mouth, by their necks, and it laid them before the traveler who had been saved from the snake. It made a sign with its snout that he should take them, and it went along behind the traveler until he reached his house. When it saw where he went in, it went to look for a hen and brought it to his house. And two days later it brought a rooster to his house. This animal eats raw meat, and also dried and green ears of corn, and green stalks, and hens, and bread, and honey. This animal is caught in a trap, or with a snare, or with a lasso, or they shoot it with an arrow. They also set traps for it in the maguey plants when it goes to drink the honey.

[Nahuatl column:] It called out, it cried out; it went quickly toward the snake, going straight at it. It spread itself out — perhaps it had done something elsewhere on the road when the coyote arrived there. And then the coyote drew itself up and rolled about; perhaps it had done something elsewhere. The coyote came again. It went to its master's house. Again it went straight toward the coyote. The coyote gave it something — a turkey hen. And then it awaited its warrior companion. Again, however many times, it gave people there in the courtyard turkeys. The food of the coyote: meat, green raw [corn]; ears of corn, beans, something round, black mushrooms, tamales, tortillas, honey. And as for the ways of the coyote: it goes about marking its territory, it moves about, it wanders about, it digs around, it goes about smelling things.

There is another animal of this species in this land that they call cujtlachcoiotl: it has the same qualities described above; except that in its fur it resembles the bear [cujtlachtli]: and it has a thick ruff, very fine: and on its chest and face it has a crest of large hairs, which makes it look frightening.

There is another animal of this species which they call azcatioiotl: it has the same qualities described above; except that it sits on anthills, which is why it is called azcatioiotl: and also when it howls at night it makes many voices together, some thick, others thin, others even thinner.

There is another animal of this species which they call tlalcoiotl: it has the qualities described above; but it does not live in the mountains like the others, but rather near the towns. Some call it fox or little fox. It eats chickens and beans and ears of corn, and many other things.

There is another animal called ocotochtli: which also lives among the rocks and mountains; it is the size of a small [animal], low and stout: its fur is brown along its back

[Nahuatl column:]
It is called cuetlach coiotl, or cajtla coiotl, it is like a coyote: its fur is like that of a cujtlachtli, shaggy, bristly.

The azcal coiotl is also like a coyote, and it is called azcalcoiotl because it cries out, it howls, it makes sounds like a coyote, it makes rumbling sounds, it whistles, it makes small sounds.

The tlalcoiotl: its name is tlalcoiotl, it lives near houses, it is not raised among the crags, it wanders nearby: it is not a far-ranging coyote, it lives around the settlements, it goes about eating birds, it eats turkeys, it eats ears of corn, it eats cinquefoil berries: it eats all kinds of things, it eats snakes.

and on the belly whitish, with some black spots, sparse and small: it has soft fur, it has a round head, and small ears, like those of a cat: it has a round face: a short snout from which comes a rough or thorny tongue: it has a thin call like a high-pitched string, it is very agile and leaps greatly as though it flies. This animal has a singular and special property by which it hunts to feed other fierce beasts — it hunts men or deer or other animals. It hunts in this manner: seeing that what it wishes to hunt is approaching, it hides behind a tree; and when the prey arrives, it launches itself, rushes at it, and sprays its tongue into the eyes, and it is so venomous that it kills at once; as the animal or person it has killed falls, it covers it with leaves and climbs up into a tree and begins to howl, whose howling can be heard from very far away; and then the other fierce beasts such as tigers, lions, etc., who hear that howl, immediately understand that they are being called to eat, and they come to where the ocotochili is, and they see the prey, and the first thing they do is drink the blood; and afterward they tear it apart and eat it: and through all of this, the ocotochili stands apart, watching how the others eat.

[Nahuatl column:] White on the belly, slender-necked, smoke-colored on the throat; on its back dark, ocelot-colored, ocelot-spotted, resembling an ocelot, of a tawny hue, of a tan hue, wide, fluffy, with a rough nape: small and round, plump in body: meaty and round-headed; with small ears, small-cheeked, with a blunt little muzzle, with small round lips, with a prickly tongue, making a sound toward those it encounters. It is very swift, it springs forward, it leaps, it flies: its body is like a rabbit's; it is fierce, among those that devour. In this way it hunts, its function, what it does when it sees either an animal or a person: then something strikes it, it goes around behind a tree, somehow it goes around behind. And when it arrives behind the tree, it crouches down watching, it peers at it, it goes forward to face it. And after they have eaten, it eats what is left over; and they say that it does this because it has such a poisonous tongue, that if it were to eat, it would poison the flesh, and the other beasts would die from eating it.

There is another small animal they call ostoca: it is called by this name because it always lives in caves and gives birth to its young there. It is very small, has a snout like a little pig, has somewhat long and slightly rough fur, and is of a dark brown color. It eats mice and squirrels and also eats rabbits.

There is another small animal they call mapachitli, and they also call it cioatlamacazqui, and it is also called ilamatan, which means "little old woman." It has hands and feet like a person; it destroys the cornfields when the ears are still green by eating them; it climbs the trees

[Nahuatl column:]
pitzao: and it makes a piercing sound, it shows itself on the road, then it goes ahead quickly, and they will eat it. And they came forward then quickly, it went down, and it went down into mietlan, and there it nurses its young, it is cradled; and some go down it as well; then afterward they will take it down and tear it apart.

Ostooa: it is also called ostooa, it always goes about seeking caves, in the cave it makes its home, there it descends, there it crawls about; thus its beak is like a small thin bill; it is thin-necked, wide-bodied, large-cheeked; it eats small fish, and in water it feeds on small fish, it carries them into shallow water and swallows them there.

Mapachitli: it is also called cioatlamacazqui, and also called ilamaton; the mapachitli is so named because it is truly just like a person in its hands; it does not sleep, its hands are like a human hand; then it reaches into the cornfield with them.

translation:
Of Animals. Folio 11.

[The animal is called] glutton, because it eats all things, and always eats, never becomes satisfied. And from this comes the custom of calling someone a pecotli — one who eats much and never becomes full — always going about eating, or wherever he sees something to eat, he immediately rushes at it to eat it.

There is another little animal called coiametl, or quauh coiametl: it is very similar to the Castilian pig, and some even say that it is the Castilian pig. It has long, rough bristles, and also its feet are like a pig's, and from its bristles they make brushes, just like from the bristles of the Castilian pig. This animal eats acorns called quauh capulin, it also eats maize and beans, and roots and fruit: it eats like a Castilian pig. And for this reason some call the Castilian pig coiametl, because of the resemblance it has to this animal; for the same reason they also call the Castilian pig pecotli, because it eats like this little animal, which they call glutton or pecotli.

[Nahuatl column:]
good, because it eats a great deal. And whoever eats a great deal takes its name, ivica pecotli: ni pecoti means: he eats much. It is also said: anoco njxixicunti, anoco njtlaquativetzi, anoco canjnox vicamati.

The cuiametl, or quauh coiametl; it is also called pecotli; it is just like [the pig], no one could tell them apart: and it would not be possible to distinguish them; the Castilian pig is not like it in appearance. It comes from Castile: it is fat, pot-bellied, broad-bodied; its flesh is like honey in sweetness, it is nourishing, watery, firm, salty, juicy; its hair is called ichoatl. Its food is: wild avocado, wild cherry, tonacaioti, tlanchoatl, fruit: it eats just like a Castilian pig. For this reason they gave the pig the name cuiametl. And the reason it is also called pitzotl — pig — is because it feeds on filth and rolls about wallowing in it.

translation:
The Eleventh Book

Third paragraph concerning other small animals like squirrels and similar ones.

There are many kinds of squirrels in this land: some of them are somewhat large and elongated, and are brown in color; they have soft fur, small ears like acorn cups, a bushy tail, with coarse fur dark at the tips. They eat whatever is available — bread, meat, and fruit — whatever they can get; even when driven away, they are not frightened, and for that reason do not leave off; they steal imperceptibly and eat whatever is stored. And for this reason thieves are called Tezhalutl. The cry of this little animal is thin and lively.

There are other squirrels that are raised in the mountains and in the trees; these squirrels eat pine nuts, and the tender buds of trees, and the worms that breed in the trees; they strip the bark from the trees in order to extract the worms that are inside.

[Nahuatl column:]
The third paragraph: concerning yet other [animals], what they are called and how they are described.

The Tezhalutl: it is slender, long, elongated, narrow-faced, somewhat round-bodied, with wide ears, narrow-mouthed, long-tailed, with a divided tail, a tufted tail, a short-haired tail, and a thick tail base.
All the produce of the land and the fruits it eats entirely. And it at once begins to steal: it does not fear for the stored provisions, nor does it abandon them; it is very bold in stealing; and for this reason thieves are called tezhalutl: they are gluttonous, grabbing with both hands.

The tree-squirrel: this one lives like the tezhalutl, it eats up on top of trees; it always stays in the treetops. And it is called the tree-squirrel because it eats the tender young pine cones, and also the tree-worms; it strips off the bark searching for them.

There is another kind of squirrel, which they call tlaltechalutl: it is called this because they breed in the cornfields, and they live in caves and among the rocks: and there they raise their young like moles; they are very harmful to the cornfields.

There is another little animal called Motutli; it is small and dark-colored: it has a long, somewhat whitish tail, and very soft fur: it eats all the same things that squirrels eat.

There is another little animal called motoiavitl: it resembles the one described above, of the same kind: it is dark gray, the color of mice, and it lives underground, just like them.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is a small animal called the tlaquatl or tlaquatzin. It is about the size of a small cat, and is dark grayish: its hair is long and very soft; and when they are old, their hair falls out. It has a long snout, and its face is marked like a cat's. The old females are small, with a long bare tail: it has no hair on it. It lives among the cornfields and among the rocks, where it makes a den in which it lives and raises its young. It has a pouch between its chest and belly, where it puts its little ones, and carries them wherever it wants to go, and there they nurse. This little animal does not know how to bite or scratch or do any harm, even when it is picked up. When they bother it, it squeals and cries, and tears come out of its eyes, like a person. When they take away its young, it cries a great deal and squeals for them. This little animal eats corn and beans and the scrapings of the maguey plants that are taken from them when they are tapped to extract the honey-water; it also eats honey. And the meat of this animal is edible and tasty, like rabbit. And those...

[Nahuatl column:] It is called tlatlaquaton, pacoltzintli, or it resembles an opossum. When it is old, when it is aged, it is wrinkled, thin-lipped, with a pointed snout; its tail is smooth and hairless, even when fully grown. And when it is healthy, it nests in rocky crevices, along walls; it hangs by its tail and goes somewhere, carrying its young, placing the foreign ones to nurse; it takes them up, it brings them out, carries them to eat; it goes quickly, harmless, not aggressive, not biting. translation:
On Animals
Folio 14

[It] raises its young and makes a nest to place them in hidden, secret spots. It is edible and has tasty flesh.

[image of a weasel]

The weasel is slender; it has a rather long little tail, a spotted face, and is somewhat reddish; it has a white chest. It eats rats and mice, especially those called nextecujlin and tlalomjtl. It also eats chickens, sucking out the contents; its dung is very foul-smelling. It is very fond of chicks and eggs and eats many of them; it greatly desires to encounter hens that are sitting on eggs to eat them. It is not itself eaten.

[image of a skunk]

There is an animal in this land that gives off a great stench, and the smell carries for a great distance. It is the size of a cat; it has long hair and is black in color; it has a bushy tail. It is low to the ground; it has sharp, small ears; it has thin bones. It lives among rocks and in caves, and there it raises its young. Its food consists of beetles —

[Nahuatl column, right side:]

— it hides, it burrows into the ground, it conceals itself, it rolls itself up; yet it cannot move about freely, it cannot fly, it can barely walk.

The coati: also called coatl. It has a slender elongated snout; it bristles up; it sways its tail; it is very hard, very fierce. Its food: it eats nextecujlin [mice] and tlalomjtl; it eats the chicks and scratches along the ground; it greatly fears the smell, which is very rank and repulsive; it greatly frightens the turkeys and turkey chicks; it goes about seeking them out and harassing them, rolling them about.

The skunk: it is called pacoltec, pacoltontli, papacoltec, tlaltec; it is filthy, it has a divided tail; it is compact; it has notched ears, a small mouth. It is found in ravines, between walls, between rocks, where it raises and shelters its young.

Its food: grubs, maguey worms, nextecujlin [mice], ground beetles.

translation:
On Animals. Folio 15.

They shout and whistle, they bite and throw stones and sticks at travelers. They have faces almost like a person's; they are hairy and shaggy; they have thick haunches, and they raise their young in the crags. They give birth to only one offspring at a time. They eat corn and beans, and fruits, and meat — they eat like a person. They also eat pine nuts and acorns; they also eat the sap of green trees. To capture these animals, hunters use this trick: they make a great bonfire in a place where these animals frequent, and they surround it with ears of corn; and they place in the middle of the fire a stone called cacalotati. The hunters of this prey hide themselves, or bury themselves in the ground. When the monkeys see the fire and smell the smoke, they come at once to warm themselves and to see what that thing is. The females carry their young on their backs, and they all sit down around the fire, warming themselves. And when the stone gets hot, it makes a great loud crack and scatters the coals and ashes over the monkeys. This is

[Nahuatl column:] what is called "the thing that makes a noise like papavians [?]," they are dazzled; it scorches them, it singes them, it burns the hair off them. As for what is said of their flesh — it is said that their meat, their limbs, their body is very fine indeed. They do not eat just any coati, nor just any wild tomato or ground tomato, nor tree-celery. And for the fire to be made well: the corn is arranged around it in a circle, or shelled corn is used; and the stone rolls into the fire, and the cacaloteti [stone] goes right to the middle of the flames. The hunters hide themselves, burying themselves wherever they are, so that the monkeys do not sense them. They approach the fire and the smoke; then they come, carrying their young on their backs, and they crowd together around the fire. They begin to warm themselves; they begin to singe themselves by the fire; they turn this way and that around the fire; they rock their young, whom they are warming, and they spread them out [to warm them]. And suddenly — for indeed the stone bursts out of the fire — it goes off with a great crack, scattering [coals and ash].

translation:
Of Animals                                                         fol. 16

[The deer of] the mountains are tall of body; they have long and well-made legs; they are of large body and stout; they have a belly; they have a long neck and a long, thin snout; their ears are long, pointed, and concave; their hooves are tender and greasy; their hooves are cloven, they have fetlocks; they are thick in the hindquarters; their tail is short and wide. They are good to eat; their meat is savory; they are ash-colored. As soon as they are born they get up and walk like lambs and colts. They are very swift. They eat green maize, and beans, and bean leaves, and graze on grasses and the leaves of trees; they eat rotten wood and the worms that breed in timber; they eat hay and the leaves of shrubs.

The male deer have antlers the color of dry wood, and they are branched. They shed their antlers by pressing them into the fork of a tree to pull them off; in this manner they tear the antlers from their head, and thus become young again like a fawn.

[Nahuatl column:]
Tall of stature, lank and strung out, lean and slender, tapering, long-legged: with savory, fragrant flesh; pleasant-tasting. It is so: as soon as it is born it rises and stands, just as a lamb is born, just as a horse: it is woolly-coated, fine-haired. Its food: ears of maize, green maize, bean pods, beans, greens; also the tender shoots of trees, tree bark, forest mushrooms, rushes, and herbs.

The male deer with antlers: the antlers are hard, the antlers are dry, wrinkled. When the antlers dry out on the animal, it scrapes them against trees to strip them; thus it sheds its antlers: it ties them off, then pulls them free.

In this land they raised dogs without any hair, smooth and hairless, and if they had any hair at all, it was very little.

Other small dogs they kept, which they called xoloitzcuintli, which likewise had no hair, and at night they would cover them with blankets to sleep. These dogs are not born this way: rather, when they are small they are rubbed with a resin called oxitl, and with this their hair falls out, leaving the body very smooth. translation:
Book Eleven

There are other dogs called tlalchichi, small and round, which are very good to eat.

There is another animal called the water dog, because it lives in the water. These are what we call otters: they are the size of a hound, have dark and very soft fur, water does not penetrate it, nor does the water soak in — the water slides off it as if it were greasy. This animal eats fish and everything found in the water.

The moles of this land are large, like big rats; they have reddish fur, they are fleshy and fat with low feet, so that they almost drag their belly along the ground. They have a not-very-long tail, long and curved claws, and teeth: two long ones on the lower part and two on the upper part, also long, and other small ones. On each side near these, the four large teeth are straight and somewhat curved. They have small round ears. This animal is edible and tasty, and very fat, and whoever gnaws its bones will have their teeth fall out or become ground down. It has poor eyesight, and in bright light it cannot see at all. It makes burrows.

[Nahuatl column:] Tlalchichi: it is said that it has a small body, patitiontli, tlalyanton, tuitopil.

Atzcuputli [otter]: just like the tlalchichi, it lives in the water, it lives always in the water, it always goes into the water. It is sleek, wide, soft, never [gets wet properly]. And the water never truly soaks it — as if it were buttery. Its food is all the fish that are in the water.

Tocan [mole]: it is reddish, fleshy, round-fleshed, compact-tailed, its eyes are sunken and narrow-set, its face is flat and squashed, its face is rough, biting at the snout, smooth-bodied, flat and even-skinned: it is good, flavorful, tasty; it fattens, it crackles when cooked, it is crisp, it softens. It always lives underground. When it goes out to the surface it can no longer find its way back; its burrow collapses. Its food is whatever it finds underground — roots of trees and plants.

It lives underground and always lives underground; and when it comes above ground, it cannot find its way back to its burrow. It immediately makes a hole where it takes refuge. It eats roots of all kinds of trees, and of plants, and of magueys. It eats the roots of corn stalks, and the stalks themselves when they are tender, and also the ears of corn it buries underground, and green beans and green corn; it gnaws and eats them there. Even if it is a large corn stalk, it pulls it underground and eats it there.

Seventh Chapter on Rats and Other Similar Animals.

Rats are of many kinds and have many names. They are called quimichi, which means rat; and they are called tapanchichi, which means wall-breaker; and they are called tepanmamal, which means wall-borer; and they are called calxoch, which means household dweller. Rats are ash-colored, their fur is smooth, they are dark brown on the back, they are slender, they have long tails, and their snout is sharp. They eat our provisions: corn, chili, squash, squash seeds, and chia; they eat ground cacao and almonds; they eat everything we eat, all kinds of fruits, and everything.

(Nahuatl column:)
It eats all manner of things: corn, husks, the inner stalk, green cornstalks; it gnaws everything, dragging it underground to eat it there; it burrows underground.

Seventh paragraph, which speaks of the small animals, their nature, what they are called, and other things of the same kind.

Quimichi: it is also called tepanchichi, and also called tepanmamal, and also called calxoch. This quimichi has many descriptive names: nextontli, chichimtontli, poiactontli, iaiamazpil, iaiamazton, viacapil, cujtlapile, cujtlapilviacatontli, tompisaton. It is called tepanchichi because it goes about inside walls. It is called tepanmamal because it bores and gnaws through walls. It is called calxoch because it always lives inside houses.

They make nests from straws and other soft things. They gnaw at clothing, and damage rich blankets and feathers, and everything kept in chests and trunks — they find it all and destroy it; and they steal precious stones and hide them in their holes. From this they took a name for those who spy and lie in wait: what is said and done in other matters, in order to go and report it elsewhere. These are called quimichin, or rats. And from this comes a proverb that says: niquimichti, meaning: "I knew secretly what my enemies were doing and saying," sending spies to see and hear their words and deeds. They eat maize, they eat chili, squash, and various greens. They eat cacao beans, cacao pods — they truly eat as people do. They eat tamales, tortillas, they eat meat and fish, they eat everything — nothing is spared. They dig holes in walls, they drag away cloaks, they gnaw feather-capes, they tear apart blankets and destroy all that lies stored. They enter everywhere, no matter how carefully things are locked away. For this reason they are called quimichtin. Because of this there is a saying among children: "I am like a rat" — meaning: I go about secretly, I listen, I spy. Cats hunt and kill rats.

...with wooden cat-traps, and with an herb called quimichpatli [mouse medicine].

There are water mice that live in the water, called Aquimichin or Atocanme. They know how to swim, and cross the water paddling; they are fat and fleshy, have a long tail, and are the same color as other mice.

There are other mice that live in the mountains; they are large.

There are other mice that live in the cornfields.

The mice that live in the house are called calquimichti.

There are others that also live in the house and have small eyes; they are called tecoconton or tecocon.

There are other mice called viacotl: they have long tails and a long, slender body.

There are some little animals, like rats or like moles. They are not blind; they burrow underground in the cornfields, eating the corn and the beans. They steal as much as they can, and when they have had their fill they store it in their burrow. They have pouches on both sides of their face like a monkey; they fill these with what they steal and carry it into their burrow, into some ho[les]...

Aquimichim: also called Atoca canicich among the mice: they live in the water. They are called lloanj, panonj; their forepaws are small, their flesh is thick, their tail is long.

Quauh quimichim [forest mouse]: it lives in the forest, its tail is long and thick.

Hal quimichim [field mouse]: it lives in the milpa, dwelling in the open field.

Cal quimichim [house mouse]: it lives inside houses.

Tecocon, tecoconton: it is just another mouse; it has a thin tail-tip, is small and slender, with dull eyes.

Viacotl: also called cuitlapilhujac [long-tailed]; the body is long, slender, with a long thin tail.

Chachaoatl: it has pouches on both cheeks; it stuffs them full; it goes about hiding things; it eats everything in the cornfield, especially it fills itself with seeds. It is also called camaxi xiqui; it fills a whole fanega [bushel]; it eats everything; [there are] two kinds...

Chapter Two: Of Birds.

First Paragraph: Of birds with rich plumage.

There is a bird in this land called the quetzaltototl: it has very rich feathers, of diverse colors; it has a sharp beak, and yellow, and yellow feet; it has a crest on its head made of feathers, like a rooster's comb. It is as large as a bird called the tzanatl, which is the size of a magpie or jay from Spain. Its tail has the form and composition of those birds called tzanatl, or tue tzanatl, which are raised in the towns. The feathers that grow on its tail are called quetzalli; they are very green...

[Nahuatl column:]
...from below it is dusty-hued; it goes there to seek food, goes there to scratch about, in whatever manner, and settles among the rushes; there it goes raising its head: thus it goes feeding itself.

Here is the second chapter, which speaks of all the various birds from many places.

Here is the first paragraph, which tells of all the various birds from many places, how they appear.

The quetzaltototl is brilliant, its beak is yellow, its lower beak is yellow, it is brightly colored, its wing feathers are like paper, its tail feathers are of equal length; the great tzanatl, whose tail feathers rustle as it walks. Its prized feathers, called quetzalli, its tail feathers are numerous, green, intensely green, herb-green, turquoise-colored, blue-green: they are like broad reeds; they sway, they wave, they shimmer, they dazzle, they ripple, they undulate...its tail feathers...

They are the color of a grape, and a little curved: they are somewhat wide and sharp, and they rest upon the shafts of the long wing feathers, which are called quetzalviztli; they are green, clear, long and straight, and sharp at the tips, and their greenness shines. These birds inhabit the province that is called Tecolotlan, which is toward the lowlands, or nearby; they live in the groves and make their nests in the trees to raise their young.

There is a bird in this land that is called timitzan, or teutimitzan: this bird has black feathers and lives in the water. The precious feathers that it has grow on its chest, under the armpits beneath the wings; half of them are dark and the other half are shining green.

There is another bird called tlauhtquechol, or teuquechol, and it lives in the water; it is like a duck. It has feet like a duck, wide and red; its bill is also colored. It has a bill like an apothecary's spatula, which they call an espatula. It has a small crest...

On the head it is red; it has the chest, belly, tail, and wings of a very fine crimson color; and the shoulders and the elbow joints of the wings are very red. Its beak is yellow, and its feet are yellow. They say that this bird is the chief of the white herons, which gather to it wherever they see it.

There is another small bird of rich plumage called xiuhquechol: it has feathers green like grass; its wings are blue, and so is its tail. This bird breeds in the regions called Anáhuac, which is to the east of Mexico, toward the South Sea.

There is another bird called çaquán; it has a sharp beak, and the feathers above the beak are reddish; it has tawny feathers all over the body. The feathers of its tail are very fine yellows, and brilliant; it has the same tail with other black feathers, with which it covers the yellow ones. When it flies and spreads its tail, then the yellow feathers appear; the tail shimmers, the yellow ones mixed with the black, and it looks like a flame of fire and like gold. They breed in Anáhuac.

[Nahuatl column:]

Xiuhquechol: it is green in its feathers, its wings are yellow, and its tail feathers — it lives in Anáhuac.

Çaquán: it is whitish-gray, red-crested everywhere it is seen, it is dark-tawny. And when it fans out its tail feathers they are yellow, very yellow, deeply yellow, gleamingly yellow. And its black [feathers] spread out; whenever it opens its tail feathers it shines yellow, or it casts light, as people say, like fire, like a flame: like gold it gleams.

translation:
Book Eleven.

There is another bird called the Aioquan; it lives in the mountains of Cuextlan and Njshvacan. It has a sharp, black beak; all its feathers are black, except for the tail feathers, which are half white and half black.

There is another bird also called Aioquan, and it is a water bird. All water birds accompany it as if it were their prince. It has a yellow beak and green wingbones; the large feathers of the wings and those of the tail are mottled with white and green. The feathers covering the whole body are reddish, tending toward red.

There is another bird called the Chalchiuhtototl; it is raised in the mountains, it is small, it has a sharp beak, its head and tail are green, and likewise its wings; the wing-coverts are also dark green; the feathers under the wings and over the whole body are of a clear sky-blue color.

Aioquan: it is a dweller of the forests, it dwells where the tlaquatzi is, it lives in Mcextlan, and in the region of Mjshoaca; its bill-tip is pointed, it is stout, it is also a flier. And its tail feathers are white, spread out: thus it is called Aioquan.

Aioquan: it is a dweller of the water. How it lives: it flies in a curved path, it mixes among the birds, it dwells in the water. And where it gathers, there the birds collect together, and the small birds cluster there. Its bill-tip is sharp; [illegible] it is yellow-green; its wing-coverts are greenish; it flies about everywhere. It has a reddish bill-tip; it glows: it settles in rows.

Chalchiuhtototl: it dwells in the forests, it is small, its feathers are fine. Its head and its tail are green, and its wings likewise; it flies about crying out, and also it drinks water, which is sky-blue. And under its wings and all its feathers are blood-red, yellow, turquoise-green, yellow-green, and deep turquoise-blue; it sparkles and shimmers.

translation:
Of Birds                    folio 22

There is another bird called Xiuhtototl, which is found in the provinces of Anahuac, toward the coast of the South Sea, in towns called Acepalla, Hapilollan, and Ototlan. This bird is the size of a jay; it has a sharp, black beak; the feathers of its breast are purple; the feathers of its back are blue, and those of its wings are light blue; its tail has metallic feathers, of green and dark blue. This bird is hunted in the month of October, when the plums are ripe; they kill them then, with blowguns in the trees; and when one goes to pick it up, one gathers some herb to use when taking it up, so that one's hand does not touch the feathers, because if it does, they are said to lose their color.

There is a bird called Xioapalquechol, also called Tziuhtli; it has a long beak and black feet; its head, tail, wings, and back are light blue in color; its breast and belly are tawny, and the wing-coverts are also tawny.

There is another bird called Xochitenacal, which lives in the mountains in the trees; it is raised in the province of Totonacapan and Cuextlan; it builds nests in palms; the nest it makes is like a sack hanging from a branch of the tree; it has a concave and long beak, very yellow; it has its head and neck [text continues]

[Nahuatl column:]
The Xiuhtototl lives in Anahuac, it goes about in Anahuac, carrying all the traits of the tzanactl bird. It is sharp-billed, sharp-featured; its back is greenish-yellow, its tail truly very green, of the color of jade; its wing-feathers are broad, and its tail-feathers are wide and spread; one side of the tail is very green, turquoise-colored; the other side is black, spread wide.

The Xioapalquechol, also named Tziuhtli, has a long bill, black-legged; its throat, its tail, and its wings, on one side of the feathers, and also its tail-feathers, are turquoise-colored, brownish, whitish; and its color: it is very green, it becomes very green, it becomes brownish, it becomes brownish.

The Xochitenacal lives in the forest, in the mountain, the forest is its home; it is especially found in Totonacapan and in Cuextlan; it hangs in the treetops. It only raises its young suspended, it carries them hanging. Its bill is long; it is narrow-billed, thick-billed, its beak is dull-colored, its beak is smooth-surfaced. This is why it is called Xochitenacal — from its hanging-place and its neck-region: co pa [continues]

translation:
Of Birds.                    Folio 23.

Neck: and the back and the wings and the elbows have green and yellow [feathers]. The small feathers of the wings that cover the large feathers of the wings, and the feathers of the chest and belly are dark yellow. They are called xollotl. The edges of the feathers of the wings and of the tail are reddish. They build nests on very high crags. They frequent the tops of very tall trees. In these places they make their nests and lay their eggs, and they brood over their eggs and hatch their chicks. In these same places they are captured and tamed.

There is another kind of parrot called tostli. These are the same birds: when they are fully grown and flying, they molt; at that point their feathers become very yellow and shining. The more years this parrot grows, the more yellow it becomes. And for this reason it is called tostli, which means: a very yellow thing.

There is yet another kind of parrot called Alo. They are raised in the province called Cuextlan. They live in the rough mountain crags; they breed in rugged woodlands. They can be domesticated. The beak is yellow and long, like a hook. Their beaks and legs are calloused. The tongue is rough, hard, round, and firm. Their eyes are red and yellow. Their chest is yellow, and likewise their belly. Their backs are purple. The feathers of the tail and wings are nearly reddish-colored. This [color] is called fire-colored. The coverts of the wings — those covering the tips of the large feathers, and also those covering the tips of the tail feathers — are dark, with some red markings.

[Nahuatl text describing the same birds:]

Tostli: when it is mature, it molts. It becomes yellowish, it turns yellow, it brightens — and at that point it is called tostli.

Alo: it lives there, in Cuextlan, in Taxcalco, in the wooded places, dwelling among the trees. It has a rounded beak, a beak like a little curved hook, a curled tongue, and a tongue that curves back; the eye is fire-colored. Its back is bluish-green; its wing feathers and tail feathers are dark reddish, very bright. The parrot has a yellow upper side; its tail feathers are yellowish, brilliant, glowing — cozcamilivi [a term for a glowing, reddish-orange color].

translation:
Book Eleven

There is a kind of parrot called cocho: it is very similar to the one called toznene. It has a yellow, curved beak; its head is red, and all the feathers of its body are purple, as are the elbows and all the outer part of the wings. It has a dark reddish color mixed with yellow. The small feathers that lie close to the flesh of the wing, called xolloti, are yellow mixed with red. The fine, soft down near the tail and near the wings is red mixed with yellow. This bird sings and speaks, and whatever language it is taught, it responds to other animals: it replies, saying what they say, singing what they sing. It is very tame and docile.

There is another kind of parrot called quiliton: these are small ones. They have a red head and a completely green body, with red wing-shields. They eat corn and beans. They learn to speak: they say what they are taught.

There is another kind of parrot called tlalacuecali: they are raised in the mountains. They have a yellow, curved beak; they have a red head; the elbows of their wings are dark crimson in color; they have a dark yellow chest; their wings, tail, and back are green in color.

[Nahuatl column — Cocho:] It resembles the toznene; yellow-beaked, yellow-lipped, with small spotted markings; its body color overall, its wing-feathers dark-spotted, shading to dark. Its inner-wing feathers are greenish; its tail-feathers, its wing-feathers, turquoise-blue mixed. It is a singer, a warbler; it speaks, it responds, it mimics, it sings along, it chatters; it trills, it calls, it sings, it repeats.

[Nahuatl column — Quiliton:] It resembles the toznene and also the cocho; it is small, round, plump; it is entirely green all over. Its wing-coverts are reddish-shaded, somewhat heavy; it eats grain, it husks grain.

[Nahuatl column — Tlalacuecali:] It is a forest bird; it has a yellow beak, a yellow-tipped beak, with small spotted markings; its wing-elbow is smooth-feathered, its breast-color; its tail-feathers, its wing-feathers are greenish; its side-feathers spread out; it is blue-green; its tail and its wing-feathers [continue].

translation:
Of Birds. Folio 24.

There are some little birds in this land that are very tiny, looking more like horseflies than birds. There are many kinds of them: they have a small beak, black, and their little tongue is like that of a bee: it makes a buzzing sound in the bushes, and there it lays its eggs and broods them, and hatches its chicks: it lays no more than two eggs: it eats and sustains itself on the nectar of flowers, like bees. It is very nimble and flies like an arrow: it is brownish in color, it molts every year, in wintertime, they hang from the trees by their beaks, and hanging there they dry out, and their feathers fall off: when the tree begins to turn green again, it comes back to life, and its feathers grow back. And when it begins to thunder, before it rains, it then wakes up and revives and is resurrected. It is medicinal for syphilitic sores, and whoever eats it will never have sores, but it makes sterile those who eat it.

[Nahuatl text:] Hummingbird: vitili, dark-colored, slender-billed, with a projecting lip, with a protruding beak, with a curved beak. It is a tree-clinger: it clings to trees, it plasters itself against them, it covers them, it spreads over them: it lays only one egg. It sips flowers: its food is flower nectar, flower syrup. It is hollow inside, fluffy, ash-colored, able to hang. It smooths the ground, licks up nectar, clings to trees: it drips, covers, spreads out, it flutters; it glides, it hangs, it squeaks. In its interior: it makes a sound, quauh-sound at its tip: there it cries out in the trees, scrapes along, begins to peel away. And in the cold season: it stiffens, it constricts, it shuts down: and then once more it revives. And when: it gurgles when it rains, then it rises, then it stirs, then it awakens. As a medicine for skin disease: whoever uses it will never have skin disease, it eats away the skin many times: yet it is swift, it makes itself erect.

translation:
Of birds.                                  folio 25.

¶ There are some called totoçiatleton; they have a throat that is colored and shining, like a live coal. They are ashen in body, and the crown of the head and the throat are brilliant like a live coal.

There are others called talolovitzim; they are roundish and ashen, with some white streaks.

¶ And another little bird called iollo totol, which is raised in the province called Ttuilixco, which is toward the South Sea. It is a small bird, like a quail. It is called iollo totol because the inhabitants of that province say that the hearts of the dead, or their souls, return in this bird. Its song is sweet and gentle. The head, breast, and back are between brown and yellow. The tail is black. The feathers of the wings are tawny, and the tips are white. It is edible.

¶ There is a bird called pohpocales, which lives in the mountains. It has this name because it calls out "pohpocales" at sunset, and before the sun rises it also calls "pohpocales." It lives in the ravines of the province of Tuzllan.

¶ [In Nahuatl:] Totoçatleton, toçratleton, toçcatle: it is ashen, grayish; it drinks at the water's edge; and it is grayish; it is truly green, [with a call] iuh quinticti, pepepetica, xoxotla.

¶ [In Nahuatl:] Telolovitzili: ololtontli, nextontli, ticetontli; it rolls about, it makes a sound, it is ashen.

¶ [In Nahuatl:] Yollo totol: it lives in Teutlixco, near the Huitzilatenco; each one sings like a quail. And this is how it is described: it spreads its wings; when you are about to die it burns your heart. And it speaks: it draws one, it calls one; truly it gladdens the heart, it delights the heart. Its bill is small; its breast and rump are somewhat yellowish. Its tail is black, with some white stripes extending along it; the tips are white. It is edible.

¶ [In Nahuatl:] Pohpocales: its home is in the forest. This is why it is called pohpocales — it always calls when the sun is entering [setting], and also before the sun rises.

translation:
Book Eleven

And the Catemafico: it eats fish, it is the size of a duck, but has long legs; it has a pointed beak, rounded and red; its eyes are also red; it has a dark yellow head; the neck, back, chest and tail are grayish-brown, and the feathers under the tail are also grayish; it has red feet. And it is edible.

There is another bird called the tecuciltototl: it is called this because when it sings it says "tecucilton, tecucilton"; it has a thin voice; it is the size of a quail and has feathers like a quail; it is edible. It is found in the provinces of Teuilixco and Toztlan.

There is another bird called the ixmatlartotl, which lives in the mountains toward the southern sea. It is called by the name Ixmatlatorotl because its song sounds like human speech: when it sings it says "Campavee,"

[Nahuatl column:]
…it calls out pohpocales. And it follows the water, it lives in Toztlan, the Catemafico swallows fish whole. Its eyes are chili-red, its pupils very red. Its beak is yellowish. Its wings, back, and flanks are ashen-colored; it rests facing one direction, and below it rests; its feet are chili-red, and it is edible.

The tecuciltototl: it always calls out in this way, saying "tecucilton, tecucilton"; its voice is thin; it is the size of a quail; it is edible; and it also comes from Teuitixco and Toztlan.

The Ixmatlatototl: it dwells in the forest. It lives in the vicinity of water. It is called ixmatlatototl because its speech sounds like that of people, and it says…

translation:
Of birds. Folio 26.

"Campa vee" is a word used by the people of those parts, and it seems to orient them. It has a silvery beak, its head, chest, wings, tail, and entire body are ash-colored, and so too its feet. It is good to eat. —

Third section on birds that live in water or that have some association with water.

There are many kinds of ducks in this land, which live in the water and eat fish, small shells, worms of the water, and other small creatures of the water.
There is one kind of duck called concanauhtli — they are somewhat large, low to the ground, ash-colored, with a broad beak and broad feet. They breed on the lakes among the cattails, build their nests there, lay their eggs, incubate them, and raise their young. This is the largest of all the ducks.

There are other ducks called ca—

"Campa vee": it is as if one makes the bird call toward that place where those people dwell. Its beak is yellow-tipped. Its head is streaked, its back is streaked, its tail is streaked; it appears uniformly colored, somewhat grayish in appearance. It is edible. —

Third section: it speaks of those birds that live in the water.

The canauhtli lives in the water; it eats fish, water-fly eggs, worms, and water snails.

The concanauhtli: it is ash-colored, large, brownish on the back, broad-faced, broad-beaked, broad-winged, broad-winged. It dips its head, opens its wings wide, lives here on the water; and it preens itself, washes itself; it dives, submerges, and splashes about.

The canauhtli: white as ice, dipping its head,

translation:
Book Eleven

[They have] a white chest and belly, and a grayish-brown body; on the wing joints they have dark green feathers; they are of medium size, smaller than those mentioned above; they have a wide, black beak; their backs are also wide and also black; they have quill feathers on their wings; they have feathers like shells; underneath they have delicate feathers like cotton.

There is another kind of duck also called canauhti tioniaiauhqui: it has dark, shining green feathers on its head; in other respects it is like those mentioned above. All these birds already mentioned are good to eat.

There are many wild geese called Halalacatl. Among the native animals here, they are large, like those of Spain; they have red feet and somewhat flat beaks; they have good meat; underneath they have white and soft feathers. These feathers are used to make cloaks; the outer feathers are stiff and have good quills for writing.

There are cranes in this land called tucuflcoiotl; they are like those of Spain; they have a large, sharp beak like a nail; they are brown or ash-colored; they have a long neck and long, black legs; they are lean; they are good to eat.

There is a kind of duck called xomotl; they have a small crest on the head; they are short-legged, black, and flat; they live in the water, and also in the hills; some of them are dark, others black, others white, others ash-colored.

translation:
On Birds
Folio 27.

They have very soft feathers, from which cloaks are made. These eat fish, and also corn.
There are little ducks, like teals, which are called tecolotli: they make noise when they fly.
There are certain birds in the water called atotoli, which means "water hen." They have a wide mouth, very deeply cleft down to the throat; they hold their beaks open, or open their beaks like a net to catch fish. They are about the size of a turkey cock. Some of these birds are white, and others are metallic-colored.
These birds mentioned above go to breed in various places, and they come to these parts in winter, at the time of the cornfields.

There is another bird in the water called quachilton; it has a red head, a sharp beak, and black feet, and is ash-colored. It breeds among the reeds in the water. There is another bird similar to these called yacacintli: it has long legs and a long beak, and they are good to eat. They eat fish and breed in the water.
There are other water birds called verocanauhtli; they have long, dark green legs, a sharp, long, green beak, and dark brown feathers.

[Nahuatl column:]
Dark-colored. Dweller of the water. One who hunts.
Tecolotli: small, round.

Atotolin: large, wide-billed, like a quechmatle. White, like a turkey.

The water-reeds: the tocuilcolotl, the atotolin, the canauhtli: the white one. Their plumage is dark: the xomutl, the tzcolotli: truly water-dwellers. Along the great shores, at the sandy beaches in the ravine: food comes there where they gather to eat. And when they have all come together, they eat there.

Quachilton: it lives in the water, it surpasses the duck; its cheeks are red, its bill is pointed. Nowhere else around here does it breed. Its bill is like cotton on the quachil.

Vexocanauhtli: it is long, its plumage is dark, its bill is sharp, its bill-tip is blunt, the edge of its bill is serrated, its bill is sharp, its bill is pointed: its cheeks are red, it flaps its great wings, it extends its neck.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another water bird called the açolin, which means "water quail," and by another name it is called coquiçaçolin, meaning "mud quail," or a quail that lives in the mud. It has a long beak and long legs; its feathers are like those of the quail; it lives among the reeds in the water.

There are other small birds in the water called Azitziçujtotl; they are round-bodied, with long sharp dark beaks and long feet; they are ash-colored with white breasts. They say they are born in the province of Anahuac and come to this lake of Mexico among the waters or rains; they are very good to eat. They say that these birds, and the divers of the water, in time turn into fish; they say they are seen entering the sea in flocks, going into the water and never appearing again.

There are swifts in this land, like those of Castile; they nest like those of Castile in their little mud houses.

There are also swallows like those of Castile; they breed, sing, and fly like those of Castile.

[Nahuatl column:]
The açolin: also called coquiçaçolin; it is slender, very elongated, its side is folded, it bows its side-feathers, its home is in the rushes; it bows its side-feathers.

The atzi tziçujtotl: its back is rounded, it has a pointed spine-tip, its beak-tip is spiny, its beak-tip is sharp, it is flat-tipped, it is thick-billed, it has spreading bills, it has very spreading bills, it has a deep throat, a very deep throat, it chatters, it opens wide. It is from Anahuac, it is white-faced, great water-tziçujtotl, a water creature; it multiplies, it gathers.

The açuiçujalotl: it is from the cliff-face; it also nests on walls and wall-ledges; it opens its throat; it blows out its breath; it is small; it is swift-sounding, ash-colored; it makes its nest, it feeds its young, it feeds them insects.

The çuiçuizcatl: it is little and black, with a flat small face; it is dark, grayish, fluffy-feathered. [Remainder partially illegible.]

There are some white birds called astatl, or teu astatl; in some parts of Spain they are called dorales, and here the Spaniards call them white herons. They are very white, like snow; they have little flesh; they have a very long neck, folded; they have a long, sharp, black beak; their legs are tall or long and black; their tail is short; they have no other color. They grow plumes on their thighs and under their wings; they eat fish; their flesh is not edible.

There is a bird in this land called Axoquen; it is the color of cranes, but much smaller; it has long legs and a long beak; it walks in the water and eats fish, and it smells of fish.

There are wild hens and roosters; they are like the domestic hens and roosters of this land; likewise —

[Nahuatl text:] Astatl: also called teuastatl: white, very white, pale white, uniformly white, gleaming white, appearing white from a distance, appearing to reflect white, appearing somewhat dark below the tail, with pointed bill tips, with bill tips like spines, with a black bill, with shimmering blue-green legs, with legs that shimmer, with legs that are dark, with a short, protruding tail.

Axoquen: its voice is like a hissing sound; it is ash-colored, ash-toned; it smells of water-weed; its body is water-weed-colored; its water-smell is water-weed-like; it tastes of water-weed.

Quauhtotolvj [wild turkey]: it is quite like the domestic turkey, but it is dark-speckled; its wing is white; it is good to eat, tasty, flavorful, fat; it is said to be filling. As for the male [vexolotl]: [it makes a] gobbling sound as it runs about calling.

It comes to this lake of Mexico when the other water birds arrive, which is in the month of July.
