It is always in the middle of the water, and rarely appears. It submerges the canoes in the water along with the people: they say it cries out and calls the wind. And then a strong wind comes and submerges the canoes. It does this when people want to catch it. To catch it, they stalk it for two or three days. On the third day they can catch it. On the fourth day all the water hunters prepare themselves, and they go to where it is, as though prepared to die, like someone going to their death. Because they have the custom of pursuing it for four days, every one of those days. This atotoli [water bird] waits for the hunters over the water, and when they come it watches them and does not flee from them. And if on the fourth day they do not catch it before sunset, they consider themselves defeated, and they know it must go free, because their allotted time in which they could kill and shoot it has ended. And when that fourth day ends, this bird begins to cry out like a crane and calls the wind. And then the wind comes and the waves rise. Then it begins to [move away]...

[Nahuatl column:] It always lives in the water, it delights in the water, it loves the full water; it feeds rarely. It does not surface easily; it surfaces with difficulty, since it pursues the wind: it rushes, it runs. Only when it surfaces does it want wind. In order to catch it: for two days, for three days one pursues it; or for four days. And if one cannot catch it within three days, within four days: the fishermen all gather together, and they prepare themselves together, knowing they go to their death — they are the fishermen. Because there is a saying among the fishermen: therefore the atotoli, for four days, constantly watches over the people, lying face-down on the water, watching over them. Because if they cannot catch it within four days — by afternoon, when five bells ring — they know that the fishermen have died, for truly it cannot be caught. The water birds gather in flocks, flap their wings, and the fish come to the surface. And then the hunters cannot escape — even if they want to row, they cannot; their arms go dead, they sink below the water and drown. And if during any of the four days of hunting they catch this bird, they take it immediately, seize it by the beak, throw it into the canoe, and then open its belly while it is still alive, with a three-pointed dart called a minacachal.

The reason they take it by the beak is so that it does not vomit what it has in its belly; for if they did not do this, it would vomit what —

of the water; and when she goes away to where they breed, all the water birds also go with her, and they head westward. The hunters and fishermen regarded this bird as their mirror: they said that in it they could see who would prosper or not in the trade of hunting and fishing.

There is another water bird called the acioti; it is of the kind of water hen, like the one described above. It also comes at the time of Saint James's day to this lagoon of Mexico. Its head is as large as a hen of this land; it has a sharp, black, rounded beak; the edges of the beak are yellow; it has a white breast; its back, wings, and tail are brown, like a duck. Its body is long and thick; it has short legs, and wide feet like a person's hand, set very far back toward the tail. This bird is also rare and seldom seen; it also tends to approach those who travel in canoes. Everything that is said of the atotoli described above is said also of this acioti. It is very good to eat.

[Nahuatl column:]
It goes along gazing about; it is of many kinds. When it flies westward it enters there. These are those who fish for it; by its name one may tell — it appears only rarely, when the other birds come back; it lives in the water. It comes from the direction of Santiago. Its entire head, toward the west — its bill is pointed, its coloring dark; its bill-edges are yellow; its breast is white; its back is grayish; its wings on both sides are also alike; it resembles a duck in flight. It is fat, not light; it spreads its feet when landing; it fans out broadly; it is taken in the hand — it does not flee, it does not leave the place.

...as was said, with respect to the Atotolin: just the same as the Acoiotl.

There is another water bird called Acitli, which means "water hare." It also rarely comes to this lake of Mexico, at the same time as the others already mentioned. It has a small black head and a sharp, long beak; its eyes are red like embers; it is rather long and thick-necked, has a white breast, and its back is black; the outer feathers of its wings are white, the elbows black, the feet black, and toward the tail it is like the ducks. It always goes toward the middle of the lake; they catch it with a net. This bird does not fly much; when someone goes after it in a canoe to shoot it with arrows, when they get close enough to kill it, it ruffles up completely, and begins to cry out calling the wind, and then the water rises in great waves, and in this way it disappears before the fishermen, going under the water. It can rarely be shot from nearby, only from far away. It is good to eat.

Acitli: it is only pleasantly alive, it also comes from there; when it comes, it comes with many birds. Its head is small: its beak is greenish, its bill is pointed, its inner beak is chili-red. Its face within is like fire, it is quite elongated. Its breast is smooth, quite extended; its chest is truly white; toward its tail it is black; toward its wings it is white; its elbow feathers are black. Its feet are black. It always stays somewhat apart, just as the duck does. It lives out on the great lake, always going about there; and thus when it wants to flee — this Acitli — it cannot fly up very well. It only runs along the water surface in the direction it wishes to go; and when someone shoots at it, pursuing it by canoe, when one nearly catches up to it and wants to shoot it, it then begins to cry out and calls the wind; there is great turbulence; the great water rises suddenly...

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another water bird called the teniztli, which means obsidian-stone beak. This bird flies at night and does not appear during the day. It is the size of a dove. It has a small, black head; its chest is as if smoked; its back is black; the feathers of its wings are small; its body is round; its tail is small; its feet and toes are like those of a dove. It has three bills, one above another, and two mouths and two tongues; it eats through both mouths, but has only one gullet. It is held as an omen: whoever catches this bird will soon waste away, and all those in his household will die one by one. For this reason, this bird was called a bird of ill omen. It eats water flies and flying ants. The flesh of this bird is good to eat.

[Nahuatl column:]
Teniztli: it goes about always at night, flying upward, going about over the great waters; its face is toward the sky. Its head is somewhat dark. Its chest is somewhat white, somewhat grayish. Its back is dark; its wings are small, little. Its body is quite round, like a small disk. Its wing feathers are small; its feet are like those of a dove in their spread. The teniztli is so called because all its bills are together. It enters swallowing its food on one side only, yet it speaks with two voices, not one; each one calls out separately. And the teniztli fish — whoever catches it, it is said, will soon die. And it is said that everyone in the household will perish.

On Birds                    folio 32.

There is another water bird called quapetlavac, or quapetlanquj, which means "bald-headed," just like the bird they call Aroque, which I believe is a heron. It has a large head like that of a turkey-cock or parrot. It is bald and has reddish claws. It has a long neck and a thick, long, and round bill, in the manner of a curved hook. It is dark-colored overall; its wings and entire bill are ash-gray; the elbows of the wings are very black; its tail is short and black. It comes to this lake when other birds do. It is a bird that is rarely seen. They considered it a bird of ill omen: they said that when one of them was caught, some important person or lord was going to die, and if they were going to war, that they would have bad fortune.

among the people: for this reason they called it tetzauhtotototl [omen bird]. Its food, its sustenance: it does not eat worms from azcapatlan; it does not go to azcapatlan to live.

Quapetlaoac: quapetlanquj — it is large, eagle-like, with a thick body at the neck. Its head is large; as wide as a turkey's neck it spreads out around the neck; the quapetlanquj is very smooth and shiny, lying stretched out at the nape; in its throat area it is pale whitish, which runs along its throat and is light-colored. Its neck is very thick, just like the shaft of an arrow in width, cylindrical; it is dark-colored; its back is spotted, mottled; its wings are greenish at the tips when they spread; they are very black when spread, with a fine dark color. translation:
Book Eleven

...it is called the "ateponaztli-duck" because from afar it seems as though some kind of teponaztli drum is being played. This bird always lives on this lake, and here it nests among the cattails: it lays up to four or five eggs. The fishermen and water-hunters make their conjecture about rain from the song of this bird — whether it will rain, or whether it will rain much or little: when it sings all night, they say that it is a sign that the rains are coming soon, and that it will rain a great deal, and that there will be an abundance of fish; and when it is not going to rain much, nor will there be many fish, they know this from the fact that it sings little — and this from every third day or at greater intervals.

There is an animal in the water that they call Acujtlachtli: it is the size of a small dog, and it resembles...

[Right column — Nahuatl:]
...it makes a rumbling sound. It is called Atoncuepotli because its cry is a loud, resounding sound that spreads out. And it is called Ateponaztli because from afar it sounds like a teponaztli drum being struck. As for the reed grebe, it always lives here, it perches here; it lays three or perhaps four eggs. The reed grebes that live in the water are always fouling the water; when they cry out, when they call out loudly, one knows by this, one can see by this — and one can also see clearly — that the fish will be plentiful, that many fish will be in the water. And when they do not call out much, when they do not cry: if only a long time has passed since they last called, it means the fish will be scarce.

Acujtlachtli: it lives just as a forest predator does, though it is small in all its [dimensions]...

...in all its features like the caqtlachtli that lives in the mountains, except that its tail is like an eel's, its length is about a knot, it is sticky and clings to the hands. They catch this animal sometimes. The fishermen — not many years ago — caught one at the place of this lake called Santa Cruz, Quavacalco, which is the spring that flows to Tlatelolco. This animal makes the water boil, and the fish come up to the surface. Sometimes it goes under the mud and disturbs all the water. Some of those who saw this animal are still living. One is called Pedro Daniel, who was forty-three years old when they caught it, during the lordship of this Tlatelolco, Don Juan Avehitue. And afterward it appeared to him, and he was frightened to see it, and had it buried near Tepepinto.

...its snout, its ears, its tail, its arm, its foot, its claw: it moves only through the forest. It is a beast of prey: its tail is all one piece, quite long, and flat, so that its tail resembles the tail of the acuetspalin [a kind of lizard]. It is not forked at all; it is simply pointed at the tip, and there is nothing that it wraps around. Whoever its tail touches, that person has no way to escape. When the acuetlachtli is caught — the Michoacan acuetlachtli, as it is also called — its heart is in the water. It dwells at Santa Cruz Quavacalco, and also where the spring is at Santiago. When the acuetlachtli appears there, it causes the water to smoke and boil, and the fish come to the surface floating. And when it enters at Coquishtlan, it slides mightily under the ground, as though moving through water beneath the earth. In this way it truly frightens people.

It has a small, white head, a longish neck, the chest and back are white, and also the tail, which is short. The exterior of the wings is black, and the interior white, and the elbow joints of the wings are black. It molts its feathers each year, and when they renew, the new feathers come out reddish. It nests in this lagoon, raising three or four chicks during the rainy season. It is good to eat, and it also departs when the other birds depart.

Iexi xoxouhqui: it lives in the water. The reason it is called iexi xoxouhqui is because its feet are green. Its legs are cylindrical and slender, somewhat dark. Its beak curves upward; its head is small, white, somewhat long-necked. Its breast is white; its tail feathers are also white; somewhat small in the wings, on the wing surfaces: below on the back it is dark, and underneath it is indeed white; on its shoulders it is dark, where it nestles. Here it lays its eggs: three or four eggs it lays when the rains come; it is also edible. And it likewise departs when the other birds depart.

...and it also departs: what it eats is fish; its flesh is edible.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another water bird called quetzaltecolotlon; it is called this because it has rich green feathers. It is a duck. It has green feathers on its head; the head is striped near the eyes with green feathers. In the middle of the head it has dark yellow feathers. It has a dark, wide beak, and a dark yellow neck. On its wings it has some shining green feathers. The back, wings, and tail are ash-colored. The chest is white; the feet are ash-colored tending toward reddish, and wide. It breeds in these parts. This bird is good to eat.

There is another water bird called metzcanauhtle, which means a duck that has something like a half-moon on its face, made of white feathers. In the middle of the head it has ash-colored feathers, and likewise on the back and on the tail, somewhat like the color of a quail. On the wings it has feathers of three colors: some of them are silvery, those being the first; the second ones are white; the third ones, which are at the tips of the wings, are green like [plumas tar]; the

[Nahuatl column:]
Quetzaltecolotlon. It is a duck; it is called quetzaltecolotlon because of how it appears: its head is thus, and its feathers are made thus: in the middle of the head it is yellow; the top is dark, broad; the bill is yellow, and its feathers are shiny; all of its body-surface colors are described: on the back it is grayish; on the shoulder-blade area it shows a pale color; its wing area is also visible in a certain way; it has small flat spots; it does not hang down. It is edible.

Metzcanauhtli — it is called metzcanauhtli because of its face, which is made thus: white in color, like the shape of the moon in the middle. In the middle [of the head] it is ashy; on the shoulder-blade area and on the tail-feather area, altogether grayish, bending back and forth; its feathers are of three kinds. Its tail is greenish-blue. It is white [in certain parts].

The feathers underneath are white and soft like cotton; they use them to weave cloaks. They do not breed in this lake but go far away to breed. They are very good to eat.

Book Eleven

[It has] black stripes across its face in honor of the air. It is the size of a duck: it has a small head, it has a little crest on it, on its head: its feathers are dark tawny, it has a white breast, it has some black bands on its belly, it has black and wide feet: they do not breed in this lake but rather in other regions, and from there many come to this lake: they are good to eat.

There is another water bird called the amanacoche: it is called that because it has white temples like paper — as if to say, a bird that has paper ears. It is the size of a teal: the top of its head is ash-colored; its neck is also ash-colored, and its head is ashen, its breast white, its back black and also its tail; it has two white feathers in its tail, one on each side; the elbows of its wings are white on both sides: half the feathers of its wings are dark, and the other half black; the quills of its wings are black; its feet are black: it also does not breed in these parts; many come to this lake: they are good to eat.

translation:
On Birds. Folio 37.

[The bird lives on] the lake, and is seen before all other birds. They call it atapalcatl: because when it wants to rain, one day before and all through the night, it makes noise in the water with its wings, beating the water with its wings. The fishermen of the water understand from this that it is going to rain. It is called matatotli: because it has a blue beak, wide and flat, and has a white stripe above the beak; the head is tawny, the wings, the back, the tail and breast are tawny, the belly is mottled black and white; the feet are black and wide. For this reason they lay ten, fifteen, or twenty eggs; in some years many of them remain here. They are good to eat.

There is another water bird called tzitzioa: it is a duck; it is called tzitzioa because it has some very white feathers on its tail. There are two of these long white feathers, one over the other, in the middle am-

[Right column, Nahuatl text:]
It does not come promptly. It is called atapalcatl: when there are clouds and it is going to rain, it begins at the shore, and all night it makes a rumbling sound; from this the fishermen understand that it will rain, that the lake will be rough. And it is called iacatexotli because its beak is blue, its throat feathers are white, its head feathers are brownish, its wings and back and tail are all brownish; its armpits are whitish-gray, its feet are black; it nests here; it lays ten, fifteen, twenty eggs; they are good to eat, though not all, since some cause one to become ill. They are edible.

It has white feathers on both sides; its wings are silvery, half white, and the quills of the wings are black; the joints of the wings are tawny; it has black feet, broad ones. They do not breed here — they come in flocks to this lake at the time of winter, and they are very good to eat.

There is another water bird called yacapitsaoac; it also has another name, which is nacaztone. It is called yacapitsaoac because it has a thin, round bill with which it strikes; it goes almost always underwater. In the middle of the head the feather is dark ashen; its eyes are like burning coals; the neck and shoulders are dark ashen; the breast is somewhat whitish; the tail is also small and dark ashen; its wings are black, and the feathers underneath are white—

its beak is smooth and shiny; its eye is white; its throat is reddish; it dives beneath the water; it perches nowhere; it comes here too, in the same way; many come to feed, to eat.

...it has feet like a hen's, somewhat broad, with wide toes. They do not breed in these parts; they go elsewhere to nest. Their food is their own feathers; sometimes they eat fish, but they do not taste of fish as other water-birds do. They are good eating.

There is another water-bird called tzoniaiauhqui, and it is called tzoiaiauhqui because its head is like charcoal, black up to the neck; its eyes are yellow; the neck and breast are very white; the back is dark ashen-colored; the tail is the same color and small; the belly is black near the tail; it has some white feathers on both sides; its feet are black and broad. They do not breed in these parts; they go far away to nest. Great flocks of them come to this lake. They eat sand from the burrows, and the seeds of the algae are good to eat. These birds are very fat.

[Nahuatl column:]
...its back is somewhat white, and likewise its small tail-feather is whitish; the underside of its wing-feather is white on the inner surface; it is smaller than a turkey, like a quail, like a parrot. It does not breed here; it goes elsewhere. It eats things — its flesh is fragrant, its meat is tasty.

Tzoniaiauhqui: it is called tzoniaiauhqui because its head is very black; it is named for its neck, which extends downward; its eyes are yellow; its breast is very white; its back feathers are grayish-white; its small tail-feather is also grayish; on its flanks it is white and cream-colored; it places itself nicely; its tail-feather, its wing-feather, is parrot-green. It does not breed here; it only comes and goes. Many of them feed on what lies in the water — flat gravel, water-moss. Its flesh is tasty, flavorful, and therefore it is prized.

translation:
Of Birds. Folio 39.

There are other water birds called colcanahuhtli: meaning ducks the color of quail, because their feathers resemble those of a quail. They are the size of the ducks of Peru. Only the wing joints are white; they have a broad beak and black, broad feet. They eat the water plants called atatapalacatl and others called achichilacachtli, or they feed on water insects. They do not breed in these parts; they come from far away. They are found in great numbers and are good eating, these birds.

There is another water bird called chilcanahuhtli, and it is called this because its head, chest, back, and tail are the color of tawny chile, and also its eyes. Its wings have silvery feathers, and the black wing feathers also have silvery tips. The feathers of the armpits are silvery and metallic yellow. Its belly is dark, and its feet are red and broad. It eats fish. It does not breed in these parts; it goes to breed in other places.

Colcanahuhtli: it is called colcanahuhtli because it is made entirely in the likeness of a quail in its coloring; it is as large as the ducks of Peru. Only its wing joints are white, and it preens itself on both sides. It has small spreading wings. It goes flapping along. It comes to feed on atatapalacatl, and it goes away again too. It does not breed here either. Many come together. It is tasty, its flesh.

Chilcanahuhtli: it is called chilcanahuhtli because its head is chile-colored, its back, its tail, its wing feathers are all made thus, with a dark forest color. Its eyes are the same; they are greenish. Its wing feathers are dark greenish, metallic. They are scattered, the tail feathers are greenish-yellow, striped. Its belly is dark, its wing tips are very dark, it goes flapping along...

¶ The Ayoha, a water bird called Achalalactli: it is called by this name because its song goes cha cha cha, chu chu, cha la chala chala: it is the size of a teal. This bird does not dwell on the great lake, because it is an enemy of salt water: it lives in fresh water and inhabits ravines; it does not stay on the water itself, but rather in the trees, and from there it dives down to the water to fish, for it eats fish or frogs, and once it has caught its prey, it returns to the trees to eat. It has a head covered entirely with ash-colored feathers; its temples are white; its bill is black, sharp, and rounded; its neck is rather long; its feathers are mixed with white and black; its breast is white; its tail is dark brown and small; the elbows of its wings are white; the feathers of its wings are dark brown; it has

¶ Achalalactli: it is a duck, called achalalactli, a bird that cries out: cha cha cha, thu thu, la thala thala — so much does it resemble the colocin. And this bird does not dwell everywhere along the shores; it does not go just anywhere; it lives along the cliffs; it does not settle on the water, but rather perches on the hillsides, on the treetops, and moves about in the highlands. ¶ There is another water bird called pipíztli; it has a black head, and its eyes are also black, its eyebrows white, and they appear to be eyes; it has a long neck, and the throat and chest are white; the back of the neck, the shoulders, the tail, the feathers of the wings, and the wing blades are all black; the elbows are white on both sides; its feet are long and reddish and slender; it is not corpulent, but it stands tall on its feet. translation:
Book Eleventh

There is another bird of this lake called acachichictli, and it is called thus because its song is "achi chi chic." It moves among the cattails and the rushes of the lake; fishermen take it as a sign of when dawn is approaching, because a little before dawn it always begins to sing, and then the other water birds respond, also singing. It has a small head, a sharp beak; its feathers are yellow inclining toward brown; it has yellow feet and green eyes. It always lives on this lake and feeds on this lake. It lays four eggs as large as dove eggs. It is edible.

Fourth paragraph, on Birds of Prey.

There are eagles in this land of many kinds; the largest of them have a thick, curved, and close-set yellow beak; they have yellow feet and large, curved talons.

[Nahuatl column:]
Acachichictli: it lives in the water, it is called acachichictli because of how it speaks, saying "achichic." It lives only among the reeds and rushes. And as for the bird: its appearance is also that of a water creature; it always eats at dawn; it begins to call, then it makes the various birds of the water respond. Its head is quite small and pointed; its entire face is yellow, somewhat grayish; its body is yellow, its back greenish. It always stays here, it always perches here. It lays four eggs; it is edible.

Fourth paragraph, which tells of all the birds of prey.

Eagle: the eagle is yellow-beaked, its beak tip is sharp, its beak is wide, its beak is broad, its beak curves, its beak hooks, its beak is open: it is sour-colored, tawny-colored.

...precious; they have gleaming eyes, like glowing embers, great of body. The feathers of the neck and back down to the tail are shaped like shells — they call them tapalcatl. The wings of this bird are called ahazili or mamazili. The tail they call quauhquetzalli. The feathers found beneath the large feathers are soft like cotton — they call them quauhtlachcaioth.

[illustration of eagle with wings spread]

The eagle has keen sight; it stares fixedly at the sun without looking away. It cries out and shakes itself like a hen. It is dark brown, it has a crest; it hunts and eats living animals, and does not eat dead flesh.

[illustration of second bird]

[Nahuatl text:] Yellow-throated, with a slender yellow throat; marked like a totol bird, white-feathered, white-necked; it rests upon the dead, upon the neck of the dead, upon the shoulders of the dead, upon the back of the dead. Its name: quauhtapalcatl; its wing-feather name: ahazili; also hapalli and mamaz̄tli; its tail-feathers are called quauhquetzalli; it fans its tail out, the name for that being quamolocli or quappoiaoalli. And when it rests, its breath is called tlachcaioth — hence it is called quauhtlachcaioth. As for the eagle: it is not fearful of anything; it faces things boldly; it stands erect before the sun; it is strong-armed, broad-winged; it makes a sharp cry; it scatters things; it is ash-colored, dark; it flaps its wings repeatedly.

¶ The obsidian eagle: it is good; it is the young man himself.

There is an eagle called Iztac quauhtli: it is as large as those above, it is ash-colored, and has a yellow beak and yellow feet.

There is another eagle called toalquauhtli, which means nocturnal eagle: it is called this because it is rarely seen during the day, and at night it hunts prey.

There is another eagle called tlacoquauhtli, which means half-eagle; in color it resembles the kestrel, it has yellow feet and a yellow beak.

There is another eagle called aquauhtli, which means eagle of the water; it is medium-sized, lives on the rivers, and hunts water birds.

There is an eagle called Itzquauhtli, which is as large as the one described above; it has a yellow beak and yellow feet as well. It is called Itzquauhtli because the feathers of its neck, shoulders, and breast are beautifully golden: it has

Mixcoa quauhtli: it goes swiftly like the cuicheltli.

Iztac quauhtli: ash-colored, not dappled, very agile, its beak is yellow, its feet are yellow.

Iooalquauhtli: it is also said to resemble the eagle: it is called the night eagle, it rarely appears during the day: at night it hunts prey, striking them.

Tlaco quauhtli: it is also called Thienquauhtli, it imitates itself: its beak is yellow, its feet are yellow.

Aquauhtli: it is quite handsome and large: it dwells along the water, it swoops upon and catches those water birds that live along the water.

Itz quauhtli: large, just as the one first described, beak yellow, feet yellow: it is called itzquauhtli because of its feathers on its shoulders and at its tail: it is very impressive, gleaming, variegated in its many colors: [continues]

[The osprey] hunts fish in the water from high up in the air, where it flies about. When it wants to fish, it throws itself down from above onto the water, and goes under the water; and it seizes the fish it wants to eat and takes it up in its talons, without receiving any harm from the water, and eats it while flying.

¶ In this land there are certain eagles they call mixcoa quauhtli; they are not as large as those already mentioned. They are the size of a domestic hen. They are called mixcoa quauhtli because on the nape of the neck they have some large, straw-colored feathers, two of them raised upward. No other bird has feathers of this kind; these feathers are called iquappilol. They have a black head, and a white stripe crossing over the eyes; the beak is yellow and curved, and all the feathers are black with a halo of dark yellow; the feet are yellow. There are many of them and they are hunters.

And to hunt them they use this trick: they take a large basket of canes or palm-fronds, put it over their head, and the hunter begins to climb up the crag with his basket over his head. When he gets close to where the eagle is, the eagle swoops; the hunter throws himself down, and the eagle seizes the basket with its talons and carries it off through the air, thinking it is carrying a person. It flies very high, then lets itself drop and comes down upon it, beating itself against the ground. Meanwhile the hunter takes the chicks and goes off with them. All eagles eat the meat they kill, and nothing else.

The tecolotl [owl]: it is round-eyed, broad-faced, smooth-faced, with tufted feathers; round-headed, with a large head, thick-necked, with mottled eyes. It lives in rocky places, inside trees. It calls out at night. It feeds [on prey] because it sees very well in the dark. It calls in the night... it hoots, it cries out.

The cacatecolutl [a type of owl]: it is small, striped, and it resembles the tecolotl [owl]; it is called the cacatecolotl; it nests in cornfields.

The cacalotl [crow], also called calli or cacalli: it is completely black, very dark. It is agile in flight, swooping down swiftly; it is greedy, it snatches things, it steals; it makes great noise and clatter; it settles upon the ears of corn; it also eats meat.

There are also sea crows, or water crows, like those of Spain; they are called acacalotl.

There are some birds in this land called pipixcan; they are white and about the size of a dove. They fly high, and they breed near the sea. At the time of harvesting maize, they come inland. When these birds appear, people understand that it is time to harvest the maize.

There are also in this land falcons, like those of Spain, and great hunters; they are called tlhotli or thotli.

There are also hawks like those of Spain that hunt rabbits; they are called tlhoquauhtli; among them there are sacres [a type of falcon].

There is a kind of falcon in this land that goes about in pairs, male and female; the female is larger and a better hunter. When hunting here, she does not strike the prey with her wing but seizes it with her talons, and then she drinks the blood through the throat; and when she is to eat the flesh of [the prey]...

Acacalotl: [it is] black, it lives by the water, it feeds by the water, it calls xovivilla, xovivitlats, it has a dark beak, its beak is yellow-tipped.

Pipixcan: white, resembling a dove, smooth-faced; it lives on great waters, it lives on the open sea. It is said of the pipixcan that when the wind blows, it cries out, and when it stops it falls silent.

Thotli: and its name is also Thotli; it is ash-colored, it hunts, it swoops swiftly, it makes a rattling sound, it seizes flesh; its beak is pointed, yellow-tipped, greenish-tipped, blue-tipped, herb-colored at the tip.

Tlhoquauhtli: and its name is also tlacothotli; very ash-colored; it hunts.

Quauhthotli: and also tloquauhtli; the female is somewhat larger, but the male is somewhat smaller. The female hunts continuously. Its name is also Alcon [falcon]; it is yellow at the beak, its eyes are like those of a cat; it is dusky-ashen; its tail feathers are two hand-spans long; its feet are yellow. It hunts only with its talons. When it swoops down upon [prey]...

translation:
Book Eleven

[The] bird that has caught [its prey] first plucks [it] at the place where it is going to eat it.

Even though they [the eagles] swoop down on them [their prey], they strike them with their talons on the paper mat: only with their beaks do they wish to tear them. And those two [birds]: they can no longer fly, [even though] they wish to fly, they can no longer go far. They just fall tumbling down. And when the [great] bird catches [prey] well: immediately it grabs it in its talons and twists it; then it wrings its neck, draws blood from it, and finishes it off; it plucks it somewhere there, pulls out its feathers, [and eats it] in the cave. And how much it eats: first it scouts around, going about its [hunting] territory: the first time it eats [prey] in a day. The first time: it goes out at dawn, and does not go far. The second time: it goes out at midday. The third time: it goes out at late afternoon, it hangs and soars about [over] its domain, at the rocky bowl of water: only twice does it swoop down. And also the water-snake [heron]: it would swallow the hummingbirds whole, pulling them down; those [birds] called tothotin, it eats throughout the entire day: just as it is said [to do].

¶ The white hawk: its name is sacred, and it is strong, not very approachable in the wilderness. These are the ones that hunt rabbits, hares, doves, and turkeys. The appearance of the white hawk: its feathers are streaked with white, truly white, somewhat mottled; it hunts the whole day long, four times, or perhaps five times it makes a kill.

¶ The reed hawk, also called the Acatlhotli, in Spanish called the cavillan. The reason the reed hawk is called Acatlhotli or reed hawk is because its beak is as sharp as obsidian, dark and dusky in color. And as for its talons: they are white and sharp. And this hawk and the reed hawk, these are the ones that glide and soar upward through the air, hunting doves and turtledoves, etc. They are somewhat approachable...

translation:
On Birds.                    200.

[image of a bird of prey]

There are also alcotanes and merlins, great hunters. They call them Itzlotli, or Hetleuhhim. Some of these can see and hunt at night, and they call those iooaltlotli, which means a bird of prey that hunts at night.

[images of small birds]

There is in this land a bird of prey which seems to me to be a merlin of Spain. They call it Necuiílictli, and by another name they call it hecachichinqui, which means "one who sucks the wind." By yet another name they call it cenotzqui, which means "one who calls the frost," and they also call it tletleton, which means "fire." It is small, has a sharp beak, and is agile. It eats mice and lizards; it also eats small birds called quacilm. It is spotted in russet and black, like a crow. They say that this bird does not drink; after eating it opens its beak to the air, and the air serves it in place of drink. Also in the wind, it feels when the frost is coming, and makes gestures at those times. It comes to these parts in winter; it is not fit to eat.

[Nahuatl column:]

...and it merely lives amid its food; wherever it spots doves, or there it catches them; it is tawny-colored.

Itzthoth: also called tlehtleuhtim, small, not wise, it makes a rattling sound; it strikes; the night-Itzlotli: it is only the same as the Itzlotli. It is also called iooaltlhotli; it sees in the dark of night; or it hunts, it strikes well.

Necuiílictli: also called necuislotli, or hecatchichinqui; it is also named cenotzqui, and tlehtleuhton. It is fine, small-bodied, sleek-tailed; it eats worms, it eats lizards, it eats grasshoppers; it sucks the wind and rolls over in the air. And when it senses the wind, when it is a cold north wind, it then begins to cry out.

It darts up, it darts up spreading out like paper-wings...

There is a small bird called tetzompan mamana. Its wings are mottled black and white, and its beak is sharp like an awl. It is called tetzompan mamana because after it has eaten its fill, it does not stop hunting mice and lizards — yet it does not eat them, but rather hangs them on the tips of agave plants or on the branches of trees.

There is a bird called xochitototl, which means "flower bird": it has a throat, chest, and belly as yellow as a flower, very yellow. It has streaks on its face; its head, back, wings, and tail are mottled black and white, and its feet are black.

There is another bird called aiacachtototl; it is tawny in color. It is called aiacachtototl because it sings as the rattles called aiacachili sound. It says: chacha cha, xi xi xi xi, charexi, chare chi, cho cho cho cho.

There is a bird in this land called quauhtotopotli, which means one that bores holes in trees. It is also called quauhtchopitli, which means one that pecks trees; and it is also called quauhtatala, which means one that strikes the trees. It has a sharp beak like a pointed awl, and hard and strong like razor-stone; it is intelligent, very agile, climbs up trees, and flies from one tree to another. It bores into trees with its beak, boring through even the hardest trees; it eats worms, makes a nest and raises its young inside the hole it makes in the tree.

There is a bird called poxaquatl, which means roughly the same as "sisón" (a type of bustard). It resembles an owl, has ruffled feathers, flies like an owl, unsteady and wide — for this reason it is called poxaquatl.

There is another bird called vitlaloti, which lives in the mountains; it is like a wild hen, dark brown like something smoked, and it has a small crest of feathers. It is edible.

[Nahuatl column:]

caitlatl, it utters its speech; tachitouja. Whoever sees it passing by, making a sound — so it makes the sound tachitouja.

Quauhtotopotli: it is also named quauhtchopitli, and also named quauhtatala. Its beak is sharp-pointed, its beak is of metal hardness, its beak is dry and hard, its beak is greenish, its beak is dark; its beak is grayish and firm, its beak is hardened: it eats wood, it strikes trees and makes them resound, it makes the trees creak and split; it eats worms fit for it, the bird that makes the heart pound; when it pecks, it settles in one place.

Poxaquatl: it is plump, it appears plump; it is short-legged, small-faced, it flies low, it flies along close to the ground — hence it is called poxaquatl. It is yellowish, its eyes are yellowish in color.

Vitlalotl: it walks through the treetops, resembling the quauhtotolin (wild turkey), it is dusty-colored, it is dark, it has small feathers on its nape; it pulls out its own small feathers.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are owls, and they have the eyes and all the other characteristics like those of Spain.

Chiquatli: its feathers are ashy-colored, its eyes are round and wide, its beak is hooked, it is slender; its feathers are ash-gray mixed with a greenish-yellow color, its head is somewhat raised; its wing feathers are leaf-like, nocturnal in color, shining at night like a mirror; it goes about at night, it looks about at night, it eats, it catches things, it swoops. It goes along hunting; it stares fixedly, it does not see very well by day; it catches lizards and eats them, that is what it is called.

There is another bird called tapalcatçotçonguj, it is like the owl, except that when it sings, it sounds like when one roof tile is struck against another.

Tapalcatçotçonguj: it is just like the chiquatli: it is called tapalcatçotçonguj because of its voice, which sounds like roof tiles [striking]; it speaks in the milpa fields; and wherever it calls out, that is how it speaks.

There are little owls in this land, no more and no less like those of Spain; they are called tlalchiquatli.

Chidhtli: it is also just like the chiquatli.

Tlalchiquatli: it is just like the chiquatli, but smaller; just as the tlalchiquatli [behaves], it lives in the ground among people, among the rocks, it spreads out there; it goes about in burrows, it is not good [for eating].

translation:
Of birds. Folio 51.

It lives on the ground. It goes about on the surface of the earth, flying low.

There is a small crested bird called the llamatototl, which means "bird like an old woman." It is plump and round, and has a thick, short beak. It has a little crest and goes about among the houses and through the towns.

There is another small bird called the tlatvicicítli, which is similar to the one above in its plumpness and color, but it differs in its song, because this one has the habit of singing before dawn. Its song is "tlatvicicili." It sings on the flat rooftops and on the walls, and wakes people up with its singing. Tlatvicicítli means "hola, hola, day is breaking."

There is a bird called the chiquatototl; it has a sharp beak and a yellow breast, and its back and wings are of a partridge color, flying about in a dull grayish-brown color like a quail.

There is another bird called the çacatlatli, or çacatlaton; it is roundish and smoky in color, and is said to be a çacatlaton because it goes about in the savannas among the hay. It eats the seeds of the pigweed (bledo).

There is another bird called the tlapaltototl, which means "red bird." It has entirely deep red plumage throughout its body, and its wings and tail are grayish —

The llamatototl: it is ashen, chalky white, dust-colored, yellowish; it has a puffed-out throat, a rough, scaly head; it calls out everywhere.

The tlatvicicítli: it is just like the llamatototl. The reason it is called tlatvicicítli is this: when night falls and dawn approaches, it begins to speak, as if to say "tlatvicicítli": it goes about on the flat rooftops and on the walls, waking people up.

The chiquatototl: it has a hard beak, it is yellow-bellied; its back and wings are ashen, its tail is spotted; it bobs its head.

The çacatlatli, or çacatlaton, is a small, skinny little merchant-bird: it is called çacatlatli because it lives among the grasses; its food is hay-seeds.

The tlapaltototl: its flesh is entirely red, as is its plumage. But its wing-feathers and tail-feathers are ashen, very richly colored, and beautiful —

...dark ones: it sings at night, singing four or five times each night: it is good to eat and has no fat.

There is another bird called chiltotopil, and it is red, like the one described above: but it is not good to eat, nor does it have blood: it has a kind of watery fluid in place of blood.

There are sparrows in this land but they differ from those of Spain in that they are somewhat smaller, though just as mischievous as the others; they sing very well, and people raise them in cages to enjoy their song; they molt their feathers each year: and the males have some red feathers in the middle of the head and on the throat: they live in the towns, and nest in buildings, and they are good to eat, and people catch them with birdlime.

The males of these birds are called quachichil, they are called this because they have part of the head colored red.

translation:
Of birds.                    folio 52.

These birds are also called nochtototl, which means "birds of the prickly pear cactus," because their most common food is the prickly pear, and they also eat chia seeds and ground maize, and cooked ground maize.

[illustration of a bird with plants]

There are some little birds in this land called cocotli, and the Spaniards call them turtledoves. They are not as large as those of Castile, but they are the same color; they are small. Their wings are tawny and they are speckled; their feathers are very smooth; they have reddish-orange feet and they are small. They are called cocotli because when they sing they say "coco, coco." They eat seeds of grasses and also chia seeds. They mate only once; and when one of them dies, the other goes about always as if weeping and alone, saying "coco, coco." It is said that eating the flesh of these birds cures jealousy: jealous women are given the flesh of these birds to eat so that they forget their jealousy, and the same for men.

Sixth chapter, of quails.

The nochtototl: it is simply like the turtledove, or like the quachtlil. That is why it is called nochtototl, because of the color of the quachtlil; and its beak is edged in a dark hue: very much because the nochtli fruit is good for it; it eats it; it eats the nochtli, the seeds, the tlaolterxli, the nextamaltextli. —

The cocotli: it is small, it is a ground-dweller; its wings are like amate paper in color, clear yellow, pale yellow, slightly small: it is flower-red, slightly greenish. And its voice, its call: that is the sound of the cocotli, its speech as it speaks: "coco, coco." Its food is: small seeds, chia, quelite greens. When it mates with its companion: when one dies, it becomes like one abandoned; it calls out: "coco, coco." And it is said it cures sadness: it is said it dispels melancholy; it fortifies the body; it restores us; it improves one's body: and so they say it will cure sadness. —

The sixth chapter: it speaks of them all together, all the birds. / — . —

translation:
Book Eleven.

There are quail in this land, which are called çuli or çulli; they are as large as those of Castile, and they are better to eat, because they have breasts like a partridge. They have a sharp beak, and are between green and brown in color. They are the same color as the quail of Spain. They run a great deal, lay many eggs, and hatch thirty to forty chicks. They eat maize and chia.

The males of these birds are called tzcucoli; they have large breasts, their chest is tawny and patterned, and they have a small crest.

The female quail are called ooaton, and they are smaller than the males. They make their nests — some of them narrow enough that only one can fit inside, others make them wider so that two can fit — and so the male and the female sit together upon the eggs. But in the narrower ones, the male and female take turns. They can be raised in cages.

Colin: also called colli, [it is] dark-throated, grayish, white, speckled on the throat, [illegible]. It is tawny-speckled, edible, tasty, flavorful, very savory, very crispy when cooked. It fattens people up. One makes it multiply; it goes off in flocks. When it multiplies, it goes in groups of twenty. Its food is maize and green xoxocosol.

Tecuçoli: it is just the same as the caoqujthtli; it is smoky-colored, speckled, deeply speckled, [illegible].

Ooaton: it is just like the col, but smaller, grayish, [illegible] speckled. To breed them: some people raise them one way, others another way; one feeds them, nourishes them, makes them plump. One raises them, one breeds them. [illegible]

translation:
Of Birds.                                    fo.53.

These little birds go about in flocks together in the field, and when they are scattered, they come together again by calling to one another. Those who hunt them, when they scatter them, spread the net right there where they rose up; and the one that stayed hidden, once the hunter goes away, begins to whistle, calling the others; and then they return, and if they fall into the net, they are caught. When someone comes upon the chicks of the quail, which cannot yet fly, their mother is always with them; she begins to flutter around the one who found them, and pretends she cannot manage to flee, and draws near so as to wound that person, so that he will not take her chicks, giving them time to hide; and once they are hidden she then flies off, and from a little way off she lands on the ground. This stratagem, they say, is also used by the partridges of Spain.

[Nahuatl column:]
They go about always in motion together. And when one of them settles: only by voice, by calling, by the sound it makes: it calls out loudly. And when one of them hears: then it sees where it is. It recognizes it there, it knows it, or it answers back: then it turns toward one of them, then indeed it calls, it clucks together, some take flight; then they come, they come flying toward it, they come alighting there, they fall to the ground at once, on the net: and then he covers them, keeps watch over them: that none escape, that none get free. Then they flutter about, they flap, just as if indeed they could fly: but on the ground they are held down again, the small chicks hide there: then it departs, it flies. And then in a little while, it called out, when they were gathered together again. Its chicks: then it stands there, then it calls, they cluck together: then they are assembled, and so once more none of them comes to any harm.

translation:
Book Eleven

Seventh chapter on thrushes, jackdaws, magpies, and doves.

There is a bird called the tzanatl: it is black, has a curved beak, and is the size of a thrush. They are not good to eat.

There is another called the teutzanatl: it has a somewhat long beak, strong and sharp; it has a long, spread-out tail; it sings well and cries out with a loud voice. The females are not very black, but the males are a very fine black and are larger than the females. They are called teutzanatl, which means "rat bird" or "precious tzanatl," because they are not native to this land. It has not been many years since they came to these parts. When Axayacatl was lord, they were brought to these parts of Mexico by his order, from the provinces of Cuextlan and Totonacapan. At that time they were cared for and given food, and as they began to multiply they spread throughout all the regions of Mexico. These birds eat lizards and other similar small creatures. translation:
Of Birds. Folio 84.

In the beginning no one used to kill or catch them, because it was forbidden by the lord.

There are other kinds of these birds called tzanatl, some are brownish, others black; there are many of them, and they go about in flocks eating the maize, doing it great damage; they are not good to eat.

There is another bird called coioltototl, they are like the thrushes already described, except that they have red throats and red breasts, and also the wings and the feathers near the tail; some of them have a yellow breast and white wing-joints, and they sing very well. For this reason it is called coioltototl, which means a bird that sings like a rattle-bell; they nest among the cattails.

There is another bird called vilotl, which is like a dove; it has a thin, sharp beak; it is ashen in color, it has [continues below]

[Nahuatl column:]
...it places them together, it says to the demons: "Do not call me, do not speak to me," it leaves the water-creature. The Acatianatl, or acatiunatl: some are quite black, others are smoky-colored; they live among the reeds, in the marshes, they feed well on the water-creatures; they also eat small worms, and they fly about.

The coioltototl: it is just like the acatzanatl, but some are red-throated, truly red, paper-wing-red, lip-edge red, some are yellow-breasted, tawny-breasted, greenish-necked. And it is very good; its voice is truly like a rattle-bell: it is delicious, sweet; for this reason it is called coioltototl; it lives among the reeds, in the marshes, it spreads its wings, it moves about.

The vilotl: its beak is blunt, its beak-tip is pointed, it is ash-gray, it is smooth-skinned, it is lean, its tail is long, its tail is white; it has a small greenish head, a small neck.

translation:
Book Eleven

[The bird has] long and slender legs, and the tail is long, ringed at the feet; it has a rather long neck. It eats maize and chia seeds, and seeds of amaranth, and other herbs. This bird is foolish: when it makes a nest it gathers a few straws poorly arranged, and it does not drink during the day; until the evening it is bleary-eyed.

It shares the qualities of the turtledove. These birds are good to eat.

[Nahuatl column:]
Its food: maize, chia, Chicalotl [prickly poppy seed], watercress, and so on. It is called Hatzituhqui. It arranges its nest loosely, twisting and interweaving. And this Hatziuhqui does not drink during the day; it opens its eyes wide, it ruffles its feathers, it runs quickly about, it searches for water. And it is truly like the cocotl [dove] in its nature; it resembles the cocotl; it goes about with its mate, with its companion hen; and being sorrowful, it laments constantly, the bird is always sad. And then it runs along calling out, it coos, it gives its cry. And the vilotl [dove] speaks thus; it speaks its words. And when the vilotl goes away, others follow behind it, they peck at things, they go here and there, they flee; they seek cover, they hide themselves, they scatter about, they take fright and flee; they call out together, they say to one another: "Behold, it is not well to remain." And when they find water, they all drink it together.

Book Eleven.

...is called the cujtlacoch bird because of its song, which says: cujtlacoch, cujtlacoch, taratz, tarat, tatatati. People take the young ones and raise them in cages for love of their song, which is very sweet. They sing for three months of the year. They are raised everywhere; they make nests in trees and also in holes in rocks in high places. They eat worms, flies, meat, and ground maize. In winter they do not sing; they sing in summer, and they always position themselves facing into the wind in order to sing.

There is a little bird in this land called the centzon tlatole [mockingbird]; it is grayish-brown, has a white breast, its wings are mottled, it has some white streaks on its face, and it is rather slender. It is raised in the mountains and on the cliffs. It sings sweetly and makes diverse songs, and it imitates all other birds, which is why they call it centzon tlatole [four hundred voices]. It also imitates the hen...

[Right column, Nahuatl:]
...the cujtlacoch bird, its song, cujtlacoch, cujtlacoch, tarat, tavat, tatatati, and so forth. It is found everywhere, on rooftops, on walls; it builds its nest in many places. Its food: insects, worms, lizards, meat, maize kernels. In winter it does not sing, it does not call; when it wants to sing, it faces into the wind, opens its beak, and faces toward wherever the wind comes from.

Centzon tlatole: it is ash-colored, its throat is yellowish, its wing feathers are white, its wing [feathers are...], its body is slender. It lives in the forests, it dwells [in various places]. It does not sing in the dry season, only in the rainy season. It is called centzon tlatole because it imitates all birds and also imitates chickens...

translation:
Of Birds — folio 86.

...and to the dog: when it goes about, it sings also at night, and they are kept in cages.

There is another little bird called myaoatototl, or xopan totytl: it is like a little greenfinch; they sing very well. Its song is very pleasing; it is a small bird in this land.

There is a bird called chiquimolli: it is the size of a thrush, and resembles the woodpecker of Spain in its nature; it has on its head a small crest, somewhat reddish-faded; its beak is white; the feathers of the whole body are black spotted with brown; the front of the throat is yellow; its feet are like those of a thrush; like worms that burrow in trees, it works inside the wood of trees, boring with its beak; its song is sharp and thin; it warbles at times, gives whistles, and at other times chatters as if many birds were together; and when it turns back like a tahin [?], it is a sign of anger and bad omen from peppers [chilis]; and those who hear it say it cries out against us, the chiquimolli. Look, take care, for some misfortune is going to befall us. And when it goes along joyfully, those who hear it say: if the chiquimolli brings good news it will come well for us; but to those you see together with other women or men, it says they are chiquimollis, because they are doing things with each other. If someone enters from outside near those who are together in merriment and conversation, with or without purpose, they say to him: go away, chiquimolli! — and by this name they call those who always stir up quarrels or fights among others.

There is a little bird in this land called chachalacametl: it is the size of a jackdaw. The feathers of the whole body are a dull yellow color; the tail is mottled, in white and dark; it eats fruit and corn; it nests in the branches of trees. It sings loudly when many of these birds gather together; one of them begins, and then all the others follow; they have in the throat something like the sound of a hen of this land, though smaller; and at night they sing three times like a rooster of Castile; they say they do this to wake up those who are sleeping.

[Nahuatl column, right side:]

The xopan totytl [spring bird], also called ololtyntli, coziaiachic-tlatole [it of the slender yellow speech], iamanca tlatole [it of the gentle speech], cuicani [singer], tiolpaquisti [it causes spiritual joy], teiolavielti [it causes spiritual satisfaction]: it makes one feel good, it gratifies, it soothes.

The chiquimoli: it is like a nuthatch; it is pleasing, it feeds on maize-worms inside the corn; it eats the little worms in the tree-trunks. And it goes making noise, rattling; sometimes it makes a sound as if striking with its beak: it makes a tubi-tubi sound with its bill. And when it chatters rapidly and quarrels, as the saying goes, it does not please those who hear it; it drives them away. It climbs up the tree, goes all around the trunk — and when it makes noise and chatters, as the saying goes, it belongs to merchants or tradespeople. Let it utter its pipitoa [sound]! It is also said that it is called so because it disturbs the people, or blames them, or causes one to be pointed at — so it is that they name it chiquimolli — it does not please the people; listen, it will call attention — and thus it goes proclaiming.

The chachalacametl: its voice is like that of a teutkanatl [divine crow]; its color is yellowish; it is a beautiful bird; it has a fine plumage; its food is grain; it climbs up and chatters upon the tree branches; it speaks clearly and repeats itself over and over — and then, like a rooster, it rouses those who sleep; it scatters its voice; and thus it is called a vexolotl-sayer, a face-revealer.

translation:
Book Eleven

Ninth paragraph concerning the roosters and hens of this land.

The hens of this land and the roosters are called totoli, and also hiviquentzin, and also xiuhcozque: they are domestic and well-known birds. They have a round tail; they have feathers on their wings, although they do not fly. They are very good to eat, the best meat of all birds. They eat ground maize when they are young, and also cooked and ground amaranth greens, and another herb they call torialchichicaqujlti, and another they call quanacaqujlti.

They lay eggs and hatch chicks; they come in various colors — some white, others rare, others black, others brown. The males are called vaxolotl, and they have a large wattle and large breast; they have a long neck; they have red wattles; their head is [text continues on next page]

Ninth paragraph, which treats of the turkey, the bird called pisca.

Turkey: also called hiviquentzin, also called xiuhcosca. They live in households, they are raised at home, they live near people, they are reared alongside people. They hatch, they are of good size, their feathers spread wide, they are not good fliers, their flesh is edible and nourishing, tasty and savory. Their food when they are young is ground tortilla dough; they are fed maize kernels; when they grow larger they eat on their own: they are sun-colored, vigorous. The female turkey: some are ashy-white, some black, some like the color of cacao; some are whitish, some are salt-white, grayish, some are flat-feathered, some are puffed. The male turkey: large, very large...

translation:
Book Eleven

The female hen is smaller than the rooster; she is low to the ground, has wattles on her head, and a crest in place of a comb.

She takes from the rooster, lays eggs, sits upon them, and hatches her chicks. Her meat is very tasty and fat; she is plump. She tucks her chicks under her wings and gives her little ones food, searching for worms and other things. The eggs she first conceives curdle and form a little membrane, and inside develops a tender shell; then the hen sits upon them, and after she leaves them, the shell hardens.

The female turkey hen: she is good, round, broad-backed, wide-backed, flat-backed; she spreads her wings, she raises herself up, she struts, she drags her wings on the ground, she crouches low; she is tasty, very tasty, dark, spotted, fine-feathered, finely feathered, with fleshy neck wattles. She spreads her wings, she struts, she makes a nest, she prepares a nest, she drags her wings, she spreads her wings, she flattens herself; she feeds her chicks. And they enter beneath her; they enter under her, she covers them, she keeps them warm, she shelters them, she rocks them, she clucks, she is born, she grows feathers.

Tenth chapter on the parts of birds, both internal and external

All birds of rich plumage are called by these names: çaquea, quechol, tzinitzcan. Common speech uses: iaquaoan, iotovon, iquecholhoan intotzcujo, meaning all the richly plumed birds that the Lord made. Of these, and of all other birds, all their parts are set down here, both internal and external. The first is the feather, which is called hivitl; and the head feathers of nearly all the precious birds are called tzinitzcan, and the neck feathers are called tapalcaiotl, or quauhtapalcatl. The feathers of all birds, both on the belly and on the back, are called alapachlli and itapalcaio. And the soft feather that is near [the body]...

ea, polaoa: totolconerontti, vitolconetl, moxinquej: they roll up, telpochtotvlm, iehpochcotolimmaci, maconsja, xelsioas quiça

Tenth chapter: it speaks of their various natures, the diverse birds.

All the various richly plumed birds: çaquan, quechol, tzinitzcan, and among them is included the falcon, as the saying goes: Içaguaoa, itooan, iquetholhoan in totecujo. Of all the various birds and their feathers, their possessions and their property: hivitl. And the feathers on the crown of the precious bird are called quetzal tzinitscan. And the feathers on the neck are called tapalcaiotl, itapalcaio; likewise quauhtapalcatl. The breast feathers, and the back feathers, are called alapashtli and itapalcaio, which are found abundantly there.

translation:
Book Eleven

The flesh is called tlachcaiotl, or quaethtlachcaiotl. The feather that birds have near the tail, which lies over the tail feathers, is called olmcaiotl, poiaollotl, or quam moloctl. This last name is used only for the feathers that eagles have at the base of the tail, or at the root of the tail feathers.

[illustration of birds in flight]

The wings of birds are called hatlapalli, or aztlacapalli. The small feathers that are on the outside of the elbows up to the tip of the wing are called timiztcan. The second ones that come after these, which are somewhat straighter, are called ticoliuhqui. Others that come after these, closer to the large feathers, are called chilchotic or tuepatle, and these have sharp points.

The large feathers of the wing are called mamaztli. These are large and hollow; with these the bird flies. They are also called quam mamaztli. Those of hens are called totolmamaztli, those of other birds totumamaztli, and those of all birds are called totolacatl, or haztli, meaning: all the large feathers as they are arranged in the wing.

The whole wing spread out together, for flying or for covering, is called ahaztli: especially those of hens, with which they cover their chicks. translation:
Book Eleven

[On parts of the bird's body:]

"Hatlatilli, tlatlatiloni, tlagera xiquipilli, cujtlatecomatl, cujtlamatlati" — this means the crop of the bird.

"Mametlatl, tememmetlatl" — this means the gizzard of the bird. "Tlatecitla cuechoa, tlaaxilia, tlaaxoa" means to grind up.

"Cujtlaxcolli, totocujtlaxcolli" — the intestines of the bird. "Conexiquipilli" means the small sac where the egg is formed.

"Tetl, itzmtempanea" — this means the little vessel that is above the rump of the bird. "Chipaiac, quipiac" — it is foul-smelling. "Tototin itleiuh" — that little vessel of the hen.

"Xomatzalli" — the toes of the hen, and also the whole leg up to the knee. They tell a story that merchants on that account walk a great deal, because they have a devotion to the feet of the hen.

translation:
On Fish. Folio 62.

Those resembling the fish of Castile are called mjchi; they are similar in having a forked or divided tail, and also in their fins and scales, and in having a broad body and a thick neck, and in being swift and in slipping away like monkeys.

The fish of the sea are called tlacamjchi, which means large fish, fish that swim in the sea that are good to eat. These large fish eat the small ones.

Eels, or conger eels, are called coamjchi, which means serpent-fish: it is called serpent because it is long like a serpent and has a head like a serpent; and it is called fish because it has a tail like a fish and fins like a fish.

The sea turtle is called chimalmjchi, which means shield-fish, because its shell is round like a shield; and it is called fish because it has fish flesh inside.

There is a fish in the sea that is called [continues on next page]

Tlacamjchi: meaning great fish, dwelling in the great water, in the ocean: tasty, flavorful, edible, greatly prized. And it devours fish greedily; it devours the young fish.

Toamjchi: like a serpent with a stone head. And its tail, its fins, its face, it is in every way a fish, truly good.

Chimalmjchi: it dwells in the great sea, it is round: like a shield; with a tail, with flat fins: its head is its shell.

Of shrimps and turtles. Folio 64.

[Spanish, left column:]
°[Sea] turtles wait at night for them to come out of the water; and then the fishermen run toward them, and they turn them over — shell down and belly up — and then another, and then another; and so they overturn many of them quickly. And since the turtles cannot right themselves, they stay like that; and the fisherman catches them — sometimes twenty, sometimes fifteen.

[Illustration: upper panel: a large spiral conch shell; lower panel: a figure flipping sea turtles on a sandy beach near the waves]

¶ The sea snails are called tecciztli; they have horns and are edible. The shell is white, very white like bone, and is twisted. That shell is like a cave where the animal hides. Sometimes it puts out half its body and its horns; other times it hides inside completely.

[Nahuatl, right column:]
They go forth upon it by night. This is how one gets hold of a turtle — they come out at night from the great water. And there on the sand they lie in wait to catch them; when they come out they line up, they come out one by one; they come rushing toward them as they are catching them, for the people stand upright there, they fall down; one goes here in the water, another goes there, the people stand upright; they just barely seize the people, then quietly they are taken. For this reason: once they have fallen, they cannot right themselves again; they are old, they are sluggish. Fifteen, sixteen, twenty in all are taken.

translation:
Book Eleven.

[Illustration of shells]

The water shells are called tapachtli, or atzcalli; this name applies both to river shells and to sea shells. By this name they also call the creature living inside, as well as the shell itself. The shell is also called ticicaxitl, because the female healers use it for divination. These shells are concave and broad; in some of them pearls are formed, and they are rough like bone. They come in various colors — some white, others green, others reddish. Some of them have an enamel on the inside that displays various colors. These are the ones in which pearls are formed, which are also called oysters.

The small river clams are called atzcalli. They are sold and eaten; they have a black shell like those from Spain that are found in rivers.

The pitch that is used in this land as a kind of tar is called chapopotli. It forms in the sea; the sea casts it onto the shore, and it is gathered from there.

[Nahuatl column:]
...it is called so; its tail is formed thus; from its mouth it proceeds. It goes there and enters there; it goes in; it simply descends.

Tapachtli: they use it — all that lives in the water bears the name tapashnacatl. The shell is also called atcoli; its color is variegated — tlapaltic, iztac (white), xoxotla (greenish); it is smoky, faded; it shines. The shell of the atzcalli, its interior, is pearlescent.

Atzcalli: the atzcaltonth — it comes from the water; it is not truly a river creature; it is small, tubular, rounded; it is edible.

Chapopotli: it falls greatly; it thus descends and falls down.

translation:
Of the armadillo and the iguana. [folio]

Fourth paragraph, of the animal they call the armadillo, and of the iguana, and of the river fish, or of the lakes.

There is a small animal in this land called aiotochili, which means: a gourd-rabbit. It is entirely armored with shells, and is the size of a rabbit. The shells with which it is armored look like pieces of gourd rinds, very hard and tough.

There is another animal in this land called quauhcuets

[Nahuatl column:]

The fourth paragraph speaks of living creatures, of each one's food, and of the fish: those that live in the water, or in lakes.

The aiotochili lives in the forest, it dwells in the forest: that is what its name means. Aiotl [gourd] + kvhim [rabbit]. Regarding the aiotochi: its head is like a rabbit's head, its ears are pointed, its ears are broad, its snout protrudes. And its feet: they are indeed like a rabbit's, shell-covered: the shell-covered one, just as an aiotl's shell covers it as it goes along; its bones are shell-covered, just like the shell of a gourd: it is very strong, very broad, very hard, very firm.

The quauhcuetspali: it dwells in the forest trees, it is indeed like a cuets

translation:
Book Eleven

There are some little fish called xalmjchi.
There are other little pot-bellied fish that are raised in the mud; they are called cujtlapetvtl: they are medicinal for children.

There are some very tiny little fish called mjchicaquan, which means "tiny little fishes." They go about together swarming; they dart like an arrow from one place to another; they are quick in moving from one place to another.

All of these fish are tiny little ones that are shown below here.

Toasted fish wrapped in corn husks are called mjchpictli.
Little fish toasted on a griddle are called mjchtlacatli.

Cujtlapetvtl: a fish; it curls up, is rounded, has a neck; it is like a small clay pot; its head is bitter-tasting, rough.

Iaiaiuhquj mjchi: or iaiaiuhquj fish — it behaves in just the same way.

Iztac mjchi: tiny; it is produced in springs.

Aljchteuhtli: meaning "tiny mudfish"; it may dart about; it spreads out; meaning tiny fish of the mudflats.

Mjchpictli: fish toasted on a griddle, that is what it is.
Mjchtlacectli: tiny fish toasted on a griddle.

There are some little water creatures called axolotl; they have feet and hands like lizards, and they have a tail like an eel; their body is also broad, their mouth is wide and they have barbels at their throat. They are very good to eat; they are food for lords.

There are some little water creatures called acocili; they are almost like shrimp, they have heads like locusts, they are grayish-brown, and when they are cooked they turn red like shrimp. They are eaten boiled and also toasted.

There is another little water creature called aneneztli; it is somewhat long and round, it has hands and feet, and it has a wide head; it is grayish-brown. They are eaten. They transform into those little beetles that have four wings and fly, which in Castile they call avirones [water boatmen].

There are some little water shells...

Axolotl: it is like a lizard, its hands, its tail, its tail is flat; its mouth is wide, it is bloated, it is fleshy, meaty: it is tasty, not at all bad; good, fine; edible, savory, nourishing.

Acocili: like a shrimp, its head is like a small gourd, small, yellowish, fleshy. And when cooked it becomes red: reddish, smooth-skinned, flat-shelled; edible, it crackles, it pops. One eats the acocili, one pops the acocili, one crunches the acocili.

Aneneztli: slender, small, bumpy, fleshy; flat-headed, made with a flat head, shiny, glistening: edible, it transforms; it becomes a water boatman, it turns into a water boatman.

Axaxaiacatl: it is round like a small gourd, round, flat...

There are other small creatures called Michpiltetci, or amilotetl: they are like those described above, and people eat them.

Michpiltetci: or also amilototl, round, roundish: like amaranth seeds, white, they make a sound, they roll about, they are smeared, or they smear themselves, they have tails: this is what amilotl is called.

There are other water worms called Iscavitli: they have no heads, only two tails; they are like lizards; people make food from them.

Iscavitli: slender, quite thin, with points at both ends, yellowish; they are alive; I gather them, I take them, I fry them, I prepare them with sauce, I sell them.

There are certain serpents that breed on the water, which are called tecujtlatl: or acoqvitl, or amomextli; they are of a clear blue color. After it has become thick and dense, they collect it, spread it on the ground over ashes, and afterward they make little cakes of it, and when toasted they eat them.

Tecujtlatl: acujtlatl, acoqvitl: amomextli: greenish, fluffy. When acoqvitl wells up, it spreads over the surface of the water, it coagulates there; they scoop it up, they roll it onto a mat; they spread it out, they dry it over ashes. I press the tecujtlatl, I spread it out, I flatten it; I sell it, I toast it.

Chapter Four: On other water animals that are not edible.

First paragraph: on caimans and other similar animals.

In this land there are very large lizards, which the native people call acuetzpalin; the Spaniards call them caimans. They are long and thick; they have feet, hands, and long tails, with the tip divided into three or four parts. They have a very wide mouth and a very wide gullet; the largest of them can swallow a whole man. They have black skin and very hard shells on their backs. They give off a foul odor, and they attract with their breath whatever they wish to eat. These do not go into the sea but only along the banks of large rivers.

[Nahuatl column:]
The fourth chapter, which tells of other water creatures that are not good to eat.

The second paragraph tells of water creatures that are not edible and that live in the water.

The caiman: it is large, wide-bodied, long, very long, with large hands, with claws, with a long tail, its tail extending out — just like a caiman in appearance, with a large head. Its mouth is very wide, its jaws are wide and flat; it can submerge, it can dive deep, it can dive swiftly. Its skin is rough, dark, hard. Its shell is like stone; it is hard, woody, firm, stiff, thick, dark-colored, rough-fleshed, with a sharp spine. It breathes out and inhales; it dives and submerges. It lives in the great waters and along the riverbanks.

There is an animal in the sea called the Acipaqujtli: it is large, long, and thick. It has feet and hands, and great claws, and wings, and a long tail, full of segments like a tree branch. It strikes and kills with its tail, and cuts with it whatever it wishes. It eats fish and swallows them alive, and it even swallows people whole, and tears them apart with its teeth. It has a face and teeth like a person's.

The otter is called aitzcoujntli; it also lives in the water.

There is a water animal called the acoiotl; it is the size of a greyhound or a hunting dog. It has long, smooth fur and goes into the water. It has a white chest. This animal has already been described among the coyotes.

Acipaqujtli: It lives very well in the water, in the heavenly waters, in the interior of the heavenly sea. Its body is thick, its torso is thick; it has hands, it has feet, it has claws; and it has something like paper-wings and a tail. Its tail is slender and long. With that tail it strikes everything around it, and is notable for its power — when it strikes something, it splits it, severs it, cuts it, shatters it. Its food: it consumes all living things in the water. It strikes them, beats them, bites them, swallows them, gulps them down, seizes them in its jaws, gnashes at them, rolls them over, turns them flat, crushes them, grinds them, cracks them.

Aitzcoujntli: it has already been spoken of above.

Acoiotl: it dwells in the water, it enters the water, it submerges, it plunges into the water. It resembles the coyote in appearance, though it is somewhat tawny-colored. It dives into the water, floats, knows the water, soaks itself, and submerges.

Second paragraph, about a small animal called the ahuizotl, notably monstrous in its body and in its habits, which dwells in springs or underground veins of water.

There is an animal in this land that lives in the water (never before heard of) which is called the Ahuizotl. It is about the size of a small dog. It has very fine, short fur; it has small, pointed ears; its body is black and very smooth; it has a long tail, and at the tip of the tail a hand like a human hand; it has feet and hands, and its hands and feet are like those of a monkey. This animal dwells in the deep springs of the water, and if any person comes to the edge of the water where it lives, it immediately—

[Right column, Nahuatl text:]
[It is white-boned; some of its story was already told in the section on the coyote.]

Second paragraph: here is told about one living creature called the ahuizotl. The ahuizotl: it is said to be greatly feared, and is said to be very much respected, and concerning its appearance — it lives in the water, in whirlpools, and wherever the water wells up.

The ahuizotl: it looks just like a small dog, smooth, short-tailed, with pointed, spine-like ears, like a small dog; black as rubber, slippery, very slippery, very smooth, with a long tail. And at the tip of its tail is a hand-like appendage: truly like a human hand, it grasps. And its hands: just like the hands of a small child, or just like the hands of a monkey. It lives in the depths, in whirlpools; and when anyone approaches there, or comes near, it immediately draws them under the water: it pulls them in, swallows them, and they disappear into its lair.
