[They would] take [him] out: they would inform the keepers of the idols, and they alone would remove him, because they said that the others were not worthy to touch him; and they also said that he who had drowned, the gods Tlalocs had sent his soul to the earthly paradise.

Third paragraph, concerning a water snake or serpent, most monstrous in its ferocity and deeds.

There is a snake in this land called Acoatl, or Tlilcoatl, which lives in the water and in the mud: it is as thick as a man can embrace, and very long: it has a large head, it has whiskers behind its head like the whiskers of a large barbel fish: it is very black, it shines with blackness: it has eyes like burning coals, it has a forked tail, it dwells in caves

[Nahuatl column:]
...Tlaloc, the rain priest... they had been drinking pulque... he was sent back to where... the old woman... it says: perhaps it will destroy me... I have merited it, I have deserved something from it...

Third paragraph: it moves swiftly, the water serpent, in the water, very [fearsome] indeed.

The Acoatl, the Tlilcoatl, dwells in the water, lies in the mud, is thick-bodied, very fat, of a single color: long, wide, broad-flanked, four-cornered, with a wide neck: dark, black, flat-scaled, with a tail spread like a mat, dwelling in springs and caves; its food is fish; it bites people, it causes people to bleed.

A notable cunning of this serpent or snake.

To hunt people: this serpent has a notable cunning. It makes a pit near the water the size of a large basin, and takes large fish such as barbel or others of another kind, and carries them in its mouth, and throws them into the pit it has made: and before throwing them in, it lifts its neck up high and looks in all directions: and then it places the fish in the little pool, and goes back for more.

[illustration of a serpent/snake with fish in water]

And some bold ones, while it goes out again, take the fish from the little pool and run off with them, whereupon...

And when it goes to fetch some, where no one can stop it; it spreads fear, it stirs up the bank of the water, it sets its coils there in the water like a vessel: and there in the cave it gathers the fish together, and when it is time, it drags them all out, and comes swiftly back: it comes pouring them into the rocky pool by the bank of the water, and there they vanish as it gathers its fish: then it goes back for more, beating the ground again, going back in again: and they stay submerged for a while. And as for the bold one who dares: as he is running, the serpent uncoils: then it rushes and pursues him...

translation:
Book Eleven

The snake comes out again; then it sees that its fish have been taken, so it raises itself up tall upon its tail and looks all around. Even if the thief has gone some distance, the one who carries the fish can be seen by it; and if it cannot see him, it tracks him by smell, and chases after him as straight as an arrow, seeming almost to fly over the grasses and the bushes. And when it reaches the one who stole its fish, it coils around his body and squeezes him tightly.

And its tail, being forked, it inserts into the nostrils — each tip into one nostril — or else pushes it into the mouth. Having done this, it squeezes the body of the one who stole its fish very tightly.

[Nahuatl column:]
It turns itself around repeatedly, raises itself up, turns itself about. It mounts upon him. Then the snake straightens itself up, stands erect upon its tail, looks all around, and turns its gaze in every direction. Then it sets off in pursuit, running fast, gliding over the grasses and the brush, tracking wherever the thief has gone, following him everywhere. Then it reaches him and coils around him, wrapping itself tightly about him. And its forked tail it inserts into his nostrils, each tip into one, or into his mouth. Then the serpent begins to tighten, squeezing him, so that it crushes him there.

Fourth Section, on other water snakes and water creatures.

The water snakes are called acoatl, and they are like those of Castile.

The text sets out the features and characteristics of these snakes, and how they slide with great swiftness, and what they eat. In this account there are many very good words, and many of them.

translation:
Book Eleven

[Nahuatl text describing the toad's sounds and movements — partially cut off at margin]

There are toads in this land, like those of Spain, and they are called tamaçols: on account of the clumsiness with which they move and jump — moving little and stopping many times. From this they derived a proverb against those who are slow when sent somewhere: they say to them, "Go quickly like the toad, which gives one jump and then stops, dumbstruck like a fool." In this account many words are set down, and very good ones, concerning the form and nature of these toads.

The tamaçoli: it is clumsy, dull-witted, stumbling in its speech, slovenly in talk, utterly incoherent in what it says, dim-sighted, with splayed feet, ungainly. It does not walk steadily; it does not move along continuously but leaps in one place. And when it leaps it does not spring up properly — it tumbles along, or it leaps this way and that, moving in a coiling, singing motion. When it falls it is put to shame, for it cannot right itself properly. It scrambles here, it scrambles there, tumbling and dragging itself; it lands face down. This snake is fiercer and bites more often during the rainy season, because at that time its venom is more potent — and this especially in the morning, because at midday and in the afternoon its venom loses its strength. Where it bites, the area immediately swells and begins to discharge fluid, and if this bite is not treated promptly, the bitten person dies. And if it bites the foot or the hand, even if the person does not die, the foot or hand where it bit dries up and withers.

There is another snake called colcoatl, which means: the snake that is the enemy of the quail — because it deceives them with its song and eats them. It is medium-sized, neither very thick nor very long. It is spotted like quail; it has a white chest and a yellow mouth. It is very venomous; whoever it bites has no remedy. It is deceitful and lures the quail with its song...

Tilcoatl: it lives in the water; it was mentioned in its own paragraph above.

¶ There is a serpent in this land called Macacoatl, very large and very thick, dark brown in color; it has scales on its tail, and on its head it has horns like a deer's, and for this reason it is called Macacoatl, because it has horns like a deer. It lives in very rugged mountains. When it reaches full maturity, it settles in some place and stays there; without going out, it draws to itself by its breath rabbits and birds and deer and people, and eats them, and sustains itself thus, remaining in its cave.

translation:
On Horned Snakes

Fourth chapter on certain horned snakes and their monstrous properties.

There is another snake that is also called maçacoatl; it is small and has horns; it is dark-colored, does no harm, and has no dangerous qualities. The flesh of this snake is used by those who wish to have potency, in order to be with many women. Those who use it too much or take too great a quantity always have their member aroused, and they continually emit seed, and they die from it.

There are also certain snails in this land, like those of Castile; they are also called maçacoatl. They are provocative of lust, and whoever uses them without restraint dies from it, as was said above regarding the snake.

[Nahuatl column:]
Maçacoatl: it is small and horned, striped; it is not fierce, it does not bite. This snake transforms itself, changes itself — let no one approach it; it faces one directly, it stares one down; this snake, if one comes near it, it stiffens itself, and then it makes the eyes flow; one dies from it.

Tlalmacacoatl: it lives in the fields; it is dark-striped, dark-colored, small and rough, and small like a corncob in the field — thus is described the tlalmacacoatl: it lives everywhere in the cornfields; and the deer fear it; it makes one dizzy. When it appears before one, when it approaches, something like a liquid comes from it, something sticky. Whoever encounters it becomes inflamed, loses their mind, and grows faint; they die from it, they become ill with internal sickness.

translation:
Book Eleventh

There is a snake in this land called tetzauhcoatl; it is not very thick, nor very long; it has a reddish chest, and its neck glows like an ember. It is rarely seen, and whoever sees it is seized with such fear that they die from it, or remain very ill. And for this reason it is called tetzauhcoatl, because it kills by fright.

There is another snake called tlapapalcoatl; it is not large, but medium-sized. It is called tlapapalcoatl because it is painted in almost all colors.

There is another creature, a monster of snakes, called coapetatl, or petlacoatl. It is said that many snakes come together and interweave themselves like a reed mat, and they move from here to there —

Tetzauhcoatl: it is not very large, not very thick, and not very long; it lives in the wilderness and in the mountains, and it glows very brightly, just like a flame. And thus it is said, thus it is called tetzauhcoatl; it only rarely appears, and only rarely kills anyone. Whoever sees it is seized with great terror and nearly dies of fright, or becomes very ill — and for this they named it tetzauhcoatl.

Tlapapalcoatl: it is not very large, just modest in size. And thus is said of the tlapapalcoatl: its scales are truly of all colors; they say it moves along, and it is called njsiaoacoatl, and it is simply a fine creature.

Cooapetlatl: or petlacoatl. This one does not live alone; it gathers together with other snakes and they truly weave themselves together like a mat; a multitude of snakes, and also —

translation:

[illustrations of the Metlapilcoatl snake, shown coiled and flat]

There is a snake called Metlapilcoatl, which means "mano-shaped snake," like the grinding stone that women use for grinding. This snake is thick and rounded, and if you look at it from a distance, you cannot tell where it has its tail or where it has its mouth — from both ends it looks like a tail. It is dark brown, it slides when it moves, and sometimes it rolls along like a grinding stone. It is not venomous, nor does it do any harm to anyone. It is found in the province of Totonacapan.

[Nahuatl column, upper right:]
The Chichimec people call it citlalcooatl; it lives among the rocks for that reason. And they use it to clean their arrows with it; and we, the Chichimecs, clean our arrows with it. And it is known when a star falls, that it can be found there, or one can hear it. And the star pursues it from afar; it does not harm people much. If one looks further, in the dark places, it is said to be good for the sick.

[Nahuatl column, lower right:]
Metlapilcoatl: it is quite stout; it looks the same from a distance; it appears the same at both ends of its mouth, so it seems like a grinding stone, pointed at both ends; it is very flat, it is smooth; when it travels it glides along, and sometimes it rolls just like a grinding mano stone. It is not dangerous, it does no harm. It lives especially there in Totonacapan.

translation:
On a monstrous serpent

Paragraph five, on a monstrous serpent, great in size and in venom, with others of its kind

There is a serpent, very large, called the Aueiactl. It is as long as a beam of ten fathoms; it has rattles on its tail, or links; it has teeth and fangs. It is very slippery, it is dark brownish — the color of the snake called tlilaatl. Its chest is yellowish; its snout is reddish. It is venomous, and this venom has no remedy. This snake is found in the hot lands, especially in the province of Totonacapan. It bites, stings, and swallows. It lies in wait for travelers on the roads; it places itself across the narrow parts of roads so that no one may pass, without being seen or caught. And if someone who sees it flees, it immediately goes after them, as if flying. Those who already know of this snake or serpent carry many [things against it]...

[Nahuatl column:]
Fifth paragraph: of one serpent, and what is said about it.

The Aveiactli is very large — just like a beam, perhaps ten fathoms in length. It has a rough mouth, a rough snake-like throat; it is slippery, smooth, shiny, dark-colored. It is a predator; it is almost impossible to escape from, it is deadly. It dwells on the ground. It is seen very often in the hot lands. It bites, it coils around one, it drags one into its lair, it crushes one, it swallows one. Wherever it goes out from, it comes right back there, it slides along, it crawls on its belly, it goes sideways, it crawls upside-down — there is no escape from it. Or else it swallows one right there. And if one runs away from it...

translation:
Of a serpent that rots.

Flies eat it wherever it goes, it goes stinking, and the flies follow after it, buzzing and humming around it. It is very poisonous. Whoever it bites cannot be cured, there is no medicine for it; the person rots and thus dies.

There is another serpent called hecacotl, or hecava: this snake is medium-sized, not very thick, but it is long — it reaches three or four fathoms in length. It is yellow, and reddish and green, and white along its back, striped with these colors. It is not venomous. But when it does harm, or when it attacks, it wraps itself around whatever it wants to kill and kills it by squeezing. This snake is called heca coatl, which means serpent of the wind, because when it goes somewhere, if the land is flat, it goes raised up on its tail as if flying, and if there are thickets or reed-beds it goes flying above them; and wherever it passes, it seems to give off a thin breath of air.

Hecacooatl: also called iccaoa — it is of moderate size, neither too fat nor too long; it is the length of an arm-spread, a double arm-span. It is yellow, red, and green; it is white on its back, striped in this way, not harmful. But when it is angered, or when it falls upon something, it causes pain, it causes numbness, it grabs one by the throat. This is how the hecacooatl behaves: when it moves it raises itself, it travels upright upon the ground, its tail trailing behind it as it goes, as if it were flying. And in the grasslands, in the thickets, it comes out making a sound; and it goes there, going out like a heca-patztli (wind-burst).

There is another snake called tzoalcoatl: it is small, neither very thick nor very long; it has no rattles nor teeth, it is a dark brownish color: it is the color of the tamales called tzoalli: it has no venom, nor does it harm anyone; it is a simple creature, and goes about without doing harm to anyone.

There is another snake called cincoatl, or cencoatl: it is of medium size, has no rattles, and does not bite; it is yellow, and red, and dark brown, resembling the snake called tecatlacauhqui: it has a wide head and a large mouth, it does not give live birth, but makes a nest and lays eggs, and from there draws out its young; it wraps its body around whatever it wishes to kill: it strikes with its tongue.

Tzoalcoatl: it is just moderately sized, not at all long, nor does it bite; it is described by its name as resembling the tzoalli tamale, being darkish in color; it does no harm, it is not dangerous, it is a harmless little snake; it just goes about simply, causing no trouble.

The sixth paragraph speaks of all those snakes that are truly remarkable, each one in its place.

Cincooatl, also called cencoatl: it is good in all respects, not a true biting snake, not dangerous; it is yellow-colored, spotted, painted; it resembles the motecutlacocauhqui; it has a wide flat head, wide-jawed; it lays eggs; it goes about simply, not truly harming, not splitting, not entangling; it wraps itself around one [illegible].

They call them quatzoncoatl: they are thin, almost like the hairs of the head; when they move, they go in coils; these snakes are rarely seen.

There are other snakes called Mecacoatl; they are as thick as the fist of a hand, but their length is not known, because when someone sees one, they never manage to see the end of it. They live in warm lands, in rocky places and scrublands, in very dense mountains.

There is another snake called tetzmolcoatl: it is of the same kind as the cimoatl in thickness and length; it is green and mottled with brown. It is very venomous, and it attacks people, it charges like —

[Nahuatl column, right side:]
...as if its hair were spread out... it moves without touching the ground... it slides along... it is called quatzoncoatl... it moves and goes [along]...

Mecacoatl: its thickness equals that of a hand's span; it is very long — its full length is not known, nor can its end be seen. It lives in warm, rocky lands, in scrublands, in forested mountain areas, underground...

Tetzmolcoatl: it resembles the cimcoatl in appearance, it is striped and mottled; it is very fierce, it bites people, it strikes and coils around them — this is why it is called tetzmolcoatl...

flying; it coils around the neck, and grips so tightly in killing that no one can free themselves from it, whether beast or person.

There is another snake called quetzalcoatl; there are many of them in the hot lands of Totonacapan. It is medium-sized: it is about the size of water snakes, or close to it. It is called quetzalcoatl because it grows feathers in the same manner as the precious feather called quetzalli. Around its neck it has some feathers called tzinitzcan, which are bright green and small; and on its tail and along its segments it has feathers like the bird called xiuhtototl, which is the turquoise bird; and on its chest it has red feathers. This snake is rarely seen; nor is it known what it eats. When it does appear, it is to bite whoever sees it, and its venom is mortal — whoever it bites dies immediately. This snake flies.

[Nahuatl column:]
Whoever, or whatever it fastens upon, it cannot easily be shaken off; it will bite as many times as it can, and it is very strong, very hard-bodied.

The quetzalcoatl: it is seen in Totonacapan, it is only medium-sized, only about as long as a water snake, or perhaps one fathom, more or less. Its name: it is called quetzalcoatl because of its appearance; along its back it looks just like the quetzal feather, its spine is dark-colored; and its plumage forms itself, and just as the plumage of the quetzal, its underside is very dark, its back-scales being rough and ridged. And its quetzal-plumage is very green; indeed it lies coiled, like one spread out at rest, lying spread out. And around its throat it is like the tzinitzcan bird; and its tail is like a skirt, like the xiuhtototl bird; and on its breast it is very red,

When it wants to strike, it raises itself up high and throws itself upon whatever it wants to bite. And when it bites, it also dies, because in one blow it expels all its venom, and with it, its life.

¶ Seventh paragraph on other monstrous serpents, their nature and their properties.

And it cannot [fly freely] ... and nothing that it bites survives long: when it bites, [the victim] appears [afflicted]; it strikes and poisons: and immediately [it is all over], one cannot last even one hour, nor can one escape. There is another snake called xicalcoatl, which means "gourd snake." There are large ones and small ones. They live in the water. When they are grown, they have on their back, naturally formed, a very brightly painted gourd, of all colors and all designs.

This snake: when it wants to hunt people, it goes to a place where travelers pass by, and it displays the gourd on top of the water,

swimming along, while it itself hides beneath it so it cannot be seen. And those who pass by, seeing the gourd, enter the water to take it. The snake little by little draws back, moving toward the depths, and the person who goes to grab it follows after it, and upon reaching the deep place, the water begins to churn and the snake acts thus.

The xicalcoatl: the gourd is part of it, and also the snake — some are large, some are small. It is a creature of the water. It is said: the large one looks just like a flat gourd floating on the surface. And the young one looks just like a small gourd floating on the surface. And the gourd on it is perfectly formed, of very vivid color, very beautifully painted, brilliantly colored, and covered in designs. This snake lures people very well with the gourd: when it wishes to hunt, it spreads itself out on the surface, yet the gourd alone appears, just its tail region extending behind it, truly dazzling to the eye, as if swimming on the surface. And those who are foolish: they go in after it, thinking they have a chance at that beautiful gourd; they descend into the water, and in taking it they go only to their death, for it carries them away thence.

On the Round Snake

There is a snake called cooatapatolli, which means: round snake. It is like a ball, round and black, like rubber; and it has a snake's tail and a snake's head in the middle of the roundness.

¶ In this land there are those creatures we call centipedes, no more and no less than those of Castile. Set down here in writing are the features and characteristics of these creatures; there are many and very good words for them.

[Nahuatl column:]
...it speaks. And whoever grabs it or strikes it, or frightens it, it hisses greatly, it raises itself up, it acts fierce and also it bites. ¶ Petlacolcooatl: it takes its name from petlacolli [mat] and cooatl [snake], because the snake resembles a woven mat. And it is also called petlacolli, because of its flat, mat-like appearance; and also it is very commonly said to have four hundred [legs]; just as a mat, the petlacolli spreads itself out, and because of its many legs its edges move like a fringe; on account of this it has also come to be called petlacolcooatl; for it is very strong there...

translation:

[The scorpion stings:] they are accustomed to suck the sting and rub it with ground tobacco. But better still are bruised leaves placed over the sting.

There are some spiders in this land that are venomous, which they call tzimiLatlauhqui; they are black and have a red tail. They bite: the bite causes great distress for three or four days, though it does not kill. The oil of these spiders is very medicinal for many ailments, as is written here. They find as a remedy to ease this pain to drink strong pulque, which they call vikhi.

[Nahuatl column:]
The scorpion's speech: it stings very well, and the pain subsides quickly; the swelling from the sting goes down; it cleans itself off.

Concerning the tequeani spider: it is also called tzintlatlauhqui; it is round; it is quite dark, or black. And the tzintlatlauhqui bites: it is reddish, biting in the manner of a chili pepper; its underside is white, and smooth, like a cotton boll. It wraps up and rolls up its prey just like an avocado seed, and more. When one lives in a hot place and is bitten, and has drunk, and lives in a place of cold water, it stings and spreads like a yellow serpent; it stings and causes great pain, much inflammation; in a little while the pain somewhat subsides. But then the pain intensifies greatly; the person becomes nauseated, even if it has been a long time. The person writhes in pain, wherever they are struck.

Concerning spiders

Folio 93.

It falls upon everything, it goes down everywhere; it truly agitates itself, it spreads itself wherever it feeds, or it makes everything wet around it; and thus it falls upon the spittle of the ground: it truly burns the heart, it truly stings. How one treats oneself: one presses it, one places it upon oneself; and quickly one squeezes it, and one applies something to it, and thus for two days, for four days one will endure it, one will recover. The venom: it truly inflames the bite, and indeed the nanaoatl sores appear; for there where it settles, wherever the spider has bitten, it heals; yet only on the surface: then immediately there comes the craving for cold water, chills, trembling, and one faints: it causes one to lose consciousness. This spider lives in the warm lands; it is just as they say of the rain spirit: whoever is struck by it will simply become confused and faint, and where it has shot its venom — the heart and the body truly burn within: truly —

There are other spiders, which they call Tocamaxaqualli: they are not venomous, nor do they cause harm.

There are bedbugs in this land, like those of Castile, and they call them texcan.

There are certain little cockroaches which they call caltatapach, and they are brownish, and have two kinds of wings with which they fly. They are venomous: where they bite, they cause itching and swelling. They are attracted to candles at night.

[Description of the tocamaxaqualli spider]: it moves about, it rolls up, it is small and round, it causes no harm; it only turns greenish at the mouth, it lives thus, it goes about thus, it moves somewhat with its eyes wide, and then runs away.

[Texcan — bedbug]: flat-little, broad-headed, with legs, its bite stings, it grasps, it bites, it sucks, it pinches the skin, it causes swelling.

[Caltatapach — cockroach]: it is grayish, flat and small, the color of paper; it has two kinds of coloring, entirely stained with color, its mouth is foul-smelling; it bites and causes itching and swelling along the legs and armpits; it does no real good; it falls upon candle flames at night.

translation:
Book Eleven

Some reddish, rather large ants bite and are venomous — they do not kill, but they cause pain.

[Nahuatl column:] ...their feet strike the ground, they gnaw; they are irritating, they bite sharply, they bite repeatedly, they spread out, they scatter, they make a great noise; they spread out widely, they travel far. There are other ants called Tlatlauhtqui azcatl ["red ants"]; they are somewhat larger than those already mentioned; they bite more than those already described; the venom travels up toward the groin and into the armpits.

[Nahuatl column:] The Tlatlauhtqui azcatl, not a gentle ant — it is not a good little thing, it is strong, it causes swelling, it is a red ant, it is sandy-looking, it is rough-surfaced, it is bulging: it spreads over one's body, it causes swelling along one's surface, it causes swelling all over one's surface, it causes burning. It stings the entrails, it stings the inner body, it causes a chilling sensation in the groins; it stings the hand...

translation:
Of Ants                           fol. 95

There are other ants called "icel azcatl": they are redder than those already mentioned. They do not make burrows, nor do they live together, but rather go about alone. For this reason they are called "icel azcatl," which means: solitary ant.

There is another kind of ant called "quauh azcatl," which means: ants that are raised in trees. They are almost similar to those called "tlatlauhqui azcatl," and they bite and are venomous.

[Nahuatl column:]

...it wanders about and rolls itself up.

The icel azcatl: it surpasses the tlatlauhqui ant, it is very shiny, very red. It is as if restless, it is worth nothing, it just goes about on its own. Its companions, the icel azcatl, go about entirely alone; they do not go about accompanying others, nor do they go about following others, unlike other ants. Nevertheless they are seen in many places, encountered everywhere, going about meeting one another.

The quauh azcatl: it is said to be powerful, and the ant: because of the trees, it lives in rotting wood, it is born there. And in being great it surpasses the tlatlauhqui ant — it is bristly, very bristly, fiercely bristly. Some are black, some are whitish, some are somewhat reddish; all are strong. They also bite, they also sting, and likewise the tlatlauhqui ant — it is quite the equal of the icel azcatl.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are other ants called cujtla azcatl: some of them are brown, others whitish, others yellow and dark. They are harmful: they breed in mulberry groves and at the roots of maguey plants. Their bite stings and burns; many of these travel in swarms.

There are other ants called Tlilazcatl, or tzicatl: they breed in cold lands, they are small, they are black, and they bite; their eggs are white. In some places people eat them, and for that reason they are called azatl molli [ant sauce].

There are other ants called tzicatl: they are almost the same as those described above.

[Nahuatl column:]
Cujtla azcatl: it is said of it that it partakes of filth and of ant: they are called cujtlatat, and many of them are called nertique, camjlteque, coqu[i], costatactique: they are born among hairs, between filthy places, in tangled places: they spread themselves out, they arrange themselves, they go forward in a line: they go all gathered together continuously.

Tlilazcatl: they are said to be bold biters: they come out biting, they are small: they are born underground, among roots: and they also bite somewhat. And when it is summer they multiply greatly, they spread and cover [things]; they look as if they were white, they eat milpa [cornfield] plants, they taste good, many people catch them to eat: they are also called azcamolli [ant stew].

translation:
On the snake, mother of the ants.

folio 96.

The aforementioned [ants] breed in humid places and where there is food to eat.

There is a snake called Tzicanantli, because they say it is the mother of the ants. It is thick and breeds deep inside anthills. It is painted in all colors and is frightening.

There are other ants called hzicatana. They breed in hot lands and destroy trees and everything around them. They march in columns like warriors, and they are also called tepeoanj, which means destroyers.

[Nahuatl column:]
They fall upon and devour [things], or else they swarm boiling up from there; they spread across the ground. Nothing can escape them, nothing can flee from them, nothing can get away from them. Then they devour and eat whatever comes in their way.

Tzicanantli: it is a thick serpent that lies coiled at Azcapotzalco. The tzicame ants are there with it, or the ascame ants; it lies there beneath the ground, very striped. It is painted in many colors; it is terrifying and causes fright.

The tzicatana, also called tepeoanj, march like an army of ground ants; they live in filthy places. And they do not walk straight, they walk in a winding path. They are called tepeoanj because they eat everything that is tender, and whatever they find hanging they no longer leave behind — they devour it and consume it. When they go somewhere they spread out as they travel, and they go as destroyers.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are other ants called Nequazcatl, which means honey ants. They breed underground and carry on their tail a round little vessel full of honey. This vessel is like an amber bead; the honey is very good, and people eat it just as they eat bee honey.

Tenth paragraph: on other creatures of the land.

In this land there are worms which in Old Castile are called catralexas, which breed in vineyards. Here they are called tlalxiquipilli; they are very venomous — they kill when they bite.

The Nequazcatl lives underground and dwells there, is born and raised there. And the reason it is called Nequazcatl is that at its rear end it has something sweet and honey-like, like tree honey, which is eaten.

Tenth paragraph: concerning the small living creatures that move about on the ground.

The tlalxiquipilli: it is covered in filth, it is rounded with filth, it has a hanging neck, it is bristled, it has a pointed snout, or perhaps it has a broad head; it is spiny, it has quivering hairs, it is dark, it is pitch-black. And it lives only on the surface of the ground; it is not edible. And when it bites, it is very bad — whoever eats it will die; it causes pain in the intestines; it causes swelling in the veins; it burns inside; it causes the body to dissolve. And...

translation:
On other small creatures.
Folio 97.

Wherever it spreads across our food supply, it makes the water bubble up and settles there. My fellow creature the worm causes it to crackle and makes it rot.

There are some cockroach-like creatures called Tlalacatl: they breed under the earth, they have feet and hands, some of them are reddish, others whitish, others white; they breed in damp places, they have no venom and do no harm.

Tlalacatl: very small and smooth, with legs and feet; some are reddish, some quite white, some pale white. They live among the plants, among the weeds, by the water, in the underbrush; they do not sting or bite; in their manner of living, they burrow into the ground, and in this way they go drilling underground.

There is a small creature called Tapaxi, or Tapalaxi; it goes along the roads; they are something like cockroaches, a little bigger, and they have spines all over their body and one large one on their head; they go in pairs: when the male joins with the female they look like people.

Tapaxi: or Tapalaxi, with a broad flat back, wide-legged, with feet, with a small tail; rounded, with a shell-like covering; they look like a little metal pot; they live along the back of the neck [i.e., along pathways]. They have awareness of earthly things; they stand looking about, they crouch looking about, or they spread out flat, then slide along, going along one by one side by side.

translation:
Book Eleventh

When the female gives birth she bursts and dies, and her young come out through the opening in her belly. They then go in search of a small herb that grows along the roads, called Memeia — it is called this because when broken it produces a milky sap. With that milk the young of this little creature sustain and nourish themselves. After they have grown somewhat, they eat flies.

There are certain worms in this land, which are also found in Spain; they are called coiaiacal. In the Spanish language I do not know what they are called. Some of them are dark yellow; others are red; others are whitish; others are dark brown. They are somewhat long, about half a finger, and as thick as a hen's feather from Castile at their thickest. They have many legs and stumble about on them; then they curl up and remain so.

[Nahuatl column:]
…it resounds loudly, it is wise in earthly matters. And as for how it is made: it is not easy; it does not stop calling out; it sounds chichi; it pierces through [its cry]; there its young are born, then it runs about, it enters into the grass; another one comes seeking it; it enters into an enclosure, comes out from within; it feeds only a little upon grass; it goes about satisfying itself; it devours the caioltsitsin.

¶ Contaiacal: it is a worm, yellowish, somewhat dark, somewhat flat, somewhat greenish; some are somewhat burning; one kills the contaiacal — whoever sees it and touches it with the hand, it immediately rolls up, and causes much [discomfort]. Its victims: whoever picks it up; it causes a burning sensation. And it is used to cure loss of appetite.

257
translation:
On Bees                    fo.99.

Small and round; these little spiders are otherwise worthless, having no other good quality whatsoever.

¶ Eleventh chapter. On bees that make honey, of which there are many different kinds, and on butterflies.

¶ There are certain large bees in this land, which they call Xicotli; they make honey and dig caves in the ground where they make their honey. The honey they produce is very good. They sting like bees, and the sting swells up.

[Nahuatl column:] Just as hair moves along, it goes scattering, it rises up and goes. And the little marrow-like thing that stirs within it is very slender, pointing in only one direction, causing great swelling; it inflames greatly, and it causes throbbing in the flesh and in the blood.

¶ Twelfth chapter: Concerning the Xicotli bee, which shapes and forms the honeycomb.

¶ The Xicotli: it is round, quite rounded, yellowish-sour, with paper-like wings, it hums, it buzzes, it makes a crackling sound, it wraps itself about, it makes a rattling noise, it needs things, it hisses; and when it smokes out those who approach, when it is born in spring, it wraps things, it rattles, it sucks, it collects; it becomes irritated with its own dung, it hisses: it numbs the face.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another kind of bee they call Pipiioli: they are smaller than those already mentioned, they also make caves in order to make their honey; they make very yellow honey, which is good to eat.

Pipiioli: they are small, like the bumblebee, round and little, yellowish. They make their home inside [trees/walls]; they transform: they can be seen underneath, like [something], they also drink nectar from flowers; they fly in groups, they hover and suck, they transform, they move about hovering: they fly, they flutter about, they go flying [continuously].

There are other bees that they call Mimjatoatl: they make honey in the trees; they make a kind of box in the manner of a still, and inside they make their honeycombs, and fill them with honey. They do not reproduce as other animals do: rather, inside the honeycombs they generate their young, like little white worms; they were like the bees of Castile, and they make very good honey.

Mimjaoad: it is slender, it is also called vitztonti; it lives especially in that place in the forests. And in the woods: it has paper-like wings, it has hands/legs, it gathers [honey], it moves about, it builds: its product comes out clear; when it is born it needs [sustenance]: it is just like the bumblebee, just like the pipiioli. What it makes is honey: it is that which is a source of syrup/nectar. And how it multiplies: how it reproduces, it does not simply increase of itself, as other living things do: it is only by the honey that it lives; if one is not careful, if one does not remove [the honey in time], [it may be lost].

Of Butterflies     Book     folio 100.

¶ There are many kinds of butterflies in this land, of diverse colors, many more than in Spain.

¶ Butterfly [papalotl]: it is something that flutters about, it is whitish, slender-necked, thin-necked, fluffy, like smoke, paper-winged, or spreading out like paper, feathered, having legs, having a snout, it flies up, it flutters, it flies about: it sucks from the flower cups, it sips from the flowers, it hums softly, it is lively: it fans its wings, it flutters, it beats its wings, it sips, it does not alight long — it is of two kinds of butterfly.

¶ The gourd-butterfly [xicalpapalotl], or gourd-cup butterfly, or gourd-cup [variant]; it is somewhat large, it resembles in appearance a gourd and a butterfly: because its body [thorax] is very yellow, quite yellow: and it is painted with black, it is painted — thus it looks very beautiful, it is admired, it is marveled at: it is desired, it is coveted, it causes longing, the heart is not sated,

¶ Tlilpapalotl [Black Butterfly]: it is just the same, just like the xicalpapalotl [gourd butterfly]; but it is black, white in some parts, striped with tiny lines, its wings are iridescent.

¶ There are other butterflies called tlilpapalotl [black butterfly]: they are black, sprinkled with some white spots.

¶ There are other butterflies called tlecócospapalotl, or quappachipapalotl: they are tawny-colored, and their color shines.

¶ Tlecócospapalotl [Fire-colored butterfly]: and likewise the quappachipapalotl. ¶ There are others called Iztacpapalotl [White Butterfly]: they are whitish, between yellow and white.

¶ There are others called chianpapalotl [chia butterfly]: they are very spotted.

¶ Chianpapalotl [Chia Butterfly]: it somewhat resembles the xicalpapalotl, because it is patterned, just as chia seeds are scattered all over its body...

translation:
On Butterflies                    fo. 101.

[Nahuatl:] ...and their wings are spread open, they spread them constantly.

Texopapalotl [blue butterfly]: some are large, some are small, and they are found nowhere in particular; their color is that of texotli [blue pigment], not quite deep blue, rather somewhat whitish, somewhat pale, somewhat faded; their wings are somewhat green, somewhat broad-winged; they are broad-winged, they flutter about.

There are others called Texopapalotl [blue butterfly]: they are light-colored blue.

Xochipapalotl [flower butterfly]: some are large, some are small; they have many colors on them, by which they are beautiful; they are very green, or mottled; they are very gray, they are very admirable; they are mottled, they are mottled, they are flower-like.

There are others called Xochipapalotl [flower butterfly]: they are very painted, with a thousand marvels [on their wings].

Vappapalotl [colored butterfly]: quite fine, red in the way they are beautiful, their wings; they cannot be surpassed, they are admirable. It is also the name for this: the leaves of the amaranth plant become strong, and the amaranth seeds mature; then the vappapalotl name is applied, because of the reddish-yellow color, or they become red.

There are other butterflies called vappapalotl: they are red and painted, very beautiful; by this same name are also called the leaves of the amaranth plant when they are ripe, some of which are yellow and others red.

translation:
Book Eleven

Twelfth paragraph, on the many varieties of locusts and other creatures similar to them, and of caterpillars.

There are many kinds of locusts in this land; they are like those of Spain.

The twelfth paragraph: it speaks of the grasshopper/locust (chapoli), and how it is classified.

Whatever kind of grasshopper: some are slender, some are thin-beaked, some have broad heads, some are rough, some have wide lips. Some have paper-like wings, they have legs; some are large, some are small; some fly, some only glide along, some just hop. And their life, their way of living: they are found clinging to things, they are found where people perish; they are heard in the cornfields pulling off the tassels of the corn, there they feed upon them. And there they are born: if they should destroy something, those who know say that they emerge having devoured the grasshopper plants, they make a crackling sound. And what they eat: what they very well eat, they feed upon, they cut things up, they destroy things, they jump, they fly, they leap rapidly, they scatter quickly, they roll about.

translation:
On Grasshoppers.                    fo. 102.

Some of them are called acachapoli: these are large ones, they are called acachapoli, which means grasshoppers like an arrow, because when they fly they go swiftly and make a rushing sound like an arrow. People are accustomed to eat them.

[illustration of grasshopper]

There are others called Necti chapoli: they are medium-sized and are reddish, and during the time of harvesting the maize they go about and are good to eat.

There are other grasshoppers called Xopan chapoli, which means summer grasshoppers; they are large and fat, they do not fly but go about on the ground; they eat many bean plants. Some of them are dark, others are brownish, others are green; people are accustomed to eat them.

Acachapoli: large, very straight and elongated, slender, thin in body, with greenish wings, flying, making a crackling sound, buzzing; their name comes from the reed; they resemble an arrow in their manner: they fly, buzz, crackle, crackle, make a rustling noise as they fly, they make a crackling-flying sound.

Necti chapoli: quite good, reddish on its underside, red on the chest; when the harvest season comes it is fat and good; it reddens as it burns.

Xopan chapolin: very fat, round and squat, thick, yellowish-white, it just goes along without flying, it just moves along the ground: it eats, it gnaws things, it makes them disappear where it goes. Some are greenish, some are yellowish, they all together just go about indiscriminately.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are others called tlalchapoli, or ixpopoiochapoli, which means to say "blind locusts." There are many of these and they are small, and they walk through the fields; they do not scatter even when stepped upon. They are edible.

There are other locusts called Colcachapoli. They are painted in the manner of quail, and they are also edible.

There are others called Cacatecuglichtli, called thus because they sing saying "chij, chichi, chi, chi," and they always move about among the hay. They are also edible.

Tlalchapoli: they are also called ixpopotochapoli, which is a kind of grasshopper. The tlalchapoli is found everywhere, and lives throughout the land. The ixpopotoli does not dodge or flee; it just wanders about. It settles in the middle of things, and when one finds it on the road, it does not leap away from people, nor does it jump up when approached, in the manner of one who cannot see.

Colacachapoli: it is not like other grasshoppers. It is called colacachapoli; it has striped wings, and its underside is colorful.

Cacatecuislichtli: it is ash-colored and small. Its underwings are colorful; the catecuiglichtli always settles in the same place, making the sound "chij, chichi, chi, chi, chi," and it flies up...

translation:
On Caterpillars [worms/grubs]
Folio 103.

...they live there, it is called tyvacaletl: it makes a rustling sound. Tyvacale, tyvacale, tyvacale, chichichichi, chi.

The caterpillars that are raised on cherry trees or on other trees are called capolocuyli, and also Avatl. These make cocoons on the trees, they eat all the green leaves of the trees, and they turn into butterflies. They are not edible.

Capolocuyli: it feeds on the cherry fruit, it is born from the cherry tree; first it rolls itself in the cherry fruit, then it is born inside the cherry; it is innumerable, the capolocuyli: it gnaws and shrivels the cherries, it sucks them dry; it becomes very numerous in the cherry trees; it greatly multiplies in the cherry trees; and finally it turns into butterflies.

There are other caterpillars called Avatecolotl. They also grow on trees; some are black, others are reddish-brown, they are very hairy, and the hairs they have sting: the stings hurt like the sting of a scorpion. They also turn into butterflies.

Avatecolotl: it is a worm, somewhat like the paçotl, hairy, very hairy in its hairs. Its hairs sting and irritate, as if they were fire-thorns. Some of these avatecolotl form on cherry trees, some on sour fruit trees, some near water; and they do not all develop the same way, only some of them feed in their place. And when one is stung by them: immediately one develops blisters, one turns yellow; and then one's hair stands on end, then it becomes a butterfly; and their shed skins become very numerous and edible...

translation:
On Worms                         folio 105

...it rejoices and is satisfied; and when it is stroked, it becomes lively.
All worms are called "oculin." Those that are found inside rotting fruit live within it.
The chia worm — also called "chian cuetla" — is thick and somewhat dark, somewhat greenish, quite rough, very long, about a forearm's length, and easily handled. It is called "chian cuetla" because it lives on the chia tree and is found upon it.
The nexteuyli worm: it resembles the cinch worm, is ash-colored, pale, and brownish. It is found underground, living in the soil, which it eats. When it does not rain, it gnaws the roots of the maize and dries it up. It has feet but does not walk with them; instead it moves on its back. And even if sometimes it does travel about, from this comes the saying that those who do things backwards are called "nexteuyli," because most of them do not move in the normal way.

There are other worms that are raised on the green chia plant, which are called "chian cuetla," or "chien cuetla"; they are also called "tetepol chichic." They are thick, somewhere between white and green; they grow as long as a handspan; they have horns on their head. They are neither good nor bad, but they seem to frighten those who see them.
There are some worms called "nexteuyli" that are raised underground. They are about the length and thickness of a finger. When it does not rain, they gnaw the roots of the maize and dry it out. They have feet, but they do not walk with them; instead they move on their backs. From this comes a saying: those who do things backwards are called "nexteuyli."

translation:
Book Eleven

There are other worms called Cinocuyli, which means "worms of the maize." They breed inside the ears of corn when they are green, and they eat them and destroy them. They are edible.

There are other worms called tlacolocuyli, which means "worms of the dung." They are medium-sized and grayish-brown. They are neither beneficial nor harmful.

There are other worms called Cistlal ocuyli, which breed in the prickly pear cactus trees, and in the prickly pears themselves, and they damage them.

There are other worms called Cistlal ocuyli, which breed in the limbs or members of rabbits and mice. They are also called Cistlal myl. These kill rabbits and mice, and they lodge themselves inside the flesh.

[Nahuatl column:]
Cinocuyli: they are also called coocuyli; they emerge thus, they are born thus in the maize, they eat it, they gnaw it, they split apart the ear of corn, they are numerous on the maize; they strip it, they gnaw it down, they destroy the surface, they cause it to fall, they shake it loose.

Tlacolocuyli: they are only eaten with difficulty, they are born in filth, they are only a little bit meaty, only a little bit fatty; no one really eats these worms.

Citlal ocuyli: they live among the bones of the prickly pear, they are spotted like stars; they live in the woody part, they are born in the nopal cactus.

Citlal ocuyli: they grow inside, they develop inside mice, much like the nextecuyli worm; once they have grown, they move through the flesh of the mouse, crawling about inside, they cause the creature to waste away.

The temoli: it is tawny-rounded, small and rounded at its back, with a broad wing-cover like a potsherd: when it spreads itself on the flat surface of a leaf, it appears when summer comes, when [the rain] falls, when it blooms.

The dung-beetle: it lives among dung and urine; it is just like the temoli.

The Aloxochquijl-temoli: it lives on the aloxochquijl flower, which it gnaws and cuts; it is of no great harm.

The quauhtemoli: it is born within wood, it originates within the wood itself; it causes some trouble.

The wood-worm: it is born within wood, it lives within it; it is white, very white indeed; it only sees daylight rarely; some are large, some are very small.

Of the oyametl [fir tree] fo. 112.

¶ There are other trees called Aiauḥquavitl: they are wild, tall, and thick. They have light wood; they are a kind of pine. It is a highly prized wood, much used in former times: this wood was used in the service of the temples and of the gods.

translation:
Of the Pochotl Tree

folio 113

There are other trees called Pochotl: they are smooth, very tall, and have wide, spreading crowns and great shade. They always have leaves; the leaves are rather broad. From them is gathered a manna that is medicinal, sweet, and white.

Pochotl: it is smooth-barked, very smooth-barked, firm, very slippery-smooth, well-rounded, well-rounded and smooth, uniform, filled with wind, it spreads its shade, it shades itself, it casts its shadow upon things, it extends shade over things; by means of it the rulers fan themselves. The Capochotl comes into being like an ahuehuetl tree: it makes a gurgling sound, it drips, it should not be gone to in the fields while one sleeps, it numbs one: from there it comes upon those who sleep; afterward it becomes quite pitiful in its presence. It makes a dripping sound upon the earth, it has come to meet us here, and thereby one falls flat and faints away. —

There are also in this land oak trees, which are called Avaquavitl.

Avaquavitl: it is the water-tree, a hard sacred tree, small, very hard, rubbery, broad-spread, round-spreading, rounded, branching out, with many forking branches, with many cross-branches, with many knobby projections, a spreading round thing, compact, corky and knotty, full of knots: it spreads out at the water's edge, it spreads again, it is very hard and firm, it is very firm, it makes itself grow twisted and round like a spinning top, it makes itself spread out...

translation:
Of Willows                    folio 114.

Every kind of tree whose wood, when thrown into fire, produces a great deal of smoke, is called pocquavitl: which means smoky wood or smoky firewood.

There is a small wild tree called teocutl; the root of which, when burned, smells like incense. Only lords and nobles used to use it; common people were not permitted to use it or burn it carelessly.

There is a wild tree called omata, also known as coatli, from which they make poles for doors, which they call vacales; it is very flexible: and if placed in water, it parts the water, and this water is medicinal for the urinary tract.

There is a wild tree called topocan: it has thin bark, forms a canopy, is short, has wide leaves of two colors — on one side they are very green, and on the other side white and hairy. The root, boiled in water, is good for purifying the urine, for aiding good digestion, and for reducing fever.

There are willows in this land of two kinds: some that are coarser, called vexotl, and others called omceavexotl.

Pocquavitl: it smokes, it produces smoke, it billows smoke, it emits smoke, it soots things, it makes eyes water, it makes the eyes smart, it causes the eyes to discharge, it makes the eyes water.

Teocutl: it is fragrant, it is pleasant-smelling, very fragrant, it has a pleasing aroma, it is a slender tree, it casts shade, it provides shade, it gives shade, it can be rubbed.

Coatli, the door-tree: it is flexible, pliable, very pliable, supple, it is soft, it is watery; it is a medicine, and one that provides a purging, it is smooth of surface, it purifies the urine, [it has properties listed in Nahuatl], it relieves, it soothes.

Caiolitzcan: the same applies as for coatli; it is similar.

Toyocan: it is similar, it is wide-leaved, its bark is broad, its paper-like leaves are wide, very wide, its papery leaves are shiny on one side, powdery on the back side, it is slightly rough, it is fibrous, it is a medicine, and it causes urination, it purifies the urine, it calms, it relieves fever, it aids recovery, it soothes, it comforts, it heals, it gives color/dye.

Vexotl, avexotl, and miceaavexotl: they hang down drooping, their branches are flexible and pendulous, they are soft, [further properties listed].

translation:
Book Eleven

There are also other willows, which are more prized than those already mentioned, and they are called quetzalvexotl or oquetzaluexotl: they have small and very green leaves, straight branches, and hard, rough wood.

There are some trees called yccotl: they are thick, with bark that is dark reddish, like palm bark, and their leaves are like those of a palm. It is a soft and tender tree at the core; it bears flowers, very white, like those of the palm, but it bears no fruit. They used to place them before the temples.

There are some small, wild magueys; they have points and leaves like magueys, and thorns like briars from Castile.

In this land there are natural palm trees, which are like those of Spain; they call them coyatl. They are tall and thick like the palms of Spain; they bear flowers and fruit, and their fruit is sweet and edible: it is like dates; this was done toward Panuco.

translation:
Of the bitter tree     folio 115

There are wild trees called tlacuĩlol quavitl, which means "painted wood," because they are beautiful and have black grain that looks like paintings on a red background. It is a very prized tree, because from it are made teponastles [slit drums], tambourines, and vihuelas [lutes], and these instruments sound very well when made from this wood. Because it is very colorfully grained and attractive, it is highly valued.

There are wild trees called tlacaloas quavitl. They are tall, slender, and straight; blowguns are made from them, because they can be bored through easily.

There is a wild tree, not very tall, called Aiotentli. It has reddish leaves, and its wood is also reddish.

There are other wild trees called chichic quavitl, or chichic patli, which means "bitter medicine." The bark of this tree is medicinal; it aids digestion, cleanses the intestines, and is good for the urine. The buboes, ground up and drunk with water, are used as a remedy. The wood of this tree is very hard; from it are made plugs for vessels, in place of stoppers.

[Nahuatl text — right column:]
Tlacuĩlol quavitl: it is variously colored, sparkling, thick, smooth, lustrous; it takes on painted designs, it becomes fully decorated. From it drums are made, and large drums are made; it produces a clear, resonant, bell-like sound in speech and calls. It is pleasing to look upon, gladdening to the eyes, desirable, attractive, resounding, bell-toned, pleasing, gladdening.

Tlacalhoasquavitl: it is slender, hollow, very slender, fit for making blowguns, fit for being bored through, fit for being blown through, fit for being smoothed inside, fit for being cut. One bores through it, smooths it, works it.

Aiotentli: it is dark greenish.

Chichic quavitl, chichic patli: it is drunk as a purge, it clears the intestines, it purges the bowels, it cleanses the bowels, it clears the intestinal passage, it sweeps it clean, it clears the way greatly into our entrails. It causes urination, it opens the urinary passage. When one has much blood, it expels it; it is good for one to drink so that nothing [ill] remains.

Libro vndecimo

¶ Ay en esta tierra vnos arboles q se llaman, ama guavitl: tienen lisa la corteza, y las hojas muy verdes; son del tamaño de duraznos, de la corteza del hazen papel, y quando ya es viejo, cortanle, y torna a echar renuevo.

¶ Ay vna manera de arboles, que se llama, copalquauytl: son sylvestres, tienen la madera muy liuiana y rezia, y haze desta madera xi caras bajos.

¶ Ay otros arboles que tambien se llaman, copalquavitl: de estos mana aquella resina blanca, que se llama copal; que es el incienso q ofrecian a sus dioses mucho dello se vende agora a los hangues: porque es muy bueno para muchas cosas y es medicinal, haze se en las provincias de tepequacuillo, y de iovatla, y en las provincias de tovetno.

¶ Ay otra manera de arboles q se llaman, ocolsoquavitl, oxochiocotsoquavitl: son altos y gruesos, y tienen las hojas como alisos mana dellos vna resina della hazen las cañas de humo q chupan.

¶ Ay otros arboles que se llama olquavitl: son grandes altos, y haze gran capa, destos arboles mana aquel la resina negra que se llama olli: para que mane cortanle la corteza, y por alli mena el olli. Esta resina que se llama olli, es muy medicinal casi para todas las enfermedades es provechosa es medicina para los hojos, es medicina para personas y pudrimientos, y tambien se bebe con cacao es provechosa para el estomaco y para los intestinos, y provechosa para los pudrimientos interiores y para la amata, quando se ccierta. Esta resina haze se muy correosa hage della las pelotas para jugar y saltan mas, que pelotas de viento.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are in this land certain trees called amatl-tree [amate]: they have smooth bark and very green leaves; they are the size of peach trees. From the bark they make paper, and when the tree is old, they cut it and it sprouts anew.

There is a kind of tree called copalquahuitl: they are wild trees, their wood is very light yet strong, and from this wood they make low relief carvings.

There are other trees also called copalquahuitl: from these flows that white resin called copal, which is the incense they offered to their gods. Much of it is now sold in the marketplaces, because it is very good for many things and is medicinal. It is produced in the provinces of Tepequacuilco, and of Iovatla, and in the provinces of Tovetno.

There is another kind of tree called ocolsoquahuitl, oxochiocotsoquahuitl: they are tall and thick, and have leaves like alders. From them flows a resin from which they make the smoking tubes that people inhale.

There are other trees called olquahuitl: they are large and tall and produce a great canopy. From these trees flows that black resin called olli [rubber]. To make it flow, they cut the bark and the olli seeps out through it. This resin called olli is medicinal for almost all illnesses; it is beneficial — it is medicine for the eyes, it is medicine for sores and rotting wounds, and it is also drunk with cacao; it is beneficial for the stomach and for the intestines, and beneficial for internal decay and for the amata, when it is properly prepared. This resin becomes very tough; they make balls from it for playing, and they bounce more than balls of air.

[Nahuatl column:]

Amatl-tree: it peels, it peels on its surface, its leaf, it sheds, it sloughs, its inner bark: it renews itself, it turns back, it revives.

Copalquahuitl: it drips, it oozes.

Ocutsoquahuitl: it is round like a cypress, it is hard, it is round, it oozes, it oozes outward; it produces liquid outward, from which the ocotzotl flows.

Olquahuitl: it is thick, it is stout, it is wide, it oozes outward, from it flows the olli. It is a medicine, it cures all internal diseases; it cures decay, it cures putrefaction; it is drunk with cacao, it warms the innards, it purges the bowels; it cleans the inside, it heals rotting within, the olli flows out, it congeals, it stretches, it is sticky, it is supple, it is springy, it bounces.

translation:
On the vitsquavitl [thornwood tree].
Folio 116

There are other trees called vitsquavitl: they are reddish and their wood contains the substance called todoiontl. They are the size of peach trees. These trees have leaves like those of the madroño [strawberry tree].

The density of trees is called Quappotzalli: meaning the crowding of many trees that stand close together, with the branches of some intermingled among others, casting shade — it is dark.

Where trees stand sparse, it is called quauhcaiachi: meaning the openness of trees, because they stand apart from one another and the field is clear and bright.

The name quavitl is applied to a green tree, or one that is small and still growing and being watered; or to a tree already large, or to one that is already old.

It is called quavitl: one that is transplanted, one that grows from seed, when it is a young seedling, and when it sprouts, and when it grows it is called quauhconah, or quauhpilli, or quauhcali — referring to the properties of trees in their birth and growth.

When the tree is already large, it is called yiolloco quavitl. Trees, if they take root and are transplanted, thicken; the seed beneath the earth becomes moist and rots.

[Nahuatl column:]

Vitsquavitl: it is reddish, dyeable, capable of being reddened, it makes things very red, it reddens things, it daubs [with color], it is pleasing.

Quappotzalli: it is thick, it darkens greatly, it rises up in many places, it stands erect in many places, it becomes shaded in many places, it becomes dusty in many places, it becomes shadowy toward evening, it drips with moisture in many places, it billows like smoke in many places.

Quauhcatactli: it is open, it is clear and bright, it becomes clear in many places, it becomes open-aired in many places, it resounds with the noise of many creatures, one can go about freely.

Quavitl: what it truly is — it is green; it can be watered, it can be set upright, it can be taken hold of by the roots; the yiolloco quavitl is the second kind of quavitl, or the old one.

Quavitl truly — it is one that can be seeded, that can be set upright, that can be made to branch out, that can be stripped of bark, that reforms itself, that revives itself, that buds forth in many places, that is propagated from cuttings, that is called quauhconeli, quauhpilli, quauhichi, and iollocoquavitl: it spreads out, it sprouts abundantly, it becomes leafy, it becomes weary [heavily laden], it bursts forth, it takes solid root, it becomes consolidated.

translation:
On the Parts of the Tree
Folio 117.

The parts that a tree has are the following: roots — thick, thin, and round or cylindrical. These roots go down beneath the earth and reach deep into the ground; by means of them the tree holds fast to the earth and has its foundation.

The stock of the tree is thick and round; it has rough bark. From this stock the roots extend in all directions. The stock, where the roots are born, is strong and sturdy, very firmly pressed against the earth. The roots are its bonds; this stock sustains the whole tree, holding it upright.

The trunk of the tree rises from the stock; it is thick at the bottom and thinner toward the top; it is stout, cylindrical, and round.

It is knotty; from it grow twisted branches and straight ones. It has bark; it has hollows; some branches are cut; it has forks; it has dense and strong branches; it has some [branches...]

[Nahuatl column:]
Inguavitl: it has extensions, has fibers, has surface-spreading roots, has aerial roots, has thin hairlike roots, has fine hairlike roots, is firm, is even-surfaced, spreads along the ground, nourishes, gives water, gives food.

[Trunk terms:] The tree stock is rounded at the base, is tapering, is compressed-round, is dense, is slender-round, is peppered with nodes, is broad-spreading, is spreading-flat, is firm-fibered, has striations, has fine striations, has very fine striations, is hard, arches down, supports loads, bends under loads, is fully load-bearing.

[Branch/wood terms:] The wood of the tree; has fiber-wood; its fiber goes inward; at the tree's stock it emerges fitted; is thick; is hairlike; follows along; is cylindrical; is straight-growing; is broad-cylindrical; is flat-cylindrical; is forking; is forked; is smooth-going; has tree-hollows; has tree-clustered-nodes; has tree-spine-hairs; [continues...]

translation:
Book Eleven

Fifth chapter, concerning dry trees that are standing upright or fallen on the ground, and of hewn timbers used for building.

Dry trees, whether standing or fallen, are called quavitl. They can be worked and planed. There are some dry trees with which people dye.

There are some dry trees that are split for burning. From trees, beams and planks are made. Also from trees, firewood is taken for burning.

There is a tree from which boards are made, and whose wood burns very well; it is called tlatlapanhtli, or tlatlapan quavitl. Whether it is green or dry, it is called the same, otlatzatantli.

The boards are called oapalli; some of them are thin, others thick; some flat, others curved.

The planks are called tlapech vapalli, xopetlatl; they are narrow and wide, some long and others short.

[Nahuatl column:]
The fifth chapter speaks of dry wood — that which no longer grows, that has died — how it is split, how it is worked with metal tools, how it is topped, how it is smoothed, how it is planed with a metal instrument, how it is cut crosswise, how it is sawed, how it is shaved, how it is planed flat, how it is beveled.

Tlatlapantli, tlatlapan quavitl, tlatlapanalli — it is broad and flat, it becomes flat and wide; it is split, it is divided. Tlatzatantli.

Vapalli — it is thick, it is wide and flat, it is smooth; one goes upon it, one walks upon boards.

Tlapeth oapalli, xopetlatl — it is thick, it is long, it is broad, it is wide, it is long, it is small. It is stumpy, it tapers, it is smooth, it is narrow, it is close-grained, it is fine-grained.

translation:
Book Eleven

These are also called ilhujcatl, because they support the structure.

The sill-plates are called quauhtentli: they rest on top of the wall, at the edge, and the other timbers rest upon them.

The timbers that are placed over the stone foundation, in order to set adobe bricks upon them, are called quauhtepanjsl. Because it sits on the stone foundation, and from there upward the wall is made of adobe.

The timber at the front of the door, the one that sits above the lintels, they call calixquatl, or ylhujcatl.

The wooden columns and the doorway lintels they call tlaquetsalli, otlaquetsalmjmjlli, or otlaxillotl.

The doors they call quauhttzaccaiotl, or vapalttzaccaiotl. The wooden columns that stand around the courtyard they call quauhtlaiaoa lo.

Ilhujcatl: it is also what is called that which supports, which bears up the woodwork, which carries things, which helps carry things together.

Quauhtentli: it is also what is described as being placed alongside the woodwork, lying along the edge of the wall, or at the border of the thatching, or of the basket-work.

Quauhtepanjth: it is that which lies on top of the stone base of the wall, alongside which the timber is smoothed, which supports, which spreads out and levels.

Calixquatl, also called ilhujcatl: it is strong, wide, broad, thick, very finely wrought, it carries the load, it helps carry the whole together.

Tlaquetsalli: also tlaquetsalmjlli, tlaxillotl, quauhtep — it is thick, strong, firm, sturdy, it supports from below, it carries the whole thing, it holds everything together, it bears things up.

Tlaquetsalli: it is wide, tall, slender, somewhat slender, smooth, strong, very strong in holding things, it carries loads.

Quauktzaraiotl: it is used to join things together, to bind the woodwork. Vapaltáacaiotl: likewise it is that which is described as the surrounding wooden columns.

translation:
On Worked Timbers
Folio 120

The logs of wood are called quauhtzontle: some of these are square, others round, and others concave.

The beam on which the lower hinge of a door rests is called quauhpechtli.

The wood shavings are called tlaximalli, or quauhtlaximallo, or tlaximallotl.

The wood splints are called tzicueallotl, or quauhtziuceoallotl.

The round timbers that are placed beneath the beams when they are being dragged are called quammitl: these are made of hard wood.

The pegs or stakes are called tlaxichtli.

The sawdust of wood is called quauhtextli.

Rotted wood is called quappalan.

Sixth paragraph, on the incidental things pertaining to trees, and on trees.

Quauhtzontle; quauhtzontetl: from which beams are made, or it is a log that has fallen; it is dark, round, and knotty.

Quauhpepeohtli: it lies flat against the lintel, fastened in place.

Tlaximalli, tlaximalquavitl, quauhtlaximalli, tlaximalutl: it is smooth, soft, crumbling, flaking, peeling: I shave it, I plane it smooth.

Tzicuevallotl, quauhtziucuevalli: it is hard, knotty; I split it, I cause it to crack.

Quammitl: it is thick and strong, a timber roller; I roll the logs along with it.

Tlaxichtli: it is sharp-pointed, sharply pointed; I drive stakes with it into the ground.

Quauhtextli: it is fine and powdery; I grind it fine, I scatter it.

Quappalan: it is crumbling, rotting, decayed, and soft.

Here in the sixth paragraph I speak of how the tree grows.

translation:
Book Eleven

The tree. It is planted and sown, and mastic is made from trees; the trees are transplanted.

There are certain trees called tzapotl, or tzapoquavitl: it is smooth, with green bark, round leaves, white and soft and light wood, from which sedan chairs are made. The fruit of these trees is like large apples; on the outside they are green or yellow, on the inside white and soft; they are very sweet. They have three or four pits, white inside, and if one eats many of them, they cause diarrhea.

[Right column, Nahuatl text:] The tree: it can be felled, its branches lopped off, transplanted, pruned; it sprouts, takes root, puts forth shoots; it spreads out, its branches spread, it flowers, bears fruit.

[Second Nahuatl section:] The zapote: the zapote tree is smooth-skinned, elongated, round; its flesh is savory, sweet, of good flavor, round; it is juicy, soft, spongy, frothy, dripping, sour, very sour; it becomes ripe, it is edible. It falls on the ground; it falls to the earth's surface.

translation:
On the Zapotes [Sapodilla fruits]
Folio 123.

[upper illustration: two trees with yellow fruits]

There are other zapotes called cochitstzapotl, because they cause sleep. They are like those described above, except that they are smaller.

There are other zapotes called tlacacoltsapotl, which are like those described above, but they are very large.

There are other trees called Atsaputl, which are smooth.
The fruit of these trees is called Atsaputl. They are yellow inside and outside, very sweet, firm, with a flavor like egg yolk; when ripe they have pits of a dark chestnut color.

[lower illustration: two trees with yellow fruits]

[Nahuatl text:] It spreads outward: one cuts it, one cuts it repeatedly, one bites it. The atsaputl, the flower-fruit. It is round, sweet, soft, smooth, watery, pulpy; one strips away its rind, it is rough to the taste, somewhat bitter. When one eats it, it draws out saliva, it refreshes the throat; it is thirst-quenching, it satisfies, it makes one full.

The cochitstzapotl is just the same: it causes sleepiness, it induces great sleepiness, it darkens the vision, it is heavy, it brings on much drowsiness.

The tlacacoltsapotl is just the same: it is very large, big, rounded, very round, bulging, very bulging, swollen, very swollen.

Atsaputl, atsapoquavitl, xipetstli, xixipotstli, tlalstli.

The atsaputl flower-fruit is edible, good, excellent. It is juicy, honey-sweet, honey-dripping, honey-crystallizing, hot, very heated, heart-filling, yellow, dripping with juice, slippery, slick, foamy, foaming, watery, full of pulp. And in the manner of a remedy for the mouth-palate, it is said: I eat atsaputl, I chew it, I move it around my mouth, I —

translation:
Book Eleven

[illustration: two fruit trees and a grasshopper]

There are other trees called xicohzapotl; the Spaniards call them peruchanos. They are very sweet and very good to eat, and they grow in hot country.

There are other trees called totolcujtlatzaputl, or totolcujtlatzapoquavitl; they grow in hot country. The fruit of these trees is called totolcujtlatzaputl. They are large, like big apples; on the outside they are green, and on the inside black. They are very sweet and very good to eat.

There are other trees called tecontzaputl. They are the shape and size of a sheep's heart; their bark is rough and tight. They are red on the inside, very sweet, and very good to eat. They have black pits that are very smooth and shiny.
There are other trees called hekapuytl, and the fruit is called heciotzaputl.
These are the anonas, which contain inside many black seeds like black beans. These are also called quauhtzaputl.

[Nahuatl column:]
...it glorifies, it praises, it makes one worthy of esteem...

The xicozapotl fruit: it is round, of fine quality, smooth, with a sweet nub, very sweet, honey-like, honeyish; it ripens in the sun, it comes to be in warm places.

The totolcujtlatzaputl, totolcujtlatzapoquavitl: it comes to ripen in warm places, it bursts open; the fruit is dark, somewhat fibrous, somewhat stringy, resembling turkey dung in shape; it is called totolcujtlatzaputl because it is greenish on the outside.

The tecontzaputl fruit: it is called tecontzaputl because it is shaped like a teconte [a type of vessel]; it is somewhat rough, somewhat matte-surfaced, somewhat pale, dark inside.
The hetzaputl is likewise the same, the eiotzaputl is likewise the same.

The quauhtzaputl is likewise the same; one cuts it, one splits it open, one eats it, one selects it, one tends to it, one harvests it.

Of plums
Folio 122.

There are other trees called aoacatl, or aoacaquavitl: they have dark green leaves; their fruit is called aoacatl, and they are black on the outside and green and white on the inside; they are heart-shaped and have a pit inside, also heart-shaped.

There are other aoacates called tlacacol aoacatl: they are large, like those described above. Nursing women do not dare eat them, because they cause diarrhea in the children they are nursing.

There are other aoacates called qujlaoacatl; their fruit is also called qujlaodacatl; they are green on the outside and very good to eat, and they are prized.

Seventh chapter, concerning small fruits such as plums, guavas, and cherries.

The trees on which plums, guavas, and little apples grow are called xocoquavitl.

The trees on which the small native apples grow are called texocotl or texocoquavitl: they are medium-sized, spreading trees with dense wood; their fruit is called texocotl: they are yellow and red on the outside and white on the inside, they have small seeds within, and they are very good to eat.

Aoacatl, aoacaquavitl: green on the surface, broad-leafed, with a small green throat; the interior of the throat is dark and tart; inside it is greenish, somewhat salty, moderately thick, broadly rounded, bitter-tasting, soft-fleshed, with a center.

Tlacacolaoacatl: it is large, very big; nursing women do not eat it, for it empties the milk from their breasts.

Qujlaoacatl: rough, small-branched, good, a type of tecpilaoacatl.

Here begins the seventh chapter, which speaks of the trees from which good fruit comes.

Xocoquavitl: from this tree comes fruit that is truly sour, or somewhat sour.

Texocotl, texocoquavitl: a dark-wooded tree; spiny, very spiny, watery, rubbery, nourishing, low-spreading, branching wide, with a divided trunk; the fruit is yellow, rounded, smooth, causing sneezing, causing one to salivate, making the mouth water, making the lips smack; its flower is white, causing the lips to pucker.

The tree from which cacao is made is called cacaoaquavitl. It has broad leaves and a spreading canopy. The fruit it produces is medium-sized, shaped like ears of maize or somewhat larger, and they contain the cacao beans inside. On the outside the fruit is purple, and inside it is reddish. When it is fresh, if one drinks too much of it, it intoxicates; but if drunk in moderation, it refreshes and cools.

[Nahuatl passage:] The cacao tree [cacaoaquavitl] has spreading branches; its foliage is like that of maize, like ears of corn. Its cacao pods come in varieties: some are reddish, some are yellowish, some are rough-surfaced. Inside they are hollow and firm, resembling maize kernels. The cacao drink [cacaoatl] is good to eat and to drink. This cacao drink, in great quantity and spoken of widely — it intoxicates, it makes one dizzy, it confounds one, it makes one giddy, it makes one's heart whirl, it corrupts one's heart. Only when taken in proper measure does it invigorate, refresh, and gladden the heart. One says: I drink cacao, I refresh myself, I become content.
