translation:
Of the mesquite tree.
Folio 124.

There are some trees called mesquite, or mesquite tree: they have rough bark, and the interior of the bark is very white and corky; it is medicinal — one drinks it, and a poultice is made from it. This tree has very hard wood; its leaves are like those of the agave, and its bitter leaves are medicinal for the eyes, dropping the sap of them into the eyes.

The fruit consists of small rounded pods that contain seeds inside, and the pods are sweet and good to eat; but if one eats many of them they cause the belly to swell. To eat them, one chews them —

[Nahuatl column:]
Mesquite, mesquite tree — its surface is rough-barked, rough-skinned, scaly-barked; its interior is white, it is dried-out, firm-fibered, watery, astringent, drinkable. It is useful: it relieves, it restores, it nourishes. This mesquite wood is very hard, firm, compact, strong, tree-like, knee-jointed, branching, many-limbed, many-branched, forking, canopy-spreading, summit-spreading. The mesquite gum is sticky, smooth, oozing, splitting, cracking, peeling, fragmenting, crumbling. It is a remedy for the eyes, and also for mouth-soreness: it drips into the eye, it spreads, it disperses, it tingles, it soothes. As for the fruit of it: it is an astringent thing, foreign-looking, broad-chested; it is said to be of one pod, double-podded, draping in clusters, sweet, fragrant, savory, filling to the heart, flavorful, flat, fluffy —

This is the eighth paragraph, in which I speak of the nopalli and its characteristics.

The nopalli, as it is known, is broad-leaved, smooth, green, watery, [and has various other qualities described in Nahuatl]...

There are other trees of this kind called Tlanexnopalli. Their fruit, the tlanexnochtli, consists of these dark purple tunas; they are round like capotes.

There are other trees of this kind called camaxtle. Their fruit is also called Camaxtle. They are white tunas, with a thick and sour skin, but the flesh inside is sweet.

There are other trees of this kind called xoconoch nopalli. They are very thorny, with sharp and long spines. The tunas of these trees are called xoconochili, which means sour tunas. They are whitish, with sour and thick skins that set the teeth on edge. They are eaten raw and also cooked. The inner flesh is small and sweet.

There are other wild trees of this kind called tenopalli, which grow among the crags, on the rocky hillsides, and in the ravines. The fruit they produce is called Cacanochdi. They have sour skins; these little tunas are small, and are eaten cooked and raw.

[Nahuatl column:]

Its name is tzaponochili; it is rounded in form, shaped like a gourd, like a bowl, smooth and rounded on all sides.

Tlanexnopalli: its fruit, also called by my name tlanexnochtli, is pale, whitish, reddish, somewhat reddish, rounded.

Camaxtle: its fruit, also known by the name camaxtle, has a white, thick skin; it is sour on the outside, tender inside; the flesh is fibrous, becoming fibrous as one eats it.

Xoconoch nopalli: it is wide, its skin is wide and thick; its fruit is called xoconochili; it is white, sour; on its surface are rows of thorns, spines standing apart, spines standing upright, whitish protruding spines, causing scratches, causing irritation, whitish cutting spines. Its flesh, though its inner part is syrupy sweet, is hot, spongy, fibrous, and full.

Tenopalli: in the forests, on the hillsides, among the reeds this nopal grows. Its fruit is called cacanochili; it is sour, rough-tasting, small and round; it scratches the throat going down, greenish, edible.

There are other trees of this type called Tecolonochnopalli: they have long, narrow leaves; the prickly-pear fruits that grow on these trees are called tecolonochitl, and they have thick skins.

Ninth Chapter, concerning edible roots.

The roots of the tree called Quauhtcamotli are edible, as has already been said.

There are other good roots to eat, which grow like turnips underground; these are called camotli: they are the sweet potatoes of this land. They are eaten cooked, raw, and roasted.

[Nahuatl column:]
Azcanonopalli — it grows on the plains and hillsides, in rocky and sandy places. Its name: azcanochtle. It is pale, white, yellowish, orange-colored, purple, very sweet, round, small — like a tomatl.

Tecolonochinopalli — it is very slender-leafed. It has colorful, flowery markings; its name is colonochtli; it has a leathery rind.

This is the ninth chapter, which speaks of things that grow inside the earth — good flowers, good to eat.

Quauhtcamotli — its root is woody; it is thick and cylindrical, ridged and firm.

Camotli — its root is cylindrical, round, sweet, smooth; camoxalli — a small camotli; it is like a common villager, split open at the base.

translation:

It spreads out, it puts forth shoots, it trails its vines along the ground: it is the green runner bean; it is the camote [sweet potato] — here it settles, here it puts forth its leaves, here it spreads along the ground, here it lies flat, here it goes; here it is the green one.

There are other roots that are eaten raw, which they call Jícama: they are white and sweet, and they quench thirst greatly.

The jícama plant: it spreads out, it sends out runners, it is leafy and full of foliage; its root is the edible part; the jícama is round, wide and flat, soft and tender, with a thin skin, snake-like on the outside, pale and watery on the outside, white within, white and clear, like a gourd, like a tree mushroom, watery, green and crunchy, firm; I dig up the jícama, I rake around the jícama, I prepare myself to harvest it, I gather the jícama.

The cimatl root: it has thin fibers, its plant-stem names are these: it is wide and flat, it is the runner bean, it can be cut easily, it is not so crunchy, it makes one feel full, it tightens the belly; I will say this about it: upon it grow small pointed things, small hairs; it has been smoothed: it is truly hard to bite.

There are other roots that are also eaten, which are called Cimatl: they are eaten cooked, and if not, they are by nature white; when eaten raw they cause harm; they are by nature white, but when cooked they turn yellow.

translation:
Book Eleven

Chapter Seven, which treats of all herbs.

First Paragraph, concerning certain herbs that cause intoxication.

There is an herb called Coatl xoxouhqui, and it has a seed called ololiuhqui, or coatl xoxouhqui. This seed causes intoxication and madness; it is given as a drink to cause harm to those one wishes ill, and those who eat it seem to see visions and terrifying things. It is given mixed into food or drink by sorcerers, and those who hate certain people use it to harm them. This herb is medicinal, and its seed is used for gout: grinding it and placing it on the spot where the gout is.

There is another herb, like a truffle of the earth, which is called peyotl. It is white; it grows toward the north. Those who eat or drink it see frightening or amusing visions. This intoxication lasts...

[Nahuatl column:]
This is the seventh chapter, which speaks of the many kinds of herbs.

First paragraph: it tells of many kinds of herbs that disturb the mind.

Coatl xoxouhqui — or ololiuhqui — is slender and vine-like, with a narrow leaf. It causes drunkenness and makes the heart wither; it confuses and deranges the heart. Whoever takes it sees many fearful and terrifying things. It is said it is a serpent-eater. Its water is bitter and bad-tasting. It damages the heart and deranges it; yet it is fragrant and not bitter. It is used as a medicine, applied to the affected area.

Peyotl: its peyotl is white. It is found only in the desert region of the Mexhua, in the Teuhtelolpa region, in the Mictlan direction. Those who eat it — or those for whom it goes to work — [experience visions] just as with nanacatl [mushrooms]...

...for two or three days, and then it passes. It is a common food of the Chichimecs, who sustain themselves on it, and it gives them courage to fight, and to feel neither fear, nor thirst, nor hunger, and they say it keeps them from all danger.

¶ There is another herb called tlapatl: it is like a shrub, it produces small heads without thorns, like lemons; they have a green rind, wide leaves, white flowers; it has a black seed, and it is foul-smelling, and it takes away the appetite of those who eat it, and it intoxicates them, and does so continuously.

This seed is good against gout; rubbing it on relieves the pain; its smell too is harmful, like the seed itself.

And here they say a proverb against the arrogant and presumptuous: they say that such people eat this herb, and another herb that

[Right column, Nahuatl text:]
...two things it removes from a person's composure, or it causes one to fall, not even for a whole day, or two days, it does not properly settle within; it no longer allows the heart to hear, it causes one to lose things, it makes one feel bad, it makes one grasp at things: I destroy myself, I am nothing.

¶ Tlapatl [jimsonweed/datura], standing upright: its surface is rough-textured, its herb-like parts are white and spreading, its inner part is grayish-white, its interior is speckled black, it has a foul smell, it harms the heart, it prevents proper nourishment, it makes the spirit wretched, it intoxicates. Whoever eats it no longer desires food in any way, as I have seen; and if someone eats it repeatedly, the heart will forever be disturbed, the spirit will forever be troubled, forever wandering in madness, no longer fit for human companionship. And wherever the herb lies, it greatly harms by making things wet where it rests, one must not pick it up, for it harms the heart, it prevents good nourishment, it injures the spirit, it makes the spirit wretched, it prevents proper nourishment: I am destroyed, I am undone, I go about in misery. Let the one who goes about boasting, counting himself above all, be wise about this.

translation:
Book Eleven

It is called Mixitl, which means that those who eat these plants go mad as if out of their minds.

There are other plants like these, called tzitzmtlapatl: they are called this because their heads are spiny; they have the same properties as the one described above.

There is another plant called maxitl: it is quite small and branching, it is green and has seeds; it is good against gout, by applying the crushed plant where the pain is. It is neither edible nor drinkable; it provokes vomiting, tightens the throat and the tongue, provokes thirst, and splits the tongue. If one eats or drinks it, it does not give a bad flavor or bad taste, but soon it takes away all the strength of the body. If the one who eats it has his eyes open, he cannot close them anymore; and if they are closed, he cannot open them anymore. If he is in this state, he cannot bend over or lower himself, and he loses his speech. Wine is the remedy against this plant.

There are some small mushrooms in this land called teonanacatl: they grow under the hay in the fields. Their caps are round, and they have a rather tall and thin round stem. When eaten, they have a bad flavor; they harm the throat. They make one drunk; they are medicinal against fevers and gout. One should eat them:

[Nahuatl column:]
Nemjmjxitl: tlapatl quiquatinems: momjxivitinems, motlapavitinemy.

Tzitzmtlapatl: it is likewise a tlapatl, but a different kind. Its leaves are greenish...

Mixitl is roundish, its leaves are dark green, shining; where the coacivitl plant is found, it spreads there; it is not to be eaten, not to be drunk; it constricts the throat, stops up the neck, makes the speech slur, makes one thirsty, makes one parch, makes one lose one's senses, makes one feel as though bound — one sees all things double; once, twice, many times affected, one sees everything with blurred vision, and it helps by means of wine; it makes one rub one's eyes, makes others rub their eyes.

Nanacatl [mushroom]: it is called teonanacatl; it grows in grassy places, among the cacao trees; it is rough, peppery, very peppery, intoxicating, round-stemmed, maddening; it cures fever, gout — two or three [are taken]; blood [follows]...

translation:
On Poisonous Plants.
folio 131.

Two or three [mushrooms] only: those who eat them have visions, and feel nausea of the heart, and see visions that are at times frightening, and at other times laughable. Those who eat many of them are made to vomit, and even if only a few are eaten.

And to foolish and mischievous young men, they say that they have eaten the nanacatl [mushrooms].

¶ There is another poisonous plant called tochtetepo: it has small leaves, like those of the petu tree, it has white roots; if anyone eats or drinks it, they die immediately, because it tears their intestines to pieces. And if this plant is put into pulque or water, even if it is taken out right away, it leaves its poison behind, and whoever drinks it dies.

This is also said of sorcerers who bewitch with this plant.

¶ There is another plant called Atlepati: it grows on the banks of water and near swamps; it is deadly, whoever [eats it]...

[Nahuatl column:]
It is edible [only in small amounts]; it causes heart palpitations, chest tightening, fear, dizziness, terror. He who eats many of it sees many frightening things, or goes mad; he flees, hangs himself, throws himself off a cliff. He is frightened. Thus by eating it one takes on the mushroom spirit, one embodies it. Those who boast of it, those who are reckless, those who are vainglorious — it is said they embody the mushroom.

¶ Tochtetepon: it is a small plant, they say, slender, its leaves split apart, its skin is white; it is deadly, it tears the intestines. Whoever takes and eats it, it burns them, it twists their intestines: it seizes all of them at once, only briefly does it show itself [in effect], it is seen internally, it is seen killing; it comes out [in them]. It can no longer be shaken out, it can no longer be expelled. By means of it, it is said, one becomes a devotee: one who belongs to tochtetepon, I belong to tochtetepon.

¶ Atlepati: it is a small plant, it makes the earth quake, it grows in muddy water; it is deadly: whoever [eats it]...

translation:
Book Eleven

When an animal eats or drinks it, the animal dies immediately and develops blisters like fire. If it is placed on flesh, it is a remedy against the skin disease called xiah.

There is an herb called haquiztli: it has long, thin branches, it is like a bush, and it has this property — if someone urinates on it or spits on it, their face swells up immediately, or their entire body, and if it touches the body it immediately causes blisters. Drunk against smallpox, its juice drives the disease out.

There is another herb called tenroxoli: it has leaves like thin cattails. The root of this herb induces vomiting, and it also causes bleeding.

There is another herb called qui—

[Nahuatl column:]
They die from eating it; those who eat it die; in the throat area it causes the flesh to swell and blister. It is called xiopathi; it causes blistering and great burning of the mouth; it drives away diseases for a year.

Haquiztli: it is vine-like, fibrous, and flexible. It burns the mouth, it clings to the teeth, it causes one to breathe heavily, it makes things swell and pop. When someone is fully covered in blisters all over, and their mouth burns and blisters everywhere: the person whose whole body is erupting loses all sensation in the joints. Regarding haquiztli: it is green-colored, it does not quench thirst; it maintains people, it always restores the body; it cures diseases in a year.

Tenroxoli makes the throat narrow, it is slender-stemmed, it pains the insides and compresses them, it contracts things, it tightens, it finishes—

Quimichpyatl, tlacotonlli, it burns, it singes the tongue—

translation:
On Mushrooms [fo. 132]

Michpatli. It is like a deadly herb. This herb kills rats when mixed with some food that they eat. Placed on putrid sores, it consumes all the rot in them and reveals the living flesh.

Second paragraph on mushrooms.

Mushrooms grow in fields and in the mountains; they are good to eat, they are cooked before eating. If they are eaten raw or poorly cooked, they cause vomiting, cramps, and death. To remedy the harm that mushrooms cause, the yellow ointment called Axin is good. It is applied with a syringe.

There are some of these mushrooms called Bontecomananacatl; they are large and round.

There are others called Xelhuasnanacatl; they grow in many clusters on one stem, some tall and some short.

[Nahuatl column:]

They are deadly. They intoxicate, they make one speak deliriously, they cause one to drink excessively. This is why they are called michpatli: they present good food to the mice; when the mice eat it they die; it spreads corruption in their bodies. When placed where something is rotting and is eaten, it cleans away the rot, removes the covering, reveals the flesh beneath; it cleanses as michpatli does.

Second paragraph, which speaks of mushrooms.

Mushrooms, forest mushrooms: they are not to be eaten raw, they can be eaten cooked, they can cure; when eaten they do not intoxicate, nor do they cause one to be unable to stand, nor do they warm one, nor do they stupefy: they help one recover. The mushroom that swells up and becomes dry is treated with axin dissolved in water, so that it may become soft and pliable.

The Bontecomananacatl is round, very wide, just like a bontecomat vessel.

The Xelhoaznanacatl is split, cylindrical, bristly; it looks just like a xelhoaztli.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are other mushrooms called chimalnanacatl; they are flat and round in the manner of plates. All these mushrooms are edible and they must be well cooked before eating.

There are other mushrooms called Menanacatl; they are white and round, they are not tough to cook, they cook quickly, and they can also be grilled on comals, and they are very tasty.

Others are called Çacanacatl. These are tall-stemmed and have a thin stem. They are round and flat. They cook quickly and are good to eat. They grow in the high plains when the rains begin.

There are other mushrooms called quauhnanacatl because they grow on trees; they are good to eat roasted and boiled.

Chimalnanacatl: it is round, like a water ripple it spreads. Like a shield it is set, like a tortilla it lies. This edible thing grows in the forest. It grows with a yellowish interior, somewhat reddish; it is somewhat large, and it heals well.

Menanacatl: it is round, white, somewhat dusty, not tough, it cooks quickly, it softens, it can be grilled on a comal, it is edible, it is savory, pleasant.

Çacanacatl: it is tall, somewhat yellowish-brown, somewhat roughened, somewhat fibrous, not tough, like a green herb, it softens, it is edible, savory; it grows among the grasses; only when it has just rained does it grow. All these mushrooms should not be eaten raw.

Quauhnanacatl: it grows in the forest; it is edible, it can be peeled, it can be grilled. All these mushrooms should not be eaten raw; they can be peeled, they can be grilled: [illegible]

translation:
On the root called cimatl: The herb of this root is called quavetoc, and it is also called cimatl. This herb produces pods like large beans, and they are wild beans. This herb sends out long, spreading branches along the ground. The root of this herb, if eaten raw or poorly cooked, provokes vomiting and hiccups, and can kill. Against this harm, the yellow ointment called axi, applied by sunning, is the remedy. To eat these roots, it is necessary to cook them for two days, as the herb is always [potent].

There is an herb called hamolli; it has leaves like small cattails and has a white stem. The root of this herb is like soap for washing clothes. With the thinner roots, they wash the head. They are also used like a stupefying agent to intoxicate fish. If anyone drinks of this root, they either die or suffer great harm. If someone has swallowed a leech and it remains in the body, by drinking the water of this root it [expels it—]

[Nahuatl column:]
Cimatl — its sap is described: it is called mixiuhio, it is called quaveco, it is also called cimaquilitl. It tastes like aiecotl [a type of bean]; it is said: it tastes like cimaquilitl greens. It spreads and multiplies; it is watery, juicy, soft. The sap is quite green; it is not easy to digest when one takes it raw; it causes dysentery, diarrhea; it is drinkable. The way one is cured by cimatl: that which one craves greatly — it goes by way of the buttocks. And the way one eats the sap of cimatl: one boils it well in water until fully cooked; and first it scalds, the water bubbles, with saltpeter; into the fire I place it; I treat myself with cimatl, I apply cimatl to myself.

Hamolli — it is flat like a reed, it is juicy; it is white-colored, it foams; the great thick [root], hardened like stone, is peeled; the smaller, thin, soft one is used for rinsing, for cleansing the hair, for washing, for purifying: I wash my hair, I bathe myself; it stuns fish, it makes their hearts faint: thus they are caught — as is said of the fish; it reaches the little fish. And further, as it is said, one who drinks hamolli — thus it catches and stupefies [them].

translation:
Book Eleven

There is a root called tecpatl or tecpaolotl; it is sticky like birdlime and resembles a soaproot. It is medicinal for broken bones, and it is also used like birdlime for catching birds: straws are smeared with it and placed where birds come to eat, and in this way they are caught. This birdlime is also called tlacali because it is very sticky.

There is another herb called hyiamoli. On it form little black knobs, and they are very bitter; they are a medicine for dandruff of the head.

[illustration caption:] Amaranth greens (vauhquilit)

Tecpatl, tecpaolotl, cacalite — and likewise mamolli, petequizpati. Whoever has a bone set or adjusted, who has had bones straightened — it smooths the bones; it relieves pain and fatigue, it relieves weariness, it settles into the joints; it spreads through where the joints are, in the bends of the arms, in the places where birds perch: there it reaches and spreads; it is known by the name tlascali. It is very hard and dry, and birds eat it; it makes a cracking sound, it is dry and crackling. It straightens, it stretches, it causes one to be nimble.

Yiamoli, cahadat: its leaves are slender and green; its surface is spotted, it is narrow-leafed, round, not orange-colored; it is a medicine for the head: cacapollo.

translation:
Book Eleven

Third paragraph concerning edible herbs that are cooked.

One of the herbs that is eaten cooked is called vauhquilit, which is amaranth. It is very green, has slender and somewhat tall branches, and broad leaves. The plants of this herb are called Vauhtli, and the seed of this herb is also called Vauhtli. This herb is grown to eat; it has a slightly sour taste. The water in which it is cooked is squeezed out before eating, and with salt, tamales are made from this herb, which are called quiltamalli. Tortillas are also made from ground maize and the leaves of this herb, and these are called quillaxcalli. This is a very common herb, and like the spinach of Castile, people eat a great deal of it.

Another herb that is eaten cooked is called quiltonilli. It has somewhat broad leaves when it is small. This herb is edible; when it is fully grown it is called petlicatl or opitsicatl. It is boiled with saltwater and the liquid is pressed out.

This is the second paragraph: it speaks of edible greens and their properties.

Edible greens, vauhquilit: smooth amaranth greens — I eat them boiled, I eat them as they come from the hand, greens, papalo herb, tender: I eat them with something. Its name is vauhzontti: I prepare it under its name vauh tli, malacattontti, or malacachtotontti, paoaxon, sour, aquixalon, mepaco iotzin, papatz, tamale-like — its name is quiltamalli, tlatlacioio — its name quillaxcalli: I sauté it, I fry it with chili, I make it into tamales, I roll it up, I eat it as quilpi. Vauhzontti: its surface is that of vauhquilitl, it is known as thaialeic, thachaiaoac, sandy, greenish, paoaxon, patzconi, good to eat. When it is dried out: it is no longer good for paoax, it is no longer good to eat, it becomes nashtli.

Quiltonilli: it has a somewhat spread-out surface, very small when edible. Its name is potzicatl, or pitsicatl, paoaxon, tequixqui, vilons, patzconi, papatzconi. Its amaranth-like inner part: [illegible] injutil.

To eat it. This herb produces a small black seed and is called petzi.
There is another herb that is also eaten cooked, called ytzmiquitl; it is a spreading plant, it has small thick branches and round, flat leaves.
The flowers of the squash plants are called Ayoxochquilitl; these are also eaten cooked; they are very yellow, they are spiny; one prepares them for cooking by removing the outer skin before cooking them.

The tips of the branches of the squash plants are also eaten cooked.
There is another herb called axoxoco; it has long and wide leaves. It is eaten cooked and is flavorful and sour.
There is another herb called mizquiquilitl; it is also eaten cooked; it is somewhat tall and very green; it has jagged leaves; it is pleasant to eat cooked.

There is another herb called tlatlainquilitl or tzivienquilitl; it produces

[Nahuatl column:]
It is the petziati, or else the pitziati.
Ytzmiquitl: it has smooth, soft, tender leaves, with small round leaves like a rosette.
Ayoxochquilitl: it is flowery inside; the squash blossom is cylindrical, yellow-green, puffed up, yellow-green, soft in its interior. The squash blossom is washed, scraped, and cleaned; its interior fiber is pulled out; it swells and opens; it is soaked and softened.
The water-herb (atioacaquilitl): it smells of squash; it is fragrant and pleasing in smell; it is like a squash vine, tender, edible, and tasty.
Axoxoco: broad-leafed, straight; somewhat vine-like; tasty with its squash-like flavor.
Mizquiquilitl: vine-like; greenish like mesquite; with mesquite-like blossoms; fibrous, edible, tasty; one soaks it and chews it.
Acuytlacpalli: smooth-stemmed, broad-leafed, growing near water, spreading along the water's edge.
Tzivinquilitl, or else atzivicquilitl, dwelling along the water's edge and riverbank.

translation:
On Raw Herbs. fo. 136.

On the herbs that are eaten raw. There is one called tzitziquilitl; it is very tender, has flowers and seeds, is greenish, and is very good to eat.

There is another herb called eloquilitl. It is very green and tender, produces flowers, and is very tasty.

There is another called quauh eloquilitl. It is wild. It grows especially among the prickly pear cacti. It is very tender and good to eat.

There is another called moroquilitl. It is very green and very tender, and it is hairy; it is very tasty.

There is another herb called taianalgujlitl, which grows in the water; it has hollow, jagged branches, and is good to eat.

There is another herb called achochogujlitl; it is light green, grows near the water, and is good to eat. They say of this herb that boys or girls who eat it develop swellings, and afterward everyone eats it together. This herb is also called auaxcaqujlitl.

There is another herb called tenqujlitl. It is very green and has small hollow stems like needles, and one called haxalli; and the lagoon water that soaks it cures one before eating them.
There is another herb called eystaglitl; it is tasty and somewhat flat, has a salty flavor, and is eaten cooked and raw.

Tzitzqujlitl: tender, smooth, fresh, greenish, xothio, xoxothio, xinathio, haviar, quyliaractic.

Eloquilitl: greenish, somewhat smooth, tender, greenish-yellow, moxothiotanj, avixtic, avixpatic.

Quauh eloquilitl: it is long-stemmed; it grows in the forest and among the prickly pears: celia, cecelia, somewhat smooth, cecelspati.

Mocoqujlitl: ashy-colored, ash-like in appearance, of moderate taste, fragrant and flavorful.

Taialanalqujlitl: it grows in the water; its joints break easily, it is reed-like; its name is taianalgujlitl; it bursts its pith.

Achochoqujlitl: it is firm, rough, somewhat wrinkled; it grows at the water's edge.

Avexotaqujlitl: it is known by no other name than achothoqujlitl.

Tehtzongujlitl: greenish, slender, reed-like, porous; it crumbles, it breaks; one crumbles it, one breaks it.

Istaqujlitl: whitish, flat, broad-leaved, edible, and also edible as a relish, bitter, somewhat bitter.

text:
Libro vndecimo

¶ Ay otra yerua que se llama tepicquilit tiene las hojas larguillas. Y punti agudas, si comen mucha da camaras.

¶ Ay otra yerua que se llama ecoqililt. Son las hojas y ramas delos frisoles: son vnpoco asperas. y vellosas: comense crudas. Prouocan a regoldar.

¶ Ay tra yerua que se llama vitzqiulit. Son cardos dela tierra, tiene espinas, y las hojas de abaxo son cenicientas y los de arriba son verdes: so buenas de comer, yn se masca suena entre los dientes, tiene dentro hilachas como los cardos de castilla haze se ala orilla del agua, y tabien es jarua ofiese.
¶ Ay vnos cardos Syluestres que son como los de arriba dichos saluo que se crian en las montanas llamarl: quauitzqiulit. Y dizen yo como alqueme come porque so espinosos y pican alque los come.

¶ Ay otra manera de yerua como hble que se llama chidhicaquilit cria se cerca delagua y en tierra dulce y labrada, es muy tierna, tiene las rayzes blancas, y es algo amarga.

¶ Ay otra yerua que llaman tonalchidhicaqiulit, haze se en tierrase ca y en los paramos y en las montanas es verde cenicenta es muy amarga. Es contra el calor interior.

translation:
Book Eleventh

There is another herb called tepicquilit, which has elongated leaves with sharp points; if one eats too much of it, it causes diarrhea.

There is another herb called ecoqililt. Its leaves and branches resemble those of bean plants; they are somewhat rough and hairy; they are eaten raw. They provoke belching.

There is another herb called vitzqiulit. These are thistles of the land; they have spines, and their lower leaves are ashen and the upper ones are green; they are good to eat; when chewed they make a sound between the teeth; they have fibers inside like Castilian thistles; they grow at the water's edge, and they are also used as a remedy.
There are some wild thistles that are like those described above, except that they grow in the mountains, called quauitzqiulit. They say I eat like one who eats aloe, because they are spiny and they prick whoever eats them.

There is another kind of herb, called chidhicaquilit, which grows near water and in soft, cultivated land; it is very tender, has white roots, and is somewhat bitter.

There is another herb they call tonalchidhicaqiulit; it grows in dry, barren places and in the mountains; it is grayish-green and very bitter. It is good against internal heat.

[Nahuatl column:]
Tepicquilit: its leaves are elongated, it makes the face narrow, it causes the nose to be pointed; one should not eat too much of it; it draws out the sun's heat.

Ecoqiulit: it is rounded, hard, firm on all sides, it strengthens the back; it tightens, it draws together, it makes one contract.

Vitzqiulit: it has a watery surface, it crackles, it is rough, it has a fragrance, it blooms, it spreads on the water's surface.

Quavitzqiulit: it is just like the vitzqiulit: it grows on the plains, in the forests among the vitzqiulit; it defends itself. For this reason it swells and becomes inflamed.

Chidhicaqiulit: it grows along ravines, in moist places, in good land, in shaded areas; it becomes tender, it is somewhat salty, somewhat pleasant to taste.

Tonalchidhicaqiulit: it grows in dry, barren, wooded areas; it withers and dries out, it crackles inside from the heat.

translation:
Of Raw Herbs — folio 137

[left column]
Good for digestion and purifying the intestines, especially for those who eat it on an empty stomach.

There is another herb called Cotocuexi, which resembles the vitzquili described above. It is not thorny, it grows and flowers, but neither boys nor girls use it to eat, because it is bitter and harmful, and damages the throat — it makes the voice hoarse, especially in boys and girls, and that is why they do not eat it.

There is another herb called Popoiauh, which grows like a bush and is marked with black and green. It is eaten raw and cooked, mixed with maize dough, and tortillas are made from it.

There is another called Mexixi. It is a spreading plant with small leaves. It is eaten raw and cooked, mixed with maize, and used to fill tamales. If too much of it is eaten, it causes blisters and excessive heat. The tamales made with this herb are called mexixquil tamalli, and the tortillas are called mexixquillaxcalli.

The seed of this herb is yellow and shaped like lentils; doves eat it a great deal. A medicine called natil omacamoza is made from this herb for those who have sores of matter and blood. This seed has the property of purifying the intestines.

[right column]
It is very warming inside the body, causes sweating, loosens the bowels; and when one is very cold inside, it warms the intestines.

¶ Coiocuexi resembles the vitzquilitl: it is somewhat large, tender, bitter-tasting, and its flower is somewhat small. It is not to be swallowed carelessly; it constricts the throat and is very bitter.

¶ Popoiauh: it is something like a small stump, somewhat like a small tree. The use of popoiauh is: it is very soothing and calming; it can be drunk dissolved in water, and can be strained, and cooked on a griddle.

¶ Mexixin is very peppery and small; it can be dissolved in water to drink. If too much is eaten it causes burning, thirst, and looseness; it can be strained and made into tamales: thus are made the mexixquil tamalli and mexixquillaxcalli. Its inner part is yellow, pale, dripping — very appetizing; and it disturbs digestion in the sick; and the tlaclpatli herb: it expels bile from the intestines; it goes down fiery hot in the throat; its seed makes the belly descend, it acts on the intestines, and purifies the bowels.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another herb called xoxocoioli; these are the sorrels of this land, they are sour, and they are eaten both cooked and raw.

There is another herb called xoxocoiol papatla; it has tall and slender stems and round, wide leaves, and the leaves at the base of the stem are tasty to eat when cooked.

There is another herb called Xoxocoiol cuecuepoc; it has thick and round stems, it has sparse leaves, it blooms, and it is as savory as tomatoes. This herb sprouts when the rains begin.

There are other herbs of this type called xoxocololujvila, spreading ones; they have small, round leaves and are tasty.

There is another herb called mjera xoxocoioli; it is of the same kind as the one described above, xoxocoiol papatla, but the stem is somewhat woody and hairy, and the wide leaves are very sour and set the teeth on edge.

There is another of these herbs called guauh xoxocoioli. It is like the one above. It is pleasant to eat, and they are larger than the ones above.

Xoxocoioli: sour, of good quality, whitish in appearance. It is called xocoioli; it is what is known as xoxocoioli.

Xoxocoiol papatla: it has a pleasant smell, is slender-stemmed; one takes its leaves. It is said of xoxocoiol papatla: it is very tasty and fragrant, and somewhat tart.

Xoxocoiol cuecuepoc: it is fragrant, slender, curling at the tips. It is said of xoxocoiol cuecuepoc: it is very tasty, resembling the tomato; it grows when the rains come.

Xoxocoiolhujvila: it is spreading, branching, small-leafed, tasty.

Mjcaxoxocoioli: it is like xoxocoiol patla, puffed up, hairy, with peeling bark, sour-tasting, and astringent; [it grows] among the rushes.

Quauh xaxocoioli: it is broad, or spreading, stout, like the mjcca xoxocoioli, but tasty, fragrant, good, [and it is also called] nixoxocoiolpipi.

Estas son las cerrajas de castilla, Disen que no las avia en esta tierra, antes que venjesen los espannoles y agora, ay tan tas, que toda la tierra esta lle na dellas, y como la semjlla tie ne alas y buela, ase multipli cado por todas partes.

translation:
On Raw Herbs
Folio 38

There is another herb called quanaaquisitl. This means the herb that the hens of Castile eat. These are the sow-thistles of Castile. They say that these did not exist in this land before the Spaniards came, but now there are so many that the whole land is full of them, and because the seed has wings and flies, it has multiplied everywhere.

There are small onions in this land called xonacatl; they have the flavor of the onions of Spain. These plants are from the caves.

There are other wild little mushrooms that grow in the fields, and they smell strongly.

There are other small wild onions called Maxten; they flower, but they are bitter. The root or the head of these is eaten cooked. They grow in great clusters. From this comes a saying: those who father many children are called maxtenpilva.

There is another herb called papaquisitl. It is fragrant and tasty, has round leaves, and grows in warm lands.
And another herb called Atarosa grows in the fields and among the shrubs; it is similar to the one above, it is wild and produces a kind of resin. It flowers, and its flowers are fragrant.

[Nahuatl column:]
Quanacaquisitl: it is said to resemble the coiocuetchi; it spreads out like lettuce; the lettuce grows mixed with it. And wherever it falls and spreads, it was named quanacaquisitl because the birds fatten on it; it is edible, it makes one speak.

Xonacatl: it is flat, it is bitter-smelling, it is sharp-tasting, it has a beard, it is pungent, it is cooked, it loosens the bowels, it covers and cleans the intestines.
Tepexonacatl: it forms in bundles; it is not fully developed like the cultivated xivitl plant; it is like xonacatl but sharper.
Maxten: it resembles xonacatl, it is juicy, it is crunchy, somewhat firm, somewhat clean; it is shiny and reddish. It is truly very crunchy when chewed, and it is said of one who cannot raise children that his children go wandering. Maxtenpilhoa.
Yapaloqujsitl: it is dark, it is good, it grows in soft places.

Aiauh tona: it grows on the rocky hillsides; it is blue-green, flat, like a wooden rattle, reddish-flowered.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another edible herb,
and it is the herb of the sweet potatoes.

And also the leaves of the jicamas
are eaten.

There is another herb called
tolcima quilit. It is edible.
The flowers of this herb are very
beautiful and very delicate.
The root of this herb is edible;
it was discussed above.

The sweet potato plant: it flowers, it blooms, it puts out runners, it spreads along the ground, it opens its blooms, it has rounded leaves, it is slender-leaved; when planted in sandy soil, it spreads out underground. Its name is camotli; one kind is white, called iztac camotli; another is called porcauh camotli; another is yellowish, called xochicamotli; another is called tlapalcamotli [red sweet potato]. What grows on the surface is not sweet; it is called camoxalli. It can be roasted and eaten raw.

The jicama plant: it is flat, disc-shaped, it blooms, it is fragrant. Its peeled [root] is called jicama; it is round, smooth, crunchy, sweet, fragrant, fresh, with a watery juice, and it makes a crackling sound when bitten.

The tolcima quilit herb: it puts out runners, it twines around things, it opens its blooms, it is soft, it bends back upon itself, it is tender. Its blossoms change color, they are pale, they are blue-green, they have a reddish interior. Its peeled [root] is called tolcimatl; it is ash-colored, fibrous, and woody. The tolcimatl is quite hard; one should not eat too much of it.

text:
delas xicamas                    fo. 139.

¶ La rays delas espadanas tan bien son comestibles.

¶ La rays de la yerua que nace enel agua que tiene las hojas sobre el agua tan anchas como platos que se llama atlacuecona, tiene una rays negra aspera que se llama atlatoMoli, lo interior desta rayz es comestible cozida.

¶ A y una rayz que se llama cacatztli, es redonda y blanca, comose cozida y es sabrosa.

¶ Una frutilla que se llama Xaltomatl o xal totoMatl que es fruta, que se haze en una ierua que se llama xaltoma xihuitl. Esta frutilla alguna della es plana y otra negra, es muy curiosa, y muy dulce y redonda. La rayz desta ierua. Eso comestible cruda y assada y cozida.

¶ A y una yerua que se llama Cototomatl o oio tamatl, nace en ella una frutilla: que es como los tomates chiquitos que se llama miztomatl, tiene su fruta amarilla son dulces traen un poco de la garganta: son comestibles. La rayz desta yerua si se bebe no muy mucho sino templadamente, es medicinal, limpia los intestinos. Las mujeres que dan a mamar la beben purifica se les la leche con ella.

¶ Aca xilotl: tolpatlaetli methoaio, xoxouica guaqua lonj, paoaxviy: nacaxilo tataca, nacaxilo quaqua.

¶ Aha tsamotli methoaio, matla cueconan: chachaquachtie, tecontic, tliltic: mjiollo, paoaxonj, iuh quin quauh nextamalli.

¶ Cacatztli tlaneshoatl, ololtic, paoaxonj, tocio, veli, aviac.

¶ Xaltomatl, xaltotoMatlica pollo: in xaltomaxivitl, cequi tic, cequi tliltic: neuitzopatic, neuttzopiltic, aio, aiopiltztic, ololtic, teosoltic, ololpatic: njxaltomacuycuj, njxaltimaeoa, njxalto on quaqua, vjcpitzinja, njcamapalla, njcamapatca. Injneshoatoins: xoxouicaqualonj, yoan ixconj, yoan paoaxonj, velic.

¶ Coiototomatl, coiototomatl: injcapollo. injtla aquillo, veliuh; quj tomatl: in miztomatl izoaio, cocotic, cocoztic, corpiltic, tzopelic, achitzca chichic mjneshoato. Inatllin vel omjf, tlanoqjlonj, mjcam vel ipam tececjtlax colietti. Intlachin thioal huja, iehoatl conj, icthipasa, icieltia injmaio.
translation:
On Jicamas                    folio 139.

¶ The roots of the cattail are also edible.

¶ The root of the water plant that grows in water, whose leaves spread over the water as wide as plates, called atlacuecona — it has a rough black root called atlatoMoli; the interior of this root is edible when cooked.

¶ There is a root called cacatztli; it is round and white, and is eaten cooked, and it is tasty.

¶ A small fruit called Xaltomatl or xaltotoMatl, which is a fruit that grows on a plant called xaltoma xihuitl. Some of this fruit is flat and others are black; it is very curious, very sweet, and round. The root of this plant is also edible raw, roasted, and cooked.

¶ There is a plant called Cototomatl or oiotamatl; it bears a small fruit like small tomatoes, called miztomatl. Its fruit is yellow; they are sweet and leave a slight tickle in the throat; they are edible. The root of this plant, if drunk in moderation and not too much, is medicinal — it cleans the intestines. Women who are nursing drink it; it purifies their milk.

[Right column, in Nahuatl:]
¶ Aca xilotl: it is called tolpatlaetli; it is yellowish, it dries out quickly, it is somewhat fibrous on the outside, it is fibrous within.

¶ Aha tsamotli: it is called methoaio; it has a tough, fibrous skin; it is firm and dark inside, like a corn-dough tamale.

¶ Cacatztli: it has a white skin, it is round, somewhat firm, fragrant, and tasty.

¶ Xaltomatl, xaltotoMatl — its fruit: on the xaltoma plant, some are firm, some are dark; they are spiny on the outside, somewhat spiny, round, very firm, roundish — one eats them crunching, they spread in the mouth, they spread in the hand. As for its being eaten: it is yellowish, one sucks it, one eats it with chile sauce, it is tasty.

¶ Coiototomatl, coiototomatl — its fruit: if one eats it, it is good; like a tomato: the skin of the miztomatl is thick, dark yellow, somewhat wrinkled, tart, slightly bitter. It is described thus: it is wholly digestible, one swallows it easily, one may eat it with tortillas. If someone is feverish, one drinks it; it passes through them, it refreshes their spirit.

There is a plant called Atltliliati, which produces small dark fruits, somewhat sweet and slightly sour; the leaves of this plant are good for the sweat baths [temascales], for preparing the water with which the sick are bathed.
There is a plant called Halxilotl. It is edible.
There is a plant called Tlalaiots. The plant itself is edible.

Fifth paragraph concerning medicinal plants.

Atltliliati: its fruit is like a dark cherry, blackish, somewhat greenish; its herbal properties benefit the sweat bath, it is administered for ailments of the body.
Halxilotl, edible.
Tlalaiots: it spreads along the ground, like a small waterfall; its juice is drunk, it is decocted. One does not go thirsty with it; it quenches thirst; it makes one speak clearly.

Fifth paragraph, which speaks of trees and of the various kinds of trees.

White medicine [Iztac patli].

Cajeajtlapile, cujtlapile. It is mixed together; it is placed in the hand and rubbed; and everything is ground up with the reddish medicine, acacaxilotic, avatoton, tochtetenpati, cacacilin, white cacalic, atopucapatli, iztac chichicpati; it is all combined together and given to the sick person to drink; and if within three or four days it has not taken effect [illegible].
Iztac cacalie: it flows along the ground, its herb blossoms in a rounded form, it spreads on its own; with it those who spit blood are treated [illegible].

It expels filth; and with this it makes one well, and it is ground with maize; one then grinds it and drinks it as a remedy for the sick.

Maize, small maize: its husk is white, slender; its leaves are rough and mixed, yellowish-brown, and of a rustic sort; in this way it grows in the woodland forests. It cures one who has sores on the skin: one takes some and mixes it alone in water, when it has settled; some scrape off the white outer skin, the tender pale part; one grinds it and drinks it as a remedy for the sick, and it warms one up.

The painted gourd plant, the yellowish-red tladielis: it does not grow tall like a tree, but like a small herb; the yellowish liquid of the leaves is mixed together; it grows in Tepecosco. It is necessary that one who has butterflies in the stomach take it; one mixes a little of it in water and drinks it, not to excess; nothing is mixed in with it, it is taken alone.

The plant called tlanoquitloni: its leaf-skin is white, slender; it is like a turnip; it grows like a small herb in the same manner, in the same way; its mixed juice is small and slender; it grows in Tepoztlan. 32.
There is a medicinal herb called cocoiactic, which the physicians use at the beginning of their treatment. It is shaped like a head of garlic, found underground. When they begin to treat a sick person, they grind this herb together with its roots, and they put a little of its seed into the nostrils of the patient. If applied in greater quantity, it draws blood from the nostrils. It is found in a place called Moctlauhrauhcan, which is on the edge of the forests of Quauhnahuac.

33.
There is another medicinal herb called pipitzaoac; it is something like a dried thing. The root of this herb is ground and given to drink to one who has excessive internal heat, and with it he purges by vomiting; it also causes bowel movements. With it the internal heat is relieved. It also causes purging through the urine of matter, both in men and in women. After the patient has purged with this, he will drink and smell what is made of ground maize. This herb is found in the forests of Chalco.

34.

[Entry on a root plant, continued from previous page:]
...the roots are thick, and it [the plant] is very white, somewhat sweet and spongy. It is good against fever; the water of this root — those who know use it as a purge; after purging it cleanses and purifies the genital parts and heals them, both in men and in women. If there is any abscess, it draws it out. And this same root — if someone has been wounded in the mouth and it is applied to the head, ground and applied green to the head — it also heals. This root helps those who have bad eyes, whose eyelids are swollen and red from heat; anointing them gently with it, they are healed. The leaves of this herb are somewhat reddish-purple; the branches are thin and jagged and are not medicinal. This herb grows in the mountains.

35.

There is another medicinal herb called Coanerepilli. Its root is white, firm, somewhat sweet, brownish on the outside, and white within. One of these roots, ground up, is taken in four doses to purge; it expels bad humors through the mouth and through the bowels. Only a little is drunk for purging. It also tempers excessive heat. Its leaves are clear green, round, and smooth, and are of no medicinal use. If by chance the bowel movements become too many, one should take a little broth of plucked birds called yolatolli. This herb is found in the province of Texcoco, in the open fields and plains, and is rare in the mountains.

translation:
On Medicinal Herbs, folio 144

[Entry 36]
There is another herb called yacatziuhqui; it has a twisted root. This herb is burning and sweet; it is dark on the outside and white on the inside. Ground up, it is given in four doses to purge and remove humors, and it causes all bad humors to be expelled through the mouth and below. One should not take too much of it, but rather moderately; it tempers excessive heat. It has small, round leaves that are of no particular use. If it causes too much flux, the sick person should take a little broth from those porridges called yollailli. This herb is found in the highlands around Texcoco, and in the mountains it is rarely found.

[Entry 37]
There are some maguey plants called teometl that have a yellow stripe along the edge of each leaf, with the rest being green. It is medicinal: the sap is extracted from the lower part of the leaf, and after it is cooked, it is pressed out and mixed with about ten ground squash seeds and the juice of a thousand tomatoes. This mixture is given to drink to someone who has fallen ill; he should drink it with food and should not drink anything else with it — and thus he recovers. These maguey plants grow everywhere in the mountains and also on rooftop terraces. And this is to be taken as a remedy...

[Entry 38 — Nahuatl text]
The herb called yacatziuhqui, also known as tlamalintli: it is bitter like syrup, its sap is dark and watery, its heart is white. When it is ground once, it is a purge; it causes illness to come out through the mouth and also below. One should not take too much of it, and it heats the body inside. If the leaf is fully spread out, it looks like the herb called tzaquylitl; it causes great heat when consumed. And when one takes too much of it, one takes chicken broth or atolli to counteract it. It is used in warm lowland areas, in sunlit places; yet it can be found in forests and on hillsides.

[Entry 37 — Nahuatl text]
The maguey called teometl, also known by the name teumeil: one of its leaves has a yellow edge, the rest of the leaf is greenish. It is used as a remedy for burning: it is squeezed out and washed; it is mixed with tlilcoztli and ten aiovastitli and a thousand tomatoes, all pressed together. With this, the one who is sick in the throat is cured: first he eats, then he drinks it; nothing more comes out afterward. It grows everywhere — in the mountains and in towns — and it enters into the steambath house.

38.
There is a shrub or bush called Chapolxihuit; it has no branches, and the leaves grow from the main trunk itself. The wood is green. The wood together with the leaves is ground up. If someone swallows a piece of something into the body, or stumbles and gets a splinter lodged in the foot, or a bone-spine is driven in, applying this there draws it out. It also heals wounds and cuts that have become infected. This shrub grows everywhere, in the plains and in the mountains.

39.
There is another medicinal herb called Totonaxihuit; it has round, very green leaves and is not sprawling but rather upright. With the leaves and roots ground up, abscesses are healed, like those from bruises and swellings. By applying the powders mixed with water on top of the abscess, some abscesses open up and others are resolved. This herb grows in the mountains.

40.
There is another medicinal root called Huei Patli. These roots are round, like truffles from the earth, and are intertwined with one another. They have round leaves with sharp points; the leaves are of no use. But the roots, ground up and drunk with water, are beneficial. 41.
There is another medicinal herb called yxyayaoal. It is something that has small, round, greenish leaves, and its root is somewhat dark. It removes excessive heat when drunk with water; it purifies the urine. With the ground leaves of this herb placed on the heads of children, it removes their mange. It also cures diarrhea and excessive heat. The root is ground with the leaf of the herb zeloguiltic; it is good for those who have stopped having bowel movements, and then it produces them. It grows among crags and cliffs.

42.
There is another medicinal herb called zeloguiltic. It has tall, slender branches. Its ground leaves, when drunk, aid digestion and refresh, and provoke urination. It grows in the mountains.

translation:
Of Medicinal Herbs                      folio 146.

45.                                45.
There is another medicinal herb called Cacacili; it spreads itself along the ground. Its branches are long; its leaves are somewhat broad and somewhat narrow. On this herb there grow white flowers that are of no use. The root of this herb is somewhat sweet; it is good against bloody dysentery when drunk and taken with a little chia seed water as a drink. It is taken after eating. It is also good for broken bones, applied on top with something adhesive like tzacutli resin or aromatic pitch. It is also beneficial for apostemes such as swellings and similar ailments; applied on top it brings the aposteme to maturity. It is also good for drawing out a splinter, thorn, bone fragment, or piece of flesh from the body. This herb grows in the mountains of Xochimilco and in all the mountains.

[Nahuatl column 45:]
Cacacili: it spreads itself right along the ground, it grows flat, it is reddish, somewhat warm, somewhat greenish; like the leaf of the Castilian rose-flower, not bitter, somewhat round, and its flower blooms white; its skin is somewhat rough, a little fragrant, it closes up. One who has pain on the side of the foot: and also mixed with chia seed water it becomes a drink; afterward one drinks it after eating. And one whose foot is broken, or whose thigh is broken, or who has been struck, or who has been kicked, or whose shin has been injured: it is spread there; it heats like a poultice, it binds up; when it is applied the pain is relieved, and it squeezes out and flattens the injury, it drains it. And it scrapes away what is in a wound in the body — it grows in the forest, along the edges of roads, in Xochimilco, in the forest; it grows everywhere.

46.
There is another medicinal herb called Iztac palancapatli: it is a sparse plant with very thin leaves, and its flowers are half white and half colored; its leaves and flowers are of no use. It has many long, thick, white roots.

[Nahuatl column 46:]
Iztac palancapatli: it is dark green, like a broad amate-tree leaf, tattered, whitish, rough on one side, it does not make a good infusion. Its skin is somewhat bitter, not good to drink...

translation:

Tree-like herbs: the root is not drunk unless ground up, and the powder is applied to a festering wound made by a bruise when it is already beginning to heal so that it closes. It is found on hillsides and heights.

¶ 47.
¶ There is another medicinal herb called Cototsauhguxiupl. The branches and leaves of this herb are narrow and slender, like the leaves of the maguey. The root of this herb is somewhat bitter and sweet; it is purgative and causes the humors to flow. Those who have dryness in the chest and throat drink it ground up to relieve that dryness, and in this way it expels phlegm and waste matter. The branches of this herb are of no use. It grows in the highlands.

¶ 48.
¶ There is another herb called Cococ xihuipl, also known as oto coc patli or pjlxiupl; it grows no more than one vara [in height].

[Nahuatl column:]
It has a single stalk; it is altogether white, firm, and stiff, like a grass blade, it is ground. When it is placed somewhere, it is not slippery to the touch; when it heals, the copal resin mingles with it and causes swelling together with heat. If it decays, or if there is nothing to eat of it — neither fever nor congestion follows from it; it produces no condition on the mountain slopes.

¶ Cototsauhqui herb: it is of a reddish hue, like a sapling; it is somewhat small. Its inner part is acrid and bitter to taste, sharp and altogether bitter; it is somewhat watery when ripe. It cannot easily be swallowed; it is very irritating to the throat; it is very harsh; one drinks it when there is congestion. If something has rotted inside, some people use it as an emetic. When used: if there is nothing being consumed, it heals that which ails; its greenery is somewhat watery. It grows on hillsides.

¶ Cococ xiuisl, cocoepatli — it is likewise not to be applied externally; like a small half-measure, it barely [illegible].

translation:
On Medicinal Herbs                    Folio 147

[The first plant] has three or four little branches; its greenness is somewhat yellow on the branches and on the leaves; the branches and leaves are of no use. The root is like a radish; it is useful for those who are constipated. It is not drunk but given as an enema. It is pungent like chili, and should be taken in moderation, not too much. This herb is found throughout all the mountains.

49
There is another medicinal herb called chichientic. It is a shrub; it has leaves, and the leaves and branches are somewhat reddish; its root is like a slender radish. It is somewhat sweet. For those who are treated with the herb described above, it is given to them to drink, and no other water is given, as it is cold. It is found throughout all the mountains.

50
There is another medicinal herb called Coroczihujtl. It is a shrub; it has slender branches and longish leaves, and furthermore it has flowers like chia. It has many roots, dense and somewhat yellowish on the outside. It will help those who have too much internal heat and aids greatly. It is not drunk but given as an enema. The branches are of no use, but it also helps [others].

[Right column — Nahuatl text:]

49: The chichientic herb — its surface color is somewhat reddish, like the flower of amaranth. Its root is just like that of the radish, somewhat slender and slightly bitter. It is found everywhere in the hills.

With a little maize, and one who has too much internal heat drinks it. The plant cooked is found along the maize fields and in the mountains.

§4
There is another medicinal herb called Xorocosioltic. It has one long stem and other small branches growing from it. Its leaves are shaped like a heart, rough and reddish, good for nothing [on their own]. It has a single root, round as a seed. The outer surface of the root is white, and inside it is white and bitter. It is medicinal for those who have damage to the member, inserting [it] inside, and also for those who are constipated in the bowels, taking it by enema. It must be mixed with a little white pulque without mixture, and one will vomit with it, and it will also expel the material that is inside the member. Having taken it in this way, the sick person will have a little broth of the gruel they call yolatolli. Having taken this, he may eat, but he must not drink cold water. This herb is found on rocky crags and cliffs.

§5.
There is another medicinal herb called Tlacoxihujtl. It is a shrub and has all its branches green like its own leaves. Its flowers are yellow. Its branches are angular; its roots spread outward.

[Nahuatl column §4:]
Xorocosioltic: the herb is dark-colored, spreading its branches, grayish-white, with mesquite-like wood, resembling [another plant], not entwining. Its root is just one single round bulb; on its surface it is yellowish, inside white. Whoever uses it for [urinary trouble] or similar ailments: it expels [the obstruction], causing something to come out quickly. It also relieves suffering: it will remove the pain in the sides; it grows everywhere in houses. The turkey-broth [is taken] first; and after, one eats, but not [cold water]. §5. Tlacoxivitl: it spreads in many directions like reeds spreading, it is green; its leaves spread like paper leaves, yellow-veined, and it blooms in gardens. The Tlacoxiuh branches spread in four directions.

...very green, rounded; they have some purple flowers that are of no use. The root of this herb is large and great, like a tree root, enough to provide from it. Made into strips together with squash seeds and grains of maize, the water of the decoction is strained and made like porridge. It is given to drink to those in labor. If some woman, after illness, had her husband approach her and for that reason she falls ill again, she drinks it two or three times and recovers. It is also drunk raw, ground and mixed with water: when someone begins to feel sick, all this expels through the mouth bile and phlegm. Those who have too much heat and anguish in the heart also drink it, and with this it is relieved. After drinking, they take a little chicken broth. This herb is rare. It is found in the mountains.

[Nahuatl column:]
It is yellowish-green, greenish: just as the arvarcoque [plant], its color is like that of a green thing: like what is called caxtlatlapa ixothio, movitic: it does not sting. Its inner surface is dark: just like the quauhtontotl [bird]: when one needs to use it, it spreads, it crackles, it bursts. And aiovaltelli, ground: it makes one well. It boils: just like water it becomes. This must be used so that one does not become sick again, or a woman. It quickly makes one sleep, or it makes a woman sleep: drink it two, three, four times. ...and white on the inside, they are thick and long and bitter. Toasted in lard and ground, it helps those who bleed from the nose — blowing it into the nostrils — and for those who have a cough, give it to drink with water and blow it through the mouth to loosen phlegm; it softens the chest. This herb is found throughout the mountains.

[Entry 59]
There is another herb called Chichilquiltic. It is red on the surface; it has long branches and stems; the leaves are narrow at the base and wider and pointed toward the top, and it has nodes; its joints are like canes. The herb itself is of no benefit. The roots, however, are a useful drink for those who have excessive internal heat or external coldness, or who feel coldness in the nerves. With this herb, drunk as a beverage, the heat comes out from within. When drinking it, one should not eat hot tortillas nor anything else harmful. It grows everywhere, in the plains and on the hillsides.

[Entry 60]
There is another medicinal herb called tlailayotli. It spreads along the ground like wild gourds. The leaves of this plant are edible. Its root is like the tocamatl and is between sweet and bitter. Ground and mixed with the resin called ocote oil, it heals abscesses when rubbed on with it.

[Nahuatl column, right side — translation of same entries:]

[59] It is watery, its interior is white, somewhat reddish, somewhat long-stalked, dark-colored: it causes one to sneeze. Whoever bleeds from the nose and cannot stop it — one blows it in, it stops the blood; it relieves the stuffiness in the head. It grows only in the mountains. [Entry 59]

Chichilquiltic: somewhat reddish, tall, somewhat long in appearance, with a rounded top, wide-headed, very fibrous inside, its surface is striped. It warms whoever drinks it; it places fire inside: when the sun is hot it pains one, or it spreads heat throughout one's body; then afterwards it drives out all the heat that was inside. And when drinking it, one should not eat hot tortillas or chili, for it will cause chills. It grows only in the fields and on the hillsides. [Entry 60]

Tlatalaiaxihuitl: it spreads out somewhat, likewise its leaves are edible. When drunk: it is like tol-amatl; with honey it is [prepared], found where the sun is warm...

And the powders of it are also drunk in the same way. It grows in the plains and in the highlands.

[Illustration 61: a plant with round leaves]

There is another medicinal herb called tepeamalacotl. It is like the herb that grows in water called amamalacotl; it has small round and flat leaves, it has thin and long branches and the leaf is at the tip of the branch. From the branch up to the leaf there is nothing; the roots are like small balls. It is rough and is beneficial for coughs and for digestion. Four of these little balls are taken at one time, and for children, one each. It grows on hillsides and rocky outcroppings.

[Illustration 62: a plant with colored stems]

There is another medicinal herb called Ystaquyltic; it has reddish stems and greenish, somewhat ash-colored leaves. The leaves and the stem are not useful; the long stem is beneficial for those who pass cloudy urine. And it should be drunk only once, and with it the body is also cooled, and in this way it cures mange. It grows on hillsides and in the mountains.

[Nahuatl column:]

...it unites with it; when it heals, the palaxtle spreads there, it heals; and a little bit [of it] — it is produced everywhere, in the cornfields and on the hillsides. 61.

Tepeamalacotl: it truly resembles the amalacotl that grows in the water; its leaves are small and round, like a circle in its leaf surface; it resembles turquoise as it sits there, its woody part is small and tender, it is quite quickly consumed when eaten. Its medicinal use is that it relieves heat, it is slightly hot and spicy; it causes those who are burning with fever to cool; it relieves dysentery; four are eaten. And for small children, just one is to be eaten; it grows on rocky places.

62.
Istaquiltic — it truly resembles the istaquiltl. It is edible; its wood is reddish; its leaf surface is dry and ashy-looking; the leaf surface is not needed. And its skin, when scraped, resembles the cimatotl root; it is pressed and drunk by those who want cacao; it is drunk only once; it is applied to oneself; it grows everywhere, in the cornfields and on the hillsides.

Book Eleven.
63. 63.

There is another medicinal plant called Tlalmizquitl. It is a shrub that has leaves like the tree called mizquitl, but the leaves and branches are not useful. The root of this plant is yellow, like the root of the cimatl; it has only one root, which is long and flavorful. It is ground up and drunk ground on an empty stomach. It is beneficial for those who have diarrhea. And for those who have too much internal heat, it cools them, and they should eat cold things after having drunk it. This plant is found in the plains and in the mountains.

64.

There is another medicinal plant called poca vizpatli. It has wide leaves; its form is like that of a fig tree, though the leaves are small, very green, with sharp points. They spread along the ground. The leaves are bitter. It has a root like a radish — yellow on the outside and white on the inside. The root is ground with the leaves. It is beneficial for those who are swollen and who have internal sores. The ground plant is applied to the places of the sores and swellings, and in this way they heal. It is found in the mountains.

[Nahuatl column, entry 63:] Tlalmizquitl, tlacotl: its leaf is like that of the huizquitl, it is not eaten. It is said that its root is yellow like the cimatl; it causes sweating; it is fragrant, flavorful, and satisfying. It need not be eaten raw. It is needed so that one may relieve oneself; it relieves the heat of the body; it calms and refreshes the bowels in those who are ill. It grows in the plains and in the mountains. 64.

[Nahuatl column, entry 64:] Poca vizpatli, a plant that spreads on the ground, like fig leaves in shape; it is somewhat thick, firm, pointed, and rough. It spreads along the ground. It is bitter. Its root is like a radish — yellow on the outside, white inside. It is needed to apply as a poultice over swellings. Its root, ground together with its leaves, is applied to those who have sores and swellings, and thus they heal. It grows in the mountains.

There is another medicinal herb called Vavauhtзin, or white-wood, which was described above as being against excessive heat. It is also medicinal for the swelling of the male member, and for this purpose it is ground together with the leaves and flowers of the herb called marlalli and mixed with hot water. Also, this herb ground and drunk is against typhus fever, which begins to appear with spots like verdigris; and by drinking this herb it soon comes out, but it is necessary to bleed the patient. It is also useful for one who has continual loose bowels, drunk as a decoction with hot water and mixed with a little chia seed. It is found everywhere in the mountains.

(Nahuatl column 65): Vavauhtзin: and the white-wood mentioned above counters heat and matches it. When properly prepared, it matches the white-wood remedy: when one mixes it with the green herb, with ixохio, and with vavauhtзin, it reduces fever. It appears where it lives in rocky places: it grows in two or three places, spreading on the ground. When it is time, it soon spreads out; then it reduces fever. And when one always drinks it, if one cannot easily digest, for a small child, or for one who is sick with fever, one applies the white-wood remedy; and it is found everywhere in the mountains.    66.

The roots of this herb are long and white, and small and astringent; ground and taken in water, it benefits those who have recovered from some illness that caused fever and who still have too much internal heat. It causes them to expel through the mouth bile, phlegm, and matter. After expelling it, one drinks a gruel called Yolatolli. It grows in the mountains.

· 69 ·

There is another medicinal herb called Chichilquyltic; its root is like a bulb. Its branches are somewhat long; its leaves are roundish, serrated, and somewhat reddish — they are of no benefit. The root is somewhat sweet; on the outside it is black, and on the inside white. Ground with kernels of maize, it benefits those who have great internal heat, and it purifies the urine and promotes urination. After taking it, one should eat cool foods. It grows in the mountains.

[decorative border]

In other places: four times fifteen [doses]. It causes fever to rise, it causes fever to surge — but it does not make fire come out. One is rubbed with it when it is fresh: it is like a cooling herb. It is a little thing that one takes; or when one becomes exhausted internally. The root is needed for one who suffers from constipation, who is severely feverish and whose body is very hot: with it one is purged, and through it the illness comes out. It is yellowish and sour-smelling, and crusty: when it is all used up it comes out, and then the gruel of tule reeds is given; it grows in the forest.

Chichilquyltic: its appearance is like that of a small quauhtzon-tapacolton: its leaves are broad and thick, long and branching; its leaves are broad and rounded, very warm and tingling with heat; it is sharp and somewhat reddish, it just falls apart. Its inner part is not dark; it has a refreshing pleasant smell; on top it is white, its fibers mix with a matlactetl [ten-root], moconteci. For one who has internal heat: it also causes the urine to come out swiftly, and causes vigorous urination.

¶ 70.
¶ There is another medicinal herb called Vauauhtın; it is a low plant, and it has narrow leaves, and its shoots and branches are reddish and somewhat sickly; its leaves are somewhat ash-colored and hairy; its roots are dense on the outside, yellow, and the interior is also yellow, and the innermost part is white. Ground up with its branch it is good for numbness and cramps of the feet when drunk with water. It is also good for ailments of the chest. This herb grows in the plains and on hillsides.

¶ 71.
¶ There is another medicinal herb called Aztaquiltic, and by another name tepeatocoxochitl. It is a bush; it has long branches; it has small leaves like those of the cedar tree; it is very green and smooth. The root of this herb is of no use; the branch is what is good. It helps those who have difficulty urinating — they must drink it ground up and mixed with water, and they must drink no other water but this. It also helps those who spit blood. It purges bad humors through the mouth. And those who have epilepsy, if it is given to them to drink at the onset of the illness, they are cured. It also helps those —

[Nahuatl column:]
— so that the fevers that afflict people pass; and also this food improves one. It grows in the forest.

¶ Vauauhtın: it resembles quelite greens; likewise it spreads out and spreads flat; its leaves are rough; its stem is woody; it is pale, somewhat whitish-green, bitter. This plant's herb cures, and also its sap, which is yellowish-white in color; it is good for chilling of the feet and for swellings. This plant heals fevers; it likewise grows on hillsides.

¶ This one is greenish, also called tepeatocoxochitl; it has long thin branches like those of the ahuehue cypress, four-sided, with flower-like markings, somewhat rough. Its wood is not used; this plant's herb likewise has no use. It helps those who cannot urinate frequently, and it purges things. And for one who spits blood, or yellowish, dark discharge — it expels illness. And for one whose illness has just begun, if he drinks it —

...for those who spit up matter, and for those who spit up matter it should be mixed with the herb mentioned above called hauauhtzin, to purge the humors downward. It grows in the mountains and rocky places.

72.
¶ Now another medicinal herb called quauhelo quiltic. And by another name it is called quauhelo xochitl, and by yet another name cerochitl. It is a shrub; its branches have sections; it has wide leaves, pointed and long and somewhat thick; the flower of this herb is a clear blue. The leaves and branches are of no use. The root is medicinal; when ground up and drunk with water, it helps those who have excessive internal heat and should drink no other water but that. It is also drunk when in good health and it benefits the veins. They are found everywhere, but are rare.

73.
¶ Another medicinal herb called hujujtoquiltic — it is like the thistles of Castile that are eaten, but they are chilies; the leaves like a palm, and it grows and flowers; and the flowers are yellow. The herb itself is of no use. The root smells of urine and on the outside is black and on the inside is white; it is cooked in water...

[Nahuatl column:]
...or else boiled in water. And it is used for those who have a sore throat, so that they may swallow and relieve the inflammation there, so that the soreness and burning may cease. It grows in wooded places and on hillsides.

72.
¶ Quauh eloguiltic, and also called quauh eluxochitl, or cerochitl — a vine: it has woody stems and its leaves are broad and flat and spreading, not very thick; its leaves are dark green, and it falls easily. It is said that one must grind it fine; it is not bitter, quite palatable: it causes one to vomit somewhat, and truly one recovers from it; it helps when a fever comes on with great heat. It grows everywhere in the forests and in various places.

73.
¶ Vivizquiltic: it is also known as Castilian vizquiltic; it is small, entirely fragrant, also having a pleasant smell, with yellow flowers, not causing burning to the herb. It is not bitter when eaten; it is beneficial, whitish inside. For those who are sick it relieves them, with constipation:

And that water, drunk, benefits those who have relapsed into some illness. It should be drunk on an empty stomach, twice. It calms the whole body, and the one who drinks it should not eat anything with chili. It grows in the mountains and on the rocky slopes.

74.

¶ Ayotia is a medicinal herb called memeia, which means "it gives milk." It has a single branch, with long and broad leaves, pointed, and a white flower. The branches and leaves have no benefit; the roots do. The color of this herb is chestnut-brown on the outside, and white on the inside. It has no flavor at all, only like water. It should be taken ground up with some grains of maize and mixed with warm water: one of these roots, or bulbs, is divided into three or four portions for drinking. Drunk in this way, it benefits those who have stomach trouble, whose intestines rumble, and whose belly is swollen — with this it heals. It causes the expulsion of bile, phlegm, and matter through the mouth. It should be taken on an empty stomach, and after taking it the sick person should drink a porridge called yolatolli, and afterward eat, but not anything with chili. It also provokes the bowels and expels worms. It grows on all the mountains and hillsides.

[Nahuatl column:]
Twice [it should be taken]; it is wholly mixed; for it is thus that the small round one is mixed together when one drinks it, when one does not vomit it up; it comes out everywhere through the nose. And one should not swallow it all down: on the ground, on the hillside is where it grows. 74.

¶ Memeia is a small herb: it grows as a single stem; its root is round and elongated; its interior is fibrous and small; its surface is smooth; its leaves are spread wide and flat; broad and somewhat flat; its flower is white; it does not produce milk. When the root is chewed it is not bitter, not astringent, not harsh — it tastes nothing at all different. Its root, when dried, is yellow inside; together with salt it cannot be taken as a single dose, nor can it be taken when large. One full dose is taken twice: it is necessary that it be administered to a young person whose joints are cracking as he goes about, and whose flesh is not swelling up; and one whose sides are always cold — whether a woman or a youth — whose joints ache; the root is ground and mixed together with vachtli liquid; one takes it alone, and one drinks the water [of it].

75.
There is a medicinal herb called tetzmjtic. It resembles the plant called tetzmeth. It is also called quauholli. It has very green, tough, and rounded leaves; it also produces a milky sap, and its branches are reddish. The milk flows from the leaves and from the shoots when cut. This milk, applied to the eyes, reduces their heat and removes their redness, and it also clarifies and purifies them. The roots of this herb are sweet, thick, and somewhat long; on the outside they are chestnut-colored, and on the inside white. The inner part of the root, ground up, stimulates urine and purifies it; it also reduces excessive heat. It grows in the mountain marshes.

[right column]

Or in just the same way it serves as medicine: it draws out what is yellow, what is greenish-white, and also phlegm. When nothing is being eaten, afterward one washes out, one does not vomit what one has drunk. And it expels whatever is rotten inside the body, whether lice or worms. It grows everywhere in the hills and forests.    75.

The tetzmjtic is quite similar to the tizmietl; it grows in the hills just as the tetzmeti does, and its other name is quaolli. Its leaves are green, leathery, somewhat round, smooth, and thick-veined; the surface of the leaves is shiny, and their underside is like the surface of the tlatlaoatl plant, dripping: whoever wipes their eyes with its white milky juice, or if one whose eyes are irritated uses it — it is applied, it is smoothed on, one rubs the eyeball with it, and it draws out the heat that has settled there.
