76.

This is a medicinal herb called Batsayanalgujtic. The small branches of this herb grow abundantly above the ground; it has leaves like the herb called Bayanalgujlit, with small leaves and very green stalks. It is not remarkable. The root of the herb is single and looks like beads strung together; on the outside it is light chestnut-colored, and inside it is white. It is ground up and mixed with water and drunk; it benefits nursing women when their milk has dried up — drunk many times, it purifies the milk. They also give it to drink to a child who has diarrhea, and with it the diarrhea stops. They also extract the gum from it, which purifies the veins of children. Women who are nursing should not eat [certain foods] because it causes diarrhea in the children they are nursing. It grows in the mountains and on the cliffs.

77.

This is a medicinal herb called Ycheayo; it has long, narrow leaves, many of them, and they rise up —

[Nahuatl column, entry 76:]
Tzatsaianalgujstic — the herb sprouts from the ground and its roots spread out; its leaves resemble those of the amate tree, it has no fragrance, it is only small. Its color is greenish; it does not cause thirst, nor does it bind. Its root looks like small round beads lined up in a row, reddish on the outside, white inside, rough to the touch. It is used when a child has diarrhea; it is ground up and given to drink. It purifies the urine of small children. Nursing women should not eat [certain things] because it will cause the children they nurse to die. It grows in the forests.

[Nahuatl column, entry 77:]
Its name is xcviii; it is flat along the ground, its leaves lie spread out on the surface; it is one handspan wide, and it has many [branches] —

Beneath the ground are the little spines, like a finger of the maguey plant; they are somewhat ash-colored and have small hairs and are not tall; they are medicinal. These leaves, when ground up, are applied on top of the sores of those who have buboes. Those who have buboes should not eat fish or meat. This plant grows in the mountains.

It has thin roots and thick leaves. The leaves and roots of this plant are pungent. When ground up together, roots and herb alike, they are beneficial for hemorrhoids — the powder is applied on top of the hemorrhoids and they heal; the powder should be applied many times. It grows everywhere, in the fields and in the mountains.

translation:
Book Eleven

Chapter 79

There is another medicinal herb called Mexihujtl. It has many small branches growing from a single base; its leaves are reddish, and so are its branches. It produces flowers that are also reddish. Its leaves are broad and jagged, and somewhat rough to the touch. They grind its roots and leaves into a powder, which is useful against swollen glands and hard knots. They mix the powder with a little pine resin and apply it with feathers pressed on top. This herb grows among the scrublands and also in the mountains.

Chapter 90

There is another medicinal herb called Hujtso cujtlapil xihujtl. It is a shrub. Its branches are somewhat reddish; it has no more than one straight main stem, from which smaller branches grow, tapering as they go upward. Its leaves are broad, jagged, very green, and sharply pointed at the tips. It produces yellow flowers. The leaves and branches are not useful. The root is useful: it is black on the outside and yellow on the inside, and it has a burning quality.

[Right column - Nahuatl:]
It is found everywhere: also in the valleys, on the hillsides, on the sandy plains, and in the forests.
Mexiujtl: it is thick, sharp, somewhat reddish on the underside of its leaves, and also rough-textured; its surface resembles the coloring of the tlapalhoauhtli plant; its leaf surface is rounded and small; it contracts slightly; it is altogether rooted and sprouts. One who is afflicted with swollen growths, or wherever the flesh is consumed — it is applied there: at times, a small bird nests in it; it is very hot; it is found abundantly in the maguey fields and in the forests.

Chapter 90

Vitocujtlapilxivitl: it is somewhat thick, chili-red in its rough texture, in its herbage; it stands up tall; it spreads like water; it rises in a column; it is cloud-like in its leaves, which are small and spiny, very green and sharp-tasting; its sap is yellowish; it is not good to eat; it has a burning quality in its upper parts; the interior is sharp and hot; it is ground [rest illegible].

Ground and mixed with lukewarm water, it is administered as a suppository, and it purges the clotted matter and congealed blood of the male or female member. It also helps with pain in the urinary passage and with constipation; it is to be taken on an empty stomach and one should not eat until one has purged. It is found everywhere, in the plains and on the hillsides.

91.
There is a medicinal herb called Iztacpatli [White Medicine] that spreads over the ground. Its leaves resemble those of the cedar ahueverl. They are small, light green; it has little flowers armed among the leaves. Its roots are white, thick and bitter to the taste, and numerous. These ground herbs are useful: ground up they help with swellings or abscesses that are under the skin, applied on top as an ointment. One should drink water from the root called Iztacquauhyil. This herb is found everywhere, in the plains and on the hillsides.

[Nahuatl text:] It draws out and expels the filth; or it stops bleeding; it relieves the pain of the bowels. It does not harm anything; it spreads on the ground. And one may use the Castilian measure of it; otherwise it will not go well; it will make one faint and vomit; if one takes too much of it, one will become ill; and then it acts as a purge on the bowels, spreading over everything and causing it to happen.

91. Iztacpatli, a small herb, it spreads on the ground surface: it is like a mature, broad-leafed plant, slender-stemmed, with whitish leaves; it bears flowers, it spreads its flowers everywhere in the grass; its leaves are white, it is very bitter; it spreads widely, covering the ground; it is medicine. It is necessary for one who has rotten flesh: it is a hot white thing, it causes evaporation; only where rot is, where there is no decay, it greatly reduces it; it is a medicine, it is placed over it. It goes, it reaches mountain-lions. It is found everywhere here in the mountains; and one should not eat the fruit.

Book Eleven, page 92

There is a shrub called quauhtlacalhoastli; it has broad, sparse, and rounded leaves with fringed edges, and tawny-colored flowers. The roots of this shrub are medicinal — they are thick, white, very bitter, and tough. These roots, cut into splinters and soaked in water for some time so that the water takes on the essence of the root, are given as a drink to those who have the skin disease of this land called tlanavail; it is to be drunk on an empty stomach. It can also be drunk ground up in water. It also purifies the urine. Likewise, the powder of this root is applied to the skin disease called Nanavatl. It is also beneficial for those who have ailments of the chest and suffer from poor digestion. It is also helpful for those who relapse from some illness. It also purifies the milk of nursing women. This root, prepared in water, is very beneficial. The plant grows in the mountains, on the plains, and in the fields.

[Nahuatl column:]
Quauhtlacalhoastli; it is a small tree, a small shrub. It is wide-leafed and spreading, its leaves spread out broadly, they are rough-surfaced, greenish, somewhat dark-colored, not shiny. Its root is called quauhnelhoatl — it is thick, white, very bitter, astringent; it can be split apart; it is soaked in water and the water is drawn off. It is needed for one who is continuously afflicted with the itching skin disease nanavatl; and it purifies one's urine, and one bathes in the water in which it has soaked, and it heals the one who can no longer eat well, who finds food sour in the mouth, and who can no longer drink cacao. And it also heals nursing women who have weaned their child, or who have fallen ill; and it also purifies a woman's milk. And it is said that the root, when ground up or prepared, is given to drink like an atole; it thickens like a cooked dough. In the mountains [it grows]...

It is said to be somewhat sweet, and one portion is enough to drink three times. It grows in the mountains and on the plains.

¶ 95.

¶ There is another medicinal herb called Yztauhiatl. It is like wormwood of Castile. It is also bitter. The leaf or herb, like wormwood of Castile: this herb ground or crushed benefits many things; drunk ground with water, it expels bile and phlegm; it is also a good drink for those who suffer from chills. It also expels excessive internal heat; it also purifies the urine; and it also somewhat benefits one who has a burning sensation in the head. It is also beneficial ground together with the pith of the branches of the herb called quauhyayaual, for those who have anguish of the heart due to some humor that oppresses them — drink it boiled with water and it heals. It grows in all parts of the fields.

[Nahuatl column:]
Iztauhiatl, it causes warmth, it is greenish, it has fine feathery leaves, just like Castilian wormwood in appearance: it is ground, mixed together, its various properties meet one with another. When phlegm settles, it dissolves it abundantly, it purges. And for one who is feverish, drinking it: it relieves the burning sensation in the heart; and also for one whose head throbs with heat — it is applied there. And when one is very ill with fatigue of the heart, it is gathered and ground; the iztauhiatl and the quauhiaiauh snake's pith are combined with it; and also what is mixed with it, being taken, the heart becomes refreshed; it heals.

[Entry] 96.
Another medicinal herb called Quauhyayaval. It has small, longish green branches toward the tips; the leaves are thin, somewhat rounded, a little hairy and rough. The herb is ground dry and mixed with incense; it is good for fumigation. The root is not useful. It grows throughout all the mountains.

[Entry] 97.
Another medicinal herb called Mamaxila; the herb is edible both raw and cooked. The roots are medicinal for bruises and bumps on the feet. It grows in marshes and swampy places.

[Entry] 98.
Another medicinal herb called Saltomatl. The root of this herb, ground together with the root mentioned above, is good for those who have trouble urinating. These are also mixed with a few grains of maize and drunk on an empty stomach, or after eating, and no other water should be drunk besides this. In this way it purifies the urine and makes it flow more freely. It grows everywhere in the cultivated fields and in the ravines.

...it is used as medicine, one drinks it, mixing it; it is needed when one cannot urinate easily. As for the Quauhxinanal: the herb is dark; its surface is reddish, its leaves yellowish-green, somewhat rounded and not wide, not entirely smooth; it is needed when one mixes its sap alone and fumigates with it; and it is also used alone. It also grows on hillsides; it is well suited for cooking and eating.

[Entry 97 in Nahuatl:]
Mamaxila: an herb that is edible, that can be sucked, yellowish-green, somewhat small and round; it serves as medicine. Its juice is needed to make things shrink a little; its surface is reddish, somewhat flat; underneath it is somewhat yellowish, glossy; it cures foot sores.

[Entry 98 in Nahuatl:]
As for the Saltomatl, as has been mentioned: it is combined with the juice of the Mamaxila, and also the root of the Saltomatl is likewise used for drinking as medicine. It is needed for one who has pain in urinating, who urinates with difficulty, who urinates in drops; it is also well combined, ground together with dried maize kernels; even before eating or after one has already eaten, one drinks it with epazote. Thus it purifies the urine that comes out in drops; it also grows on the hillsides and in open, flat country.

There is another medicinal herb called Quapopultzin. It has long, slender, forked branches; from the forks grow the leaves. The earth is very green and a little foul-smelling; it has flowers among the branches and leaves. This herb, ground up, is good for abscesses that arise from heat. Ground up and placed on them, it opens them; it is also mixed with a little tequixquitl salt. After the abscess has been opened with the tequixquitl mixture, soaked wicks are inserted into the opening and it heals.

103.

There is another medicinal herb called Tonalxihujtl; it has ashen-colored leaves. It grows spreading close to the ground; it has tender leaves that are brittle, and they are somewhat narrow. It produces small white flowers with a yellowish center when ground: its leaves and branches are good against mange — place them ground upon the mange. The roots of this herb are of no benefit, and the herb harms the tongue if it dries it out. This herb always grows near water and in every place: in the lowlands and in the highlands.

White and somewhat small, tending toward purple; the branches are of no use. The root of this plant is blackish on the outside, and is thick like a turnip; the inside is white and somewhat sweet. This root, ground together with the branches of the plant called chilparto, is good for stopping nosebleeds — applying the ground root inside the nostrils. It is also beneficial for those who have great internal heat; it should be drunk on an empty stomach mixed with water. It also purifies the urine when it becomes thick. It grows in the mountains and everywhere.

[illustration: a tree with leaves]

And there is another medicinal plant called Ocopiaztli, or Tlilpotongui. Its leaves come out of the ground without branches; they are as long as a palm, paddle-shaped into a stalk, and the flowers are green and cup-shaped or round. It has thick, thin, and long roots. The leaf ground with the root is beneficial against swellings that arise from heat — it is applied ground on top of them. It is also drunk in a small amount mixed with water on an empty stomach; if drunk after eating it aids digestion afterward. Placed on swellings, sometimes it opens them, sometimes it resolves them. It must be applied many times, mixed and ground together with the root of the plant that [continues on next page]...

It is called xalacocotli. Mixed with white pulque, it is drunk against the swellings mentioned above. This herb xalacocotli is hollow like a Castilian reed, but it has many branches beginning from the root; it has many small branches like little forks divided into small tendrils that are green; and the flowers it produces are yellow. The branches are of no use. The root is useful as stated above. It grows throughout the mountains.

106.
There is a medicinal tree called topocan; it has wide, rounded leaves that are pointed at the tip, they are green and somewhat whitish and hairy; it has a somewhat bad smell; it is used against excessive heat of the head, whether in children or in adults. It has thick and long roots.

[Nahuatl text:] It is white and hot; some drink it well when someone has been bitten by a deer, or when a swelling has come down. And wherever the heat is, there the medicine is applied; some use it to purge; some only use it as a tonic. It is placed repeatedly, it meets [the illness], it disperses the root of xalacocotli: it is thick, just like the root of a great tree, very bitter; in the white pulque it goes, or in water. And the xalacocotli, its nature is hollow, just like Castilian reed: it spreads its herb-leaves; but it has no fruit at all; its herb is hollow inside, as has been said. It grows everywhere, in the forests, on the hillsides. 106.

Topocan is a true tree; its leaves are small, flat and broad, wide, large; on the surface they are somewhat yellowish-green, and underneath they are lime-colored, and downy; its herb is blue-green; it is applied to the heads of small children, or also of grown people, when fire is placed upon the head [i.e., when they have fever]. For those who have bloody dysentery, they should drink it on an empty stomach, or a while after eating. With this, the bloody dysentery is stanched. Best for this purpose are the piths of the stripped branches, and also the leaves of this same tree, ground up and placed on the head. There is a medicinal herb called Tlayapalonj xihujtl. It has branches and leaves like the xoxocoyolli; they are somewhat reddish. The branches of this herb are round, and the leaves are green. The leaves are at the tips of the branches; they are notched and divided into five small leaflets. This herb puts out a stalk and blooms with a tawny-colored flower. It is not useful for anything. The root of this herb has a thick bark; on the outside it is purple and on the inside reddish; it has many roots, split and boiled in water, and well boiled so that half the water evaporates.

[Nahuatl column:]
It spreads right upon the surface of the ground. Its foliage is somewhat reddish, very small; it is somewhat sour-tasting, somewhat bitter; its leaf-tips are rather pale green. Its appearance is as though sprinkled with something; its foliage binds nothing together. Its inner sap: its bark is thin, somewhat purplish on top; its interior is very red; it is thick, has many roots; it crumbles, it does not compact; it swells when cooked.

translation:
Book Eleven

He who has continuous loose bowels, drinking it [this plant] heals him. It also helps one who has relapsed from some illness, drunk before or after a meal. And the woman who has relapsed from having lain with a man, or the man who has relapsed from having lain with a woman — they should drink it on an empty stomach. And children who have loose bowels: grind this root with five cacao almonds, mix everything in water and drink it. It stops the loose bowels.

109.

There is a medicinal herb called hueipatli. It has long, dense branches; its leaves are green, somewhat rounded at the base and sharply pointed and serrated, or notched, and slightly hairy. Its flowers are like small purplish, whitish bells and they are numerous; they are of no use. Its roots are strong and thick like those of a tree; there are two or three of them, white on the outside and inside; the bark is thin. All of it is pith. The root is somewhere between sweet and bitter and burns a little.

[Nahuatl column:]
The water boils up; it is to be poured twice, then set aside to cool. For one who can no longer swallow medicine through the mouth — when it slides down into the throat it causes him to swallow. And if one has fallen ill, whether a woman or a man, none of it is to be eaten in [the medicinal] preparation; and for young children who are congested, or for [those with] phlegm — the root is to be ground: five pieces of cacao are to be combined with the preparation, and it will stop up [the looseness] in the child. 109.

Hueipatli: it is tall, long, thick, craving to spread out, having a rough surface, reddish-tinged, [the stem] is somewhat square-shaped, brownish, grayish; the flowers hang down like bells and form clusters, orange-colored, with many branches; there is no grass-scent to it. Its root is like the root of a tree, broad; there are two or three of them, sandy inside, white on the outside and underneath; the bark is not [illegible]

And for one who has great discomfort, and whose temples and veins throb: it should be drunk mixed with water on an empty stomach; and with this it purges, and expels bile and phlegm through the mouth, and with this the throbbing of the body is relieved. The water that is to be drunk should be warm, to purge through the urine. For those who have tertian or quartan fevers, it should be given to drink when the fever is coming on, and with this it subsides and is calmed. It grows everywhere on slopes and ravines, but it is rare. In another place it was mentioned under the name Ololiuhqui, but they are different plants.

These flowers are edible and relieve hunger; they make tortillas and cook them to eat. The root is round, black on the outside and white inside; the bark of the root must be removed before grinding. It is beneficial for one who cannot urinate: it should be drunk on an empty stomach whenever one wishes, and with this one urinates. It also expels the gravel and stones that impede urination. It grows everywhere along the banks of fresh water.

112.

There is another medicinal herb called Coaxoxouhqui, Oxoxouhapatli. It is a plant like ivy that climbs trees and walls; it has green branches and small round leaves with pointed tips. It produces small white flowers and makes seeds, and each flower produces only one seed. The leaves and seeds, ground together and mixed with water and ink, when the body is washed with the mixture, are good against gout. It is also applied directly to the place where the gout is, mixed with a little resin. When the gout has spread throughout the body and causes great pain, it goes away —

[Nahuatl column:]
The tortillas are made from it and taken as a remedy. Its outer skin is round and small, dark inside, white when squeezed: and when it is ground and rubbed, it becomes warm; it is not sweet. It is needed so that one can urinate well, because one can no longer pass urine, it drips slowly; when one has not eaten yet and one wants to expel it: it draws it out from the earth below, whether it is something hardened, going down through it: and it likewise forms everywhere in Acellopan. 112.

Coaxorouqui, and also Xoxouhcapatli: it is an herb, it clings to things, it wraps around trees, it is very warm, it is hairy, whitish, it makes itself white: and when its seeds are dry, it wraps around itself again, the seeds fall in the same place, they form small black round things. Its leaves and seeds come together, and with them one bathes. Or one just rubs it on: for it cures gout. Or it is mixed with ocote pine resin and boiled where the gout has settled. For one who has already advanced gout, it relieves the gout, because —

There is a shrub called tepetomatl. It has dense green branches, and its leaves are somewhat broad and jagged at the edges; it makes yellow flowers that grow in clusters; its leaves are of no use; it makes little berries that are not to be eaten; it has thin but strong roots, which, when touched to the tongue, burn it. The roots ground up together with some of the leaves are beneficial for those in whom urine and stool have accumulated; it is also beneficial for those whose seed is corrupted, such that they cannot urinate or move their bowels or eat. It expels [these things]: a little warm water, drunk on an empty stomach or after eating when digestion is complete, will then drive out the bad humors from below, and one is healed.

...concerning what was mentioned first: and the one who smells it, when entering the sweat bath, will no longer feel the heat of the bath; and also when one comes out, one should smell it again: and so they will come out well, let the sick person not worry: it causes sweating, it relieves the fever; when there is no food to eat, or when one has been purged: in all forested areas everywhere. 114.
Tepetomatl: it is somewhat compact, somewhat flat and spread out, somewhat longish and firm, with small round branches: it goes along only with its own leaves, it gives off a smell as it goes, it is yellowish, it tastes good, it does not cling: its berries are not to be eaten. Its root is very dry and hard, like coarse wood, it is astringent; it is ground up, it gives off a reddish liquid. It is used for one whose urine is blocked, or whose stool is blocked: and one who is tormented in the belly, who is very constipated, who can no longer defecate, who can no longer move about: who is very cold, who no longer eats: it will soften things, the water will pass through the intestines again, and so once more...

There is another medicinal herb called Tlatlacotic. It is tall and large, has many thick branches, has long green knotted branches along its thirds, and at the nodes it has leaves. The leaves are broad and green, and pointed, sharp and elongated, they are not [useful in themselves]. The roots are dense, many and thin: on the outside they are black, on the inside somewhat yellow. They have a thin bark and are tasty. This ground root is drunk after a person has been purged. It must be ground and mixed with water and can be drunk before eating and after eating, after having eaten the porridges called yolatolli. It is found everywhere in the plains and in the mountains.

Tlatlacotc, tlacotontli: it is a rough plant, with many branches, firm, its surface: where its face is, where it extends its face to: its leaf is broad and flat, somewhat reddish, small and rounded, it does not make a sound like a snake, it has no taste. Its inner part is fibrous, with many branches, thin, its surface appears whitish on the underside, somewhat hollow inside, it does not rustle, it is flavorless. When one is greatly troubled in the throat, or when the belly hurts greatly, or when one has pain in the sides: it is ground up; and when one is troubled with coughing, when one has chest pain: it is drunk as a remedy. When one cannot eat, or when one is not yet eating: one must drink it, when one is troubled with thirst, and when one is very feverish and cannot eat well: it should not be eaten dry, in the forest, across the ravine, on the hillside. 116.

This ground root mixed with the root of the herb called chilpanton is useful for those who have swelling of the belly on account of some internal abscess; it is to be drunk on an empty stomach with water, and thus it purges downward the abscess that was causing harm. translation:
Book Eleven

117.

There is another medicinal herb called Hatlanquaye. It is somewhat tall and has no more than one stem like a tree; above it has some nodes and it has many leaves, wide and striped. On the lower part they are wide and on the upper part they are pointed and reddish. They have flowers among the leaves that are tawny, somewhat long and roundish. They produce a white seed similar to that of blite (quelite). Grinding the flowers together with the leaves, they are of good flavor. These leaves and flowers, ground and boiled with water and drunk before eating, or with plain water, are beneficial for those who have bloody dysentery; with this it is stanched. It is also good against flux of the belly and against vomiting, drunk as said above. It is also good against pain, taken as a drink as stated.

It gives warmth, gives breath to the sick; when one is dying, it will not cause bleeding of the leaf veins; with its juice one is washed. It is also said that it removes headache, being taken as medicine. And when nausea arises, it becomes thick, it does not cause loosening; it does not cling anywhere — only in the forests, in the mountainsides, in the temperate ravines, in the gentle hillsides does it set itself. Also it is said that it expels illness with fever: taken as medicine; it removes whatever illness is within, and it cleanses the interior; and it gives warmth, and causes shivering; it presses together the sinews; it washes the head; thus it grips the heart and fills the throat: all of it, if you press it, it will vanish.

translation:
Book Eleven

118.

There is a medicinal flower called Tonacaxochitl. It is fragrant, and it spreads along the ground and climbs up through the trees and over the rocks. Its leaves are not long and wide and green; it has flowers among its leaves. These flowers are yellowish tending toward red, long like a finger, hollow, and somewhat downy; they have a sweet smell. These flowers are ground together with the herb called Tlachichinoa xihuitl; the drink mixed with water is good against internal heat. It also clarifies the urine. This flower is commonly drunk by both the sick and the healthy, prepared with cacao. This herb and flower grow in temperate lands, among the rocks and among the trees.

119.

There is another medicinal herb called Tlachichinoa xihuitl. It is a small plant; it has green, slender branches, and its leaves come in threes, slender and sharply pointed. Ground up, it is good against heat of the mouth and stomach, and it should be drunk with water. It is also useful against festering sores and against mange, applied ground upon them. The root of this herb is of no benefit. It grows

Tonacaxochitl: it cannot be picked just anywhere; it grows on rocky cliffs, it spreads and climbs; its flower is reddish and somewhat orange, elongated, slightly cylindrical, hollow at the tip, yellowish, smooth; it is fragrant, like a little finger in size. It is used: the Tonacaxochitl flower is ground together with cacao and drunk; if one suffers pain in the legs, it is gathered from the rocky cliffs where it grows everywhere throughout the land.

119.
The Tlachichinoa xihuitl is a small plant, somewhat reddish, very slender and small; it comes out at two places, its flower is reddish-orange and elongated, it is hot; it is ground and taken medicinally; if someone has a sore in the mouth, it quickly dissolves it. And wherever there are sores or scabies, it is applied there [and heals them].

                    120
   There is another medicinal herb called Tlacoxochitl. It is somewhat tall, has leaves divided in pairs or in threes, they are green, somewhat broad and hairy, somewhat downy. Its flowers are orange, roundish and hollow, and are of no particular use. This herb has fairly thick roots, dark on the outside and white within, with a thin bark, and its taste is between bitter and sweet. It is good against excessive heat and faintness of the heart; it should be drunk ground and mixed with water and with some grains of maize, about fifteen or sixteen grains altogether, ground together and drunk with water many times, on an empty stomach and after eating — this relieves the heat. It is found everywhere in the mountains and in the moors.
                    121
   There is a medicinal tree called Quetzalmizquitl. It is a small tree, has many branches, its leaves are like those of the cedar, very green and about a palm's length, it produces small yellow flowers which fall off, and it likewise bears no seed.

Tlacoxochitl, a small herb, it grows upright, is of medium height, yellowish-green; its leaf spreads out on two sides and three sides, quite broad and wide at the edges, somewhat crinkled along the margins; its flower is orange-colored, cylindrical and tubular, it has no odor. Yet although it is common everywhere and small, it is somewhat hairy on the surface, white within, not rough to the touch, not sticky; it is ground many times and one drinks it, about fifteen pieces, or ten, or eight cacao-measures: then one sips it, or one drinks it warm as food for one who has indigestion, or for one who has no appetite. For the person who is very ill in the stomach, who has a fever, who has chills, who has pain in the chest: it relieves the heat everywhere in the mountain forests.

Like a fig tree, its leaves are very green, long and wide and pointed at the tip; they have a bad taste and bad smell. The leaves of this tree and its ground seeds are beneficial: against the swelling called ystac tolonquj, applying it on top heals it; sometimes it resolves and other times it ripens and the matter comes out. Also against mange and blisters, applied on top ground up. It has white flowers, which open only at night; these flowers give off a great fragrance, and by day they close. This tree is rare. It is found in the mountains and on the moors and in the town called Hecatepec.

And there is another plant called Coscaguauhxihujtl, it is a shrub. This plant has many branches and they are green on the outside; it has broad and somewhat long leaves pointed at the tip. On it form small round green berries, and inside them develop seeds. When dry, the leaves are ground

[Nahuatl text, right column:]

It is also needed, according to how one applies it for fever; just as ystac totonquj, when the body heats up, one applies it there to cool the body's heat, which then spreads, and afterward it dissolves, or it loosens, and somewhat quenches the fever. And altogether: for thorns, or for pustules: it refreshes the body, it unblocks the interior of the body in the manner of a thorn-fruit. ¶ And there is another medicinal herb called Hatlapultic. It has tall, straight branches, and its leaves are thick, broad, and long, growing in pairs along the stem. The flowers grow right alongside the leaves; the flowers are green, roundish, and smooth, and contain seeds inside, but they are not useful. The roots of this herb are thick and slender; on the outside they are somewhat reddish. And also from within, these roots, when ground, are beneficial for those who have excessive internal heat — one drinks them mixed with clear water; this drink is to be taken after eating and also while eating. With this, one will expel pus through the urine. This water is also drunk when a sick person enters the bath. And it is also good for healthy people when they enter the bath. It can also be drunk ground with cacao, so that the cacao drunk with it may be beneficial. It grows in the mountains among the trees.

¶ Tlatlapaltic. It is a plant: it spreads out widely; its leaves are broad and flat; it spreads out smooth and level, standing wide; it goes along fresh and green: it stretches out; just as if it were flat and level, it goes filling out, spreading sideways. Its inner skin is not fragrant, it is astringent, and very round in its stalk; on its surface also the same: it grew. It is needed by one who has internal heat dwelling in him, who has a fever: so that he may eat nothing, or so that he may eat a little; and then it will cool him. And it is useful both for the sick and for the well, combined with cacao, it makes the cacao good. It is found everywhere in the forest, in the woods. 127.

It is especially good for those who have relapsed from some illness, drinking it mixed with a pod of chili pepper and with seeds of squash, all ground together and mixed, drinking it two or three times and then taking a bath — this is how it heals. Also the leaf of the fresh maguey, roasted in the embers. The sap of this maguey, or the water in which it was boiled, heated with salt and applied to the wound of someone who has been cut or injured — whatever kind of wound — it heals. Also the dried maguey leaf, ground and mixed with pine resin and applied with a feather to the place of pain, whether it oozes or something else is wrong, it heals. Also pulque is mixed with the medicine called chichic patli and boiled together; it is beneficial for one who has pain in the chest or in the belly or in the back, or who has some illness that is causing him to waste away — drinking it on an empty stomach, once or twice or more, it heals. This medicine called chichic patli is the bark of a tree called chichic quauitl. Only the bark of this tree is beneficial. This tree grows in the mountains of Chalco.

[illustration: maguey plant with two figures, one treating the other]

[Nahuatl column:]
It is mixed with white octli [pulque] in the manner described above. As has been said, for one who has been scraped or cut, it is applied, mixed with salt — twice, three times, and then relief follows. The maguey spine is used to pierce it, to prick it, so that the small gods may be appeased; the commoner is healed, the swelling subsides. The maguey sap, or if it greatly blisters, or if it erupts in sores — it soothes wherever there is a burning sensation, wherever there is a sore. And as for the copal resin, when it dries and the ocotl resin becomes hard, it mixes together and dissolves: the medicine called chichic patli is recognized by this — it is bitter, it blisters. It is said of one who goes about eating nothing, emaciated throughout the body, having no appetite — once or twice it is taken. The chichic patli heals him.

These maguey thorns are also good for scrubbing the back with them, so that lashings are not felt.

128.

There is a medicinal herb called Cihuapatli. It is a bush with many branches, as tall as a man. Its leaves are somewhat thick, broad and sharply pointed; it has many branches; it has yellow flowers and other white ones; it makes a seed like the seed of the bledo plant. The leaves of this bush are very useful when boiled well in water. A woman who is pregnant and ready to give birth drinks this water in order to give birth well and without pain. Blood then comes out, and this is a sign that the child is ready to be born. She drinks a little more, and with this the child is soon born. The roots of this bush are thin and long and numerous; on the upper surface they are black, and underneath they are yellow; they have a strong smell.

[Nahuatl column:]
It causes pain; its bark peels off somewhat; it is called chichic quahuitl [bitter tree]. One need only strip its bark; it does not cause any irritation. It grows in the forests, not found in the lowlands. And this same remedy for anyone who has been gravely frightened — it is said to be used as a whip, so that he no longer feels the harm done to him. It causes great itching on the skin.    128.

Cioapatli: it is merely a stalk; it branches out greatly; it reaches one full measure in height; its internodes are somewhat flat and wide, small and round. Its juice is white. It is used dried. It is like white amaranth. What is needed is its herb — it is not toasted, only chewed until it becomes a soft mash; it is good for a woman in labor, so that she may deliver the child. She drinks it; she sleeps. It will not torment her any further; once more she rests. And thereafter it will no longer afflict her.

The tree called Tuna [prickly pear cactus] has large, flat, green, and spiny leaves [paddles]. The seed of chia, ground up with a little of the tail of the animal called the tlaquatzin [opossum], about half a finger's worth, all mixed with water: if a woman who cannot give birth drinks it, she gives birth immediately. This drink is better for giving birth than those mentioned above, though not many people know this. The root of this plant, green and fresh, together with the root of the willow called Quetzalhuexotl — all ground up — is made into atole with it. It is beneficial for those who spit blood and who have ongoing discharge from the chest and spit blood. This also heals an old cough, or one of many days' standing. It is also good for those who have intestinal discharge of matter, drinking it two or three times. The seeds of this plant are ground raw and the sap is extracted from them; drinking it purifies the chest. And drinking this sap mixed into atole before eating does the same thing. The sap of this chia is like linseed oil from Castile, such as painters use to give luster.

And it also cures the illness called vacca tlatlaciztli [a bowel disease]; it makes one expel waste twice, not more, and then it stops. The chia plant ripens quickly, as they say; its husk is ground and treated; [when taken,] one improves. The herb is somewhat rounded, as long as a palm's width; on the outside it is white; it is somewhat hot/burning. The outer bark of this root is useful, but the pith is not. Ground up and drunk with water, it is useful against tabardillo [typhus fever]; when drunk it immediately purges bile or phlegm, and thus the heart and body are calmed. This herb grows in the plains, on hillsides, and everywhere. In winter the herb dries up. In summer the same root sprouts again.

[illustration no. 132]

This branch hair is used by the Chichimecs to start fire. It has white flowers; in a cluster they are fragrant, and they are called Tlacorochitl. The branches of this herb are of no use. There is another medicinal herb called Ystacpatli or Oteconpatli. It grows like a green and rather stiff stalk; it has leaves like those of wild amaranth, broad and very green. On it grows a small round fruit that is not edible; it is like a wild gourd. Its flowers are of no use. It has longish roots, some of them roundish; the bark is rather thick; on the outside they are dark, and inside white and bitter. The bark of the roots is not good, but the ground pith is beneficial for those who have internal heat and swellings — with this the swelling and the heat are relieved. It grows everywhere, in the plains and in the mountains, though it is rare. It grows abundantly in the town of Tequixquiac.

Istacpatli, also called Teqmpatli, Tlacotontli: it is greenish-white, flat-leaved, like the quelite of huauhtli in its leaf arrangement, broad-leafed, with a tart, astringent taste, not sweet. The swallow-wort plant has very green leaves, round like lentils, somewhat pointed at the tips. The flowers and leaves are placed in between one another like small white feathers; the wind carries them to the flowers. The flowers and leaves are of no use. The root is a small round thing as long as a palm's breadth, yellowish on the outside and white within; and where this root grows, it is as if interwoven. This root, ground up, is very beneficial for a man or woman who has failed to expel human seed, or through fear or some other incident that occurred and it remains cut off or corrupted; and for this reason the person goes on drying up and develops a continuous cough and the body begins to turn black and waste away, even if it has been one, two, or three years since it happened. Thus, taking it as a drink, it expels a very foul humor over the course of two or three days; the corrupt humor comes out, and through the member it passes white urine, like lime-water, and very foul-smelling. The same applies to the woman.

This same thing is medicine for when—

[Nahuatl column:]
It is yellowish-green; the surface is somewhat warm; just as the swallow-wort leaf, it is like a feather, whitish; it spreads out like a mat covering; nothing sticks to it. As it rises up, it is very hot, very frightening, and quite malodorous; on the outside it is yellowish, within it is very white. And the inner part is hardened and compact; it presses together tightly. It relieves those who have swollen testicles, or a woman, who has had a miscarriage, when the corrupt matter has not come out properly and the illness reaches them; and it frightens those who, wandering about, feel their flesh darkening; and when it rushes to attack their flesh: even if the sickness has lasted one year or even four years, it is necessary to give it to them from behind; it soothes the illness; then the illness passes out, very foul-smelling, within five days the great illness diminishes. And also there comes out a rushing thing like lime-water, burnt, foul; so too the woman passes it outward in her urine. And also—

There is a medicinal shrub called Hamacazqui y papa; it has very dense branches, as tall as a man's height; they are like quince switches, grayish on one side and green on the other. The branches go straight; it has yellow flowers and rough ones; the flowers have no leaves; neither the branches, nor the flowers, nor the leaves are of use. Its roots are thin and many and long, about a hand's span, and dense like a bundle. These roots are slimy in the throat; on the outside they are somewhat reddish and inside crimson; the bark of the root is thin. The pith has many fibers, like those of the nequen plant, oily and thin. These roots, ground and drunk with water on an empty stomach, are beneficial for the illness described above, when for some reason the seminal humor is cut off; drunk as described, it purges by

whoever has had a nocturnal emission, or a woman likewise: it is given to drink. Also, it requires nettloatl, vmellacatl, or altlacatl seeds; and each day one finger's width is needed; it is spread in Tullantzinco. 135.

Tlamacazqui ipapa: the stalk rises up, it spreads out in many branches; it is truly very knotted, with many woody parts, somewhat like a quince fruit in form; likewise it has a kind of bark; inside it shows through, its surface is yellowish-green, cold to the touch, somewhat bluish. It bears fruit coolly. Its flower is truly yellow; just like the tlaconti, nothing drips from it; nothing takes hold in it. Its inner bark is thin, very fine; it has much of something, the surface fiber is very smooth, yellowish, slightly rough; inside it is reddish; its inner part is somewhat pale yellow; its surface is slightly rough; and its pith is just like thread, very fibrous; it is compacted. There is another medicinal herb called Cicimatic; it grows as a vine, has many leaves, very green, with small tendrils in sets of three. It is like beans in form; it does not flower; the herb is of no benefit for anything. The roots of this herb are bitter and thick like a trunk, and round like a person's head, and as long as a forearm. It has a thick bark; on the outside it is black, and on the inside it has dense reddish spots when ground. It is good for those who have an eye ailment in which flesh grows over the eye, which they call ayxnacapachiuj. Wrapped in a cloth and squeezed over the eyes, it removes that flesh that was covering the eye. It grows throughout the mountains.

137.
There is another medicinal herb called Tzonpoton; it has many small branches, green and straight.

[Nahuatl column:]
136. Cicimatic herb: it springs up quickly spreading on the ground, it is abundant with leaves, green; its leaves are broad and flat: they appear lace-like, they appear like quelite-herb leaves; it bears no fruit, it causes no harm. Its root: it is round, like a large tree-trunk, very thick; it is about the size of a head: it is hard inside, the surface is dark, inside it is red, and also white; it crumbles when broken. What it is needed for: one should squeeze out its juice and apply it as a wash — for eye-flesh ailments, for those with eye-flesh conditions, so that the fleshy growth on the eye is dispelled; it causes it to fall away and removes the discharge from the eye. It grows everywhere in the forest.

The leaves are broad and somewhat long; the flower is white, almost like a feather. The flowers and branches are of no use. The root is bitter and round, divided toward the bottom; it is long as a finger. On the outside it is white, and on the inside a clear yellow. This root, ground up and boiled well in water — drinking that water is good for one who has diarrhea, as when water cannot be held back, and for vomiting. Drinking it in small amounts stops the diarrhea and stops the vomiting. And if small children drink up to two swallows of it, they are healed by this. It is found in the mountains and along the rivers.

[illustration: two plants, numbered 138]

There is another medicinal herb called Cujrlapatli. It has long, somewhat slender branches that are hollow inside; from each foot, other small green branches grow. Its leaves are broad, like Swiss chard from Castile. The white flowers are of no use, nor are its branches or flowers. The roots of this plant are thick like radishes; on the outside they are white, and on the inside a clear yellow. They have a thick bark, like that of radishes, and so does the interior. Dried and ground, these roots are beneficial.

[Nahuatl column:]
Padactotontli, melactotontli: it is bitter, izteli mjszchic; when one drinks it again, it settles the stomach, it stops the looseness. The root: in piel hoato — it is very bitter, it spreads heat throughout, it heats one entirely, it causes the body to warm; it makes one thirsty greatly, it makes one burn: it is needed by one who wishes to purge himself so that the bowels move well; when it returns as liquid, as food — it quickly causes movement. Drink only a little at a time; and if one has diarrhea, one should take it carefully in small amounts. It is found everywhere in the hills always. 138.

Cujtlapatli — it is hollow, a hollow stalk; when two join, or the branches spread, they are small-leafed: its leaves are like acelgas de Castilla [Swiss chard], its inner part: its upper surface is entirely covered; it blooms fully; it is not to be eaten raw. Its juice is thick; concentrated, it is like radishes on the inside, yellow on the outside; its bark is like that of radishes: [remainder partially illegible due to damage].

For those who have swollen glands in the throat. And also for those who have fevers — these powders should be dissolved in resin and placed on the affected areas, covering them with feathers. This root is also good for women whose male member rots [i.e., who have genital ailments]. It is also good against the illness called Xoducivizili. This root is not drunk; it is prepared in the mountains.

139.

There is another medicinal herb called Oquichpalli, which has branches like those of a squash plant. It is also called by another name, Ayoxochquiltic. It spreads along the ground and also climbs up trees. Its branches and leaves are green and somewhat hairy on one side and smooth on the other. Its leaves are divided into three parts. It has large yellow flowers, like the flowers of a squash — shaped like a little bell. When the flowers fall, it produces a small fruit like a little pear. This fruit is quartered like a melon. Neither the branches, nor the leaves, nor the fruit are of medicinal use. It has rounded roots that converge into a single root. It is sufficient for medicinal use.

[Nahuatl column:]
It is needed for one who has been bitten by the serpent called the tochcatcoatl, and also for the swelling called potzalli: one remedy is applied for the first, and another for a second condition. It is given to the patient to take away; it is cooked and administered as a poultice, or mixed with ocotl resin, and also taken as a drink. It also cures a woman who has skin discoloration, or a man likewise. It also cures the ailment called quetilviziztli, and also xoducivizili. This medicine is not very effective; it grows everywhere in the forests and in the hills. 139.

Oquichpalli is a vine, and it is also called ayosuchquiltic. It is an herb; it climbs like a camote vine, or indeed climbs trees. Its leaves on top are flat and wide; its surface is somewhat rough and scaly, divided in two places. It has very large flowers, yellow; like the flower of the squash, shaped like a bell. Then the flower falls and the fruit becomes wrinkled; like a melon it is not grasped easily. Its inner flesh is fibrous and hard throughout; its roots are somewhat dark on the outside, and very white on the inside. It spreads and extends itself in many places.

It is good for many who have a damaged member. The bark of this root is thin on the outside, blackish, and white on the inside. The branches, as they spread out, put forth roots. This root, ground up and mixed with olli [rubber], is used to anoint a reed called Xomalli, which is inserted for a year; and with this, a substance comes out through the canal, or the urine comes out, and thus one is healed.

This same root mixed with olli and with the root of the herb called Xorocoyoltie is beneficial for women who cannot retain the seed of the man because the canal of the womb has become twisted. If this medicine is applied quickly, it heals; but if many days pass, they will not be healed. It is also beneficial for those who have become dried out from some illness, administering it through a syringe in the morning on an empty stomach, mixed with [continues on next page]

[Nahuatl column translation:]
...the root called tlaneshoatl: its bark is blackish on the outside, white inside, it is called xomali; it is mixed with rubber. It is needed when one has damaged their urinary canal, or when it has become blocked: it warms it inside, the matter comes out through it, or the urine flows out. And the woman whose womb is said to be displaced or twisted, where the afterbirth attaches, in the place where the child is nourished. If one is in this condition and can only walk with difficulty: if the child is born it heals her; but if it takes too long, she may perish from it, and no longer be able to be cured. The cure for this condition: the said root mixed with olli and xorocoyoltie: it will cure her body; her womb will be set right again, she will be able to retain the seed once more, and again she will be able to conceive. And when one becomes dried out from illness, it is given quickly, in a small amount mixed with water, as stated above.

hot water, and having applied the mistel, the patient begins immediately to sweat a very hot sweat. And then this medicine enters through the whole body, through the head, through the stomach, and then it drives out bad humors, phlegm and bile, in all ways through the mouth and below. After having purged, one must take a little atolli. As a drink, it shall be water boiled with the root called Chichicpati, which must be scraped into the water with which it is to be boiled, and not too much. And with this the fever is finally brought under control. This plant grows on all the hills and slopes; it grows especially in the hot lands, in a town called Xochiquauhyocan.

140.

There is another medicinal herb called Chichicpati. This herb has long thin stems, and a single root — sometimes it has many stems, sometimes only one. It has abundant branches. Its leaves are green, smooth, broad, and somewhat long, like the leaves of a peach tree. Its branches are knotted, and from the nodes the leaves grow in pairs, one on one side and another on the other side; arranged in this manner the leaves continue to the tip when they are cut.

[Nahuatl column:]
It is said that it quickly relieves fever; then everywhere in the body it spreads. It settles upon our skull, upon our temples; it is somewhat bitter, yellowish-green, yellow, white, from the armpits, from the groin. When the shade-house falls, corn gruel is drunk. And when one eats, or perhaps does not eat, medicine is drunk, and the pain will pass. Its name in Nahuatl is Chichicpati. It may be used thus: it relieves our fever; everywhere on the hills it spreads, it grows abundantly at Xochiquauhyocan. For joint pain it is used similarly. 140.

Chichicpati, a plant, it sprouts low to the ground. Its single root spreads out much, or sometimes rises up alone. Its leaves are smooth, its leaf-surfaces are flaky and smooth, somewhat round and broad — like the leaves of peach trees in their foliage. Its branches spread out from there along the leaves; they face one another, spreading on both sides, going along together. It is hollow inside, and its interior pulp [illegible].

It secretes a milky sap; the branches are hollow inside; it has white flowers. The clusters have no more than one flower; they are bell-shaped in appearance. Neither the leaves nor the flowers are of any use. It has only one root, somewhat bitter. These plants grow in pairs, male and female. The root of the male goes deep like a fathom, and is thick, and if it is old, it has a thick bark; if not, the bark is thin. And some are not so long but are thick, and the root does not have a thick bark. The bark having been removed and ground up, the pith, drunk with water, is beneficial for those who feel great interior heat. It is also good for one whose stomach has been damaged by the condition they call omacaxoni; and for this purpose it should be ground together with a pod of chile and drunk — it heals. The plant of this kind called female has two roots, long as was said. It is good for the above-mentioned sickness in the same way as the root of the male. The bark of the root of both the male and the female, made into powder and mixed with ink and applied over festering sores, heals them; and placed over swellings, it ripens and bursts them. Throughout all the mountains this plant grows, but it is rare.

[Nahuatl column:]
Its sap is white; only one [flower] opens at a time; it opens like a bell in form; there is nothing inside it. Its leaves are of no use, and not particularly notable in that respect. It does as described — it flowers, its sap is white, it does not have a twin, it does not have a snake [quality], it does not produce a vine. When ripe, the sap drips; it is peeled, it is squeezed; only its pith is ground up — that is what is used. It is needed: one takes it, and uses it when one has a stomach ailment called omacaxonj; one takes it with chile for medicine. And both roots [of the female] are long, two spans in length; one drinks its sap; the inner bark mixes with ink, black blended together: it cures swellings, either cold sores or festering sores — it ripens all of them; it is found everywhere in the hills, in the forests; it is simply scattered about.

Entry 141.
There is a resin found in this land that is nothing more nor less than incense. The tree from which it flows is called tepecopal quauitl. It forms when there is no rain, and when it rains the water dissolves it. It is beneficial for persistent loose bowels of a watery humor: one must grind an equal measure of it for a day's use, mix it with warm water so that it dissolves, and drink it on an empty stomach. If it is to be taken after eating, it should be mixed with a little ink. It is also beneficial for someone who has bloody diarrhea or spits blood, but in that case it should not be mixed with ink. This resin is also good for swellings and abscesses: applied to them it softens and opens them. These trees grow in hot lands, such as around Quauhnahuac and Temetztlan.

[Nahuatl column, entry 141:]
Coiopaltic: it oozes from the copal tree when it rains; it is called tepecopal quauitl. When the sun comes out one cannot see it well; it flows away; it is chewed, and it is like the chicle plant, it is thick; just like copal. In order to treat someone with it, a little bit is spread on them, applied to the inner edge of the lips; it settles on the water; there the fingers knead it, it is not sticky. And once a day it is mixed with something like an herb: when it is not yet to be drunk mixed, if one happens to have mixed it with the black [ink], or has eaten something. And if blood comes from one's backside, or one spits: it will not turn black. And for someone whose face is scorched, or who feels very hot, it is applied to them; quickly the heat will cool on the ground. Temetztlan.

Entry 142.
There is an herb called Cocopi, very similar to maize. The grains of this plant dry out in such a way that they turn into charcoal, and likewise some grains of wheat from the same [family do as well]...

[Nahuatl column, entry 142:]
Cocopi: it burns the food supply, even as the maize stalk: its kernels are numerous, very small, very smooth; they resemble those of [another plant], they are also numerous. And [continues]...

With the scrapings of the stone called Xiuhtomolteti. It also helps, in the manner described above, against the ailment of the heart that causes one to fall and to vomit, and one should drink it once or twice.

This stone is found near Xalapan, Yztepec, and Tlatlauhquitepec. The natives of those regions say that when it begins to thunder and rain in the mountains or hills, these stones fall from the clouds; in the mountains they go under the ground while still small, and each year they keep growing until they become large — some round, others long like truffles, some bigger, some smaller. The natives of that land say: wherever they see a single reed growing alone, they know the stone is there, and they go and dig it out. Healthy people may also drink it as described above; it tempers the body's heat.

[Nahuatl column:] It warms. And it is thus that it draws up the body's sustenance; it strikes fire. And it also clears one's vision. It is said of Xiuhtomolteti that it makes one sneeze repeatedly. It does not make a person very wicked at heart; it cools the passion in one's heart: once, or perhaps twice one will sneeze. The gold called teucuitlatl forms and grows within it, in its interior: it is just like the salapaneca stone. When it thunders, out there in the forest, in the ravines — not on rocky ground, but only in the flat earth — the gold (teucuitlatl) enters and falls there, just a tiny bit dropping down; it grows there for many years, becoming large, it develops. And when it has grown, the chaneques (earth spirits) notice it and reveal it: a single reed stands over the teucuitlatl, visible above the ground. When one goes to pull it out, it is very heavy, as if it were a bone — like a large bone — and some are just round. And also you should not go there when you are in a state of impurity; if our heart is troubled or agitated, it will not form properly. It is found at Iztepec, Xalapa, and Tlatlauhquitepec.

144.
There is another medicinal stone called Xiuhtomolteti. It is like chalchihuitl: green and white mixed together. It is beautiful; the scrapings of this stone, drunk as described above, are beneficial for the illnesses mentioned above. This stone is brought from around Guatemala and from around Xoconochco; it is not made here. Beads are made from it, to wear on the wrists.

[illustration: three rounded stones or beads depicted]

145.
There is another medicinal stone called Elztetl. It is useful for stopping nosebleeds by taking it in the hand and placing it against the neck, in such a way that it touches the skin. This stone has many colors; it has many red spots, others white, others green, others light green, others yellow, others black, others crystalline, all mixed together. Before it is polished, these differences in color cannot be seen, but after polishing they appear very clearly. These stones are found in many parts of this land.

146.
There is another medicinal stone called Atlchipin. It is beneficial against excessive internal heat, and also—

[Right column, Nahuatl:]
Xiuhtomolteti: it is like chalchihuitl, it appears beautiful, it is greenish, it is mottled, it looks pleasing; it also cannot be ground up easily, it cannot be crushed: just as was said above about what it cures; it also smells good, it does not strongly irritate the eyes; the xiuhtomotetl beads are also worn for illness prevention. It comes from Guatemala and Xoconochco. 145.
This stone, this flint-like stone, is mottled: it is partly dark, partly white, partly yellow-green, partly green, partly yellow, partly the color of yellow tecuitlatl, partly dark-tinged. When one takes it, it appears shiny when held up; it seems to glow. It becomes split through; when one who has a nosebleed or a wound holds it in his hands or places it on his forehead, it relieves him. See how it is made.

It purifies the urine when brought ground up and drunk in water in which it has soaked for an hour, more or less. This stone is not very hard; it is porous, has many points, has many different shapes; it is a rough stone and it is cold. It is good for grinding or scraping. When this medicine is taken, one should not eat hot foods. This stone grows on the crags and increases each year; they form like barnacles attached to other rocks, and it is easy to tell that one has grown upon another stone. It is found in many parts of this land, especially around Malinalco.

147.
In this land, bones of giants are found in the mountains and under the ground; they are very large and thick — one of these bones, or a piece of one. It is good for bloody dysentery and for purulent dysentery; for the latter, however, this medicine does not help. It should be drunk with cacao, prepared in the usual manner.

[Nahuatl column:]
Even though it is hard and rough, without odor, white, and quickly ground — it is quickly ground, as needed. It is needed for one who has a fever, for one suffering from heat-sickness, loosening that which is in the belly; it purifies the insides. Sometimes, only in certain places in the water it settles. This is the one: it does not overflow. And when one is not too hot in drinking it, only gentle food is taken. In all the craggy places it is made, always remaining there, as its shell: many times it is made, spreading along the rocky cliffs, like small hills, it rests there, growing like vitztatton; clearly it drips like chipintica. It comes from Malinalco.
Quinametzin bone: This is the bone of large, robust people, very dark, odorless, thick, dense. It is needed for one who is spitting blood; so that it does not become foul, so that the discharge stops, and there is no other fitting medicine: one drinks it mixed with water, with cacao, and also with nextamalli ground together; in this way the cacao rises, and likewise it is made.

The meat of the jaguar. They say it is medicinal for those who have been married and are now widowed, so that they do not think of women, nor are they troubled by carnal temptations; they should eat it roasted or boiled. Also, it is beneficial as food in this way: for those who lose their reason. And it is also good for those who have fevers with chills; they should eat it when the fever begins and drink a little broth. The lords also eat this meat to be strong and courageous. Also for those who are mad, a piece of the hide and the bones is good. And also the dung: all burned and ground and mixed with resin or cotzotl, and by fumigating oneself with it, they are healed.

On medicinal stones                           fol. 180.

over the place where it hurts, and thus they take away the pain. They are also good for those whose teeth or molars are decayed or hurt — ground up as described and mixed with ink and placed in the jaw where the tooth is broken or aching, the pain goes away. These worms are found everywhere.

150.

In this land they use the baths for many things, and in order for them to benefit the sick, the bath they call temazcalli must be heated very well, and it must be heated with good wood that does not produce smoke. It benefits, first of all, those who are convalescing from various illnesses, so that they may finish recovering more quickly. They also benefit pregnant women who are near delivery, because there the midwives perform certain procedures so that they give birth better. They also benefit women who have recently given birth, so that they may heal —

[Nahuatl column:]
it does not press or move them, nor does it suffocate; as though it does not affect the head. Nor does it cause the eyes to become inflamed or heated; it does not make the mouth dry, nor does it make the teeth clatter. As for women, it does not cause them to swell up; it only enters inward, it only passes through inward, it only spreads across the surface: it heals wherever one is bitten — it is applied all over. Wherever one has a toothache, it is spread on: and thus one is cured. Likewise in the milpa fields, or in the terraced gardens.

150.

¶ The temazcalli: when wood burns well, it burns brightly and very hotly, and spreads heat; but when poor wood burns, it produces much smoke and does not heat evenly. And when it does not heat evenly, it does not help the sick well, nor does it ease the head. It is there that medicine enters the body; it is there that the breath comes out of the flesh; it is there that the body becomes supple and softened. And it is also there that the milk of a woman who is far along in pregnancy comes out —

And to purify the milk. All the sick receive benefits from these baths, especially those who have knotted nerves, and also those who purge themselves after taking purgatives. Also for those who fall from above or from a height, or were beaten or mistreated and their nerves became knotted, the bath benefits them. translation:
Book Eleventh

Ayauhtona: it is light green, has wide and rounded leaves, has many branches, and on all of them it makes flowers. It is also edible.

There is another fragrant herb called Halpoyomatli. This herb has soft, ash-colored, hairy leaves, and flowers form on it. From its scent, perfumes are made to put into smoking tubes; its fragrance spreads far.

There is another fragrant herb called Yyauhili. It is very green, has many branches that all grow together upward, and it always smells. It is also medicinal for those who have diarrhea — ground up and drunk with cacao, which must be toasted and then ground and mixed with the cacao, it also helps those who spit blood and those who have fevers.

There is another fragrant herb called Yitzilxochitl.

There is another fragrant herb called Ocoxochitl. It has thin, spreading green branches; very tiny blossoms form on it. It grows in the mountains wherever it pleases, and it is always fragrant.

There is another fragrant herb called Yztauhiatl — these are the counterparts of this land; it is very bitter and fragrant, like the wormwood of Castile.

There is another herb called Ytztonquauitl: it has a sweet smell.

There is another fragrant herb called Epacotl — it is tall and slender, its seed...

[Right column, Nahuatl captions:]
Ayauhtona: light-colored, rough, resembling the plumage of the xiuhtototl bird, with branches like a small tree, with spreading limbs, with flowers blooming, edible.

Halpoimatli: smoky, smoky, ashen, soft-leafed, with blossoms, desirable, capable of being smelled from afar, delightful, spreading, lifting to the sky.

Iiauhtli: green, spreading on top, leafy on top, branching above; a medicine: it purges corrupt matter from people, is drunk with cacao — first one must fast, then swallow it; in the direction of cacao it relieves one of fevers, gives strength to the weary.

Vitzitzilxuchitl: delicious, invigorating.

Ocoxochitl: creeping, somewhat rough, green, with hanging blossoms, woody, it revives the weary, it is of pleasant scent, fragrant.

Yztauhiatl: bitter, mingled, ashen-flavored, with a fine flower-fragrance, pungent, sharply bitter.

Itztonquavitl: very fragrant, refreshing.

Epacotl: small and flat; it purges, it is edible, it causes one to become refreshed.

translation:
Common Herbs fo. 183.

The grass that horses eat in this city of Mexico is called caltoli. It grows in water and is triangular in shape; in some parts of Castile it is called carrizo [reed].

There are certain rushes called ytstoli which are triangular and produce flowers; the flowers and roots are medicinal, as was said above.

The cattails are called tolpatlactli; they are neither larger nor smaller than those of Spain. The roots of these are called azxilotl. They are eaten both cooked and raw, as was said above.

The rushes are called tolmjmjlli; they are neither larger nor smaller than those of Spain. The white part they have below the water is called aztapilli or aztapili.

There are medium-sized rushes of which [continues below]

Chaxalli: slender, fine, thin, hollow inside, growing along the water's edge and beside rocky shores.

Caltoli: four-sided, rounded, long, tapering at the tip, its leaves very broad, interlocking at the base, fibrous, rough and scratchy to the touch, so that it scratches one, shaped like a water-pointed reed: edible, smooth to swallow, it grows in the water.

Itztolin: four-sided, thick, rounded, smooth, fragrant, its fragrance pleasant; the root is medicinal: one drinks it, mixed to relieve swelling.

Tolpatlactli: broad, long, very long, flexible, like a mat of rushes, like cornhusks, fibrous inside, it is like an agave thorn; its fruit is the tomjoli; it is strong; from it comes the tolcapotl; its root is the azaxilotl: edible, good for drinking.

Tolmjmjlli: long, green, hard, of a rocky-green color, tapering at the tip, tapering like a stem, narrowing at the base, white at the base: its white part is called iztac, also aztapili, or else oztopili.

Petlatoilli: rounded, [continues]

translation:
Book Eleven

They make mats and call them petlatoli.

¶ There are certain rushes from which mats are made that are triangular in shape and have a lattice-like structure; they are called nacacetoli.

¶ There are other rushes called tolyaman or atoli that are not thick; mats are also made from them.

¶ There is another kind of rush called tolnacochti; they are short and thin, and they are tough and stiff; mats are made from them.

¶ There are rushes just like those of Spain, no more and no less, and they are called xomali.

¶ There are certain small plants that are edible, which grow in the water like jonquils; they are called ateletzon.

¶ There are certain small reeds that grow in the water called acacapacquilit.

¶ There are certain small water plants whose leaves are as wide as a coin and spread out over the surface of the water; they are called amamalacotl or amalacotl.

¶ There are certain tall, thin, leafy reeds; the leaves of these are hairy, rough, and stringy.

Nacacetoli: it is the same as the petlatoli mat-rush, except it is thicker, wider, and branches in three directions.

Toliaman: it is also called atolli; it is not thick, smooth, slender; it is used for making mats from the toliaman rush.

Tolnacochti: it is short, somewhat round at the base, small, smooth, hard, yellowish in color, reddish-yellow; it is stiff.

Xomali, also xomalli: it is green, flat, thin, very slender, growing on the ground, soft, small, delicate, trailing; it creeps along.

Ateletzon: it is a very small plant, it grows in the water.

Acacpacquilit: it grows in the water, it is tangled, slender, branching.

Amamalacotl, also amalacotl: it is flat, yellowish-white on the surface, hollow inside, smooth.

Acacuatl: it is thorny, small, flat, peeling, stripping, it scrapes, it strips the skin, it grazes the skin.

translation:
Of Flowers [folio 185]

... that they call nopal ocoxochitl [cactus flower]. ... it resembles the mocoxochitl.

There are some small ones called memealxihuid. [In Nahuatl:] Memeial, xiuhtontli, memeiallo, aio; it causes one to become thioallaioti by means of which it is used.

There is an herb called tzacutli, and its root is sticky, and they make glue from it. [In Nahuatl:] Tzacutli, mapipitzaoac [slender]; its rind: cacalic [rough]; tehoatl is what tzacutli is called; it spreads: I make glue with it.

Tlaltzacutli [Earth glue-plant].

Eighth paragraph of the flowers of wild herbs. [In Nahuatl:] The eighth paragraph: it tells of flowers in their herbaceous and arboreal [forms].

There are some very fragrant wild flowers called Omjsuchitl; they come in two kinds, some white and others red. [In Nahuatl:] Omjsuchitl, either white omjsuchitl or red omjsuchitl; its leaves are fresh green, slender, smooth; its fragrance is pleasing, it gladdens the heart, it delights the heart.

There are other flowers that are also wild, called tlalisgujxuchitl. They are very fragrant and grow on low plants that spread along the ground; they are white and very fragrant. [In Nahuatl:] Tlalisgujsuchitl: spreading, trailing, white in its flower, tasty, very tasty; it makes one's [heart] content.

There are other flowers that are also wild; they grow in hot lands and are very fragrant. The plant on which [they grow] ... [In Nahuatl:] Tilsuchitl [vanilla], stringy, hardish, green; its fragrance, and it turns black, it is called tlilse[xochitl]...

translation:
Book Eleven.

It climbs up through the trees; when it is in its herb form, it is green; when it dries, it turns black. It is precious and medicinal.

There are also some wild flowers called Coçauhqui and yesuchitl; they are yellow and fragrant. The nobles use them a great deal.

This flower called Tonal xuchitl is also called yoal xuchitl, which means night flower. This is because during the day it gives off no scent at all, but when the sun sets and throughout the night it has a very sweet fragrance.

This flower called Cacaloxuchitl comes in two varieties; some of them grow on trees and on the ground [remainder continues on next page].

[Right column, Nahuatl:]
[It is] fragrant, pleasant-smelling, good, praiseworthy, fine, medicinal, abundant. It is mixed with cacao; it is used to perfume cacao, [it is mixed] with it.

The Coçauhqui suchitl is not like the cocquch yiesuchitl; it is yellowish-greenish, yellowish, a little pale; it is pleasant, fragrant, very warming, savory.

The Chalchiuh yiesuchitl: it is very moist, greenish in its flower, as it is called, the jade flower.

The Quauh yiesuchitl: it is simply the tree variety.

The Toiac: it is just a variety of yiesuchitl, somewhat pleasant; it crackles, it bursts open.

The Tonal suchitl: it is said that the tonal suchitl forms on the ground. When the sun has gone down and it unfolds, opens up, and blooms, and when the sun sets it bursts open; it is very fragrant, very pleasant-smelling; it does not smoke, it crackles, rustles, is pleasant-smelling.

The Tlalcacalo suchitl does not reach up; it simply stays close to the ground [continues on next page].

translation:

...scents have a very gentle fragrance: but this one called Halcacaloxuchitl, which is treated here, grows in the countryside and has no scent at all, though it has the appearance of the one above that grows on trees; but it has no scent whatsoever.

This is the same one described above, which has no scent.

This flower called Texoxoli has no scent and is beautiful; they grow in large groups together, and there is a saying about people who go about very well dressed but are of low standing — they say of them: "Un texoxoli," meaning someone who wears finery greater and better than they deserve.

This flower of the herb called Tolumatl is very beautiful and has no scent.

Texoxoli: it is slender, smooth, hollow inside; it is red in its interior; it is bland, somewhat striped, or many-veined, somewhat rough. As a saying, when someone puts on too much and dresses himself up: "he is a texoxoli."

Nupallacutl: it also grows among the nopal cacti; its juice makes things greenish-blue.

translation:
Book Eleven

This flower is like white hair, and for that reason they call it Quetzalxochitl, which means "flower like white hair" [or gray-haired flower].

This flower is the same as the one above called Caxtlatlapa, which produces flowers of many colors, all growing from one single stem.

These flowers that are called Cempoalxochitl are yellow and fragrant and beautiful, and there are many of them — some grow wild and others are planted in gardens, in two varieties. Those called female cempoalxochitl are large and beautiful. Others are called male cempoalxochitl; these are not as beautiful or as large.

[Right column, Nahuatl — partial, with lacunae:]
[Description of the Quetzalxochitl:] ...its color is white... it is a round-headed flower... it is said that it shines and gleams, it is indeed a beautiful flower...

[Of the Caxtlatlapa:] ...it is many-colored, it spreads its leaves wide, it is yellow, it is red, it is tawny... one cannot easily [describe it]... it is pleasing.

[Of the Atcocoxochitl:] ...it spreads [its petals] widely... it is round, it is well-formed... it has a strong, pleasant scent.

[Of the Cempoalxochitl:] It is yellow... [its scent spreads]...
The female cempoalxochitl — this is the large one.
The male cempoalxochitl — this is the small one.
