translation:
Of Gardens, folio 187

There are others of this kind called Tlacuilsuchitl; they are small, though very yellow and very fragrant.

These little flowers called Cozatli are small and are wild; they belong to the same kind as the yellow and fragrant ones mentioned above.

This flower called teacayaetli is red and belongs to the same kind as those mentioned above.

Ninth paragraph on the flowers and trees that grow in it.

The gardens are very pleasant and cool, with many trees and plants; they have plants and trees of various flowers; they have spring or river water with which they are irrigated; it is fertile ground, a peaceful and very delightful place; they are planted with very fragrant and precious flowers and trees.

Macuil suchitl, copal suchitl — this is the one called teopnauhqui, it is such.

Cocatli — they are tiny, and they grow scattered on the hillsides.

Tetacaiaeth — it is also a kind of copal suchitl related to it, reddish.

Nextamal suchitl — grayish, somewhat shrub-like, its flower is white.

Chilpan, tlacotonli — its flower is greenish, it hangs suspended, its blossoms hang in rows.

Cacalaca suchitl.

This ninth paragraph speaks of those that are also flowers, the first being a great tree.

As for the flower garden: it is fresh and cool, rustling, murmuring, spreading, fragrant, very fragrant, glistening with fragrance, overflowing with fragrance, blossoming, bursting into bloom, full of blossoms, fading in bloom, covered in flowers, the ground spread with flowers, well crafted, [continues]

translation:
Book Eleven

Flowers. They are planted in flowering trees of very fragrant kinds, in which are made the flowers called yolloxochitl, and the tree is also called yolloxochiquijt; these flowers are fragrant and beautiful, and their shape is like a heart. Formerly only the lords used them, especially those called tlacayolloxochitl, because there are others of lesser value called ytreujn rolloxochitl which are beautiful but are not used by the upper classes — they are used by common people.

This flower called yolloxuchiquaujt grows on large trees like walnut trees; the tree is also called yollosuchitl. These flowers are precious and of very sweet scent; they have the shape of a heart, and inside they are very white. These flowers are of two kinds: those called tlacayollosuchitl are large and very beautiful, used by lords and people of refinement. There are others called ytzcujniollosuchitl which are medium-sized and of little scent, used by common people. It is very medicinal. It is also drunk with cacao, which gives it a very good flavor and makes it more beneficial.

to suchitl [the flower]. This flower is delicious, fragrant, aromatic, it becomes refreshed, it is pleasant-smelling, it has broad leaves, it has a heart, it has seeds; and one drinks it with cacao; it warms one up: it is a remedy for chills, wherever there is fever it is applied there; it is placed, it is washed, it is savored, it is enjoyed, it spreads fragrance, it is delicious, it is fragrant, it gives freshness, it gives relief: it blooms, it opens, it spreads.

¶ The elosuchitl [magnolia flower]: the elosuchitl tree, it is cylindrical, it has branches, it has ribs, it is dust-colored: its leaves are very broad; they are like spreading maize leaves; its flower pods are broad, full, well-laden, fleshy: the elosuchitl: it has veins, it has a heart, it has seeds, it has a flower: its veins are smooth, full, yellow, pale yellow, pine-scented: its seeds are round, slender; its heart is hollow, its skin peels, it is aromatic, fragrant, it is tasty, it is delicious; one drinks it, it appears modest: many of its [qualities] cause one to be repelled, they make one dizzy, they make one giddy: one arranges flowers with it, one sets out flowers with it, one gathers them.

And also in the forests there are other flower-trees called Eloxochiquaujtl, in which grow very large flowers: they are shaped like the largest ears of maize, and when they are on the stalk they are very fragrant. They are also drunk with cacao; and if one puts in too much, it makes one drunk, so only a little should be added. Also, when put into water, it makes the water flavorful.

translation:
Book Eleven

[Nahuatl text describing fragrant, pleasant-smelling flowers, their spreading qualities, and their names:]
...it is fragrant, it is pleasant, it spreads its scent, it spreads itself out, it is sought after, it is desired, it is reached for, it separates, it gains the achiote color, it is gathered...

The tree-ear flower (Quauh eloxochitl): it is small, round, it has a name like the ear of the maize-stalk tree; it is just a little bit branched, its name is the tree-ear flower; it is fragrant, pleasant, and sweet-smelling.

Also there are other trees in the forests that are called Cacavaxochitl, on which certain flowers grow, which are also called Cacaoaxochitl; they are small, and in the manner of jasmine; they have a very sweet and very intense fragrance.

[Nahuatl description of the cacao flower:]
The cacao flower is slender, large, very fragrant, sweet-smelling; it resembles the tollosuchitl flower; it is cylindrical, narrow; its name is the cacao flower; it has a slightly smoky quality; it is small, it guards five flowers, it is very firm in its base, it separates at the foot; it is cup-shaped, double cup-shaped; it is soft, very pleasant to smell; all of it is pleasant, all of it is sweet-smelling, all of it is fragrant. I gather it, I arrange it, I place it, I collect it, I make a flower mat of it, I make a flower covering of it, I assemble it together, it is assembled together; it boils, it bubbles, it is bubbling, it continues to bubble.

translation:
Tree Flowers                                     340.
                                                fo. 189

There are other flowering trees called Ysquixochiguauitl. On them grow flowers called Ysquixochitl. They are white, very fragrant, very beautiful, and very prized.

[Nahuatl column:] Isquisuchitl, isquisuchiguauitl, quauhxiaoalli, mamae, quisquisso, xipatstic, tlatstic: its name is isquisuchitl; it is white like a magnolia blossom. The isquisuchitl is delicious, fragrant, sweet-smelling, rough to the touch on its underside, dark-colored, reddish; it is truly like the copal tree in form, with broad leaves; and its underside, and its scent: it is cold in water, cold in cacao; it is chilly, cold; it bubbles up, it crackles, it spreads out, it scatters, it sheds, it rises up into the air, it spreads along the ground, it rolls about, it tumbles along. The teuisquisuchitl is none other than the isquisuchitl itself.

There are other flowers called Tlapal ysquisuchitl, and they are called that not because they are entirely red, but because they are streaked and striped with red.

[Nahuatl column:] Tlapal isquisuchitl: it is truly the same as the isquisuchitl, except that it is slightly yellowish; it spreads flat, its surface is wide; it is slightly reddish, it spreads flat.

There are some trees in the forests called Cuetlaxsuchitl, and when the branches of these trees are broken, a milky liquid flows from them, white like milk. These trees produce flowers called [text continues on next page]

[Nahuatl column:] Cuetlax suchitl, quauhxiaoalhi, it is slender, it spreads wide, its surface is broad, quisso, it is straight, [text continues]

translation:
Book Eleven

Cuetlaxochitl: The leaves of this plant are like cherry leaves, but very colorful and soft; it has a very fine red color, but the flowers have no scent. They are beautiful and for that reason are prized.

There are some flowers that are also native to the forests, called teunacastli, which means precious or divine ears. They are so named because they are very fragrant, beautiful, and useful — they are an aromatic spice that is used a great deal for drinking with cacao.

Likewise in the forests there grow certain trees called vitziculsochitl, which produce flowers that bear the same name as the tree.

[Nahuatl column:]
...called cuetlaxochitl; it is chili-red, dark greenish, blood-colored in appearance, somewhat translucent, pale on the underside, spread out, flexible, thin and soft as leather — and this is what the cuetlaxochitl is like; it grows on rocky hillsides and gorges, producing itself there on its own.

Teucujtlasochitl: This is a forest flower. The teucujtlasochitl grows on trees; it hangs down, spreading over the branches of forest trees; its surface is somewhat grayish, they say somewhat dark; its stem, they say, is pale; it is fragrant and somewhat elongated; it is yellowish, deep yellow, pale yellow, tawny, more tawny — and for this reason it is yellow, fresh, and green; its color is deep, it fades; it is good-looking, it looks well, it should be kept, it brightens things, it is good...

Teunacastli, veinacastli: Its common name is sochitl [flower]; the flower together with the seedpod; mjcel.

Vitziculsochitl: The tree and its flower are called vitziculsochitl. The tree itself...

translation:
Flowers of Trees
Folio 190.

Some are white, others purple, others colored; none has a scent, yet they are prized for their fine appearance.

There are also some trees that are planted in the forests, called Tzompanquauitl. It is a medium-sized tree, has leafy branches, has a rounded crown and a fine appearance; it has flowers called equimisuchitl, which are very brightly colored and of fine appearance, but have no scent whatsoever.

The leaves of the tree described above are called Equimitl.

[Nahuatl column:] It is slender, tall, with spreading branches, with limbs that spread out: its color turns back and becomes mottled, as it is said: it has thorny flowers, of medium size, reddish, some reddish, some whitish; it cannot be climbed, it is not desirable, it is not remarkable; it is worthless, utterly worthless, it gives no pleasure.

The Tzompanquauitl tree: it stands upright by itself, its branches spread out nicely, rounded like a parasol, its flower is the equimisuchitl: it is red, truly scarlet in color, it has no scent, it is of no use, nothing adheres to it, nothing is desired from it. The tzompanquauitl is sweet, delicious, yet somewhat biting and astringent, with a rind; its seed pod, the equimitl, is red: just like a type of bean. As for how it seeds itself: the seed pod opens, and it splits apart; it is cut so that the seeds fall out, just like a pod bursting open.

The equimitl grows along with the tzompanquauitl; it is flat and likewise called equimitl: as has been said...

There are also trees in the forests called mapil suchitl, on which flowers grow that resemble a hand with its fingers — hence the name "finger flowers." They have thick and very dense leaves.

Also, the tree mentioned above is called Macpal suchitl because its flowers are like the palm of a hand with its fingers; it takes its name from the palm and the fingers.

Tenth Section, on shrubs that are neither true trees nor true herbs, and on their flowers.

There is a shrub called Teququauhxochitl that has red flowers which last two or three days without wilting and have no scent, yet they are beautiful. This plant grows on top of other trees, on their branches, and in the forks of other trees.
There is another plant that also grows on the branches and forks of other trees, called Quauh suchitl.
There is also another plant called Tecolotl y yatlia, which likewise grows on the branches of other trees.

There are some trees that in part resemble palm trees, because they have many leaves like palms, but they do not have branches like palms. They produce white flowers and are of the manner of clusters and flowers of palms.

¶ All flowers, when they begin to bloom: first they emit fragrance, they give off smoke-fragrance; then they drip, then they unfold, then they open, they spread downward; then they blaze, they open up their petals, they spread out, then they ripen, they become strong; when they are fragrant, they give pleasure, they give joy; when they are needed, when sap comes, when they are gathered by the sap: they speak, they are splendid, they spread their splendor, they spread their glory, they are radiant; their marigold-paper spreads out, their flower-paper unfolds, they become black, they become soiled, they bind themselves, they are bound; they are great, they blossom, they dry out. He deceives people, he causes them to go astray; he causes them to be pierced by thorns, he causes them to be scratched by thorns, he entangles them with the air-vine, he causes them to be consumed. He adorns people with flowers, he strews flowers before them, or he just offers them garlands; he perhaps just scatters blossoms for them, he places flowers in their hands, he spreads flowers in their hands, perhaps he adorns them with necklaces, or he places flowers upon their heads.

The twelfth paragraph: it passes on to what the nature and quality of this one is.

Teupochiotl [a plant]: it grows in this way — it is branching, many-branched, round-leafed, foam-leafed, smooth-barked, rough-barked — truly like njtva [a comparison]; it is somewhat good, well-spreading, somewhat spreading. And thus it discerns the good from the bad. Whoever becomes ill and eats it, or drinks its seed, or its resin, thereby he becomes heavy, thereby he grows, thereby he gains flesh, thereby he becomes stout: and for this reason it makes the vital forces of living beings good in their inner senses, it fattens them, it makes them flourish. But those of bad character it reveals: it makes them suffer, it causes them to be seen as drunkards with water, with pulque, with food it causes them to be swallowed up — and then immediately

translation:
On the maguey [fo. 200]

...it is one that shouts and sings as it dies: and while it still has life, for the benefit of people, going about providing sustenance everywhere, it gives of itself, gives of itself, extends itself, offers itself.

¶ The maguey: [I discuss] the maguey with its many hands, its paper-like leaves, its spines, its dark interior cavity, its heart, its fiber, its base, its outer skin, its stem, its juice that is drunk, its nectar, its water, its fiber threads; it is thick and firm, it is widespread; it produces clusters, it droops downward, it makes a dripping sound, it is drunk, it is pressed, it flows down, it trickles, it is syrupy.

¶ The tlacametl [large maguey]: alternatively vecapan — wide-leaved, broad-leafed.

¶ The ocelometl [jaguar maguey]: it is painted, patterned.

¶ The netmetl: it is ash-colored, gray, ash-hued, bluish-green like a bluebird.

¶ The macócol: it is bitter, afflicting.

¶ The metoxactli: it is sour, greenish.

¶ The xilometl: it has very slender leaves.

¶ The tzilacaiometl: it is painted and spotted, it is whitish-spined.

¶ The vitzijtyl maguey: it is small and round, very spreading, dark blue-green.

¶ The acametl: its leaves are very slender, like slender reed-grass.

translation:
Book Eleven

Teucomitl: it is rounded, rough on the surface, rough and porous, edible, worth acquiring. Why it is called teucomitl: those whose eyes have become afflicted can no longer see clearly because of it; for it is porous, and it swells and puffs up the feet. Teucomitl grows in two places, in the arid lands, in the fearful places.

Notzoli: it is wrinkled, smooth, it sheds its skin, it has teats. It provides a sticky liquid: it was eaten as food.

Teunuchtli: what is now called simply nuchtli — it is green, edible as a vegetable, long, slender, something to be sucked, clear, something that refreshes one, cooling.

Tememetla: it is called chapaltontli, tlalpanton; it is hollow, flat; it cools one, it is clear/transparent, it refreshes and opens things up.

Tetzmitl, also called tetzynetl: it provides a sap, it is sticky, it is a medicine.

Tlaltinol tetzmitl: it is said to resemble tetzmitl; yet it is a little smaller, yellowish, reddish: its sap is a medicine for the eyes.

Tlapal tetzmitl: it is said to resemble hoatl, the burnt/scorched tetzmitl.

Chapter Eight: Of Precious Stones.

First paragraph: concerning all precious stones in general, how they are sought and where they are found.

Precious stones are not found in the state in which they now appear in the hands of those who own them or who sell them; they are not found already beautiful and polished and shining. Rather, they are formed inside rough stones that have no appearance or beauty at all, which lie out in those fields, or people bring them in from the towns.

This is the eighth chapter: it speaks of the many kinds of canes [reeds/stalks].

The first paragraph speaks of the many different kinds of canes, and of what they are properly called.

All the various kinds of canes do not emerge or appear in their goodness, in their freshness, in their fineness, in their maturity, in their desirability — rather they are there [in the ground]; they are covered, hidden, not to be admired, not to be sought, of no worth —

translation:
Precious Stones                                                fo. 203.

from here to there. And other such stones many times have within themselves precious stones, though not large but very small ones; some have them in the middle, others on the edges, or on all sides.

[illustration: a figure standing on a hill pointing, with a sun above and a person lying on the ground]

There are people who know where precious stones are found, and it is that any precious stone, wherever it may be, emits from itself a vapor or exhalation like a fine smoke; and this smoke appears when the sun is about to rise, or at the rising of the sun. Those who search for and know these stones, place themselves in a convenient spot when the sun is about to rise, and look toward where the sun comes up, and where they see a fine little mist rising, they then know that there, there is a precious stone, or that one has formed there, or that one is hidden there. And they go to that place, and if they find some stone from which that little mist was rising, they understand that inside it there is some precious stone, and they break it open to look for it.

[Nahuatl column:]
It is seen upon it: wherever it goes, it rolls along, it travels about, or somewhere it drifts along, it goes skimming along. And so the mother of the precious stone does not carry it; it is placed somewhere — it may be small, or perhaps on its surface, not very large, just a little bit, just a small amount, just a little, just a tiny bit — in the place where it was set. And those who are knowledgeable, who take heed of these things, they among themselves perceive it: by this means they recognize it, they see it clearly — for it steams, it glimmers; at dawn, just before sunrise it comes out, and they seek it where it places itself, where it stands — they go to meet the sun; and when the sun comes out, with its full face it truly gazes upon it, it shines very brightly, it dazzles; it gleams very brightly: in that place where the smoke rises like a little puff of mist, they see it clearly, the shining serpent-like gleam; it is then taken — the precious stone — whether it be a green stone, or a clear crystal, or some other sparkling gem.

Libro vndecimo

Y sino ay piedra donde sale aquel humo to caven en la tierra, y hallan alguna caxa de piedra donde estan algunas piedras preciosas escondidas, so por ventura esta en la misma tierra perdida so escondida. Tambien ay otra señal donde se crian piedras preciosas: especialmente las que se llama Chalchiujtes; enel lugar donde se crian yerua que esta alli nacida, esta siempre verde. Yes porque estas piedras siempre echan de si vna exalacion fresca y humeda, y donde esto, esta cava y hallan las piedras en que se cria estas Chalchiujtes. Las turquesas hallanse en minas: ay minas donde las cavan, y saca vnas mejores que otras: vnas que son claras y otras que son finas, vnas que son trasparentes; y otras que no lo son. Tambien ay minas donde se halla ambar fino, y el cristal o veril, y tambien las piedras deuasas, y tambien Jaspe. Y tambien las piedras donde se hazen los espejos; tan bien vnas negras que son como aguache: y tambien las piedras de sangre; todas estas se hazen en los montes y las cavan como minas. Y destas piedras dexaspes muy preciosas ay gra cantidad en los terminos del pueblo que se llama Sanctiago de Tebalco de llas hazen Aras, y otras piedras muy preciosas: hallanse a la orilla de la mar, otras preciosas y perlas y conchas blancas y coloradas. Y otras piedras que se llaman Biti Bilterl, que se halla a la orilla de los Rios en la prouincia de Totonacasa. Quando los que conocen las piedras, hallan alguna piedra preciosa dentro en ella: primeramente, la quiebran y sacan la piedra

translation:
Book Eleven

If there is no stone where that smoke comes out going into the earth, and they find some stone box where some precious stones are hidden, it may be that they are lost or hidden in the very ground. There is also another sign where precious stones are found: especially those called Chalchiujtes; in the place where they grow, the grass that is born there is always green. And this is because these stones always give off a cool and moist vapor, and where this occurs, they dig and find the stones in which these Chalchiujtes are formed. Turquoises are found in mines; there are mines where they are dug, and some come out better than others: some that are clear and others that are fine, some that are transparent and others that are not. There are also mines where fine amber is found, and crystal or beryl, and also the deuasa stones, and also Jasper. And also the stones from which mirrors are made; also some black ones that are like a dark liquid; and also bloodstones; all of these are found in the mountains and are dug out like mines. And of these very precious jasper stones there is a great quantity in the territory of the town called Santiago de Tebalco, from which altars are made, and other very precious stones: they are found on the seashore, other precious ones and pearls and white and colored shells. And other stones called Biti Bilterl, which are found on the banks of the Rivers in the province of Totonacasa. When those who know about stones find a precious stone inside one: first, they break it open and extract the stone

[Nahuatl column:] They look at it carefully; they take it up gently with their hands, saying that it is within the earth. One can discern, one can recognize that it is a fine stone, that there inside is a thing of beauty; or perhaps a green stone, or perhaps a smooth stone within the earth, or perhaps one finds it in a ravine, or in a crack, or in a hollow in the rock. One's children do not yet know how to identify a fine stone; it always shines: it radiates coolness; it emits a vapor — its breath, its fragrance, is very great: it is moist inside; it can be seen; thus the turquoise rests there, or the fine turquoise, or the blue-green stone; it is very beautiful, very bright. And thus it glows; and thus it settles in a cave, among the stones, among the crags, among the caves; in the hills; and thus immediately...

Second Paragraph: on the emerald and other precious stones of its kind.

Emeralds are called Quetzalitztli: there are very fine ones in this land, they are precious and of great value. They are called thus because "Quetzal" means a very green feather, and "itztli" means obsidian stone, which is very smooth and without any blemish. And these two qualities the fine emerald possesses.

[Nahuatl column:]
It is a medicine, it is a remedy; it comes along the edge of the water; the hummingbird appears at the water's edge; it dwells among the reeds, and in the warm lands it does not appear in rivers. And as for the green stone, it is the mother of jade; when the skilled one who knows how to see it looks at it, he spreads out a cape. He takes it up, he examines it carefully; and then he cuts it, he shapes it, and then right away he polishes it, he smooths it, he makes it gleam with the color of quetzal feathers, he makes it shine.

Second paragraph: concerning the quetzal-obsidian stone, and what it resembles.

Quetzalitztli: its name comes from quetzal and also from itztli, because of its greenish appearance, just like the quetzal feather, it is green; and its flesh-color is dark, and when one looks through it, it is precious, fine, lustrous.

The crystal of this land is called Tevilotl; it is a stone found in mines, in the mountains. Also among these grow amethysts, which are clear purple stones.

The amber of this land is called Apoconalli: it is called this because the amber of this land — these stones so named — resemble the little bubbles or blisters that water makes when the sun strikes it at rising, so that they appear to be clear yellow, like gold. These stones are found in mines in the mountains.

[Nahuatl column:]

It is truly so, it is truly it, it causes movement, it descends, it causes one to be adorned, it causes one to be adorned. It causes one to be made manifest, it is round, it is broad, it resounds, it resounds repeatedly. It causes one to be admired. Tevilotl is known. It causes light to shine.

Tevilotl: this tevilotl forms somewhere, it is named, it is of the hills, it is hollow; some are white, some are greenish, it is yellowish, it is said, it is called tlapaltevilotl. This tevilotl forms a skin, it comes out smooth, it resounds truly like water, it is clear, it is clean, it is very clean, it is exceedingly clean, some are smoky, wind-dried, it is hard, a small stick, it is admirable, it is admired, it causes admiration, it is much admired.

Apoconalli: it forms upon water, it is called Apoconalli: for this reason those knowledgeable people who named it caused it to be admired. It resembles the foam of water; when the sun comes up at dawn, bubbles appear, or it resembles the sun itself, and so they named it. Apoconalli they caused to be admired.

There are three kinds of these stones:
The first kind is called yellow amber: these appear to have within themselves a spark of fire, and they are very beautiful.

The second kind is called quetzal apoconalli; it is called this because they are yellow mixed with light green.

The third kind is called ystac apoconalli; it is called this because they are whitish yellow, they are not transparent nor are they very precious.

These apoconalli stones are located on hills, they come out of the hillside, they can be sucked up, they are very pleasing to look at. They are called by two names, this apoconalli, from which it derives its appearance. The first kind is called yellow apoconalli; it is just like a stone; it is as if it were a tlexochio that had come together, as if a small glowing ember, it sparkles from within; it is as if a fire were burning inside it, as if a candle's flame were inside it, seeking to come out; it is very marvelous: and when it is most marvelous, when a candle is placed next to it, it draws in the candle's light, it illuminates, it shines. The second kind is called quetzal apoconalli; its appearance is greenish: it is like an emerald, and it seems as if a quetzal feather were embedded within it, sparkling inside. The third kind is called white apoconalli; it is called white apoconalli because it is not very yellow, it is only somewhat pale, only a little colored, only faintly tinted. All these apoconalli stones produce vapor as they breathe.

translation:
Book Eleventh.

These stones I believe are black emeralds, by virtue of what I have experienced with them: ground into a powder like flour and applied to fresh wounds and sores, they heal them very quickly and do not let them fester. Ground as described, mixed with quince paste or any other preserve, well kneaded so that the preserve holds together with the powder or flour, taken in a quantity about the size of one or two pills, they are very beneficial against rheumatic ailments, give great resonance to the voice, and relieve any inner heat. I know this by experience of many days.

There were in former times in this land, and they are still found today, since pieces of them turn up in various ancient buildings, certain clear green stones called Tolteca ytztli; they are precious, and I believe more virtuous than those described above.

There are other stones of this type called Matlalitztli; they are dark blue.

[Nahuatl column:]
Very rough in texture, [called by various names]; some are called iztapalcatl; the dark ones are no longer so well regarded; from here comes mizteti [mirror-stone]. As for the white obsidian: it is said to be sharp, blade-like, serrated — [found at] Tlaxcala, Hatzoponja; some called white obsidian, not very earthy, somewhat whitish on the surface, and there one sees it gleaming and shining. Some yellow ones: [they say] the dog's obsidian resembles the pupil of a bird's wing in its lines. Some are greenish, somewhat blue-green.

Tolteca obsidian: it is somewhat blue-green, somewhat cooling, somewhat flower-like, somewhat rough; it was truly one's property, truly one's possession, truly one's good fortune among those who lived as Toltecs (as is recounted today) — they lacked nothing to eat, nothing to wear, nothing at all. It is said that for this reason it is named Tolteca; the obsidian is good, it is to be seen, it spreads [its quality], this obsidian.

Matlalitztli: its name comes from matlalli [blue-green color] combined with iztli [obsidian].

And other clear ones, and others very blue are precious; they are worked like those of obsidian, they are rare, and I consider them of greater virtue than those mentioned above.

[illustration: a stone with flowers growing from it]

In this land there are some stones that belong to the same kind as those mentioned above. They are called Xiuhmatlalitsli, and a second explanation of the name says it is a sapphire. It is said to be a very precious stone, more so than all others, and it is said to be like a drop of water that comes from the full green when it burns: which drop is very clear and somewhat bright blue. This stone, when cut like obsidian blades, shines in the night. This most precious stone is found in the same mines where the obsidian stones are extracted, but they appear very rarely and people prize them greatly. They are of great virtue, more than the emerald. I have experience of the virtue and beauty of this stone.

There are some black stones called Teuteil; they have the appearance of jet. They are rare, and have a very fine black without any mixture of another color. Such blackness and fineness and purity is not found in any other stone. It is not lacking in great virtue, although I have no personal experience of it.

[Nahuatl text, right column:]
Its appearance, or as it were the color of the sky-blue turquoise, blue-green, deep blue, surface-blue, turquoise-blue: and its moisture is like clear water somewhat watery; and on the other hand it is somewhat dense, very smooth and polished, gleaming here and there, making itself seen everywhere, spreading its blue-green color, very green.

Xiuhmatlalihzhtli: from it comes what is called sky-blue, and turquoise, and water; it is bell-like among precious things, so that it appears wondrous: when it is seen, it is as if water is dripping from it; and it also appears as if it were the color of turquoise, just like the turquoise-bird; and indeed it gives off smoke well when burned. A green wood is attributed to it, the turquoise-bird alights upon it, flaring up into flame as it burns: and at night, a handspan of it lights up the surroundings, wondrous, making things visible, a thing of awe, a precious thing.

Teuteil: from it comes what is called divine stone; and therefore one alone suffices to make it truly black, which is to say coal-black in color, like coal: it is said to resemble obsidian, black, dark, and so on.

translation:
Book Eleven

There are also certain stones called Ezetl, which means bloodstone; it is a brown stone speckled with small spots of color like blood, and other small greenish ones among the reddish ones. This stone has the virtue of stopping the blood that flows from the nostrils. I have personal experience of the virtue of this stone, because I have one as large as a fist, or a little less, rough as it was broken from the rock. In this year of one thousand five hundred and seventy-six, during this Pestilence, it has saved the lives of many whose blood and life were flowing out through their nostrils. Taking it in the hand and holding it pressed there for a while, the bleeding would stop and the person would be healed. Of this disease many have died, and many continue to die throughout this New Spain. There are many witnesses to this in this town of Tlatelolco de Santiago.

Fifth Paragraph: concerning the stones from which mirrors are made, and other lesser stones.

In this land there are stones from which mirrors are made; there are veins of these stones, and mines from which they are extracted. Some of these [stones are] mace tliltic, caputztic, chaputic, or cemactic tliltic, or actic in tlillan.

Ezetl: The ezetl takes its name from eztli [blood], and also from tetl [stone], because of the way it is painted in the stone, as if it were blood; as though it were dried blood that no longer has color. It drips down, some make one shiver, some cause fright, some make one scatter, some cause one to feel struck; it is painted with blood-colors, it is splashed with color, it is sprinkled with color, the colors sparkle and shine, it spatters, it sprays color over everything — and all of this because it takes its name from blood, it draws blood from things, it causes bleeding, it brings on the flowing of blood; though struck hard, it provokes great anger. It soothes anger, it calms, it cools, it heals.

Fifth paragraph: it speaks of another, separately named stone from which mirrors are made, which is called tezcatl.

Tezcatl [obsidian mirror]: it comes from somewhere — its name comes from the hill, from the cave, from the place of color, from the place of reflection; this tezcatl [mirror stone]...

translation:
Precious Stones.                    folio 210.

Some stones are white, and from them good mirrors are made; these mirrors are called "balancianos," mirrors of ladies and lords. They have very fine metal; they show the face very accurately. When they are still in the raw stone they look like pieces of metal; when they are worked and polished they are very beautiful, very smooth, without a single flaw, and they are precious. There are other stones of this same metal that are black; when they are worked and polished, mirrors are made from them that show the face in reverse from what it truly is: they make the face large and misshapen, things appear thick and long, the lips are thick and misshapen, the nostrils are large and coarse — they represent nothing as it truly is. They carve these mirrors in many shapes: some round, others triangular, others in other shapes; they are sold in the marketplaces, some large, others medium, others small.

In this land there are flints, very good ones, and of many kinds in their make, and of many colors, as is explained in detail in the text. They were used in former times to make arrowheads and knives to open the chests of those who were sacrificed.

[Nahuatl column:]
Some are white, some are black; this one is good for seeing, for reflecting clearly, bright and clear. It is called the mirror of noblemen, the mirror of rulers. The black one is not good; it does not show clearly, it does not show one truly — it is called (they say) a distorting mirror; whoever looks into it is shown: where the mouth appears large, the eyes crossed, the lips thick, the cheeks puffed out, not slim. They say it is a foul, distorting mirror. This mirror — some are hollow, some are convex. They say: a reed mirror, a mountain mirror, a cave mirror; it clatters, it spreads flat, it makes things appear large, it distorts; I scrape it, I hollow it out, I make it flat, I scrape it clean, I sand it, I polish it finely, I polish it with fine sand, I burnish it, I make it smooth, I make it shine, I make it into a mirror; I look at myself in the mirror, there I appear, there I see myself.

Tecpatl (flint): this kind comes in various forms; its name is: rounded, broad, ridged; another kind fully formed: smooth, very smooth, resonant, gritty-surfaced, rough, pointed, flat, lumpy, pocked,

Now they are no longer useful for anything except for arquebuses and for striking fire with them; nonetheless they still use them for the tips of arrows.

¶ There is a kind of green flint called Xoxouhqui tecpatl, which resembles jade. The lapidaries call them Tecelic, because they are white to work, and have some spots of light blue.

¶ As for the worked and curious stones that are worn tied to the wrists, whether of crystal or other precious stones, they are called chopilotl. This term can be applied to any stone that is curiously worked or beautiful, which they call chopilotic.

¶ There are some small white stones, very white, which have some veins and streaks of other colors. They are called Tepuchtli.

¶ In this land there is marble,

translation:
Precious Stones                    folio 211

They call it Aytzli: it is the equivalent of the marble of Spain.

There are certain precious stones called Vitsitsil-tel, which means a stone that resembles the hummingbird. This is a small white stone; but the light makes it appear in various colors, just as it also makes the hummingbird's feather appear in various colors — the hummingbird appears in diverse colors. This stone, according to the diversity of the light that strikes it: this is well explained in the text. It has a shape like that of an ant. This stone is found on the shores of the sea, among the sand; and it is also found in a river that runs through the land of Totonacapan. It is seen at night, because it shines in the manner of a firefly, or like a small candle burning; and from a distance it appears to be nothing but a firefly. They recognize it as this stone in that the light stays still and does not move. It is rare and precious; only lords and their relatives use it, or at least those of the color of a very fine pearl.

[illustration: drawing of stones/gems with a small bird]

[Nahuatl text, right column:]
Vitzitziltetl: its name comes from "vitzitzili" (hummingbird) and "tetl" (stone), because of its appearance, which is like the hummingbird's iridescence, which is also called totozcatleton. Its appearance is like the countless colors that spread and flash upon it: from it emerge red, scarlet, green, the color of the turquoise bird, the color of the roseate spoonbill, orange-red, and yellow-green. It shines like one small ember, like a tiny ant, like a small spindle whorl — just a tiny speck, just a little spark. Its home, where it appears, is in the divine waters, in the sky-waters of Acaltitlan, and also there in the Totonacapan river, at Texcalapan, where it appears. It only comes glowing, like a little spark gleaming; or like a small candle burning, when it is seen moving about at night; and when it moves, when it glows in the darkness, one recognizes the vitzitziltetl. It is hard, watery-clear, smooth, very precious, admirable, wonderfully marvelous, iridescent, sparkling.

translation:
Book Eleven

In this land there are many kinds of shells, which these native people use as precious things; they call them Atscalli. They are of various kinds and various colors; they are from sea creatures that live within them. Some are red, others white, others yellow, others of various colors. Those called Quetzal-atscalli and Chalchiuh-atscalli have such variety of colors on the inside that they look like very rich enamels, and the way the light plays on them varies their appearance in different forms. Some call these shells Vitsitzil-atscalli; others of these shells are bright red on the outside, like vermilion. All of these are used to adorn oneself at dances, and they are highly prized. All these shells are called Tapachtli.

The word Atscalli is used for all shellfish or their shells, as [the text continues...]

[RIGHT COLUMN - Nahuatl text translation:]
¶ Tapachtli: no one knows their name; they are called caomitl, having a flat surface; they are called tapachtli because they produce a ringing sound; they are wide, strong, thick, large, all called Atscalli. Those that wander along the shore: some of them are red, some are white — these are called iuopalli; some are entirely suffused with color. That which is called Quetzal-atscalli, or also Chalchiuh-atscalli: they glisten like the hummingbird stone. Some call them vihizil-atscalli; and some that are transparent are called tapachtli. These tapachtli are desired for wearing, to be placed on both sides, to be set as shoulder pieces, to be strung, to be made into necklaces, to be placed in the Toltec manner, to be used as adornments, to be worn as necklaces, to be lived with, to be eaten, to be counted.

These are the Tecucistli, which are large sea-shells. Also those called chipolli, and others called Cilli, which are small precious little shell-beads; also the abaneras which they call tapachtli, and other shells which they call tecucistli.

The sea-shells are white; some are large, others are small. All of them are coiled and are precious, and they are played like a horn or trumpet.

Some of the shells are fine red, others are whitish-red, or purple.

[illustration of shells]

Of the abaneras, or sea-shells: some are light yellow, others more yellow.

The shells of oysters, in which pearls are made, are on the outside rough and of no appearance, and of a brownish color like rotten bone. But on the inside they are smooth and glazed and very beautiful, like enameled in all colors — red and yellow and blue and crimson and light green and purple, and all other colors — and they resemble the rainbow in its diverse colors.

[illustration of shells and pearls]

...which lives in the water, having a shell-surface: like the tecuistli, like the chipoli, like the cili, like the tapaxtli, like the tecuicistli, etc.

The tecistli is white; some are large, some small, spiral-shaped, awe-inspiring; they can be blown as a flute: one blows into the teciz, one makes it sound, one clears it out.

The tlapaltecistli: broad with color, of mixed color, whitish, broad with color, of a mixed and whitish color.

The tapachtli has already been described.

The aiopalli: likewise a water-stone, broad with color, colored, somewhat colored, bluish-colored, of mixed color.

The quetzal-stone, or else the jade-stone, or else the hummingbird-stone: on top they look like excrement, as one might say they resemble smoke-stained soot, of an ashen, dusty appearance, as if they had gone stale. But inside they are glassy and slippery, very wondrous, astonishing, shining with color — red, yellow, the color of the xiuhtototl bird, of the roseate spoonbill, green, blue-green, wrapped in color, encircled by color, radiating color...

There is also silver, and copper, and lead, which grow in various places, in ravines and on cliffs. Before the Spaniards came to this land, no one paid attention to silver or lead. They searched only for gold in the streams, because where the water runs they would scoop it up with gourds, washing the sand, and in this way they found grains of gold — some as large as grains of maize, others smaller, others like sand.
After having treated in the preceding chapters and books of medicinal herbs and of the stones that have great virtue for the maintenance of health, and also of gold, which has very favorable properties for health, it seemed to me that it would be good to set down here the properties of the resins found in this land, which the native people use greatly for their health, and I have much experience of their virtues. The resin called white copal, and another resin called —

[Nahuatl column:]
They say it rains, that the stream (as they call it) is very clear; in one direction it is yellow, in another it is greenish; it looks as though it boils, it appears very bright. And it is found either in the ground or inside a hill — this yellow teocuitlatl [gold]. One must not go down, nor go rolling; it keeps one off from the ground and the hill, [it needs] a pick, a scraper, a sifter. Likewise it is found mixed with teucujtlatl [gold], with tepuztli [copper/metal], with tenextli [lime-ash]. And where there are shallow pools, there the teucujtlatl appears in the water. And for this reason, before the Spaniards came here, no Mexican, no one at all, knew how to dig out the yellow teucujtlatl; they would scoop it up with atole-gruel ladles, with wooden xicalli gourds; there they would wash the yellow teucujtlatl, and then it would come out bright as it is. All the maize husks: then they would take it up as sand, setting it aside, sifting it, knowing it, spreading it for necklaces, for bracelets, for ear-plugs, for lip-plugs. This teucujtlatl, the yellow one, is also called itediqujca, also called teul, and

cha-popotli, which is like pitch from Castile, and another gum called ulli, which is black, fibrous, and very light: these three gums, melted together and made into something like tar, applied to the legs and body, do great good to all interior and exterior members. It should be noted that the copal and the chapopotli can be melted together in a pot placed over the coals, having first ground everything up together: equal parts of one and the other. But the ulli must be melted by itself, placing it on a spit and setting it alight over the flame of a fire; as it begins to burn, it starts to drip a black liquid like ink, which should be collected in a bowl, and thus it becomes a liquid. They can melt as much as they wish, though it may not be as much as the rest; but the more of it there is, the better the pitch will be. After the ulli has been melted by itself, it must be joined with the other melted materials, and it is not necessary to do anything else but to stir what is mixed together for three or four days or more, rolling it, placed in the sun at intervals so that it blends well, so that it forms an ointment useful for many days. It can be applied to the body as many times as desired. Cut leggings from dressed deerskin that reach from the feet to the ankles, and they need not be sewn; with this ointment applied to their inner side, everything...

The sun's precious golden substance: it is wondrous, golden, good, precious, warm, and a cause of joy and learning; it is the sun's own property, the reflection of our lords, of our Lord. It comes from the place called Haviz-calpan, resembling something refined, which they call tonatiuh-icuil, very golden, very wondrous; it spreads like flowers, it resembles the golden liquid teucuitlatl, and it drips at its edges. The golden teucuitlatl does not sustain life by itself; it is directed toward the sun: thus it is not known by any single deity, the true deity who shares the mid-point of the gods, truly well-known as the emerging god, the true god — the sun liquefies it, the sun causes it to glow; in the sunlight alone it says it is nowhere, meaning it came and entered into the sun's precious substance. This gold, the yellow and white, is fully complete, fully formed, thoroughly refined; it rolls about on earth, it can be gathered, it can be retrieved, it can be cut apart, it can be lifted, it can be licked: it relieves one's fatigue, it cures one's illness, it refreshes one's spirit, it revives one. First paragraph treats of cochineal and other fine colors.
The color with which cochineal is painted — which they call nochestli, meaning the blood of the prickly pear — is so named because in a certain type of prickly pear there grow some worms that...

[Nahuatl column:]
Mirror-dust [tezca tlalli]: it is exactly like the polishing-sand of mirrors; it is the black, sandy, glistening substance used for polishing mirrors.

Certain kind of black ink [Tezcatl-tlalli]: it is like the mirror-stone, a formed thing, something marvelous, glistening, shimmering; with it one causes things to gleam.

Flint emery [Tecpa xalli]: it is rough, it is a polishing agent, it is flint-like, it crumbles, it is sandy, it is granular, it is coarse, it is very coarse, it is thick-grained, it is very thick-grained, it is like ground meal, it is dusty; it is something that can be spread, something that can be applied, something that levels out, something that scrapes, something that smooths, something that polishes. I smooth things, I polish them, I make them refined.

The eleventh chapter here speaks of all the various colors. The first paragraph here [speaks of] where they come from and how they are made.

Nochestli [cochineal]: it takes its name from the nopal cactus, and also from blood, because it is produced upon the nopal; and it is just like blood, it is like clotted blood.

There is another kind of base, mixed cochineal dye which they call Hapalnextli, meaning a certain impure grade of cochineal, because it is mixed with ash or with flour. There is also a false cochineal that also grows on the leaves of the prickly pear, which they also call Hapalnextli, and those who raise true cochineal give the prickly pear leaves — on which this false one grows — to the cochineal insects, and they also mix it in with the good cochineal to sell it, which is a great fraud.

The fine yellow color they call Xochipalli, which means the dye of yellow flowers. This yellow color is brought from and grows in warm lands.

...or red, or firm/hard: just as the green one called citli, tlatlaxcalolli. And this alone is the cochineal itself, called nocheztlaxcalli: I make tortillas of nocheztli, I spread tortillas of nocheztli, I handle tortillas of nocheztli, I eat tortillas of nocheztli.

Tlapalnextli: its name comes from the fact that it contains tlapalli [dye/color] and nextli [ash/lye]: because it is just the same cochineal in its product, like tlarelo, like texio, like tlaixnamyctilli — all of which are just cochineal — and all that is edible, the nopal cactus produces it; this tlapalnextli dye takes its name from the nopal. It does not color well, it is not firm, it crumbles apart, it fades, it peels off. To dye with tlapalnextli: it does not dye well, it does not adhere well, it spreads, it causes discoloration.

Xochipalli: its name comes from flowers and from tlapalli [dye]; as one might say, it is the dye of flowers. This xochipalli is made in hot sunny places, it is used for dyeing, for painting, for brightening things, for making things luminous...

translation:
Book Eleven

The fine blue color is called Matlalli, which means blue. This color is made from blue flowers; it is a highly prized color and very pleasing to look at. It is also called Cardenillo in the Spanish language.

There is a color that is a bright yellow, which is called Çacatlaxcalli, meaning "bread of grass," because it is made from certain very thin yellow grasses. It is sold in the marketplaces in the form of small flattened yellow tortillas. These tortillas are used for dyeing things yellow or for making yellow paint for painting.

There is a whitish red color [text continues on next page]

[RIGHT COLUMN - Nahuatl]
It blooms, it bursts into bloom. I adorn with flowers, I spread flowers upon it, I adorn it with flowers.

Matlalli: its name comes from nowhere else than the plant whose flower is the matlalli — it is deep blue-green, and somewhat greenish; it is beautiful, attractive, fresh, light-colored, lustrous, bright, fine-looking. I make it into a dye bath, I make something into a dye bath, I soak things in it, I spread it out, I apply it in layers.

Cacatlaxcalli: it comes from cacatl and tlaxcalli, because it resembles the way dried grass forms a mass — it is yellow, smooth, very thin. I make cacatlaxcalli with it. The tortilla-cake, like a proper tortilla, is wide, spread out, large, thin; it is made in the sun; it is yellow, whitish-yellow, golden-toned, yellow-hued, pale yellow. I make things with cacatlaxcalli; I coat things, I apply it as a finish, I make things firm with it.

Here in this land there is a large tree, with many branches and a thick trunk, which is called vitzquaujtl. Vitzquaujtl [brazilwood]: the spine, and the tree: it is called by this name, this great tree; and truly it is fragrant within, inside of it; the dye is made from it for coloring, for dyeing red things, for striping yellow, for making things yellow, for making things pale yellow, for exhausting the color in a vessel — only somewhat hard to cut, somewhat dense; it shows in dyeing on leather; it makes a fine chichiltic red, a pale chichiltic. Chiltic, chilpatzaltic, chilpatic. It is for dyeing; it is not for painting. I go to cut brazilwood, I go to bore out brazilwood, I give the brazilwood its color, I go to hew brazilwood, I go to gather brazilwood, I sell brazilwood.

Book Eleven.

There is a tree that grows in hot lands: the fruit of which is not for eating; this fruit is called nacascolotl, and this fruit is used together with that earth called Haliyac and haseche, and with pomegranate rinds, and with the gum called mezquicopalli, to make a very good ink for writing.

There is also in this land a plant, or shrub in the manner of a plant, which grows in the hot lands and is called tesoatl: the leaves of this plant or shrub are cooked together with alum and with laliyac, and this makes a very fine red color with which a great deal of red ochre is dyed, and it is very useful.

translation:
On Colors                                                         folio 219.

There is an herb found in the hot lands called [Tlacuillo?]. One takes this herb and squeezes it, and the juice is poured into certain vessels where it dries or congeals. With this color one dyes things a dark blue, and it is very lustrous: it is a prized color.

[illustration]

There is a light blue color, the color of the sky, which they call Texotli, and xoxouhqui: it is a color much used in garments that people wear, such as the cloaks of men and the huipiles of women. It is made from the same flowers as the matlalli, and it is a fine color.

There is a yellow stone which, when ground up, makes a yellow color that painters use; they call it tecocauitl.

[illustration]

They make a natural ink from the smoke of pine torches, and this fine ink they call Tilli, ocotl. They have certain vessels for making it called Tlilcomalli, in which it is made after the manner of distilling vessels. It is useful for many inks for writing and for medicines that —

Tlaceuilli: it is an herb that is heated and thereby made; it smokes, it turns green, it turns into a paltz color, it settles here and there, it spreads out. One takes up the tlaceuilli there. This dye is dark green. It makes one green, it makes one pale, it makes one striped in color, it stripes in color: I make something paltz-colored with it, I create the paltz-color.

Texotli: the texotli — what it is called — texotli is greenish, green, very green, quite green; it is somewhat whitish-faced, somewhat pale-faced, and wondrous.

Tecocavitl: it is called a stone that comes from somewhere, a yellowish thing. It is a yellow-orange stone, an orange stone, a yellow stone. It makes one pale, it makes one striped in color, it makes one ash-colored: I make something tecocau-colored, I spread the tecocau color, I make the tecocau color emerge.

Tlilli: it is pine-torch soot, the resin of the pine. It makes one striped with black, it makes one pale with black, it makes one dark with black, it spreads black over one; it is rough, very rough, very roughened; one becomes smeared with it, one becomes covered with it, one becomes —

translation:
Book Eleven.

...with many things that serve as medicines.

There is a substance called Tlaliyac that is useful for many things, especially for dyeing and making ink. It is found in many places, such as in Tepexic, etc.

Third paragraph: on certain materials from which colors are made.

Alum is a well-known stone called Tlalxocotl, which means sour or tart earth. There is much of it, and it is sold in the marketplaces; there is much trade in it, because the dyers use it a great deal.

There is a stone that painters use, which is somewhat brownish and produces a grayish-black color. It is used by those who make clay gourds; it is like a black pearl, and when ground, they paint the gourds with it. After firing it appears very black and shiny.

[Nahuatl column:]
...I apply color to it, I dye it, I paint it over, I apply color, I make it smooth, I make it level.

Tlaliac: its name comes from the earth, and because of its sourness, because it is of the earth, it belongs to the mountain.

Third paragraph: it speaks of how colors are made and prepared.

Tlalxocotl: its name comes from earth and from fruit [xocotl]; because of the earth it is flat, somewhat rough: and because it is sour, it is tart-tasting, somewhat whitish, it mixes among things, it cools things, it is a bit white, very white. It always purifies well, it purifies the surface, it clarifies the face.

Tetlilli, or tezauhctlilli: its name is taken from tobacco and from black; because it is needed for mirrors, and because it makes things shine. I apply it to make things shiny.

translation:
On Colors [Chapter I]                                                    folio 311

Here in this land they use vermillion a great deal, as they do in Spain, calling it Tlaujtl.

They use chalk a great deal; the women use it for spinning. It is sold in the marketplaces and is called Tizatl.

Here in this land there are stones from which varnish is made; they are called Tetizatl. These are stones that form in streams, and they become hardened. They are used a great deal for varnishing smooth stones.
There are also others called Chimalticatl, which come from near Huaxtepec. They are extracted like stone, for working. These stones are first fired; they are like plaster of Castile, and are sold in the marketplaces.

On Compound Colors.

The yellow color, mixing what is called Çacatlaxcalli with [continues...]

[Nahuatl column:]
Tlaujtl: it takes its name from a certain place; it is a stone, a flat rock, it is the substance of flat rocks, rocky in nature. It is desirable, of the hills, of the caves, something needed, something required, something to be obtained, something to spread thinly, something to apply as a wash. I apply it as a wash, I make things ruddy with it, I make things glow with it.

Tizatl [chalk]: women grind it; it is white, cylindrical, round. It is not mud; when water is added it becomes like a crust. Then in the rocky place it is refined. Chalk makes things firm. I make myself firm with it, I make things firm with it, I make things smooth with it.

Tetlcatl: it takes its name from stone; it comes from stone, and also from chalk. Because of this it is ground, it is crumbled, it is broken up, and then it is put to use. I make things firm with it.

The Inxticalitl is made with water in Tula where it is prepared; it is strained and then ground and broken up. When I want to use it, I mix it with Michoacan chalk, which is called texotlalli, and then I mix it with chia water, it firms it up, when placed in a cup or in sand.

Chimalticatl comes from Oaxtepeс, where it breaks off like a mirror. When it is worked it becomes very glossy. Then it is mixed and smoothed and applied.

Here is told, here is described: Tlapalli [red color].

Tiappalli: it takes its name from the fact that it reddens things, or because it is reddish, and...

...the sea, which they call teuatl, and this does not mean "god of the water," nor a goddess of water, but rather means "wondrous water of great depth and vastness." It is also called ylhuicaatl, which means "water that joined with the sky." For the ancient inhabitants of this land believed that the sky meets the water in the sea, as if it were a house, where the water forms the walls and the sky is the ceiling above them. And for this reason they called the sea ylhuicaatl, as if saying "water that joins with the sky." But now, after the coming of the faith, they already know that the sky does not join with the water, nor with the land, and so they call the sea veyatl, which means "great water," and fearsome, and fierce, full of foam and waves and masses of water, and bitter salty water bad for drinking, where many animals are bred and which is in continual motion.

[illustration: a sailing vessel on waves with fish]

¶The great rivers they call atoiatl, meaning "water that flows in great haste," as if

...teuatl: it is called teuatl not because it is a god, but because it means something wondrous and great; it is also called ilhuicaatl, meaning the people long ago, including those of New Spain, understood and believed that the sky was like a house whose four sides touched the water; and that the water lapped against the sky as if against a roof beam. And so they named it ilhuicaatl, because the sky met the sea. But now with true understanding it is called "great water," fearsome, terrifying, a thing to be confronted, marvelous and bubbling, swirling, bitter, briny, and brackish. Its surface is covered with trees, full of whirlpools, bitter, brackish and salt-crusted, foamy. Those who live beside the great water say: "I go along beside the sky-water, I cause the great water to splash, I go about to perish in the water, I go about beside the sky."
¶Atoiatl: its name derives from the way the water issues forth and runs — it means "the water that runs." [And it flows...]

...said the water that runs fresh: the ancient people of this land used to say that all rivers came from one place called Talocan [Tlalocan], which is like a terrestrial paradise; which place belongs to a god called Chalchiuhtlicue, and they also said that the mountains are founded upon it, and that they are filled with water inside, while on the outside they are made of earth, as if they were great vessels of water or houses full of water; and that when it becomes necessary, the mountains will burst open and the water within will pour out and flood the land. And from this they were accustomed to call the towns where people live "altepetl," which means mountain of water, or mountain full of water. They also said that rivers came out of the mountains, and that the god Chalchiuhtlicue sent them forth. But now that the truth of the matter is known as it is today, it is by the will of God that the sea enters through the land by its veins and channels, and travels beneath the earth and the mountains, and wherever it finds a way to come out, it does so through the roots of the mountains or through the plains of the land. And afterward many streams join together and form the great rivers called "atoyatl"; and although the water of the sea is salty or bitter, the fresh water of the rivers loses its bitterness, the salt being filtered out as it passes through the earth, or through...

Second paragraph: on the various names of rivers and springs.

There is a river called Chiuenavátl, which is that of Tlocan, and another river similar to it: and it is because they have nine springs, or a few more or less, from which they originate.

There is another river in the hot lands toward Covixo which is called Amacozatl; in it there breed manatees and other large fish almost like sharks.

[Nahuatl text:] It is called atoiatl: and its water is bitter, and this [water] is no longer bitter further on, it runs along the rocks and the earth, and it flows greatly from Xaltitlan where it issues forth; there it refreshes itself, there it runs, the river flows, it wells up, it surges, it speeds along, it rushes, it makes colors, it spreads out, it makes a rumbling sound, it roars, it splashes, it makes a terrifying sound of waves, it rushes downstream, it crashes, it narrows, it courses, it murmurs.

Second paragraph: concerning what is said about the different kinds, through which the river, and also the great water [sea], are divided.

Chicuhnávael: its name in Mexican is "nine waters"; it is called so because it wells up in nine places, it spreads out, it gathers, it flows together, thus it is called Chicunavatl, the white-foamed water; it stands there at Toloca.

Amacozatl: here the hot-land fish breed, it is dangerous, it causes great dread; the cotinga bird skims along upon it.

translation:
Book Eleven.

There is another river toward the province of the Cuextecs [Huastecs] which is called Quetzalatl, meaning "water like a precious green feather." They call it this because it is very clear and very good, and because of its depth it appears green.

There is another great river on the road to Guatemala, where there are many caimans. They call it Tequanatl, meaning "water in which there are fierce beasts that eat men," because those ferocious animals breed there.

The river of Tula is called Tullanatl, meaning "the river of Tula," because it passes through the middle of the town. Its water is like a dark color; it is rocky and muddy, with many stones and treacherous slime. It runs with great force, and many times the river carries away those who cross it.

It makes things sky-blue, it makes things green; it carries one along, it causes one to pass through, it brings one out at Thalapan.

On the qualities of waters fo. 225.

[Texatl], which means lye-water or water passed through ash — of this quality is [the water] between Huexotzinco and Capetlahuaca, which descends from the slopes where [the volcano] begins from up high, and in that water [snow] melts, and one can well see it come from the snow, and it goes out below between Huexotzinco and Acapetlahuaca, and the place where it sinks in is called Sanjue, and where it comes out again.

¶ There is a river called Totol-atl, which means the river where wild turkeys drink.

¶ There are rivers called prodigious or marvelous waters, because they flow and run for some time, and at another time they stop flowing and running; and there were two streams, one between Huexotzinco and San Salvador and another between Huexotzinco and Calpan, which flow and run in the rainy season and cease to flow and run in the dry season, and that which is between Calpan and Huexotzinco they call Pipindoatl.

¶ There are some streams in this land that run and have a spring where they rise, and sometimes they run and sometimes they cease to run; they say that when [someone] passes by it, it stops running or dries up, because they say it is ashamed of those who pass. And so they call it Pinaoa-tl or Pipinaoa-atl, which means shameful water; and in this same way are the two streams mentioned above that are near Huexotzinco.

¶ The springs that issue from flat ground they call ameyalli, which means water that flows; the water of these springs is sweet and is drunk and sustains [people] for the most part, and some of these springs...

[Right column, Nahuatl:]
...it becomes apparent, it is water: because of this it is drinkable, it appears, it shows red, it appears drinkable.

¶ Totolatl: its name is explained thus — it is said of it that the water is because wild turkeys reportedly come there to drink, the mountain turkeys gather there, they come swooping down, they go to feed, scrambling about.

¶ Tezahuatl: its name is explained thus — it is said of it that the water is like something coming out; it is greatly frightening, it is black, full of sediment, troubled, tezahuatl. It disappears quickly.

¶ Pinavizcatl: it is a thin water; what is said of it — it is called pinavizcatl because whenever no one passes over it, and no one crosses it running; but when someone crosses it, they are washed, scraped, stripped bare; it thus always behaves making one go naked. It makes one go stripped bare, naked.

¶ Ameyalli: its name is explained thus...

[Waters] are brackish and of bad taste and bad smell, and some cause harm to the body when drunk and cause illness.

¶ The streams that carry little water are called apitsactli, which means water that flows in small quantity.

¶ The springs that flow up from their depths lifting the sand, so that it appears the very sand flows out, are called Xalatl, which means sandy water. This water is considered very good water.

¶ An arm of the sea or of a river is called Amayitl, which means arm of water.

¶ The lagoons or ponds where rushes or sedges grow, which do not flow anywhere, are called Amanalli, which means water that stands still.

¶ They also call amanalli the lakes where water gathers together.

translation:
On the qualities of waters. Folio 226.

Cuecuexatl is a spring that is near Coyoacan, which was attempted in past times to bring to Mexico City to sustain the city, and it produced so much water that it flooded the city and the towns that are on these plains. Later, when Don Gastón de Peralta was Viceroy, they tried again to bring it to Mexico, and a great deal of money was spent, but they were never able to bring it: they abandoned the project. Then when Viceroy Don Martín Enríquez arrived, he arranged to supply the city of Mexico with great abundance from the spring of Santa Fe, as we see it serving us very well this year of one thousand five hundred and seventy-six.

The spring that used to come to Mexico, with which the city was supplied with water in ancient times, is called Chapultepec, which means something like a grasshopper or locust mountain, because at the foot of a small hill that looks like a locust the water of this spring emerges. It is poor water and not sufficient for the needs of the whole city; and so Viceroy Don Martín Enríquez did well in seeking to bring the other one mentioned above.

The small ones that are dug below ground and seep and draw water from below, and are not very deep, are called comolli, because they are dug below ground; from them they draw water for drinking and for everything else.

[Nahuatl text:]
...ticae, or mualpitzauaticae.

Amanalli: from it comes the name of this water, called tlamanalli; or it may be a standing water: it is water that stands still, does not flow, is muddy, slimy, covered with algae, mossy, permanently still.

Amanalli: it is called standing water, tlamanalli; it may be beneath a tree, or beneath dense brush, spreading in drops, dripping continuously, trickling continuously, seeping continuously.

Cuecuexatl: it is here near Coyoacan, close to Mexico.

Chapoltepetl: its name comes from chapolin (grasshopper); and the water: because of Chapultepec the water springs up among the reeds, it wells up, it is delicious, fresh, good, pure, and they drink it; by it the Mexicans are sustained, the Tenochtitlan people are sustained, it gives them life to drink, it nourishes the Mexican people.

Atlacomolli: its name comes from water (atl) and comolli (pit); one wishes to dig down into it, it is deep, far away, in one place; from there the water emerges, from there the Mexica draw water. Natlacomollahia, natlacomoltataca (they dig a water-pit, they dig out the water-pit).

translation:
Book Eleven

Concerning the shallow ones that flow and from which water is drawn: they are called Ayoluastli, and those that are not shallow are not called that, but rather atlacomollli.

Concerning the deep springs of fountains that run, they are called Axoxovilli, which means blue water: because the water being very pure and deep, it appears to be blue.

Third Paragraph: on the various qualities of earth.

Fertile land for sowing, where what is planted grows abundantly, is called Atoctli, which means land that has been brought by water; it is also called Tlalcoztli, and also xalatoetli; it is soft, loose, gentle land, where much maize or wheat grows, so that from a small sowing a great harvest is made.

Another kind of fertile land where maize and wheat grow very well is called Quauhtlalli, which means land that is filtered through rotted wood; it is also called tepetlalli, and also cuechaoac and costic, meaning loose, yellow, and hollow land.

Another fertile land is called Tlalcoztli, which means yellow land:

[Nahuatl column:]
Aiolvaztli: it appears at the surface of the atlacomolli, very far away, spread out in all directions. Naiolvaztlalia, naiolvostataca, aiolva3co, natlacui.

Axoxovilli: it is named because it looks blue in the water, spreading widely, running along in rows. xoxoctic, xoxovixctin.

This paragraph speaks of how the earth performs its functions.

Atoctli: it is named because the water follows along with it and runs. It makes things grow well, it flows alongside the tlalcoztli. Xalatoctli, it nourishes, it is soft, very soft, pleasant, refreshing. It sustains people, it is nourishing, something to be taught about. It is edible.

Quauhtlalli: it is named from wood, from the soil; the wood rots in it, whether it be large trees or shrubs, whether quauhtlatotli, or tepetlalli, or forest growth, dark, or dry wood. It produces things.

Tlalcoztli: I see it is white and yellow; because of this it is yellow.

translation:
Of Lands.          fo. 227.

The color of the soil indicates fertility.

Another kind of fertile land is called xalatoctli because it is sandy soil that the water brings down from the heights; it is soft ground.

Another kind of fertile land is called Tlacotlali, which is land where plants and grasses decompose and turn into fertilizer, serving as manure when they are buried in it.

The lands that are bought and sold and pass from one person to another are called tlalcoalli, which means purchased land; and these lands are for the most part fertile.

The lands whose owners are dead and who abandoned them are called Miccatlalli, which means land of the dead.

[illustration: skeleton with crossed bones]

Sandy soil that is barren and gives little fruit is called Xalalli, which means sandy and sterile land.

[illustration: corn plants growing in a field]

There is also a sticky soil that is good for making clay pottery...

Nahuatl entries:

Xalatoctli: this is the sandy soil that flows along, granular, that runs along, shifting, shifting.

Tlacollalli: this is where the plants rot, and the soil transforms, becoming productive.

Tlalcovalli: its name comes from what belongs to the land; tlacovalli: it is where one plants boundary markers, the sold land, the tlacovalli: I sell land, I buy land.

Miccatlalli: its name relates to the dead, and the land: it is called where the bones are, where the earth holds them, and it is called where the flesh of the dead has dissolved into the ground.

Xalli: its name relates to sand and to land: because of the sand, because it is fine-grained sand: it is not productive, it only spreads out flat, it spreads out level and smooth, it is not very nourishing, not very fleshy, not very full, not fleshy.

Tecoquijtl: its name derives from stone and from clay...

translation:
Book Eleven

...and soils for the flat rooftops (azoteas), and it is also fertile — maize and wheat grow well in it.

¶ Another kind of fertile land is called Callalli, which means: land where a house once stood and was built, and after it is dug up and sown, it is fertile.

¶ Land that has been leveled by hand and flattened on purpose in order to do something there — that flat, hand-made level ground — they call Tlahmantli, which means: leveled land.

¶ Land that is smoothed, settled, or tamped down by hand they call Tlaluitectli, which means: land beaten flat, settled by blows.

¶ Manured land they call Tlaluijac, which means soft land, because it has been worked and enriched with dung.

¶ Land where maguey plants have rotted and turned to compost they call Metlalli — land manured with maguey.

¶ Irrigated land they call Atlalli, which means: water-land.

[Nahuatl column:]
...it is said to be firm, hard, compact, rough, grainy, tough, resilient.

¶ Callalli: it takes its name from calli (house) and tlalli (land): it is the land on which a house stood; it surrounds the house. People have lived there; they are gone.

¶ Tlalmantli: its name comes from tlalli; it is even, flat land — not cracked, not uneven; a house can be set upon it.

¶ Tlaluitectli: it is that which is worked upon the earth, smoothed, compressed, made level. One beats the earth, one pounds the earth flat, one tamps the earth.

¶ Tlalaviiac: it is good, rich earth, that which nourishes and fattens the soil. One waters it, one tends it, one cares for it, one makes it bear.

¶ Metlalli: it is land in which maguey grows, is intertwined, is mingled together.

¶ Atlalli: its name tells us it is water; it is land [that is watered]...

translation:
Of Lands                                                    folio 228

Land that can be irrigated: [terms for] entertaining, watering, refreshing, splashing, rinsing, cleaning, seasoning, cooking; it is good, fine, fertile, tasty, teachable; it does things, it makes things happen; it produces grains, it shells, it scatters, it produces food; it nurtures on the slope, it is bound to the plain.

The hillside or slope, or the rise of some hill or height: they call it tepetlalli, which means land of the slope. Tepetlalli: it is what belongs to the hill, to the hilltop, to the rolling terrain; it is also called ximmilli; it is rough, ashy-soiled, sandy; it is also called good hillside soil; maize, amaranth, and beans grow there; prickly pears, maguey, wild herbs flourish there; trees stand there; there are xiuixva plants, cacalixva, cacateva, meiova; there are maguey shoots, cacao trees, oak trees; it is covered with the capachivi plant, the quaprachivi plant, nopals spread and grow in layers.

The rocky or crusty land, which is hollow and good, they call tetlilli, meaning stony land — not naturally so, but because it has been worked with stones or [tools]. Tetlalli: it is what is rough and powdery; stones are embedded in it; it sheds loose material, it stores it. Or it may be that the stones are gritty, crumbly, powdery, very powdery.

translation:
ON SOILS AND LANDS
Folio 380 / 230

Concerning the ash-heaps where the ash is thrown: in every neighborhood where they deposit their ash, they make a mound of it and call it Nextlalli, which means "ash soil." It is not good for anything.

Tecpatlalli means the spots around the bases of flint stones and other rocks where the lapidaries cast their waste. [It is the soil or grit around such stones.]

The soil used to make flat rooftops (tlapancos), and also the soil that has fallen from the flat rooftops of plastered houses, they call Tlapantlalli, which means "rooftop soil" (soil of terraces).

There is a soil that is barren because it is naturally dry, and on it nothing grows—no grasses like reeds—nor does anything else grow on it; they call it Teuhtlalli, which means "dry soil" or "dust soil."

The dust that rises from the ground they call Teuhtli.

There is a soil called [continues on next section]

Axixhalli [urine-soil]: axixhalli, one urinates upon it, one applies urine to it.

Nextlalli: everywhere the ash collects; it looks like little hills; this is nextlalli [ash-soil]; it is needed for nothing; it is used to whiten cacao, and it is dark and rocky.

Tecpatlalli: it is thin and flat-layered, full of sharp flint stones, it grinds things down, it is sandy.

Tlapanhalli: with this one plasters a house; it is a soil that lies upon a rooftop; it is that which one uses to apply a roof, to spread it, to plaster it, to level it, to close it up, to seal it, to smooth it.

Teuhtlalli: teuhtli [dust] is what it is also called; this is its name; it is like petlalli [a mat-like layer]; it is also called ximmilli. That is to say, it is dry soil.

Teuhtli: it takes its name from this, that it is the dust of the earth; from it rise bubbling [dust clouds]; they fly up, they swirl and rise, they billow upward, they whirl, they fly up and swirl spiraling aloft.
