Of the earth for making jars, etc. Folio 231.

Those provinces that are on the southern side, near the sea, in this New Spain — they are called Anahuac-lands; they are lands of rivers, gold, and feathers, etc.

Fifth chapter: on the various kinds of earth for making large water jars, pots, and pitchers, etc.

There is clay in this land for making earthenware and vessels; it is very good and very sticky; they knead it with those fibers from the stalks of the cattail reeds; it is called tecoquitl and contlalli.

From this same clay the griddle-plates (comales) are made.

[Nahuatl text, right column:]

Anahuac-land: it is where the great water lies, beside the sea, near it, where one refreshes oneself and is made happy.

Chichimec-land: it is where the Chichimecs live; they suffer hardship, they are afflicted, they are parched and lean. From there one goes forth, fleeing from want; truly it is a barren place, nothing is found there; there is weeping, there is longing, there is divine fear, there is misery and desolation.

Fifth chapter: it speaks of one kind of earth from which vessels and bowls are made.

Contlalli clay: from it are made bowls, and wide basins, etc.; tecoquitl clay, fine clay vessels, tolcapuio vessels, flat griddle vessels, small serving dishes. I form them, I make them with a mold, I smooth them, I scrape them, I join the pieces, I polish them; I make coarse fiber reinforcement with it, I make it coarser.

Comal-clay: this is what is called tecoquitl; it is for spinning and smoothing into griddle-plates.

translation:
Book Eleven

Here are set down the proper names of some notable mountains.

There is a very tall mountain, which smokes, that is near the province of Chalco: it is called Popocatepetl, which means "smoking mountain." It is a monstrous thing to see; I myself stood on top of it.

There is another mountain range next to this one, which is the snowy range, called Iztactepetl, which means "white mountain," or also "white woman." It is monstrous to behold from the top, and I have seen it from the height, and I myself stood upon it.

There is a great mountain called Poiauhtecatl, which is near Orizaba, which is a town near Chalco. Only a few years ago its summit began to burn; for many years I had seen its summit covered in snow, and afterward I saw it when it began to burn, and the flames were visible by night and by day, beyond the flows of lava. And now, since the fire has consumed much of the interior of the mountain, the fire can no longer be seen, though it still burns always.

There is another great mountain near Tlaxcala, which they call Matlalcueye, which means "the woman who wears a blue-green skirt."

There is another mountain near Colhuacan and Iztapalapan; though it is not very tall, it is very famous, and it is called [continues on next page]

[Nahuatl column:]
...ravined, gorged, cliffed, ravined again, slope-sided, hillsided: one ascends it, the mountain is climbed with fire, one goes living upon it, one reaches the mountaintop, the mountain does not transform, the mountain does not crumble, the mountain disintegrates.

Here it is told, here it is said, here we name, here we call the mountains.

ma, Vixachtecatl.

Another mountain, near Cuitlahuac, which is called Iaoaliuhqui: all these mountains have notable things.

Note

Having treated of the springs, waters, and mountains, it seemed to me an appropriate place to speak of the ancient and principal idolatries, which were and still are practiced: in the waters and in the mountains, one very solemn idolatry was performed in this lake of Mexico, in the place called Ayauhcaltitlan, where they say there are two large stone statues, and when the lake drops, they appear, and one can see the offerings of copal and many vessels that were placed there as offerings; there also: There also, they offered the hearts of children, and other things. In the middle of the lake, in the place called Xiuhchimalo, they say there is a whirlpool where the water of the lake is swallowed up; there also, sacrifices were made every year — they would cast in a child of three or four years, in a new small canoe; and the whirlpool would carry it off and swallow it, canoe and child together. This whirlpool, they say, has a vent toward Tula, in the place they call Apasco, Santiago, where there is a very deep spring; and when the lake rises, it rises, and when the lake falls, it falls; and there they say that many times they have found the small canoe in which the child had been cast.

translation:
Book Eleven

There is another spring where they used to make sacrifices, in the province of Toluca, near the town of Calimanyan. It is a high mountain that has two springs at its summit, which flow nowhere: the water is very clear, and nothing grows in it, because it is extremely cold. One of these springs is very deep; a great number of offerings appear in it. Not long ago, a certain friar went there and found that those springs had a recent offering of paper, copal, and small mats, which had been offered very recently — it was still inside the water. This occurred in the year 1570, or thereabouts. One of those who saw it was Father Fray Diego de Mendoza, who was at that time the guardian of Mexico, and he told me what he had seen there.

There is another spring, or fountain, very clear and very beautiful in Xochimilco, which is now called Santa Cruz. There was a stone idol beneath the water, where they would offer copal. I myself saw the idol and the copal, and I went under the water to retrieve it, removed the idol, and placed a stone cross there, which remains to this day in that same spring.

There are many other springs and waters where offerings are still made to this day, which one should inspect with diligence to see what is offered there.

translation:
On the heights of the land
folio 234.

Near the mountains there are other places where very solemn sacrifices used to be made, and people came to them from very distant lands. One of these is here in Mexico, where there is a small hill called Tepeacac; the Spaniards call it Tepequilla, and now it is called Our Lady of Guadalupe. In this place they had a temple dedicated to the mother of the gods, whom they called Tonantzin, which means "our mother." There they made many sacrifices in honor of this goddess, and people came from more than twenty leagues away from all the regions around Mexico. They brought many offerings; men and women and young men and young women came to these feasts. There was a great gathering of people on these days, and everyone said "let us go to the feast of Tonantzin." And now that the church of Our Lady of Guadalupe has been built there, they still call her Tonantzin, taking occasion from the preachers who call Our Lady, the mother of God, Tonantzin. From this has arisen this situation. It is not known for certain what this Tonantzin is; but this much we know for certain: that the word, from its original meaning, refers to that ancient Tonantzin. This is something that should be remedied, because the proper name of the mother of God, Holy Mary, is not Tonantzin but Dios Cinantzin, and this seems to be a satanic invention to cloak idolatry.

[Nahuatl entries:]
Sharp peak: mjltic, mjmjliuhquj.

Tlachichiquilli [a leaning or tilted mountain]: chichiquilltic — the one that leans its neck, that slopes as one descends it on the ravine side. Another type: a rounded or sloped mountain.

Tlatilli [a broad, flat-topped mountain]: tiltec, great, very broad, pachtonth, rounded on top, mjmjltic. Another type: a crag.

Tlaxixipuchtli [a mountain with projecting outcroppings]: it shows its surface, it faces outward on both sides, its face is rough and rugged. Cobre de monte [rocky face of the mountain].

Tepetlcpac [the top of the mountain]: the top of the hill spreads wide, it widens, it extends flat. The ground levels out, the ground spreads smooth, the ground is firm. It becomes lower, it becomes broader. There is a spring there, there is nothing hidden. The slope of the mountain.

Tlaelpan [the side of a mountain, between two mountains]: that which is somewhat at the base of a mountain, or somewhat at its neck. It is smooth, it is uneven/hollowed, it is flat, it stands there, it lies flat, it descends. Between two mountains.

Tlatoscatl [a mountain with a pass or gap]: where one goes threading between mountains. I thread through it, I go meeting it, I come out to its side, I go along its side, I go along its face, I go along the base of the mountain.

translation:
Book Eleven

On the topic or subject of this name Tonantzin [Our Mother]:

They come now to visit this Tonantzin from very far away, as far as before. This devotion is also suspicious, because in all parts there are many churches of Our Lady, and they do not go to those; instead they come from distant lands to this Tonantzin, as in ancient times.

The second place where there were formerly many sacrifices, to which people came from distant lands, is at the foot of the sierra of Tlaxcala, where there was a temple called Toci, where a great multitude of people gathered to celebrate this feast of Toci — which means "our grandmother" — and by another name she was called Bapoila Tenan, which means the goddess of the sweat-baths and of medicines. And afterward they built there a church of Saint Anne, where now there is a monastery and friars of our father Saint Francis, and the natives call it Toci, and people come from more than forty leagues away to the feast of Toci, and they call Saint Anne by this name, taking the occasion from preachers who say that because Saint Anne is the grandmother of Jesus Christ, she is likewise our grandmother of all Christians, and so they have called her and call her in the pulpit Toci, which means our grandmother. And all the people who come, just as in ancient times, to the feast of Toci, come under the guise of Saint Anne, but since the word is equivocal and they have regard for the old ways, it is more in secret that they come for [the old reasons]...

translation:
On the heights of the land                    folio 235.

...the old, not the new; and likewise in this place it seems idolatry persists, concealed, because so many people come from such distant lands without any miracle having occurred there by Sanctana. It seems rather to be the old devil, not Sanctana. And in this year of fifteen hundred and seventy-six, the pestilence that broke out there began; and they say there is now no one left there. It seems a mystery that the punishment began where the offense started: the covering up of idolatry under the name of Sanctana.

The third place where there were anciently many sacrifices, to which people came from distant lands at the foot of the volcano, in a town of Calpa called Tianquisnanalco, San Juan: in this place they held a great festival in honor of the god they called Telpuchtli, who is Tescatlipuca. And since they heard the preachers say that Saint John the Evangelist was a virgin, and since in their language the same word Telpuchtli is used for him, they took the occasion to hold that festival as they used to hold it of old, disguised under the name of Saint John Telpuchtli — outwardly sounding Christian — but in honor of the ancient Telpuchtli, who is Tescatlipuca. For Saint John has worked no miracles there, and there is no reason to go there rather than to any other place where there is a church.

translation:
Book Eleven

Seventh paragraph: on the differences among stones, types of stones. Item, note.

They hold this festival, and on its day a great number of people come from very distant lands, and they bring many offerings. Seeing this, it resembles what was done in ancient times, even though the sacrifices and cruelties that were once performed are no longer carried out, and this settlement has been established. In these places already mentioned: I am well convinced in my opinion that they do not do this out of love for the idols, but out of greed and ostentation — so that the offerings they used to give would not be lost along with the glory of the prestige they received from being visited by people from strange and many distant lands.

And the devotion that these people took up in ancient times of coming to visit these places — for these mountains are notable for producing from themselves clouds that rain upon certain areas continuously — the people who live in those lands watered by the clouds that form on these mountains, recognizing that the benefit of the rain comes to them from those mountains, felt themselves obliged to go visit those places and make offerings to that divinity which resided there and sent the water, and to bring offerings in gratitude for the benefit they received from there. translation:
Qualities of common stones. Folio 236.

[Left column — Spanish text:]
...those lands that were watered by the clouds of those mountains, persuaded or admonished by the demon or his satraps, adopted as a custom and devotion the practice of coming to visit those mountains every year at the feast that was dedicated there. In Mexico at the feast of Cihuacoatl, which they also call Tonantzin; in Tlaxcala at the feast of Toci; in Hanquismamalco at the feast of Tezcatlipoca. And so that the towns that enjoyed this custom would not abandon it, they persuaded those provinces to come as they used to, because what was formerly Tonantzin, Tocitzin, and Telpuchtli — which on the surface sounds as if it should not be called Santa Maria, Saint John the Evangelist, or the Baptist — in the interior life of the common people who come there, it is clear that it is nothing but the old practice, and they come for the old reasons. It is not my view that their coming should be impeded or offended; but it is my view that they should be disabused of the error they labor under — letting them understand on those days when they come there the falsity of the old belief, and that what they do is not in keeping with the ancient [Christian] tradition. This should be done by preachers well versed in the language and ancient customs of those peoples, and also in Holy Scripture.

translation:

After having passed mountains and valleys and marshes and ravines and roads of many kinds, this seemed to me an opportune place to treat of the paths by which the Church has come until arriving at this final dwelling place, where it now wanders as a pilgrim, sowing the evangelical doctrine. It is known to all that the militant Church began in the kingdom of Palestine, and from there traveled through diverse parts of the world, toward the east, and toward the west, and toward the north, and toward the south. It is known that toward the north there are still many provinces, still many uncultivated lands, where the Gospel has not yet been preached. And toward the southern regions, which were thought to be inhabited by no people at all, even now in our times many lands and very populous kingdoms have been discovered, where the Gospel is now being preached. The Church departed from Palestine — and already in Palestine faithful people live and reign and hold dominion — and from there it went to Asia, in which there are now no more than Turks and Moors; it also went to Africa, where there are no longer any Christians; it went to Germany, where now there are only heretics; it went to Europe, where throughout the greater part of it the Church is no longer obeyed; the Church now holds its seat most securely in Italy and Spain, from where, crossing the ocean sea, to...

[There] have come to these parts of the West Indies, where there were diverse peoples and languages: of whom many are now gone, and those remaining are on the path to disappearing. The most populous and best settled of all these West Indies has been New Spain, and what now prevails most and has the greatest luster is Mexico and its surroundings, where the Catholic Church is established and at peace. But as regards the Catholic faith, it is a sterile and very laborious land to cultivate, where the Catholic faith has very shallow roots, and with many labors very little fruit is produced, and with little opportunity what has been planted and cultivated dries up. It seems to me that the Catholic faith will be able to endure but little time in these parts. One reason is that the people are dying off with great speed, not so much because of the mistreatment they receive as because of the plagues that God sends them. Since this land was discovered, there have been three very universal and great pestilences, besides others not so great nor so universal. The first was in the year one thousand five hundred and twenty, when, driven out of Mexico by war against the Spaniards, they [the people] took refuge in Tlaxcala.

There was a plague of smallpox, where nearly infinite numbers of people died. After this, and after the Spaniards had conquered New Spain, and having it already pacified, and with the preaching of the Gospel being practiced with great prosperity, in the year one thousand five hundred and forty-five, there was a most great and universal pestilence, whereby in all of this New Spain the greater part of the people who lived there died. And I found myself during this pestilence in this city of Mexico, in the district of Tlatelolco, and I buried more than ten thousand bodies. And at the end of the pestilence the illness came upon me, and I was nearly at death's door. After this, the matters of the faith proceeded peacefully for a space of thirty years, more or less, and the people were restored. Now, this year of one thousand five hundred and seventy-six, in the month of August, there began a great and universal pestilence. It has now been three months that it has been running its course, and many people have died and are dying and continue to die more each day, and no one knows how long it will last nor how severe it will become. And I am now in this city of Mexico in the district of Tlatelolco, and I see that from the time it began until today, which is the eighth of November, the number of the dead has continually grown, from ten, to twenty, to thirty, to forty, to fifty, to sixty,

In this pestilence, as also in the other described above, many died of hunger and from having no one to care for them or give them what was necessary. It happened, and still happens, that in many houses all the inhabitants fell sick with no one able to give them even a jar of water, and with no one to take them to the church or even to report that they were ill. The religious men went from house to house, hearing their confessions and comforting them. When this pestilence of smallpox began, the lord viceroy Don Martín Enríquez took great pains to see that the Indians were provided for, both with food and with the sacraments, and through his persuasion many Spaniards went for many days through the houses of the Indians, giving them food; and bleeders bled them, and doctors treated them, and priests and friars — of Saint Francis, of Saint Dominic, Augustinians, Theatines — went through their houses to—

I encounter it on the road; secretly I walk the bad road, I go about following sin, disorder. In the darkness I secretly walk the bad road, I go about covering myself in sin.

A road little used, with all its qualities.
This means: very rarely one goes by a small, narrow, rough, uneven, crooked path; it is not much sought after; it destroys one's face. In the forest, in a remote place, one enters between the rocks, one passes through with difficulty, climbs in a wild place, one reverses. I follow this road, I go by this road, I step down from it, I stumble, I get entangled, those who cause people's faces to be destroyed go along it; I follow it: the quetzal feather. This means: a new road, wide, clean, smooth, straight, well-made, the royal road, worthy of the sun, very good, of good quality; one does not go about getting dusty, one arrives in good condition, without fatigue, nothing is fallen across it; it is smooth. Where no one travels the road, where one cannot pass, it is narrow.

Near there lies the great kingdom of China, and the Augustinian fathers have already begun to enter it. Book Eleven

...because of the foodstuffs that we use, and that are used in the lands from which we come, we found none here; nor even of the tame animals that we use — those of us who came from Spain and from all of Europe — did we find any here either. From this it appears that neither those people nor men from those parts had ever come to discover this land, because if they had come from there, they would have come to discover these things. In other times we would have found here wheat or barley or rye or hens like those over there, or horses, or oxen, or donkeys, or sheep, or goats, or some other tame animals that we make use of. From this it appears that these lands were only discovered in our times and not before. Regarding the preaching of the Gospel in these parts, there has been much doubt as to whether it was preached here before now or not.

I myself have always been of the opinion that the Gospel was never preached to them, because I have never found anything that points to the Catholic faith — rather everything is so contrary and so idolatrous that I cannot believe the Gospel was ever preached to them at any time. In the year seventy, or thereabouts, two religious men worthy of credence certified to me that they had seen in Oaxaca, a city sixty leagues from this city...

translation:
On the Provisions.                                     fo. 247.

...toward the east, where they saw some very ancient paintings, painted on deer hides, in which were contained many things that alluded to the preaching of the Gospel. Among others there was one which showed three women dressed like Indian women with their headdresses and hair like Indian women, seated as Indian women sit. Two of them were side by side, and the third was in front of the two in the middle, and she held a wooden cross, which, according to what the painting showed, was tied at the knot of the hair. And in front of them on the ground lay a naked man, stretched out, his feet and hands spread over a cross, his hands and feet bound to it with cords. This seems to me to allude to Our Lady and her two sisters, and to Our Redeemer crucified, which they must have held by means of ancient preaching. There is another thing that also inclines me to believe that the Gospel was preached in these parts: and that is that they practiced auricular confession in these parts of Mexico, where the penitents told their sins to the xarapa in great secrecy and received penance for them, and the xarapa urged them earnestly to amendment; and this confession they made only once in their lives.

translation:

...and concerning old age: and they held that for the penitent who had fallen back into sins there was no remedy, because sins were forgiven to no one more than once in life. This is written at great length in the second book, which deals with the feasts of the gods. I have also heard it said that in Champoton and Campeche, the friars who went there to convert the people found, at first, many things that allude to the Catholic faith and to the Gospel; and if in these two said places there was preaching of the Gospel, without doubt it also occurred in these parts of Mexico and its surrounding areas, and even in this New Spain. But I am amazed that we have found no more trace of what I have described in these parts of Mexico.

And although I say this, it seems to me that it is quite possible that they were preached to for some time; but that when the preachers who came to preach to them died, they entirely lost the faith that had been preached to them, and returned to their idolatries, which they had held before. And I conjecture this from the great difficulty I have found in the planting of the faith among these people; because I have been preaching in these parts of Mexico for more than forty years, and what I and many others with me have most insisted upon is placing them in the belief of the holy Catholic faith, by many means and trying various opportunities; and for this...

translation:
Book Eleven

...present new ministers and the Spanish nation, to return them to the principles of the faith.

There is another thing, which has become apparent partly through experience and partly through prophecy: and it is the end of this nation. What appears through experience is that from the Canary Islands to here, all the native nations — and here in this land we see through experience — that this is being verified. This also appeared through prophecy by a holy man named Domingo, that when the Spaniards arrived at this land, it was full of people, innumerable; and when by means of war they drove the Indians out of the city of Mexico against the Spaniards, and they went to Tlaxcala, a great plague of smallpox struck them, and Indians died without count. And afterward in the war and in the hardships with which they were afflicted after the war, a great quantity of people died in the mines, and making them slaves and taking them captive outside their land and exhausting them with great labors in buildings and in mines. And after these abuses were remedied by the friars having petitioned Emperor Charles the Fifth, in the year one thousand five hundred and forty-five, there came a great pestilence in which more than half the people of New Spain died, whereby all the land was left very depopulated of people, and very great towns were left deserted, which were never repopulated for thirty years after this...

On Gourds                          folio 253.

Gourds of these lands that are eaten
¶ Aiotli [squash/gourd]: or else aiotli — cylindrical, flat and broad, with a ridged back, tamale-shaped, mottled, cacao-colored, striped, flower-like, ashy-green, ash-colored, very cold, tree-hard, cord-like, blooming, flower-tendril'd, good and green to eat, offering shade, fit and proper to eat, causing drowsiness.

Another kind of gourd, smooth and painted.
¶ Tsilacaiotli [smooth gourd]: round, yellowish, yellowish-striped, with milk-like [flesh], striped. Its interior is like the aiotli — white, flat and broad, not yet mature; this tsilacaiotli has dark seeds inside, round and small: and again within, its seeds are white, very savory, bitter, sharp-flavored, strong-tasting, oily, thick; its juice drips, it is drunk as a beverage. It spreads [as a vine], it forms tamale-shapes, it puts out shoots, it branches, it clings, it gives shade, it extends, it winds about, it forms little flowers: the squash herb is used for [something], the yellow squash herb is [something]...
